<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_ix">[Pg ix]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="PREFATORY_STATEMENT_OF_SYMBOLIC">
PREFATORY STATEMENT OF SYMBOLIC
CONVENTIONS</h2>
</div>


<p>THE purpose of the following observations is to bring together in one
discussion various explanations which are required in applying the
theory of types to cardinal arithmetic. It is convenient to collect
these observations, since otherwise their dispersion throughout the
several numbers of Part III makes it difficult to see what is their
total effect. But although we have placed these observations at the
beginning, they are to be read concurrently with the text of Part
III, at least with so much of the text as consists of explanations
of definitions. The earlier portion of what follows is merely a
<i>résumé</i> of previous explanations; it is only in the later
portions that the application to cardinal arithmetic is made.</p>

<p class="nindc space-above2">I. <i>General Observations on Types.</i></p>

<p>Three different kinds of typical ambiguity are involved in our
propositions, concerning:</p>

<p class="hanging2">(1) the functional hierarchy,</p>

<p class="hanging2">(2) the propositional hierarchy,</p>

<p class="hanging2">(3) the extensional hierarchy.</p>

<p class="nind">
The relevance of these must be separately considered.</p>

<p>We often speak as though the type represented by small Latin letters
were not composed of functions. It is, however, compatible with all
we have to say that it should be composed of functions. It is to
be observed, further, that, given the number of individuals, there
is nothing in our axioms to show how many predicative functions of
individuals there are, <i>i.e.</i> their number is not a function
of the number of individuals: we only know that their number
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq 2^{\text{Nc}ʻ\text{Indiv}}\)" src="images/63.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 10.224ex; height: 2.333ex;" id="img_images_63.svg">, where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg">" stands for the
class of individuals.</p>

<p>In practice, we proceed along the extensional hierarchy after the early
numbers of the book. If we have started from individuals, the result
of this is to exclude functions wholly from our hierarchy; if we have
started with functions of a given type, all functions of other types
are excluded. Thus a fresh extensional hierarchy, wholly excluding
every other, starts from each<span class="pagenum" id="Page_x">[Pg x]</span> type of function. When we speak simply
of "<i>the</i> extensional hierarchy," we mean the one which starts
from individuals.</p>

<p>It is to be observed that when we have the assertion of a propositional
function, say "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x\)" src="images/65.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.031ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_65.svg">," the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_2"> must be of some definite
type, <i>i.e.</i> we only assert that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/66.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_66.svg"> is true whatever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_3">
may be within some one type. Thus <i>e.g.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.x=x\)" src="images/67.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.994ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_67.svg">" does not
assert more than that this assertion holds for any <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_4"> of a given
type. It is true that symbolically the same assertion holds in other
types, but other types cannot be included under one assertion-sign,
because no variable can travel beyond its type.</p>

<p>The process of rendering the types of variables ambiguous is begun in
*9, where we take the first step in regard to the <i>propositional</i>
hierarchy. Before *9, our variables are <i>elementary propositions</i>.
These are such as contain no apparent variables. Hence the only
functions that occur are matrices, and these only occur through
their values. The assumption involved in the transition from Section
A to Section B (Part I) is that, given "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.fp\)" src="images/68.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.771ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_68.svg">," where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/69.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_69.svg"> is an elementary proposition, we may substitute for <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/69.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_69.svg_1">
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!(x,y,z,\ldots)\)" src="images/70.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.862ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_70.svg">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg"> is any matrix. Thus instead
of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.fp\)" src="images/68.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.771ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_68.svg_1">," which contained one variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/69.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_69.svg_2"> of a given
type, we have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.f\{\phi!(x,y,z,...)\}\)" src="images/72.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.124ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_72.svg">," which contains
several variables of several types (any finite number of variables and
types is possible). This assumption involves some rather difficult
points. It is to be remembered that no <i>value</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_1">
contains <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_2"> as a constituent, and therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_3"> is not a
constituent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(fp\)" src="images/73.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.382ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_73.svg"> even if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/69.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_69.svg_3"> is a value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_4">. Thus we
pass, above, from an assertion containing no function as a constituent
to one containing one or more functions as constituents. The assertion
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.fp\)" src="images/68.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.771ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_68.svg_2">" concerns <i>any</i> elementary proposition, whereas
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.f\{\phi(x,y,z,\ldots)\}\)" src="images/74.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.128ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_74.svg">" concerns <i>any of a certain
set</i> of elementary propositions, namely any of those that are values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_5">. Different types of functions give different sorts of ways
of picking out elementary propositions.</p>

<p>Having assumed or proved "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.fp\)" src="images/68.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.771ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_68.svg_3">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/69.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_69.svg_4"> is elementary and
therefore involves no ambiguity of type, we thus assert
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash.f\{\phi(x,y,z,\ldots)\}, \]" src="images/75.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.757ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_75.svg"></span>
where the types of the arguments and the number of them are wholly
arbitrary, except that they must belong to the functional hierarchy
including individuals. (The assumption that propositions are incomplete
symbols excludes the possibility that the arguments to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_6"> are
propositions.) The noteworthy point is that we thus obtain an assertion
in which there may be any finite number of variables and the variables
have unlimited typical ambiguity, from an assertion containing one
variable of a perfectly definite type. All this is presupposed before
we embark on the propositional hierarchy.</p>

<p>It should be observed that all elementary propositions are values
of predicative functions of one individual, <i>i.e.</i> of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{x}\)" src="images/76.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_76.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/77.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_77.svg"> is individual.<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xi">[Pg xi]</span> Thus we need not
<i>assume</i> that elementary propositions form a type; we may replace
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/69.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_69.svg_5"> by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!x\)" src="images/78.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_78.svg">" in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.fp\)" src="images/68.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.771ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_68.svg_4">." In this way, propositions as
variables wholly disappear.</p>

<p>In extending statements concerning elementary propositions so as
formally to apply to first-order propositions, we have to assume afresh
the primitive proposition *1·11 (*1·1 is never used), <i>i.e.</i> given
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x\)" src="images/65.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.031ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_65.svg_1">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x\supset \psi x\)" src="images/79.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.815ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_79.svg">," we have
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\psi x\)" src="images/80.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_80.svg">" which is practically *9·12. This was asserted in
*1·11 for any case in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/66.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_66.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/81.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_81.svg"> are elementary
propositions. There was here already an ambiguity of type, owing to the
fact that x need not be an individual, but might be a function of any
order. <i>E.g.</i> we might use *1·11 to pass from
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash.\phi!a\unicode{x201d} \quad \text{and} \quad \unicode{x201c}\vdash.\phi!a\supset \phi!b\unicode{x201d} \quad \text{to} \quad \unicode{x201c}\vdash.\phi!b,\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/82.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 46.813ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_82.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_7"> replaces the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_5"> of *1·11, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\phi}!a\)" src="images/83.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_83.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\phi}!b\)" src="images/84.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.948ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_84.svg"> replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/85.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_85.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/86.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_86.svg">. Thus
*1·11, even before its extension in *9, already states a fresh
primitive proposition for each fresh type of functions considered.
The novelty in *9 is that we allow <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/87.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_87.svg"> to contain one
apparent variable. This may be of any functional type (including
Indiv); thus we get another set of symbolically identical primitive
propositions. In passing, as indicated at the end of *9, to more
than one apparent variable, we introduce a new batch of primitive
propositions with each additional apparent variable.</p>

<p>Similar remarks apply to the other primitive propositions of *9.</p>

<p>What makes the above process legitimate is that nothing in the
treatment of functions of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg"> <i>presupposes</i> functions
of higher order. We can deal with each new type of functions as it
arises, without having to take account of the fact that there are later
types. From symbolic analogy we "see" that the process can be repeated
indefinitely. This possibility rests upon two things:</p>

<p>(1) A fresh interpretation of our constants—<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lor\)" src="images/89.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_89.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim\)" src="images/90.svg" style="vertical-align: 0.301ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 0.529ex;" id="img_images_90.svg">, !,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_6">)., (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x\)" src="images/91.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.552ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_91.svg">).—at each fresh stage;</p>

<p>(2) A fresh assumption, symbolically unchanged, of the primitive
propositions which we found sufficient at an earlier stage—the
possibility of avoiding symbolic change being due to the fresh
interpretation of our constants.</p>

<p>The above remarks apply to the axiom of reducibility as well as to our
other primitive propositions. If, at any stage, we wish to deal with
a class defined by a function of the 30,000th type, we shall have to
repeat our arguments and assumptions 30,000 times. But there is still
no necessity to speak of the hierarchy as a whole, or to suppose that
statements can be made about "all types."</p>

<p>We come now to the extensional hierarchy. This starts from some
one point in the functional hierarchy. We usually suppose it to
start from<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xii">[Pg xii]</span> individuals, but any other starting-point is equally
legitimate. Whatever type of functions (including <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_1">
we start from, all higher types of functions are excluded from the
extensional hierarchy, and also all lower types (if any). Some
complications arise here. Suppose we start from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_2">.
Then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/92.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_92.svg"> is any predicative function of individuals,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi!z) = \phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/93.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.888ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_93.svg">. But identity between a function
and a class does not have the usual properties of identity; in
fact, though every function is identical with some class, and
vice versa, the number of functions is likely to be greater than
the number of classes. This is due to the fact that we may have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi!z)=\psi!\hat{z}.\hat{z}(\phi!z)=\chi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/94.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.975ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_94.svg"> without
having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}=\chi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/95.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.268ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_95.svg">.</p>

<p>In the extensional hierarchy, we prove the extension from classes to
classes of classes, and so on, without fresh primitive propositions
(*20, *21). The primitive propositions involved are those concerning
the <i>functional</i> hierarchy.</p>

<p>From all these various modes of extension we "see" that whatever <i>can
be proved</i> for lower types, whether functional or extensional,
can also be proved for higher types<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_1" id="FNanchor_1">[1]</a>. Hence we assume that it is
unnecessary to know the types of our variables, though they must always
be confined within some one definite type.</p>

<p>Now although everything that can be proved for lower types can be
proved for higher types, the converse does not hold. In Vol. I. only
two propositions occur which can be proved for higher but not for
lower types. These are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !2\)" src="images/96.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.018ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_96.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !2_{r}\)" src="images/97.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.927ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_97.svg">. These
can be proved for any type except that of individuals. It is to be
observed that we do <i>not</i> state that whatever is <i>true</i> for
lower types is <i>true</i> for higher types, but only that whatever
<i>can be proved</i> for lower types <i>can be proved</i> for higher types.
If, for example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ{\text{Indiv}} = \nu\)" src="images/98.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.431ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_98.svg">, then this
proposition is false for any higher type; but this proposition,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ{\text{Indiv}} = \nu\)" src="images/98.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.431ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_98.svg_1">, is one which cannot be proved
logically; in fact, it is only ascertainable by a census, not by logic.
Thus among the propositions which can be proved by logic, there are
some which can only be proved for higher types, but none which can only
be proved for lower types.</p>

<p>The propositions which can be proved in some types but not in others
all are or depend upon existence-theorems for cardinals. We can prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{array}{l} \exists !0,\, \exists !1,\, \text{universally},\\ \exists !2,\, \text{except for}\,\, \text{Indiv},\\ \exists !3,\, \exists !4,\, \text{except for}\,\, \text{Indiv},\, \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Indiv},\, \text{Rl}ʻ\text{Indiv};\,\, \text{and so on}. \end{array} \]" src="images/99.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 56.27ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_99.svg"></span>
Exactly similar remarks would apply to the functional hierarchy. In
both cases, the possibility of proving these propositions depends upon
the axiom of reducibility and the definition of identity. Suppose there
is only one individual, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_7">. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}=x\)" src="images/100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_100.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}\neq x\)" src="images/101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.319ex;" id="img_images_101.svg">
are two different functions, which, by the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xiii">[Pg xiii]</span> axiom of reducibility, are
equivalent to two different predicative functions. Hence there are at
least two predicative functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_8">, and at least two classes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/102.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_102.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda_{x}\)" src="images/103.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.673ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_103.svg">. This argument fails both for classes and
functions if either we deny the axiom of reducibility or we suppose
that there may be two different individuals which agree in all their
predicates, <i>i.e.</i> that the definition of identity is misleading.</p>

<p>The statement that what can be proved for lower types can be proved
for higher types requires certain limitations, or rather, a more exact
formulation. Taking <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_3"> as a primitive idea, put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Kl} = \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Indiv} \quad\text{Df},\,\, \text{Kl}^{2} = \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Kl} \quad\text{Df}, \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.5ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_104.svg"></span>
Then consider the proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\text{Kl} = \Lambda\)" src="images/105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.035ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_105.svg"> . We
can prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\text{Kl} \cap tʻ\text{Indiv} = \Lambda . \exists ! \text{Nc}ʻ\text{Kl} \cap tʻ\text{Kl} . \exists ! \text{Nc}ʻ\text{Kl} \cap tʻ\text{Kl}^{2}. \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/106.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 61.492ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_106.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\text{Kl} = \Lambda\)" src="images/105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.035ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_105.svg_1"> can be proved in the lowest type
in which it is significant, and disproved in any other. The difficulty,
however, is avoided if Indiv is replaced by a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_1">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Kl}\)" src="images/107.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.389ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_107.svg"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/108.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.23ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_108.svg">. Then we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻ\alpha = \Lambda, \]" src="images/109.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.642ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_109.svg"></span>
and this holds whatever the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_2"> may be. Thus in order
that our principle about lower and higher types may be true, it is
necessary that any relation there may be between two types occurring in
a proposition should be preserved; in other words, when one constant
type is <i>defined</i> in terms of another (as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Kl}\)" src="images/107.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.389ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_107.svg_1"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_4">), the definition must be restored before the type is
varied, so that when one type is varied, so is the other. With this
proviso, our principle about higher and lower types holds.</p>

<p>With the above proviso, the truth of our statement is manifest. For
we have shown that the same primitive propositions, symbolically,
which hold for the lowest type concerned in our reasoning, hold also
for subsequent types; and therefore all our proofs can be repeated
symbolically unchanged.</p>

<p>The importance of this lies in the fact that, when we have proved a
proposition for the lowest significant type, we "see" that it holds
in any other assigned significant type. Hence every proposition which
is proved without the mention of any type is to be regarded as proved
for the lowest significant type, and extended by analogy to any other
significant type.</p>

<p>By exactly similar considerations we "see" that a proposition which
can be proved for some type other than the lowest significant type
must hold for any type in the direct descent from this. <i>E.g.</i>
suppose we can prove a proposition (such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists ! 2\)" src="images/110.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.018ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_110.svg">) for the
type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Kl}\)" src="images/107.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.389ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_107.svg_2"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Kl} = \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.182ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_111.svg">); then
merely writing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/112.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_112.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Kl}\)" src="images/107.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.389ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_107.svg_3">, we have
a proposition which is proved concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_5">, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!2 \cap tʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/113.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.483ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_113.svg">, and here, by what was said
before, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_6">) may be replaced by any higher type.</p>

<p>Thus given a typically ambiguous relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_5">, such that,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg"> is a type, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\tau\)" src="images/115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_115.svg"> is a type (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}\)" src="images/116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_116.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}\)" src="images/117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.294ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_117.svg"> is such a relation), we "see" that, if we can prove<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xiv">[Pg xiv]</span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (Rʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.339ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_118.svg">, we can also prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (Rʻ\tau)\)" src="images/119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.353ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_119.svg">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_1"> is any type, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_9"> is composed of typically ambiguous
symbols. Similarly if we can prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\text{Indiv},Rʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/120.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.502ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_120.svg">, we can
prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\tau ,Rʻ\tau)\)" src="images/121.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.529ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_121.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_2"> is any type. But we
cannot in general prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\text{Indiv},Rʻ\tau)\)" src="images/122.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.515ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_122.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\tau,Rʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/123.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.515ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_123.svg">, and these may be in fact untrue. <i>e.g.</i>
we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}(\text{Kl})ʻ\text{Indiv}.{\sim}\exists!\text{Nc}(\text{Kl})ʻ\text{Kl}^{2}\)" src="images/124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.489ex; height: 2.584ex;" id="img_images_124.svg">.</p>

<p>Thus more generally, when a proposition containing several ambiguities
can be proved for the types <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.231ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_125.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/126.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_126.svg">,
..., but not for lower types, it is to be regarded as a function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_7">, and then it becomes true for <i>any</i> type; that is, given
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi (Rʻ\text{Indiv},Sʻ\text{Indiv}, \ldots), \]" src="images/127.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.605ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_127.svg"></span>
we shall also have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi (Rʻ\tau,Sʻ\tau, \ldots), \]" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.632ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_128.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_3"> is any type. In this way, <i>all</i> demonstrable
propositions are in the first instance about <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_8">, and
when so expressed remain true if any other type is substituted for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_9">.</p>

<p>When a proposition containing typically ambiguous symbols <i>can be
proved</i> to be true in the lowest significant type, and we can "see"
that symbolically the same proof holds in any other assigned type,
we say that the proposition has "permanent truth." (We may also say,
loosely, that it is "true in all types.") When a proposition containing
typically ambiguous symbols <i>can be proved</i> to be false in the
lowest significant type, and we can "see" that it is false in any
other assigned type, we say that it has "permanent falsehood." Any
other proposition containing typically ambiguous symbols is said to
be "fluctuating," or to have "fluctuating truth-value," as opposed to
"permanent truth-value," which belongs to propositions that have either
permanent truth or permanent falsehood.</p>

<p>In what follows, ambiguities concerned with the propositional hierarchy
will be ignored, since they never lead to fluctuating propositions.
Thus disjunction and negation and their derivatives will not receive
explicit typical determination, but only such typical determination
as results from assigning the types of the other typically ambiguous
symbols involved.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xv">[Pg xv]</span></p>

<p>It is convenient to call the symbolic form of a propositional function
simply a "<i>symbolic form</i>." Thus, if a symbolic form contains
symbols of ambiguous type it represents different propositional
functions according as the types of its ambiguous symbols are
differently adjusted. The adjustment is of course always limited by
the necessity for the preservation of meaning. It is evident that the
ideas of "permanent truth-value" and "fluctuating truth-value" apply
in reality to symbolic forms and not to propositions or propositional
functions. Ambiguity of type can only exist in the process of
determination of meaning. When the meaning has been assigned to a
symbolic form and a propositional function thereby obtained, all
ambiguity of type has vanished.</p>

<p>To "assert a symbolic form" is to assert each of the propositional
functions arising for the set of possible typical determinations which
are somewhere enumerated. We have in fact enumerated a very limited
number of types starting from that of individuals, and we "see" that
this process can be indefinitely continued by analogy. The form is
always asserted so far as the enumeration has arrived; and this is
sufficient for all purposes, since it is essentially impossible to use
a type which has not been arrived at by successive enumeration from the
lower types.</p>

<p>The only difficulties which arise in Cardinal Arithmetic in connection
with the ambiguities of type of the symbols are those which enter
through the use of the symbol <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg">, or of the symbol <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg">, which
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{ sm }}\)" src="images/131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 3.007ex;" id="img_images_131.svg">. For it may happen that a class
in one type has no class similar to it in some lower type (cf.
<a href="#_102_72" class="pginternal">*102·72</a><a href="#_102_73" class="pginternal">·73</a>). All fallacious reasoning in cardinal or ordinal arithmetic
in connection with types, apart from that due to the mere absence
of meaning in symbols, is due to this fact—in other words to the
fact that in some types <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_132.svg"> is true, and
in other types <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_133.svg"> may not be true. The
fallacy consists in neglecting this latter possibility of the failure
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_133.svg_1"> for a limited number of types, that
is, in taking the "fluctuating" form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_133.svg_2"> as
though it possessed a "permanent" truth-value.</p>

<p>A fluctuating form however often possesses what is here termed
a "stable" truth-value, which is as important as the permanent
truth-value of other forms. For example, anticipating our definitions
of elementary arithmetic, consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(2 +_{c} 3 = 5\)" src="images/134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 10.057ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_134.svg">. There is no
abstract logical proof that there are two individuals; so suppose 2 and
3 refer to classes of individuals, but 5 refers to classes of a high
enough type, then with these determinations <img alt="" data-tex="\(2 +_{c} 3 = 5\)" src="images/134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 10.057ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_134.svg_1"> cannot be
proved. But <img alt="" data-tex="\(2 +_{c} 3 = 5\)" src="images/134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 10.057ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_134.svg_2"> has a <i>stable</i> truth-value, since
it can always be proved when all the types are high enough. In this
case the fact that our empirical census of individuals (at least of the
"relative" individuals of ordinary life) has outrun the capacity of
logical proof, makes the fluctuation in the truth-value of the form to
be entirely unimportant.</p>

<p>In order to make this idea precise, it is necessary to have a
convention as to the order in which the types of symbols in a symbolic
form are assigned. The rule we adopt is that the types of the <i>real
variables</i> are to be first assigned, and then those of the
<i>constant symbols</i>. The types of the apparent variables, if any,
will then be completely determinate.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xvi">[Pg xvi]</span></p>

<p>A symbolic form has a <i>stable</i> truth-value if, after any
assignment of types to the real variables, types can be assigned to
the constant symbols so that the truth-value of the proposition thus
obtained is the same as the truth-value of any proposition obtained by
modifying it by the assignment of higher types to some or all of the
constant symbols. This truth-value is the <i>stable</i> truth-value.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">II. <i>Formal Numbers.</i></p>

<p>The conventions, which we shall give below as to the assignment of
types, practically restrict our interpretation of fluctuating symbolic
forms to types in which the forms possess their stable truth-value.
The assumption that these truth-values are stable never enters into
the reasoning. But we judge a truth-value to be stable when any method
of raising the types of the constant symbols by one step leaves it
unaltered.</p>

<p>In practice the fluctuation of truth-values only enters into our
consideration through a limited number of symbols called "formal
numbers."</p>

<p>Formal numbers may be "constant" or "functional."</p>

<p>A <i>constant</i> formal number is any constant symbol for which
there is a constant <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_3"> such that, in whatever type the
constant symbol is determined, it is, in that type, identical with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg">. In other words if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg"> be a constant
symbol, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_1"> is a formal number provided that "truth" is
the permanent truth-value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/137.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.816ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_137.svg">, for some
constant <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_4">.</p>

<p>The <i>functional</i> formal numbers are defined by enumeration; they
are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha,\,\, \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa,\,\, \Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa,\,\, \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu,\,\, \mu+_{c}\nu,\,\, \mu-_{c}\nu,\,\, \mu \times_{c}\nu,\,\,     \mu^\nu, \]" src="images/138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 61.537ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_138.svg"></span>
where in each formal number the symbols <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg"> occurring in it are called the arguments of the
functional form even when they are complex symbols. The argument of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta)\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.313ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_141.svg"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg">, and those of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu+_{c} (\nu +_{c} \varpi)\)" src="images/143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.489ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_143.svg"> are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu+_{c} \varpi\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 1.676ex;" id="img_images_144.svg">,
and those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 +_{c} 2\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.909ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_145.svg"> are 1 and 2.</p>

<p>Thus among the constant formal numbers are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 0,\,\, 1,\,\, 2,\,\, \ldots,\,\, \aleph_{0},\,\, 1 +_{c} 2,\,\, 2 \times _{c} \aleph_{0},\,\, 2^{2}. \]" src="images/146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 36.928ex; height: 2.439ex;" id="img_images_146.svg"></span>
The references which support this statement are
</p><p class="nindc">
<a href="#_101_11" class="pginternal">*101·11</a><a href="#_101_21" class="pginternal">·21</a><a href="#_101_32" class="pginternal">·32</a>.<a href="#_123_36" class="pginternal">*123·36</a>.<a href="#_110_42" class="pginternal">*110·42</a>.<a href="#_113_23" class="pginternal">*113·23</a>.<a href="#_116_23" class="pginternal">*116·23</a>.
</p>
<p class="nind">
Among the functional formal numbers are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta),\,\, \mu +_{c} (\nu +_{c} \varpi),\,\,(\mu +_{c} \nu) \times _{c} \varpi,\,\, (\mu +_{c} \nu )^\varpi. \]" src="images/147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.688ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_147.svg"></span>
It will be observed that <i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 +_{c} 2\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.909ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_145.svg_1"> is both a constant
and a functional formal number, so that the two classes are not
mutually exclusive. In fact they possess an indefinite number of
members in common.</p>

<p>All the formal numbers, with the exception of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c} \nu\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_149.svg">, are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg"> without any hypothesis
[cf. <a href="#_100_41" class="pginternal">*100·41</a><a href="#_100_01" class="pginternal">·01</a><a href="#_100_52" class="pginternal"></a>.<a href="#_110_42" class="pginternal">*110·42</a>.<a href="#_112_101" class="pginternal">*112·101</a>.<a href="#_113_23" class="pginternal">*113·23</a>.<a href="#_114_1" class="pginternal">*114·1</a>.<a href="#_116_23" class="pginternal">*116·23</a>, note to
<a href="#_119_12" class="pginternal">*119·12</a>, and <a href="#_120_411" class="pginternal">*120·411</a>].</p>

<p>A functional formal number consists of two parts, namely, its argument
or arguments, and the constant "form." An argument of a functional
formal number may be a complex symbol, and may be constant or variable.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg"> is an argument of <img alt="" data-tex="\((\mu +_{c} \nu) +_{c}\rho\)" src="images/152.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.786ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_152.svg">,
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xvii">[Pg xvii]</span>and of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu) \times _{c} 1\)" src="images/153.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.867ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_153.svg"> and of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}\nu)^\rho\)" src="images/154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.105ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_154.svg">;
also <img alt="" data-tex="\(2 +_{c} 3\)" src="images/155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.909ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_155.svg"> is an argument of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(2 +_{c} 3)\times_{c} 1\)" src="images/156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.566ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_156.svg">.
The constant form is constituted by the other symbols which
are constants. Two occurrences of functional formal numbers are only
occurrences of the same formal number if the arguments and also the
constant forms are identical in symbolism. Thus two occurrences of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_1"> are occurrences of the same formal number, even if
they are determined to be in different types; but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_2">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg"> are different formal numbers. Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{1}\)" src="images/158.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.352ex; height: 2.375ex;" id="img_images_158.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} 1\)" src="images/159.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.142ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_159.svg"> are different formal numbers because their
"forms" are different, though the arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_2"> and 1 are the
same and (in the same type) the entity denoted is the same. Thus the
distinction between formal numbers depends on the symbolism and not
on the entity denoted, and in considering them it is symbolic analogy
and not denotation which is to be taken into account. For example
two different occurrences of the same formal number will not denote
the same entity, if in the two occurrences the ambiguity of type is
determined differently.</p>

<p>The functional formal numbers are divided into three sets: (i) the
<i>primary</i> set consisting of the forms <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_3">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa \)" src="images/160.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_160.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_161.svg">, (ii) the
argumental set consisting only of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_1">, (iii) the
arithmetical set consisting of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c}\nu\)" src="images/162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_162.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^\nu\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_163.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c} \nu\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_1">.</p>

<p>A functional formal number has at most two arguments. But an argument
of a functional formal number may itself be a functional formal
number, and will accordingly possess either one or two arguments,
which in their turn may be functional formal numbers, and so on. The
whole set of arguments and of arguments of arguments, thus obtained,
is called the set of <i>components</i> of the original formal
number. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_2"> are
components of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu) +_{c} \rho\)" src="images/165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.906ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_165.svg">; and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_2"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_2"> are components of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.832ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_166.svg">; and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_4"> are components of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.517ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_167.svg">. The two arguments of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu) +_{c}\rho\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.906ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg">
are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_1">, and those of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c}\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.832ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_169.svg"> are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_3">,
and those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu+_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/170.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.517ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_170.svg"> are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_6"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_5">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xviii">[Pg xviii]</span></p>

<p>Addition, multiplication, exponentiation, and subtraction will be
called the arithmetical operations; and in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_4">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} \nu\)" src="images/171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_171.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_172.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c} \nu\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_4">
will each be said to be subjected to these respective operations.
The <i>arithmetical components</i> of an arithmetical formal number
(<i>i.e.</i> one belonging to the arithmetical set) consist of those of
its components which do not appear in the capacity of components of a
component which does not belong to the arithmetical set. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_8">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_5"> are arithmetical components of
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\mu +_{c} \nu) +_{c} \rho\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.786ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_173.svg">; and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_4">
are arithmetical components of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.832ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_166.svg_1">, but
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_9"> is not one; and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_10"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_6"> are
arithmetical components of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.517ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_167.svg_1">, but
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_7"> is not one; and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_11"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/174.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.397ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_174.svg"> are arithmetical components of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.408ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_175.svg">, but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \rho\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.015ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_176.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_3"> are
components of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/177.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.397ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_177.svg"> and are therefore
not <i>arithmetical</i> components of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.408ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_175.svg_1">. Only arithmetical formal numbers possess arithmetical
components.</p>

<p>A formal number of the arithmetical set having no components
which are formal numbers of the argumental set is called a
<i>pure</i> arithmetical formal number. For example
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/178.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.786ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_178.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.517ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_167.svg_2">
are pure, but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/179.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.408ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_179.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 17.139ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_180.svg"> are not pure.</p>

<p>There are many types involved in the consideration of a formal
number. For example, in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_7"> there is the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_8"> and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_8">; in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_6"> there
is the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_7">, the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_12">, and the type
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_8">; and so on for more complex formal numbers. The type of a
formal number as a whole in any occurrence is called its <i>actual
type</i>. This is the type of the entity which it then represents.</p>

<p>The other types involved in a formal number in any occurrence are
called its subordinate types.</p>

<p>The actual types are not indicated in the symbolism for the various
formal numbers as stated above. They can be indicated relatively
to the type of the variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg"> by writing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.258ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_182.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/183.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 8.875ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_183.svg">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} \nu)_{\xi}\)" src="images/184.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 7.978ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_184.svg">,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^\nu)_{\xi}\)" src="images/185.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 4.169ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_185.svg">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c} \nu)_{\xi}\)" src="images/186.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 7.978ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_186.svg">, by the notation of *65.
Even when the actual type of a complex formal number, such as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}(\nu +_{c} \varpi)\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.489ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_187.svg">, is settled—so for instance that we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{\mu +_{c} (\nu +_{c} \varpi)\}_{\xi}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 16.64ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_188.svg">—the meaning of the symbol
is not completely determined, for the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \varpi\)" src="images/189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 1.676ex;" id="img_images_189.svg">
remains ambiguous. It follows, however, from</p>
<p class="nindc">
<a href="#_100_511" class="pginternal">*100·511</a>.<a href="#_110_23" class="pginternal">*110·23</a>.<a href="#_113_26" class="pginternal">*113·26</a>.<a href="#_119_61" class="pginternal"></a><a href="#_119_62" class="pginternal">·62</a>,
</p><p class="nind">
that the subordinate types make no difference to the value of a formal
number, so long as the components are not null.</p>

<p>We can therefore make a formal number definite as soon as its actual
type is definite by securing that its components are not null. This is
done by the convention II T (below) combined with the definitions
</p><p class="nindc">
<a href="#_110_03" class="pginternal">*110·03</a><a href="#_110_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>.<a href="#_113_04" class="pginternal">*113·04</a><a href="#_113_05" class="pginternal">·05</a>.<a href="#_116_03" class="pginternal">*116·03</a><a href="#_116_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>.
</p><p class="nind">
When the subordinate types are adjusted in accordance with these
definitions and conventions, they will be said to be <i>normally
adjusted</i>.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xix">[Pg xix]</span></p>

<p>But in order to state this convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg"> we require a definition
of what is here called the <i>adequacy</i> of the actual type of a
formal number. The general idea of adequacy is simple enough, namely
that, given the subordinate types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_2">, the actual type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_3"> should be high enough to enable us logically to prove
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\sigma\)" src="images/191.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.179ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_191.svg"> when such a proof is possible for types which are
not too low. For example, all types except the lowest for which it has
meaning are adequate for the constant formal number 2. It is rather
difficult however to state the meaning of adequacy with precision in a
manner adapted to all formal numbers. Fortunately the definition of the
lowest type which corresponds to this general idea of adequacy is not
important for our purposes. It will be sufficient to define as adequate
some types which certainly do have the property in question.</p>

<p>The method of definition which we adopt is to replace the formal
number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_4"> by another one <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma'\)" src="images/192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.92ex; height: 1.742ex;" id="img_images_192.svg"> so related to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_5">
that with the same actual type for both we can prove
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\sigma'.\supset.\exists!\sigma\)" src="images/193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 10.757ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_193.svg">, whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_6">
is not equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg"> in all types. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_7"> be functional,
we need only consider its argument, or its two arguments, and can
dismiss from consideration the other components; then we replace these
arguments by others so that the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma'\)" src="images/192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.92ex; height: 1.742ex;" id="img_images_192.svg_1"> has the required property.
Thus:</p>

<p>(i) The actual types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_9">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_195.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_161.svg_1">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_5">
are adequate when we can logically prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !Ncʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha,\,\, \exists !\Sigma Ncʻt_{0}ʻ\kappa,\,\, \exists !\Pi Ncʻt_{0}ʻ\kappa,\,\, \text{and}\,\, \exists !\text{ sm }ʻʻt_{0}ʻ\mu; \]" src="images/196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 58.921ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_196.svg"></span></p>

<p>(ii) The actual types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \nu\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_8">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c} \nu\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_3">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\times _{c} \nu\)" src="images/197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_197.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^\nu\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_1"> are adequate when we can
logically prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\exists!\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\mu +_{c} \text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\nu,\quad \exists !\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\mu -_{c}     0\cap t_{0}ʻ\nu,\\ &amp;\exists!\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\mu \times _{c} \text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\nu,\quad     \text{and}\quad \exists!\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\mu^{{\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\nu}}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/198.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.255ex; width: 52.527ex; height: 5.641ex;" id="img_images_198.svg"></span></p>

<p>It will be noticed that <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_199.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.465ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_200.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_0ʻ\mu\)" src="images/201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.526ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_201.svg"> are the greatest classes of the same type as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_9">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_2">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_13"> respectively, and that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\mu\)" src="images/202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.548ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_202.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_0cʻt_1ʻ\nu\)" src="images/203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.383ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_203.svg"> are the
greatest cardinal numbers of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_9">
respectively. These definitions hold even when any of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_10">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_15">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_10"> are complex symbols.</p>

<p>The remaining formal numbers which are not functional must certainly
be constant. The difficulty which arises here is that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_8">
be such a formal number and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_1"> occurs in its symbolism,
we have no logical method of deciding as to the truth or falsehood of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.257ex; height: 1.994ex;" id="img_images_204.svg"> in any type. But we replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_2">
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.554ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_205.svg"> which is the greatest existent
cardinal of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_3"> in that occurrence. Thus:</p>

<p>(iii) If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_9"> be a formal number which is not functional, an
adequate actual type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_10"> is one for which we can logically
prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\sigma'\)" src="images/206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.806ex; height: 1.742ex;" id="img_images_206.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma'\)" src="images/192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.92ex; height: 1.742ex;" id="img_images_192.svg_2"> is derived from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_11"> by replacing any occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_4"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_12">
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}cʻt_{1}ʻ\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.554ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_205.svg_1">. Accordingly if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_5">
does not occur in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_13">, an adequate type is any actual type for
which we can logically prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\sigma\)" src="images/207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.179ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_207.svg">.</p>

<p>In the case of members of the primary and argumental groups we have
substituted the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_208.svg"> of the appropriate type in the place of
each variable. When the actual type is adequate we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\alpha ).\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha,\quad (\kappa ).\exists !\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa,\quad (\kappa ).\exists !\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa,\quad (\mu).\exists !\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu. \]" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.013ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_209.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the case of members of the arithmetical group (except in the
case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_c \nu)\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.09ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_210.svg">, we have substituted for each argument the
largest cardinal number which can be obtained in the type of that
argument, namely the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}cʻ\text{V}\)" src="images/211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.718ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_211.svg"> for the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_208.svg_1"> of
the appropriate type. Accordingly we are sure (except in the case of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_c \nu)\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.09ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_1"> that for all other values of the arguments which are
existent cardinal numbers the formal number is not null.</p>

<p>It will be noticed that normal adjustment only concerns the subordinate
types. For example <a href="#_110_03" class="pginternal">*110·03</a> secures that in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c}\mu\)" src="images/212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.517ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_212.svg">
the actual type of<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xx">[Pg xx]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_10"> is adequate, and <a href="#_110_23" class="pginternal">*110·23</a>
shows that any adequate actual type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_11"> will do.
But nothing is said about the actual type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c}\mu\)" src="images/212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.517ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_212.svg_1">.
We make the following definition: When the subordinate types of
a formal number are normally adjusted, and the actual type is adequate,
the types of the formal number are said to be <i>arithmetically</i>
adjusted.</p>

<p>We notice that for the primary set, the arithmetical adjustment of
types means the same thing as the adequate adjustment of the actual
type. Also if the arguments of a formal number of the arithmetical set
are simple symbols, the two ideas come to the same thing.</p>

<p>In the case of variable formal numbers of the primary set, it follows
from <a href="#_117_22" class="pginternal">*117·22</a><a href="#_117_32" class="pginternal">·32</a> that when their types are arithmetically adjusted they
are not equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_1"> for any values of their variables.</p>

<p>Also in the case of those variable formal numbers which are of the
pure arithmetical set (excluding <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c} \nu\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_4">) it follows
