from <a href="#_100_4" class="pginternal">*100·4</a><a href="#_100_52" class="pginternal">·52</a><a href="#_100_42" class="pginternal">·42</a>.<a href="#_113_23" class="pginternal">*113·23</a>.<a href="#_116_23" class="pginternal">*116·23</a> that, working from the ultimate
components reached by successive analysis upwards, for all values
of such ultimate components which are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC} - \iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.825ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_213.svg">
they can be reduced to the case of the formal numbers of the primary
group; and that therefore they are not equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_2"> when their
types are arithmetically adjusted. For example in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \{\nu+_{c} (\rho +_{c} \sigma)\}\)" src="images/214.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.986ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_214.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_16">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_11">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_14"> are these ultimate components;
let them be existent cardinal numbers. Hence when the types are
arithmetically adjusted, the actual type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho +_{c} \sigma\)" src="images/215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.108ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_215.svg"> is
adequate and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho +_{c} \sigma\)" src="images/215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.108ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_215.svg_1"> is an existent cardinal; we can
therefore substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}cʻ\alpha\)" src="images/216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.47ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_216.svg"> for it. By the same
reasoning we can substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}cʻ\beta\)" src="images/217.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.302ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_217.svg"> for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_c\text{N}_0cʻ\alpha\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.315ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_218.svg">, and again <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.275ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_219.svg">
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{N}_{0}cʻ\beta\)" src="images/220.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.313ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_220.svg">.</p>

<p>A definite standard arithmetical adjustment of types for any formal
number can always be found by making every use of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_1">,
whether explicit or concealed in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_1"> or in some other symbol,
to be homogeneous. Proofs which apply to any arithmetical adjustment
of types start by dealing with this standard type, and then by the use
of <a href="#_104_21" class="pginternal">*104·21</a>.<a href="#_106_21" class="pginternal">*106·21</a><a href="#_106_211" class="pginternal">·211</a><a href="#_106_212" class="pginternal">·212</a><a href="#_106_213" class="pginternal">·213</a> the extension is made to the adjacent
higher classical and relational types. We then "see" that by the
analogy of symbolism this extension can always be formally proved at
each stage, so that we are dealing with the stable truth-value. For
some constant formal numbers a lower existential type can be found than
that indicated by this method.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
III. <i>Classification of Occurrences of Formal Numbers.</i></p>

<p>A symbolic form of any of the kinds [cf. <a href="#_117_01" class="pginternal">*117·01</a><a href="#_117_04" class="pginternal">·04</a><a href="#_117_05" class="pginternal">·05</a><a href="#_117_06" class="pginternal">·06</a>]
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu &gt; \nu,\quad \mu &lt; \nu,\quad \mu \geq \nu,\quad \mu \leq \nu, \]" src="images/221.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 32.756ex; height: 1.928ex;" id="img_images_221.svg"></span>
is called an <i>arithmetical inequality</i>.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxi">[Pg xxi]</span></p>

<p>These forms only arise when we are comparing cardinal numbers in
respect to the relation of being "greater than" or "less than." It
might seem natural to include equations among these arithmetical
inequalities. Their use however, even as between cardinal numbers, is
not so exclusively arithmetical, and it is convenient to consider them
separately under another heading during our preliminary investigations.</p>

<p>In the arithmetical inequalities as above written, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_17"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_12">,
or any symbols replacing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_18"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_13">, are called the <i>opposed
sides</i> of the inequality, and either of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_19"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_14"> is called
a <i>side</i> of the inequality.</p>

<p>Symbolic forms of the kinds <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma =\kappa\)" src="images/222.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.612ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_222.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma \neq \kappa\)" src="images/223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.612ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_223.svg">, where either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_15"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_4"> is a formal number,
will be called <i>equations</i> and <i>inequations</i> respectively; and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_16"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_5"> are called the <i>opposed sides</i> of the
equation or inequation, and either of them is simply a <i>side</i> of
the equation or inequation.</p>

<p>When we reach the exclusively arithmetical point of view, it will be
convenient to put together equations, inequations and arithmetical
inequalities as one sort of symbolic form. Their separation here is
for the sake of investigations into the exceptions due to the failure
of existence theorems in low types. It is unnecessary to consider
arithmetical inequalities in this connection.</p>

<p>The ways in which a symbol <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_17"> can occur in a symbolic form are
named as follows:</p>

<p>The occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_18"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\sigma\)" src="images/224.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.914ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_224.svg"> is called an
<i>argumental</i> occurrence,</p>

<p>The occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_19"> as an argument of an arithmetical formal
number (which may be a component of another formal number) or as one
side of an arithmetical inequality is called an <i>arithmetical</i>
occurrence,</p>

<p>The occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_20"> as one side of an equation is called an
<i>equational</i> occurrence,</p>

<p>The occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_21"> in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi \in \sigma\)" src="images/225.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_225.svg">" is called an
<i>attributive</i> occurrence,</p>

<p>Any other occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_22"> is called a <i>logical</i>
occurrence, so also is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma =\Lambda\)" src="images/226.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.879ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_226.svg">.</p>

<p>It is obvious that a pair of opposed sides of an equation or inequation
must be of the same type. Furthermore, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_23"> be a formal
number, and *20·18 is applied so as to give
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \sigma =\kappa .\supset :f(\sigma).\equiv .f(\kappa), \]" src="images/227.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.035ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_227.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxii">[Pg xxii]</span>the equational occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_24"> must be of the same type as its occurrence in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\sigma\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.416ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_228.svg">), otherwise the inference is fallacious. Accordingly substitution in
arithmetical formulae can only be undertaken when the conventions as to the
relations of ambiguous types secure this identity. This question is considered
later in this prefatory statement, and the result appears in the text as
<a href="#_118_01" class="pginternal">*118·01</a>.</p>

<p>At this point some examples will be useful; they will also be referred
to subsequently in connection with the conventions limiting ambiguities
of type.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*100·35.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}\vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\lor.&amp;\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\beta :\supset:\\ &amp;\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta\end{aligned}\]" src="images/229.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 65.61ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_229.svg"></span></p>

<p>Here the formal numbers are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_12"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_1">, each of which has three occurrences. The

<p class="nindc space-above2">IV. <i>The Conventions</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg"> <i>and</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_1">.</p>

<p>Two occurrences of a formal number with the same actual type are said
to be <i>bound</i> to each other.</p>

<p>The choice of types for formal numbers, when they are not made definite
in terms of variables by the notation of *65, is limited by the
following conventions, which enable us to dispense largely with the
elaboration produced by the definition of types.</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_1">. <i>All logical occurrences of the same formal number
are in the same type; argumental occurrences are bound to logical and
attributive occurrences; and, if there are no argumental occurrences,
equational occurrences are bound to logical occurrences.</i></p>

<p>This rule only applies, so far as meaning permits, to those types which
remain ambiguous after the assignment of types to the real variables.</p>

<p>It will be noticed that if there are no argumental or logical
occurrences of a formal number, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_2"> does not in any way apply
to the assignment of types to the occurrences in the form of that
formal number.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxiv">[Pg xxiv]</span></p>

<p>The identification of types in argumental and attributive occurrences
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_3"> is rendered necessary to secure the use of the
equivalence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \gamma \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ\sigma .\equiv .(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in \sigma .\gamma\,\text{ sm }\,\alpha, \]" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.633ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_263.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_25"> is a formal number. Without the convention, this
application of *37·1 would be fallacious. The only one of our
examples to which this part of the convention applies is <a href="#_101_28" class="pginternal">*101·28</a>
(demonstration), where it secures that the two occurrences of 1 are
in the same type. It is relevant however to the symbolism in the
demonstration of <a href="#_100_521" class="pginternal">*100·521</a>.</p>

<p>It will be found in practice that this convention relates the types of
occurrences in the same way as would naturally be done by anyone who was
not thinking of the convention at all. To see how the convention works,
we will run through the examples which have already been given above.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_100_35" class="pginternal">*100·35</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_4"> directs the logical and equational
occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_18"> to be in the same type, and
similarly for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_8">. Also "meaning" secures that the
equational types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_19"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_9"> are
the same. Thus these four occurrences are all in one type, which has
no necessary relation to the types of the attributive occurrences of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_20"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_10">. Thus, using the notation
of *65·04 to secure typical definiteness, *100·35 is to mean
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned} \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !&amp;\text{Nc}(\xi )ʻ\alpha .\lor.\exists !\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\beta :\supset :\\ &amp;\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\beta .\equiv .\alpha \in \text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\beta .\equiv .\beta \in \text{Nc}(\beta)ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta.\end{aligned}\]" src="images/264.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 69.339ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_264.svg"></span></p>

<p>The types of these attributive occurrences are settled by the necessity
of "meaning."</p>

<p>In <a href="#_100_42" class="pginternal">*100·42</a> (demonstration), since all the occurrences of formal numbers
are equational, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_5"> produces no limitation of types.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_100_44" class="pginternal">*100·44</a> (demonstration), <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_6"> secures that the two
occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_21"> are in the same type. Also we
notice that the first occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_11"> is really (cf.
*65·04) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\beta\)" src="images/265.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.548ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_265.svg">, since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \mu\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.578ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_266.svg">" occurs,
and thus "meaning" requires this relation of types, and the second
occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_12"> is in the type of the occurrences of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_22">.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_100_511" class="pginternal">*100·511</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_7"> directs that the logical and argumental
occurrences are to have the same type. In <a href="#_100_521" class="pginternal">*100·521</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_8">
directs that the two occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_8"> are to have the
same type. In <a href="#_101_28" class="pginternal">*101·28</a> both occurrences of 1 are to be in the same type.
In <a href="#_101_38" class="pginternal">*101·38</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_9"> directs that all the occurrences of 2 are to
have the same type.</p>

<p>The convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_10"> in no way limits the types in <a href="#_110_54" class="pginternal">*110·54</a>, nor
in <a href="#_116_63" class="pginternal">*116·63</a>, nor in <a href="#_117_108" class="pginternal">*117·108</a>.</p>

<p>In the first example from <a href="#_120_53" class="pginternal">*120·53</a> (in the demonstration) convention
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_11"> has no application.</p>

<p>In the second example from *120·53 (in the demonstration) convention
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_12"> directs that the two occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\beta\)" src="images/253.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.541ex; height: 1.974ex;" id="img_images_253.svg_4">
shall be in the same type; and the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxv">[Pg xxv]</span> necessity of "meaning" secures that
the first occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\gamma\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.504ex; height: 1.552ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_4"> shall also be in this type.
The same necessity secures that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma +_{c} \delta\)" src="images/252.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.879ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_252.svg_3"> shall be in the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_2">; and it also secures that in
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\gamma = \alpha ^\gamma \times _{c} \alpha ^\delta\)" src="images/267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 14.018ex; height: 2.325ex;" id="img_images_267.svg">"
the first occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\gamma\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.504ex; height: 1.552ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_5"> and that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\gamma\times_c \alpha^\delta\)" src="images/268.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 8.497ex; height: 2.325ex;" id="img_images_268.svg"> shall have a common type,
which is otherwise unfettered; also nothing has been decided as to the
types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\gamma\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.504ex; height: 1.552ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\delta\)" src="images/255.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.346ex; height: 1.993ex;" id="img_images_255.svg_3"> in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\gamma\times _{c} \alpha ^\delta\)" src="images/269.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 8.497ex; height: 2.325ex;" id="img_images_269.svg">.</p>

<p>We now come to conventions embodying the outcome of arithmetical ideas.
The term "arithmetical" is here used to denote investigations in which
the interest lies in the comparison of formal numbers in respect to
equality or inequality, excluding the exceptional cases—whenever the
cases are exceptional—due to the failure of existence in low types.
The thorough-going arithmetical point of view, which we adopt later
in the investigation on Ratio and Quantity and also in this volume
in <a href="#_117" class="pginternal">*117</a> and <a href="#_126" class="pginternal">*126</a> and some earlier propositions, would sweep aside
as uninteresting all investigation of the exact ways in which the
failure of existence theorems is relevant to the truth of propositions,
thus concentrating attention exclusively on stable truth-values.
But the logical investigation has its own intrinsic interest among
the principles of the subject. It is obvious however that it should
be restrained to a consideration of the theorems of purely logical
interest. In practice this extrusion of uninteresting cases of the
failure of arithmetical theorems, even amid the logical investigations
of the first part of this volume, is effected by securing that <i>all
arithmetical occurrences of formal numbers have their actual types
adequate</i>.</p>

<p>As far as formal numbers of the primary group, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_23">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_271.svg">,
are concerned, the arithmetical adjustment of types
is secured formally in the symbolism by the definitions <a href="#_110_03" class="pginternal">*110·03</a><a href="#_110_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>
for addition, and <a href="#_113_04" class="pginternal">*113·04</a><a href="#_113_05" class="pginternal">·05</a> for multiplication, and <a href="#_116_03" class="pginternal">*116·03</a><a href="#_116_04" class="pginternal">·04</a> for
exponentiation, and <a href="#_117_02" class="pginternal">*117·02</a><a href="#_117_03" class="pginternal">·03</a> for arithmetical inequalities, and
<a href="#_119_02" class="pginternal">*119·02</a><a href="#_119_03" class="pginternal">·03</a> for subtraction.</p>

<p>We save the symbolic elaboration which would arise from the extension
of similar definitions to other formal numbers by the following
convention:</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_2">. <i>Whenever a formal number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_26"> occurs, so that,
if it were replaced by</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_24">, <i>the actual type
of</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_25"> <i>would by definition have to be adequate,
then the actual type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_27"> is also to be adequate.</i></p>

<p>For example in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} (\nu +_{c} \varpi)\)" src="images/272.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.489ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_272.svg">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c}\varpi\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 1.676ex;" id="img_images_273.svg">
were replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_26">, then by <a href="#_110_04" class="pginternal">*110·04</a> the actual
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_27"> is adequate. Hence by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_3"> the
actual type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \varpi\)" src="images/189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 1.676ex;" id="img_images_189.svg_1"> is to be adequate: accordingly so
long as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_15"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varpi\)" src="images/274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.873ex; height: 0.998ex;" id="img_images_274.svg"> are simple variables and members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}-\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/275.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.825ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_275.svg">, we can always assume <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !(\nu +_{c}\varpi)\)" src="images/276.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.366ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_276.svg">
for the type of the occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \varpi \in \mu +_{c} (\nu +_{c} \varpi)\)" src="images/277.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.974ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_277.svg">.</p>

<p>It is essential to notice that so long as the argument of an argumental
formal number, or the arguments of an arithmetical formal number, are
adjusted arithmetically, the exact types chosen make no difference.
This follows for argumental formal numbers from <a href="#_102_862" class="pginternal">*102·862</a><a href="#_102_87" class="pginternal">·87</a><a href="#_102_88" class="pginternal">·88</a>,
for addition from<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxvi">[Pg xxvi]</span> <a href="#_110_25" class="pginternal">*110·25</a>, for multiplication from <a href="#_113_26" class="pginternal">*113·26</a>, for
exponentiation from <a href="#_116_26" class="pginternal">*116·26</a>, for subtraction from <a href="#_119_61" class="pginternal">*119·61</a><a href="#_119_62" class="pginternal">·62</a>. Thus
(remembering also <a href="#_100_511" class="pginternal">*100·511</a>) in any definite type a formal number has
one definite meaning provided that any subordinate formal number which
occurs in its symbolism is determined existentially. The convention
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_4"> directs us always to take this definite meaning for any
pure arithmetical formal number.</p>

<p>The convention does not determine completely the meaning of an
arithmetical formal number which is not pure. For example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}(\nu +_{c} \rho )\)" src="images/278.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.786ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_278.svg">
is a pure arithmetical formal number when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_20">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_16">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_5"> are determined in type; and convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_5">
directs that the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\((\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/279.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.775ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_279.svg"> is to be adequate. But
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c} \text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_{c} \rho)\)" src="images/179.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.408ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_179.svg_1"> is an arithmetical formal
number which is not pure, and convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_6"> directs that
the type of the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_2"> is to be adequate, but does
not affect the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \rho\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.015ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_1">. Thus it is easy to see
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_7"> secures the adequacy of the actual types of all
arithmetical components of any <i>arithmetical</i> formal numbers which
occur, but does not affect the actual type of a formal number which
occurs as the argument of an argumental formal number. But in this
case convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_13"> will bind the actual type of this occurrence
of the argument to any logical or attributive occurrence of the same
formal number. For example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists ! \nu +_{c} \rho\)" src="images/280.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.902ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_280.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_c\text{ sm }ʻʻ(\nu +_c \rho)\)" src="images/281.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.408ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_281.svg"> occur in the same form, then
these two occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c} \rho\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.015ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_2"> must have the same actual
type. In practice argumental formal numbers are useful as components
of arithmetical formal numbers for the very purpose of avoiding the
automatic adjustment of types directed by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_8">.</p>

<p>The meaning of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_9"> is best explained by examples. Among our
previous examples we need only consider those in which arithmetical
formal numbers occur.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_110_54" class="pginternal">*110·54</a> the convention or definitions direct us to determine the
types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_28"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_13"> adequately when
forming <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/282.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.492ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_282.svg">, also to determine
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/282.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.492ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_282.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_283.svg">
adequately when forming <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta)+_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/284.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.186ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_284.svg">.
The convention does not apply to the types of
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta) +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/285.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.186ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_285.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha + \beta + \gamma)\)" src="images/286.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.307ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_286.svg">. These types must be identical
in order to secure meaning.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_116_63" class="pginternal">*116·63</a> the convention directs us to adjust the types of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\times _c \varpi\)" src="images/287.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 1.468ex;" id="img_images_287.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_172.svg_1"> adequately; it does not
affect the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{\nu \times _{c} \varpi}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.592ex; height: 2.095ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_1"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\mu^\nu)^\varpi\)" src="images/288.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.673ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_288.svg">, which must be identical to secure meaning. If we
replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_21">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_17">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varpi\)" src="images/274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.873ex; height: 0.998ex;" id="img_images_274.svg_1"> by formal numbers, by 2,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_6">, and 1 for example, we get "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . 2^{\aleph_{0}\times \text{c1}} = (2^{\aleph _{0}})^{1}\)" src="images/289.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.898ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_289.svg">."
The convention now directs that 1 is to be determined adequately. It
so happens that any type is adequate for it, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists ! 1\)" src="images/290.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.018ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_290.svg"> can
be proved in any type. Then adequate types for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0} \times_{c} 1\)" src="images/291.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 7.147ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_291.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{\aleph _{0}}\)" src="images/292.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.995ex; height: 1.932ex;" id="img_images_292.svg">
are types for which we can prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists! (\text{N}_{0} cʻt_{1}ʻ\aleph _{0}) \times _{c} 1\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.978ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_293.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists! 2^{\text{N}_{0} cʻt_{1}ʻ\aleph _{0}}\)" src="images/294.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 10.668ex; height: 2.021ex;" id="img_images_294.svg">. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_4"> is the
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg"> in both cases, an adequate type for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0} \times _{c} 1\)" src="images/296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 7.147ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_296.svg"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_5">, and for <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{\aleph _{0}}\)" src="images/292.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.995ex; height: 1.932ex;" id="img_images_292.svg_1"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\tau\)" src="images/297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.79ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_297.svg">.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_117_108" class="pginternal">*117·108</a> we find arithmetical occurrences in arithmetical
inequalities. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_10"> directs us to take the first
two occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_29"> and the first<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxvii">[Pg xxvii]</span> two of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_14"> with adequate actual types. The type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_30"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_15"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha= \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/298.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_298.svg">
is not affected by it. It is evident that the
conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_14">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_11"> are not sufficient to secure
the truth of this proposition as thus symbolized. It is essential
that in the equation the type be adjusted adequately for both formal
numbers. In fact the general arithmetical convention, that types
of equational as well as of arithmetical occurrences are adjusted
arithmetically, is here used.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">V. <i>Some Important Principles.</i></p>

<p><i>Principle of Arithmetical Substitution</i>. In <a href="#_120_53" class="pginternal">*120·53</a>, the
application of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_12"> needs a consideration of the whole
question of arithmetical substitution. Consider the first of the two
examples. We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash : \beta = \gamma +_c \delta . \exists ! \beta . \supset . \alpha ^\beta = \alpha ^\gamma \times _c \alpha ^\delta. \]" src="images/299.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 35.446ex; height: 2.57ex;" id="img_images_299.svg"></span></p>

<p>It is obvious that unless we can pass with practical immediateness
from "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = \gamma +_c \delta. \alpha ^\beta = \alpha ^\beta\)" src="images/300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 19.282ex; height: 2.438ex;" id="img_images_300.svg">" to
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\beta = \alpha^{\gamma +_c \delta}\)" src="images/301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 10.64ex; height: 2.154ex;" id="img_images_301.svg">" by *20·18, arithmetic
is made practically impossible by the theory of types. But a difficulty
arises from the application of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_13">. Suppose we assign the
types of our real variables first. Then the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_11">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg"> can be arbitrarily assigned, and
there is no necessary connection between them which arises from the
preservation of meaning. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_4"> may be in a type which is
not an adequate type for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma +_c \delta\)" src="images/303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.879ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_303.svg">. Assume that this is
the case. But the equational use of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma +_c \delta\)" src="images/303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.879ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_303.svg_1"> is in the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_5">, and by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_14"> the arithmetical use
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma +_c \delta\)" src="images/303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.879ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_303.svg_2"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha^{\gamma +_c \delta}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.082ex; height: 1.993ex;" id="img_images_304.svg"> is in an
adequate type. Thus, on the face of it, the reasoning, appealing to
*20·18, by which the substitution was justified, is fallacious; for the
two occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma +_c \delta\)" src="images/303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.879ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_303.svg_3"> in fact mean different things.</p>

<p>In order to generalize our solution of this difficulty it is convenient
to define the term "arithmetical equation." An <i>arithmetical
equation</i> is an equation between purely arithmetical formal numbers
whose actual types are both determined adequately. Then it is evident
that from "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma = \tau.f(\tau)\)" src="images/305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.659ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_305.svg">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_28"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_6">
are formal numbers and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_7"> occurs arithmetically in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\tau)\)" src="images/306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_306.svg">,
we cannot infer <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\sigma)\)" src="images/307.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.296ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_307.svg"> unless the equation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma = \tau\)" src="images/308.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.479ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_308.svg">
is arithmetical. For otherwise the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_8"> in the equation cannot be
identified with the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_9"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\tau)\)" src="images/306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_306.svg_1">.</p>

<p>When we have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = \tau . f(\tau)\)" src="images/309.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.648ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_309.svg">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_10"> is a formal
number and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_6"> is a number in a definite type, and wish to pass
to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\beta)\)" src="images/310.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.285ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_310.svg">," or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = \tau . f(\beta)\)" src="images/311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.758ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_311.svg">" and wish to pass
to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\tau)\)" src="images/306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_306.svg_2">," the occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_11"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\tau)\)" src="images/306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_306.svg_3"> being
arithmetical, the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_7"> may not be an adequate type for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_12">. Accordingly the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_13"> in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = \tau\)" src="images/312.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.467ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_312.svg">" cannot be
identified with the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_14"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\tau)\)" src="images/306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_306.svg_4">. The type of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_15">
in the equation ought to be freed from dependence on that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_8">.
Accordingly the transition is only legitimate when we can write instead
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\beta +_c 0 = \tau . f(\tau )\unicode{x201d}\quad \text{or}\quad \unicode{x201c}\beta +_c 0 = \tau . f(\beta ),\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.035ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_313.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxviii">[Pg xxviii]</span>
where in both cases the equation is arithmetical. For now all the
symbols are subject to the same rules.</p>

<p>If this modification can be made without altering the truth-value of
the asserted propositions, the substitution is legitimate, otherwise it
is not.</p>

<p>It is obvious that in the above our immediate passage is to or from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\beta +_{c}0)\)" src="images/314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.062ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_314.svg">. But is easy to see that, the occurrence of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta+_{c}0\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.058ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_315.svg"> being arithmetical, we always have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f(\beta ).\equiv .f(\beta +_{c}0). \]" src="images/316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.749ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_316.svg"></span>
In order to prove this, we have only to prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \alpha +_{c}(\beta +_{c}0)&amp;=\alpha +_{c}\beta,\\ \alpha \times _{c}(\beta +_{c}0)&amp;=\alpha \times _{c}\beta,\\ (\alpha +_{c}0)^\beta &amp;=\alpha ^\beta, \alpha ^{\beta +_{c}0}&amp;=\alpha ^\beta, \end{array} \]" src="images/317.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.859ex; width: 34.14ex; height: 8.85ex;" id="img_images_317.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{and}\qquad \alpha &gt;\beta +_{c}0.\equiv .\alpha &gt;\beta .\equiv .\alpha +_{c}0&gt;\beta. \]" src="images/318.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 43.388ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_318.svg"></span></p>

<p>The demonstration of the first of these propositions runs as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*110·4.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \beta {\sim}\in \text{NC}.\lor.\beta =\Lambda :&amp;\supset .\beta +_{c}0=\Lambda .\alpha +_{c}\beta =\Lambda.\\ [*110·4] &amp;\supset .\alpha +_{c}(\beta +_{c}0)=\Lambda =\alpha +_{c}\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*110·4.&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha {\sim}\in \text{NC}.\lor.\alpha =\Lambda :\supset .\alpha +_{c}(\beta +_{c}0)=\Lambda =\alpha +_{c}\beta     &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*110·6.\supset \vdash :\alpha ,\beta \in \text{NC}-{℩}ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\alpha +_{c}(\beta +_{c}0)&amp;=\alpha +_{c}\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta \\ &amp;=\alpha +_{c}\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).(3).\supset \vdash :\alpha +_{c}(\beta +_{c}0)=\alpha +_{c}\beta \end{array} \]" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 115.774ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_319.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above demonstration the step to (3) is legitimate since by the
hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_9"> is a determination of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.903ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_320.svg"> in an
adequate type.</p>

<p>Similar proofs hold for the other propositions, using <a href="#_113_204" class="pginternal">*113·204</a> and
<a href="#_116_204" class="pginternal">*116·204</a> and <a href="#_117_12" class="pginternal">*117·12</a> and <a href="#_103_13" class="pginternal">*103·13</a>.</p>

<p>We must also consider the circumstances under which we can pass from
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\tau\)" src="images/321.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.467ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_321.svg">" to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta +_{c}0=\tau\)" src="images/322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 10.245ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_322.svg">," where the latter equation
is arithmetical. In other words, using *65·01 we require the hypothesis
necessary for
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !\tau _{\eta }.\beta =\tau _{\xi }.\supset .\beta +_{c}0=\tau _{\eta }. \]" src="images/323.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 26.487ex; height: 2.305ex;" id="img_images_323.svg"></span></p>

<p>We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*20·18. &amp;\supset \vdash :\beta =\tau_{\xi }.\supset .\beta +_{c}0=\tau_{\xi }+_{c}0 &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*110·35. &amp;\supset \vdash :\exists !\tau_{\xi }.\exists !\tau_{\eta }.\supset .\tau_{\xi }+_{c}0=\tau_{\eta }+_{c}0 &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2). &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\tau_{\xi }.\exists !\tau_{\eta }.\supset :\beta =\tau_{\xi }.\supset     .\beta +_{c}0=\tau_{\eta }+_{c}0 &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(3). &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\beta .\exists !\tau_{\eta }.\supset :\beta =\tau_{\xi }.\supset .\beta +_{c}0=\tau_{\eta }+_{c}0     &amp;\qquad \text{(4)} \end{array} \]" src="images/324.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.547ex; width: 66.958ex; height: 12.224ex;" id="img_images_324.svg"></span></p>

<p>Now in (4) the occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta +_{c}0\)" src="images/325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.058ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_325.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau_{\eta}+_{c}0\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 6.749ex; height: 2.192ex;" id="img_images_326.svg">,
which are in the same type, may be chosen to be in any type we like.
Hence we deduce
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .(4).*110·6.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\beta .\exists !\tau _{\eta}.\supset :\beta =\tau _{\xi}.&amp;\supset     .(\beta +_{c}0)_{\zeta }=\text{ sm }_{\zeta}ʻʻ\tau _{\eta}.\\ [*100·511] &amp;\supset .(\beta +_{c}0)_{\zeta}=\tau_{\zeta} \end{array} \]" src="images/327.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.259ex; width: 65.817ex; height: 5.649ex;" id="img_images_327.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxix">[Pg xxix]</span></p>

<p>Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\beta\)" src="images/328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.167ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_328.svg"> is the requisite condition. Now since
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\zeta\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.066ex; height: 2.054ex;" id="img_images_329.svg"> can be in any type, we can also choose it in any existential
type for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_16">. Thus with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_15"> applying to the
arithmetical occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_17"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\tau)\)" src="images/306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_306.svg_5">, we have, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_18"> is a formal number and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_10"> is a number in a definite
type,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \vdash :\exists !\beta .\beta &amp;=\tau .f(\tau).\supset .f(\beta),\\ \vdash :\exists !\beta .\beta &amp;=\tau .f(\beta).\supset .f(\tau),\\ \vdash :\exists !\sigma .\sigma &amp;=\tau .f(\tau).\supset .f(\sigma). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/330.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 26.181ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_330.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the last proposition by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_15"> the equation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma =\tau\)" src="images/331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.479ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_331.svg">
is arithmetical. These equations are summed up in <a href="#_118_01" class="pginternal">*118·01</a>.</p>

<p>These three fundamental theorems embody the principle of arithmetical
substitution. The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\beta\)" src="images/328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.167ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_328.svg_1"> is really less than is
assumed in ordinary life, the usual tacit assumption being
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in\text{NC}-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.871ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_332.svg">. In fact unless
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/333.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.377ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_333.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\tau\)" src="images/321.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.467ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_321.svg_1"> is necessarily false.</p>

<p><i>Principle of Identification of Types</i>. Suppose we have proved
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\phi \sigma\)" src="images/334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 12.007ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_334.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\phi(\sigma _{\xi}).\supset .p\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 12.839ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_335.svg">,"
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_29"> is a formal number
whose occurrence in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\phi \sigma\)" src="images/334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 12.007ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_334.svg_1">" is
in an entirely ambiguous type, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi _{\xi}\)" src="images/336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 2.237ex; height: 2.237ex;" id="img_images_336.svg"> is the same formal
number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_30"> with its type related to that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_1"> by *65·01.
Then since the type of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_31"> in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset.\phi \sigma\)" src="images/337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 12.007ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_337.svg">"
is ambiguous, we can write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset.\phi (\sigma _{\xi})\)" src="images/338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 14.656ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_338.svg">"
and thence infer "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .p\)" src="images/339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.526ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_339.svg">."</p>

<p>The principle is: An entirely undetermined type in an asserted symbolic
form can be identified with any type ambiguous or otherwise in any
other asserted symbolic form or in the same symbolic form.</p>

<p>For example in <a href="#_100_42" class="pginternal">*100·42</a> (demonstration) considered above, since
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\mu \cap \nu\)" src="images/340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.965ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_340.svg"> occurs, the first occurrences of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_31"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_16"> are of the same
type, and so are their second occurrences in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha=\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_341.svg">.
But the two types are not determined by our
conventions to have any necessary connection. In fact the type
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_342.svg"> is entirely arbitrary.
Accordingly it can be identified with the other type, and thus the
inference to the next line, <i>viz.</i> to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset.\mu =\nu\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.947ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_343.svg">,"
is justified.</p>

<p>In the case of arithmetical equations, it is important to notice that
we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .*100·321·33.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\alpha .\supset :\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}(\xi)ʻ\beta .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta. \]" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 74.049ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_344.svg"></span>
Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_32"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_19"> are formal numbers,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\sigma_{\xi}.\supset :\sigma _{\xi}=\tau _{\xi}.\supset .\sigma =\tau. \]" src="images/345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 28.44ex; height: 2.287ex;" id="img_images_345.svg"></span>
Thus if we have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}.\exists !\sigma .\supset .\sigma=\tau\)" src="images/346.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 19.03ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_346.svg">"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}ʻ.\sigma _{\eta}=\tau _{\eta}.\supset.p\)" src="images/347.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 20.132ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_347.svg">,"
we can infer from the former proposition
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{Hp}.\exists !\sigma .\supset .\sigma _{\eta}=\tau_{\eta}\)" src="images/348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 20.815ex; height: 2.305ex;" id="img_images_348.svg">"
and from this and the latter proposition, we infer
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{Hp}'.\text{Hp}.\exists !\sigma .\supset .p\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 19.278ex; height: 2.263ex;" id="img_images_349.svg">,"
so the general principle of identification can be employed when the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\sigma)\)" src="images/350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.4ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_350.svg"> in the first proposition is an arithmetical equation.</p>

<p>For example, in an example given above, <a href="#_100_44" class="pginternal">*100·44</a> (demonstration),
<i>viz.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\alpha \in \mu .\supset .(\exists \beta).\mu =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta, \]" src="images/351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.38ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_351.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxx">[Pg xxx]</span>
the equation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_342.svg_1"> is arithmetical.
Accordingly we are justified in asserting the propositional function
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\alpha \in \mu .\supset .(\exists \beta).\mu =\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\beta .\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\beta, \]" src="images/352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 69.005ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_352.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\beta\)" src="images/353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.548ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_353.svg"> in
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu =\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\beta\)" src="images/354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.929ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_354.svg">" has all along been
presupposed by the necessity of meaning.
Thus the inference follows,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned} \vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\alpha \in \mu .&amp;\supset .\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\alpha =\mu .\\ &amp;\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\mu . \end{aligned}\]" src="images/355.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 42.833ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_355.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proof loses its point when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_22"> is looked on as a variable
with necessarily the same type throughout. For then the proposition
collapses into
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \in \text{NC}.\supset :\alpha \in \mu .\equiv .\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\alpha =\mu . \]" src="images/356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.954ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_356.svg"></span></p>

<p>But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_23"> be a formal number necessarily a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_1">, the proposition is really
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\supset :\alpha \in \mu .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\mu . \]" src="images/357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 34.679ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_357.svg"></span></p>

<p>With this presupposition we should have in the first line of the
demonstration
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash :\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\mu .\supset .\alpha \in \mu,\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 34.175ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_358.svg"></span>
though with "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_24">" a single variable, the line is formally correct
as it stands in the text.</p>

<p><i>Recognition of Particular Cases</i>. It is important to notice
the conditions under which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \sigma\)" src="images/359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.64ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_359.svg"> can be recognized as a
particular case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \xi\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.339ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_360.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_2"> is a real variable and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_33"> is a formal number. In the first place obviously we must
substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma \cap t_{0}ʻ\xi\)" src="images/361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.959ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_361.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_34">, wherever it occurs
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \sigma\)" src="images/359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.64ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_359.svg_1">, and thus obtain <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\sigma \cap t_{0}ʻ\xi)\)" src="images/362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.068ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_362.svg">.
Then we may find that by the application of our conventions, we can
replace this by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \sigma\)" src="images/359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.64ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_359.svg_2">. For example we have</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*100·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\mu \cap \nu .\supset .\mu =\nu \)" src="images/363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.629ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_363.svg"></p>

<p>Now put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}ʻ\mu\)" src="images/364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.548ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_364.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_25">, we obtain
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}ʻ\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\exists !(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}ʻ\mu )\cap \nu .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}\mu     =\nu &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*100·41.\supset \vdash :\nu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}ʻ\mu \cap \nu .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}ʻ\mu =\nu &amp;\qquad \text{(2)} \end{array} \]" src="images/365.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 77.029ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_365.svg"></span></p>

<p>Now by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_16">, even when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_18"> is a formal number, the
identity of types of the two occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_32"> is
equally secured in
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\nu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap \nu .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\nu. \]" src="images/366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.173ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_366.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus this is a particular case of <a href="#_100_42" class="pginternal">*100·42</a>. Such deductions can be made
in general without any explicit formal statement.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxxi">[Pg xxxi]</span></p>

<p><i>Ambiguity of</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_2">. It follows (cf. <a href="#_100_02" class="pginternal">*100·02</a> and <a href="#_103_02" class="pginternal">*103·02</a>)
from the typical ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_2"> that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_3">
is also typically ambiguous. Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC}.\nu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.762ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_367.svg">" according to our methods of interpretation would not
necessitate that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_26"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_19"> should be of the same type.
We shall always interpret "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.666ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_368.svg">" as standing
for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC}.\nu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.762ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_369.svg">" and therefore as not
necessarily identifying the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_27"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_20">. Similarly for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct}\)" src="images/371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 10.183ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_371.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC ind}\)" src="images/372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.041ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_372.svg">.
For example</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*110·402.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\supset .\exists !(\mu +_{c} \nu )\cap tʻtʻ(\mu \uparrow \nu)\)" src="images/373.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.497ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_373.svg"></p>

<p>Here the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_28"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_21"> need not be of the same type. Again</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*110·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.tʻ\mu = tʻ\nu .\supset .\exists !(\mu +_{c} \nu)\cap tʻ\mu\)" src="images/374.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_374.svg"></p>

<p>Here the identification of the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_29"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_22"> requires
the hypothesis "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\mu = tʻ\nu\)" src="images/375.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.929ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_375.svg">."</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
VI. <i>Conventions</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg"> <i>and</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin T}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.853ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_377.svg">.</p>

<p><i>General Arithmetical Convention</i>. Conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_17"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_16"> are always applied, but the following convention is not
used at first. This convention limits the remaining ambiguity of type
by sweeping away the exceptional cases in low types, due to the failure
of existence theorems. The convention will be cited as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_1">.</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_2">. <i>All equations involving pure arithmetical formal
numbers are to be arithmetical.</i></p>

<p>We have seen that from an arithmetical equation the analogous equation
in any other type can be deduced. Thus with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_3"> all
