equations between formal numbers are so determined in type that their
truth in "any type" is deducible. Thus in the few early propositions
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_4"> is introduced, the fact is noted by stating that
the equations hold "in <i>any</i> type." These propositions are <a href="#_103_16" class="pginternal">*103·16</a>,
<a href="#_110_71" class="pginternal">*110·71</a><a href="#_110_72" class="pginternal">·72</a>.</p>

<p>The effect of applying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_5"> to other propositions in <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>
is to render some of the hypotheses (usually logical forms affirming
existence) unnecessary, but also materially to limit the scope of the
propositions. Take for example</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*100·35.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}\vdash :\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\lor.&amp;\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\beta :\supset:\\ &amp;\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta\end{aligned}\]" src="images/378.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 64.855ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_378.svg"></span></p>

<p>If we apply <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_6"> to this, we can write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta. \]" src="images/379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 54.947ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_379.svg"></span></p>

<p>For the equational occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_33"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_17"> are by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_17"> to be with
adequate actual types. But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_12"> is a small class in a high
type, an adequate actual type for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_34"> will be a high
type, whereas <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_133.svg_3"> may hold in a low type.
Thus with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_8">, for the sake of simplicity we abandon the
statement of the minimum of hypothesis necessary for our propositions.
The enunciation of no other proposition in <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a> is affected.</p>

<p>The enunciation of no proposition in <a href="#_101" class="pginternal">*101</a> is affected by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_9">,
though it would unduly limit the scope of <a href="#_101_34" class="pginternal">*101·34</a>. In <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_10"> would unduly limit the scope of such propositions as
</p><p class="nindc">
<a href="#_110_22" class="pginternal">*110·22</a><a href="#_110_23" class="pginternal">·23</a><a href="#_110_24" class="pginternal">·24</a><a href="#_110_25" class="pginternal">·25</a><a href="#_110_251" class="pginternal">·251</a><a href="#_110_252" class="pginternal">·252</a><a href="#_110_3" class="pginternal">·3</a><a href="#_110_31" class="pginternal">·31</a><a href="#_110_32" class="pginternal">·32</a><a href="#_110_331" class="pginternal">·331</a><a href="#_110_34" class="pginternal">·34</a><a href="#_110_35" class="pginternal">·35</a><a href="#_110_351" class="pginternal">·351</a><a href="#_110_44" class="pginternal">·44</a><a href="#_110_51" class="pginternal">·51</a><a href="#_110_54" class="pginternal">·54</a>
</p><p class="nind">
and of many others, without altering their enunciations. There is no
proposition in <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a> whose enunciation it would alter. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_11"> is
already<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxxii">[Pg xxxii]</span> applied to <a href="#_110_71" class="pginternal">*110·71</a><a href="#_110_72" class="pginternal">·72</a>; if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_12"> is removed from these
propositions, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_133.svg_4"> must be added as an
hypothesis to both of them. The effect of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_13"> on <a href="#_113" class="pginternal">*113</a> and
<a href="#_116" class="pginternal">*116</a> is entirely analogous to that on *110; in neither of these two
numbers is there any proposition to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_14"> is applied in
the text.</p>

<p>As regards <a href="#_117" class="pginternal">*117</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_15"> is applied throughout, so that
the propositions are all in the form suitable for subsequent
investigations in which the interest is purely arithmetical. It is
important however to analyse the effect of AT on the enunciations
for the sake of logical investigations, especially in connection
with <a href="#_120" class="pginternal">*120</a>. First, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_16"> can only affect propositions in
which equations or inequations occur, and among such propositions
it does not affect the enunciations of those in which both sides
of the equations are not formal numbers, so that the equations are
not arithmetical after the application of AT. These propositions
are <a href="#_117_104" class="pginternal">*117·104</a><a href="#_117_14" class="pginternal">·14</a><a href="#_117_24" class="pginternal">·24</a><a href="#_117_241" class="pginternal">·241</a><a href="#_117_243" class="pginternal">·243</a><a href="#_117_31" class="pginternal">·31</a><a href="#_117_551" class="pginternal">·551</a>. These propositions, which are
characterized by the presence of a single letter on one side of any
equation involved, can be recognized at a glance. The propositions
involving arithmetical equations whose enunciations are unaltered
by the removal of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_17"> are <a href="#_117_21" class="pginternal">*117·21</a><a href="#_117_54" class="pginternal">·54</a><a href="#_117_592" class="pginternal">·592</a>. Propositions
involving inequations whose enunciations are unaltered by the removal
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_18"> are <a href="#_117_26" class="pginternal">*117·26</a><a href="#_117_27" class="pginternal">·27</a>. Finally the only propositions of *117
whose enunciations are altered by the removal of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_19"> are
<a href="#_117_108" class="pginternal">*117·108</a><a href="#_117_211" class="pginternal">·211</a><a href="#_117_23" class="pginternal">·23</a><a href="#_117_25" class="pginternal">·25</a><a href="#_117_3" class="pginternal"></a>.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_118" class="pginternal">*118</a> and <a href="#_119" class="pginternal">*119</a> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_20"> is not used.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_120" class="pginternal">*120</a>, which is devoted to those properties of inductive cardinals
which are of logical interest, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_21"> is never used. None of
the propositions <a href="#_117_108" class="pginternal">*117·108</a><a href="#_117_211" class="pginternal">·211</a><a href="#_117_23" class="pginternal">·23</a><a href="#_117_25" class="pginternal">·25</a><a href="#_117" class="pginternal">·3</a> are cited in it, except <a href="#_117_25" class="pginternal">*117·25</a>
in the demonstration of <a href="#_120_435" class="pginternal">*120·435</a> for a use where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_22"> is not
relevant. The application of AT to *120 would simplify the hypotheses
of <a href="#_120_31" class="pginternal">*120·31</a><a href="#_120_41" class="pginternal">·41</a><a href="#_120_451" class="pginternal">·451</a><a href="#_120_53" class="pginternal">·53</a><a href="#_120_55" class="pginternal">·55</a>, and limit the scopes of the propositions.</p>

<p>One other convention, which we will call "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin T}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.853ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_377.svg_1">," is
required in certain propositions where the hypothesis implies that
there are types in which every inductive cardinal exists, <i>i.e.</i>
in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_208.svg_2"> is not an inductive class. Among such hypotheses
are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.545ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_380.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Prog}\)" src="images/381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.577ex; height: 2.086ex;" id="img_images_381.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.257ex; height: 1.994ex;" id="img_images_382.svg">
(or typically definite forms of these hypotheses), or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \text{Prog}\)" src="images/383.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 9.173ex; height: 2.011ex;" id="img_images_383.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \aleph_{0}\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 6.584ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_384.svg">. When such hypotheses
occur, we shall assume that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_4"> induct is, whenever
significance permits, to be determined in a type in which every
inductive cardinal exists, <i>i.e.</i> in which the axiom of infinity
holds (cf. <a href="#_120_03" class="pginternal">*120·03</a><a href="#_120_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>). The statement of this convention is as follows:</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin T}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.853ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_377.svg_2">. <i>When the hypothesis of a proposition implies
that there is a type in which every inductive cardinal exists, every
occurrence of</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct}\)" src="images/371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 10.183ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_371.svg_1">" <i>in this proposition is to
be taken (if conditions of significance permit) in a sufficiently high
type to insure the existence of every inductive cardinal.</i></p>

<p>It is to be observed that this convention would be unnecessary if we
confined ourselves to one extensional hierarchy, for in any one such
hierarchy<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxxiii">[Pg xxxiii]</span> all types are inductive or all are non-inductive, so that
if every inductive cardinal exists in one type in the hierarchy, the
same holds for any other type in the hierarchy. But when we no longer
confine ourselves to one extensional hierarchy, this result may not
follow. For example, it may be the case that the number of individuals
is inductive, but the number of predicative functions of individuals is
not inductive; at any rate, no <i>logical</i> reason can be given against this
possibility, which can only be rejected on empirical grounds, if at all.</p>

<p>The way in which this convention is used may be illustrated by the
demonstration of <a href="#_122_33" class="pginternal">*122·33</a>. In the second line of this demonstration, we
show that the hypothesis implies
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \text{E}!\nu_{R} . \supset . \text{E}!(\nu +_{c}1)_{R} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \text{where by} *121·04\qquad \nu_{R} = \breve{R}_{\nu -_{c}1}ʻBʻR &amp;\qquad\text{Df},\\ \text{and by} *121·02\qquad R_{\nu} = \hat{x} \hat{y}\{\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻR(x \vdash\dashv y) = \nu +_{c}1\} &amp;\qquad\text{Df}. \end{array} \]" src="images/385.svg" style="vertical-align: -4.173ex; width: 64.831ex; height: 9.476ex;" id="img_images_385.svg"></span>
It will be seen that these definitions do not suffice to determine
the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_23">. Hence in (1), the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_24"> on the left may not
be of the same type as the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c}1\)" src="images/386.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.977ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_386.svg"> on the right. Now the use
of *122·473, which occurs in the next line of the demonstration of
<a href="#_122_33" class="pginternal">*122·33</a>, requires that the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_25"> on the left and the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c}1\)" src="images/386.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.977ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_386.svg_1">
on the right should be of the same type. This requires that the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_26"> should not be taken in a type in which we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\nu. \nu +_c 1 = \Lambda\)" src="images/387.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 14.656ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_387.svg">. Hence in order to apply
<a href="#_120_473" class="pginternal">*120·473</a>, we must choose a type in which all inductive cardinals
exist. Since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Prog}\)" src="images/388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 9.173ex; height: 2.011ex;" id="img_images_388.svg">" occurs in the hypothesis, we know
that all inductive cardinals exist in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_389.svg">. But it is
unnecessary to restrict ourselves to the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_389.svg_1">, since any
other type in which all inductive cardinals exist will equally secure
the validity of the demonstration. Thus the convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin T}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.853ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_377.svg_3">
secures the restriction required, and no more.</p>

<p>The convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin T}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.853ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_377.svg_4"> is often relevant when "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.545ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_380.svg_1">"
without any typical determination occurs in the hypothesis.
Whenever this is the case, if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct}\)" src="images/371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 10.183ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_371.svg_2">" occurs in the
proposition in a way which leaves its type undetermined so far as
conditions of significance are concerned, it is to be taken in a type
in which all its members exist.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">VII. <i>Final Working Rule in Arithmetic.</i></p>

<p>It is now (whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_23"> is used, together with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin T}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.853ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_377.svg_5">
when necessary) possible finally to sweep aside all consideration
of types in connection with inductive numbers. For by combining
<a href="#_126_121" class="pginternal">*126·121</a> *126·122 and <a href="#_120_4232" class="pginternal">*120·4232</a><a href="#_120_4622" class="pginternal">·4622</a>, we see that it is always possible to
take the type high enough so that no definitely determined inductive
number shall be null (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda)\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.45ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_390.svg">, and that all the inductive
reasoning can take place within this type. Furthermore we have already
seen that the arithmetical operations are independent of the types
of the components, so long as they are existential. Thus, as far as
the ordinary<span class="pagenum" id="Page_xxxiv">[Pg xxxiv]</span> arithmetic of finite numbers is concerned, all the
conventions (including AT), and the necessity for hypotheses as to the
existence of inductive numbers, are finally superseded by the following
single rule:</p>

<p><span class="allsmcap">Rule of Indefinite Numbers</span>. <i>The type assigned to any symbol
which represents an inductive number is such that the symbol is not
equal to</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_3">.</p>

<p>We make the definition</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*126·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc ind} = \text{Nc induct} - \iota ʻ\Lambda \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/391.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.161ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_391.svg"></p>

<p>Wherever this symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc ind}\)" src="images/392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.412ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_392.svg">" for the class of "indefinite
inductive cardinal numbers" is used, the above rule is adhered to.
In other words, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{Nc ind}\)" src="images/393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.542ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_393.svg">" can always be replaced
by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\alpha \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.115ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_394.svg">," where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_35"> is a homogeneous or ascending cardinal, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_13"> is the appropriate constant, or is a variable, as the case
may be. In the latter case, a symbolic form such as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\mu).f(\mu \in \text{Nc ind},\mu) \]" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.047ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_395.svg"></span>
can be replaced by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\mu,\alpha).f(\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\alpha \in \text{Cls induct},\mu). \]" src="images/396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_396.svg"></span></p>

<p>Furthermore by <a href="#_120_4622" class="pginternal">*120·4622</a> it follows that with this rule the result of
proceeding by induction in one type and then transforming to another
type is the same as that of proceeding by induction in the latter type.
Thus for example there is no advantage to be gained by discriminating
between <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{\xi }\)" src="images/397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 2.02ex; height: 2.174ex;" id="img_images_397.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{\eta }\)" src="images/398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 2.114ex; height: 2.192ex;" id="img_images_398.svg">; for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ2_{\xi} = 2_{\eta }\)" src="images/399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 14.756ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_399.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ2_{\eta } = 2_{\xi }\)" src="images/400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 14.662ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_400.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}2_{\xi } = \mu +_{c} 2_{\eta }\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 17.172ex; height: 2.192ex;" id="img_images_401.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} 2_{\xi } = \mu \times _{c} 2_{\eta }\)" src="images/402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 17.172ex; height: 2.192ex;" id="img_images_402.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{2_\xi } = \mu ^{2_\eta }\)" src="images/403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.044ex; height: 2.375ex;" id="img_images_403.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{\xi^\mu } = 2_{\eta ^\mu }\)" src="images/404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 8.781ex; height: 2.192ex;" id="img_images_404.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \geq 2_{\xi }.\equiv .\mu \geq 2_{\eta }\)" src="images/405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 16.669ex; height: 2.192ex;" id="img_images_405.svg">, and so on.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_1">[Pg 1]</span></p>

<p>Hence all discrimination of the types of indefinite inductive numbers
may be dropped; and the types are entirely indefinite and irrelevant.</p>
