<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_3">[Pg 3]</span></p>
<div class="chapter">
<h2 class="nobreak" id="PART_III">PART III.<br>
<br>
CARDINAL ARITHMETIC.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nindc">SUMMARY OF PART III.</p>

<p>IN this Part, we shall be concerned,
first, with the definition and general logical properties of
cardinal numbers (Section A); then with the operations of addition,
multiplication and exponentiation, of which the definitions and
formal laws do not require any restriction to finite numbers (Section
B); then with the theory of finite and infinite, which is rendered
somewhat complicated by the fact that there are two different senses
of "finite," which cannot (so far as is known) be identified without
assuming the multiplicative axiom. The theory of finite and infinite
will be resumed, in connection with series, in Part V, Section E.</p>

<p>It is in this Part that the theory of types first becomes practically
relevant. It will be found that contradictions concerning the maximum
cardinal are solved by this theory. We have therefore devoted our
first section in this Part (with the exception of two numbers giving
the most elementary properties of cardinals in general, and of 0 and 1
and 2, respectively) to the application of types to cardinals. Every
cardinal is typically ambiguous, and we confer typical definiteness
by the notations of *63, *64, and *65. It is especially where
existence-theorems are concerned that the theory of types is essential.
The chief importance of the propositions of the present part lies, not
only, as throughout the book, in the hypotheses necessary to secure the
conclusions, but also in the typical ambiguity which can be allowed to
the symbols consistently with the truth of the propositions in all the
cases thereby included.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_4">[Pg 4]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_A">SECTION A.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">DEFINITION AND LOGICAL PROPERTIES OF CARDINAL NUMBERS.</span></h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of Section A.</i></p>

<p>The Cardinal Number of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_14">, which we will denote by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_36">," is defined as the class of all classes similar
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_15">, <i>i.e.</i> as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\beta} (\beta\,\text{ sm }\,\alpha)\)" src="images/406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.432ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_406.svg">.
This definition is due to Frege, and was first published in his
<i>Grundlagen der Arithmetik</i><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_2" id="FNanchor_2">[2]</a>; its symbolic expression and use
are to be found in his <i>Grundgesetze der Arithmetik</i><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_3" id="FNanchor_3">[3]</a>. The chief
merits of this definition are (1) that the formal properties which
we expect cardinal numbers to have result from it; (2) that unless
we adopt this definition or some more complicated and practically
equivalent definition, it is necessary to regard the cardinal number of
a class as an indefinable. Hence the above definition avoids a useless
indefinable with its attendant primitive propositions.</p>

<p>It will be observed that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_9"> is any object, 1 is not the cardinal
number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_10">, but that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg">. This obviates a confusion
which otherwise is liable to arise in dealing with classes. Suppose we
have a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_16"> consisting of many terms; we say, nevertheless,
that it is <i>one</i> class. Thus it seems to be at once one and many.
But in fact it is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_17"> that is many, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\alpha\)" src="images/408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_408.svg"> that is
one. In regard to zero, the analogous point is still clearer. Suppose
we say "there are no Kings of France." This is equivalent to "the class
of Kings of France has no members," or, in our language, "the class
of Kings of France is a member of the class 0." It is obvious that we
cannot say "the King of France is a member of the class 0," because
there is no King of France. Thus in the case of 0 and 1, as more
evidently in all other cases, a cardinal number appertains to a class,
not to the members of the class.</p>

<p>For the purposes of formal definition, we subject the formula
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \hat{\beta} (\beta\,\text{ sm }\,\alpha) \]" src="images/409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.956ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_409.svg"></span>
to some simplification. It will be seen that, according to this
formula, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_3">" is a relation, namely the relation of a
cardinal number to any class of which it is the number. Thus for
example 1 has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg_1"> the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_4">; so has<span class="pagenum" id="Page_5">[Pg 5]</span> 2
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx \cup \iota ʻy\)" src="images/410.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_410.svg">, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_411.svg">. The relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_5"> is, in fact, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{ sm }}\)" src="images/131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 3.007ex;" id="img_images_131.svg_1">;
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{ sm }}ʻ\alpha = \hat{\beta} (\beta\,\text{ sm }\, \alpha)\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.162ex; height: 3.548ex;" id="img_images_412.svg">. Hence for formal purposes of definition we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc} = \overrightarrow{\text{ sm }} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 14.938ex; height: 3.167ex;" id="img_images_413.svg"></span></p>

<p>The class of cardinal numbers is the class of objects which are the
cardinal numbers of something or other, <i>i.e.</i> of objects which,
for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_18">, are equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_37">. We call the
class of cardinal numbers <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_5">; thus we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC} = \hat{\mu}\{(\exists \alpha) . \mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\}. \]" src="images/414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.963ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_414.svg"></span></p>

<p>For purposes of formal definition, we replace this by the simpler
formula
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC} = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.447ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_415.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the present section, we shall be concerned with what we may call the
purely logical properties of cardinal numbers, namely those which do
not depend upon the arithmetical operations of addition, multiplication
and exponentiation, nor upon the distinction of finite and infinite<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_4" id="FNanchor_4">[4]</a>.
The chief point to be dealt with, as regards both importance and
difficulty, is the relation of a cardinal number in one type to the
same or an associated cardinal number in another type. When a symbol is
ambiguous as to type, we will call it <i>typically ambiguous</i>; when,
either always or in a given context, it is unambiguous as to type, we
will call it <i>typically definite</i>. Now the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_3">"
is typically ambiguous; the only limitation on its type is that its
domain and converse domain must both consist of classes. When we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\,\text{sm}\,\beta\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.26ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_416.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_19"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_11"> need not be of the
same type, in fact, in any type of classes, there are classes similar
to some of the classes of any other type of classes. For example, we
have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx \text{ sm } \iota ʻy\)" src="images/417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.627ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_417.svg">, whatever types <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_11"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_1">
may belong to. This ambiguity of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_4">" is derived from that
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_418.svg">, which in turn is derived from that of 1. We
denote (cf. *65·01) by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{\alpha}\)" src="images/419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.343ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_419.svg">" all the unit classes which
are of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_20">. Then (according to the definition
*70·01) <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{\alpha} \rightarrow 1_{\beta}\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.087ex; height: 2.157ex;" id="img_images_420.svg"> will be the class of
those one-one relations whose domain is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_21">
and whose converse domain is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_12">. Thus
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{\alpha} \rightarrow 1_{\beta}\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.087ex; height: 2.157ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_1">" is typically definite as soon
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_22"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_13"> are given. Suppose now, instead of having
merely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \text{ sm } \delta\)" src="images/421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.14ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_421.svg">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists R). R\in 1_{\alpha } \rightarrow 1_{\beta } . \text{D}ʻR = \gamma . \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \delta ; \]" src="images/422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.455ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_422.svg"></span>
then we know not only that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\,\text{ sm }\,\delta\)" src="images/423.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.896ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_423.svg">, but also that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_2"> belongs to the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_23">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_1">
belongs to the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_14">. When the ambiguous symbol
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_5">" is rendered typically definite by having its domain
defined as being of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_24">, and its converse
domain defined as being of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_15">, we write it
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }_{(\alpha ,\beta)}\)" src="images/424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 7.714ex; height: 1.813ex;" id="img_images_424.svg">," because generally, in accordance
with *65·1, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_6"> is a typically ambiguous relation, we write
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_6">[Pg 6]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{(\alpha ,\beta)}\)" src="images/425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 5.524ex; height: 2.345ex;" id="img_images_425.svg"> for the typically definite relation that
results when the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_7"> is to consist of terms of the same
type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_25">, and the converse domain is to consist of terms of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_16">. Thus we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \gamma\,\text{ sm }_{(\alpha, \beta)}\,\delta . \equiv . (\exists R) . R \in 1_{\alpha} \rightarrow 1_{\beta} . \gamma = \text{D}ʻR . \delta = \text{ᗡ}ʻR. \]" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 52.929ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_426.svg"></span>
Here everything is typically definite if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_26"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_17"> (or
their types) are given.</p>

<p>Passing now to the relation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_6">," it will be seen that
it shares the typical ambiguity of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg">." In order to
render it typically definite, we must derive it from a typically
definite "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_1">." So long as nothing is added to give typical
definiteness, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_283.svg_1">" will mean all the classes
belonging to some one (unspecified) type and similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_3">. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_27"> is a member of the type to which these classes are to belong,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_283.svg_2"> is contained in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_28">. For
this case, it is convenient to introduce the following two notations,
already defined in *65. When a typically ambiguous relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_8"> is to
be rendered typically definite as to its domain only, by deciding that
every member of the domain is to be <i>contained in</i> the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_29">, we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(\alpha)\)" src="images/428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.925ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_428.svg">" in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_9">. When we further
wish to determine <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_10"> as having members of the converse domain
<i>contained in</i> the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_18">, we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(\alpha, \beta)\)" src="images/429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.212ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_429.svg">" in
place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_11">; and when we wish members of the converse domain to be
<i>members</i> of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_19">, we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(\alpha_{\beta})\)" src="images/430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.019ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_430.svg">"
in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_12">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{sg}ʻ{R_{(\alpha, \beta)}} = \{\text{sg}ʻR\}(\alpha_{\beta}) \]" src="images/431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 23.582ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_431.svg"></span>
(cf. *65·2), and in particular, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc} =\overrightarrow{\text{ sm }}\)" src="images/432.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.626ex; height: 3.167ex;" id="img_images_432.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}(\alpha_{\beta}) = \text{sg}ʻ\text{ sm }_{(\alpha, \beta)}. \]" src="images/433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 21.743ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_433.svg"></span>
Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\beta})ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.589ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_434.svg">" is only significant when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_4"> is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_20">, and then it means "classes
of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_30"> and similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_5"> (which is of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_21">)."</p>

<p>"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.495ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_435.svg">" will mean "classes of the same type as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_31"> and similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_6">." As soon as the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_32">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_7"> are known, this is a typically definite symbol, being
in fact equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\gamma})ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 9.552ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_436.svg">. Hence so
long as we only wish to consider "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_283.svg_3">," typical
definiteness is secured by writing "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg">" in place of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_7">."</p>

<p>When we come to the consideration of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_6">,
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_1">" is no longer a sufficient determination,
although it suffices to determine the type. Suppose we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC}^{\beta}(\alpha) = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\beta}) \quad\text{Df}; \]" src="images/438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 26.05ex; height: 2.755ex;" id="img_images_438.svg"></span>
we have also, in virtue of the definitions in *65,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC}(\alpha) = \text{NC} \cap t^{2}ʻ\alpha = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha). \]" src="images/439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.652ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_439.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg"> is definite as to type, but is the domain of
a relation whose converse domain is ambiguous as to type; and it will
appear that there are some propositions about <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_1">
whose truth or falsehood depends upon the determination chosen
for the converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_2">. Hence if we
wish to have a symbol which is completely definite, we must write
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_7">[Pg 7]</span>"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\beta}(\alpha)\)" src="images/441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_441.svg">."</p>

<p>This point is important in connection with the contradictions as to the
maximum cardinal. The following remarks will illustrate it further.</p>

<p>Cantor has shown that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_22"> is any class, no class contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_23"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.9ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_442.svg">. Hence in particular
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_24"> is a type, no class contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_25"> is similar
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.9ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_442.svg_1">, which is the next type above <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_26">.
Consequently, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = \alpha \cup - \alpha\)" src="images/443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 11.468ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_443.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_33"> is
any class, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\sim}(\exists \gamma) . \gamma \subset \alpha \cup - \alpha . \gamma \text{ sm } \text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha). \]" src="images/444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.751ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_444.svg"></span></p>

<p>Now (cf. *63) we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ t_{0}ʻ\alpha = \alpha \cup - \alpha \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.11ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_445.svg"></span>
and we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha = \text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha)\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.19ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_446.svg">. Thus we
find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} {\sim}&amp;(\exists \gamma) . \gamma \subset t_{0}ʻ\alpha . \gamma\, \text{ sm }\, tʻ\alpha.\\ \text{Hence}\qquad &amp;\text{Nc}(\alpha_{tʻ\alpha})ʻtʻ\alpha = \Lambda . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/447.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.113ex; width: 35.75ex; height: 5.358ex;" id="img_images_447.svg"></span>
That is to say, no class of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_34"> has as many
members as <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg"> has. Hence also
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\Lambda \in \text{NC}^{tʻ\alpha}(\alpha).\\ \text{But}\qquad \gamma \subset t_{0}ʻ\alpha . \supset . \gamma \in &amp;\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\alpha })ʻ\gamma . \supset . \exists !\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\alpha })ʻ\gamma , \end{aligned} \]" src="images/449.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.276ex; width: 49.961ex; height: 5.684ex;" id="img_images_449.svg"></span>
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\alpha})ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.707ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_450.svg">" is only significant when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \subset t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 8.855ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_451.svg">; hence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \mu \in &amp;\text{NC}^{\alpha}(\alpha) . \supset_{\mu } . \exists !\mu\\ \text{and}\qquad\qquad &amp;\Lambda {\sim}\in \text{NC}^{\alpha}(\alpha). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/452.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.096ex; width: 28.623ex; height: 5.323ex;" id="img_images_452.svg"></span></p>

<p>Now the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_2">" will apply with
equal justice to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\alpha }(\alpha)\)" src="images/453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.75ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_453.svg"> or to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{tʻ\alpha}(\alpha)\)" src="images/454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.288ex; height: 2.743ex;" id="img_images_454.svg">; but we have just seen that in the
first case we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda {\sim}\in \text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.635ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_455.svg">,
and in the second we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \in \text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.875ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_456.svg">.
Consequently "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_3">" has not sufficient definiteness
to prevent practically important differences between the various
determinations of which it is capable.</p>

<p>A converse procedure to the above yields similar results. Let
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_35"> be a class of classes; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\)" src="images/457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_457.svg"> is of lower type
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_36">. Let us consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{sʻ\alpha}(\alpha)\)" src="images/458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.46ex; height: 2.743ex;" id="img_images_458.svg">. In
accordance with *63, we write <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{1}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_459.svg"> for the type containing
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\)" src="images/457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_457.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha \cup - sʻ\alpha\)" src="images/460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.008ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_460.svg">. Then
the greatest number in the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{sʻ\alpha}(\alpha)\)" src="images/458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.46ex; height: 2.743ex;" id="img_images_458.svg_1">
will be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻt_{1}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.877ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_461.svg">; but neither this nor
any lesser member of the class will be equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.877ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_462.svg">, because, as before,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\sim}(\exists \gamma ) . \gamma \subset t_{1}ʻ\alpha . \gamma \text{ sm } t_{0}ʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.249ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_463.svg"></span>
Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.877ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_464.svg">, which is a member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\alpha }(\alpha)\)" src="images/453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.75ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_453.svg_1">, is not a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{sʻ\alpha }(\alpha)\)" src="images/465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.46ex; height: 2.743ex;" id="img_images_465.svg">; but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\alpha}(\alpha)\)" src="images/466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.75ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_466.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{sʻ\alpha}(\alpha)\)" src="images/458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.46ex; height: 2.743ex;" id="img_images_458.svg_2"> have an equal right to be called
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_4">. Hence again "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_5">" is a symbol
not sufficiently definite for many of our purposes.</p>

<p>The solution of the paradox concerning the maximum cardinal is evident
in view of what has been said. This paradox is as follows: It results
from a theorem of Cantor's that there is no maximum cardinal, since,
for all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_37">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/467.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.28ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_467.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_8">[Pg 8]</span>
But at first sight it would seem that the class which contains
everything must be the greatest possible class, and must therefore
contain the greatest possible number of terms. We have seen, however,
that a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_38"> must always be contained within some one type;
hence all that is proved is that there are greater classes in the next
type, which is that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.068ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_468.svg">. Since there is always a
next higher type, we thus have a maximum cardinal in each type, without
having any absolutely maximum cardinal. The maximum cardinal in the
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_39"> is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha). \]" src="images/469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.827ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_469.svg"></span>
But if we take the corresponding cardinal in the next type, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}(\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha )ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha), \]" src="images/470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.447ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_470.svg"></span>
this is not as great as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha)ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha\cup - \alpha)\)" src="images/471.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.438ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_471.svg">,
and is therefore not the maximum cardinal of its
type. This gives the complete solution of the paradox.</p>

<p>For most purposes, what we wish to know in order to have a sufficient
amount of typical definiteness is not the absolute types of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_40"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_27">, as above, but merely what we may call their
<i>relative</i> types. Thus, for example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_41"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_28">
may be of the same type; in that case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta})\)" src="images/472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.003ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_472.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\beta }(\alpha)\)" src="images/473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_473.svg"> are respectively equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha _{\alpha })\)" src="images/474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.121ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_474.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\alpha }(\alpha)\)" src="images/453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.75ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_453.svg_2">.
We will call cardinals which, for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_42">, are members
of the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\alpha }(\alpha)\)" src="images/453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.75ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_453.svg_3">, <i>homogeneous</i>
cardinals, because the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_2">" from which they are derived
is a homogeneous relation. We shall denote the homogeneous cardinal
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_43"> by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.123ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_475.svg">," and we shall
denote the class of homogeneous cardinals (in an unspecified type) by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_1">"; thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻ\alpha &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ \text{N}_{0}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c} &amp;\quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/476.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 30.992ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_476.svg"></span>
Almost all the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_2"> are the same
in different types. When further typical definiteness is required,
it can be secured by writing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}(\alpha)\)" src="images/477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.897ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_477.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg"> in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 3.689ex; height: 1.92ex;" id="img_images_479.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_3">. For although <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_3">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_6"> were not wholly definite,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}(\alpha)\)" src="images/477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.897ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_477.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg_1">
are wholly definite. Apart from the fact of being of different
types, the only property in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg_2">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\beta)\)" src="images/480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.359ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_480.svg"> differ when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_44"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_29"> are of different types is in regard to the magnitude
of the cardinals belonging to them. Thus suppose the whole
universe consisted (as monists aver) of a single individual. Let
us call the type of this individual "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_10">." Then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.234ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_481.svg"> will consist of 0 and 1,
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\text{Indiv}) = \iotaʻ0 \cup \iota ʻ1. \]" src="images/482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.974ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_482.svg"></span>
But in the next higher type, there will be two members, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_11">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻ\text{Indiv}) = \iotaʻ0 \cup \iotaʻ1 \cup \iotaʻ2.\\ \text{Similarly}\qquad \text{N}_{0}\text{C}&amp;(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv}) = \iotaʻ0 \cup \iotaʻ1 \cup \iotaʻ2 \cup \iotaʻ3 \cup \iotaʻ4, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/483.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 59.131ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_483.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_9">[Pg 9]</span>
the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_484.svg"> being <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \cap tʻ\text{Indiv}, \iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.15ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_485.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.314ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_486.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\Lambda \cup \iotaʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.558ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_487.svg">; and so on. (The greatest
cardinal in any except the lowest type is always a power of 2.)</p>

<p>The maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg_3"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.656ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_488.svg">; but apart from this difference
of maximum and its consequences, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg_4">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\beta)\)" src="images/480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.359ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_480.svg_1"> do not differ in any important
properties. Hence for most purposes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_4"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 3.689ex; height: 1.92ex;" id="img_images_479.svg_1"> have as much typical definiteness as is
necessary.</p>

<p>Among cardinals which are not homogeneous we shall consider three
kinds. The first of these we shall call <i>ascending</i> cardinals. A
cardinal <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\beta}(\alpha)\)" src="images/441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_441.svg_1"> is called an <i>ascending</i>
cardinal if the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_30"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻ\alpha\)" src="images/489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.796ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_489.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻtʻ\alpha\)" src="images/490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.971ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_490.svg"> or etc. We write <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{2}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_491.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻ\alpha\)" src="images/489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.796ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_489.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{3}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.338ex;" id="img_images_492.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻtʻ\alpha\)" src="images/490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.971ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_490.svg_1">, and so on. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻtʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}^{2}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt^{2}ʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}^{3}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt^{3}ʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df and so on},\\ \text{and}\qquad \text{N}^{1}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}^{1}\text{c} &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}^{2}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}^{2}\text{c} &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}^{3}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}^{3}\text{c} &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df and so on}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/493.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.826ex; width: 49.905ex; height: 18.783ex;" id="img_images_493.svg"></span>
We then have obviously
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha) \subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha). \]" src="images/494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.047ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_494.svg"></span>
We also have (by what was said earlier)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻtʻ\alpha {\sim}\in \text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha).\\ \text{Hence}\qquad &amp;\exists !\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha) - \text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/495.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.339ex; width: 35.175ex; height: 5.81ex;" id="img_images_495.svg"></span>
The members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha) - \text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.166ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_496.svg"> will be all cardinals which exceed
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/497.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.669ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_497.svg"> but do not exceed <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻtʻ\alpha\)" src="images/498.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.681ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_498.svg">.</p>

<p>Let us recur in illustration to our previous hypothesis
of the universe consisting of a single individual. Then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{c}\,\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/499.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 9.223ex; height: 2.018ex;" id="img_images_499.svg"> will consist of those classes
which are similar to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_12">" but of the next higher type.
These are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/500.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.729ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_500.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/501.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.314ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_501.svg">. In our case
we had <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}(\text{Indiv}) = 1\)" src="images/502.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.754ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_502.svg">. This leads to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}^{1}\text{c}\,\text{Indiv} = 1 . \text{N}^{2}\text{c}\,\text{Indiv} = 1\, \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/503.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 33.907ex; height: 2.185ex;" id="img_images_503.svg"></span>
or, introducing typical definiteness,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}^{1}\text{c}\,\text{Indiv} = 1(tʻ\text{Indiv}) . \text{N}^{2}\text{c}\,\text{Indiv} = 1(t^{2}ʻ\text{Indiv})\, \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/504.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.076ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_504.svg"></span>
We have then <img alt="" data-tex="\(1(tʻ\text{Indiv}) \in\text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/505.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.57ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_505.svg">.
Also
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 1(tʻ\text{Indiv}) \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv}). \]" src="images/506.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.199ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_506.svg"></span>
And in the case supposed, <img alt="" data-tex="\(1(tʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.222ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_507.svg"> is the maximum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.583ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_508.svg">, but
<img alt="" data-tex="\(2(tʻ\text{Indiv}) \in\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv})\)" src="images/509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.57ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_509.svg">.
Hence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv}) - \text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻtʻ\text{Indiv}) = \iota ʻ2. \]" src="images/510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.867ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_510.svg"></span>
Generalizing, we see that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.7ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_511.svg">
consists of the same numbers as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg_5">
each raised one degree in type. Similar propositions
hold of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{2}\text{C}(t^{2}ʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/512.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.688ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_512.svg">,
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_10">[Pg 10]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{3}\text{C}(t^{3}ʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/513.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.688ex; height: 2.557ex;" id="img_images_513.svg"> etc.</p>

<p>It is often useful to have a notation for what we may call "the same
cardinal in another type." Suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_30"> is a typically definite
cardinal; then we will denote by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg"> the same cardinal in
the next type, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻ\mu . \]" src="images/515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.668ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_515.svg"></span>
Note that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_31"> is a cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap \mu = \mu\)" src="images/516.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 16.247ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_516.svg">;
and whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_32"> is a typically definite cardinal or not,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻ\alpha \]" src="images/517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.123ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_517.svg"></span>
is a cardinal in a definite type. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_33"> is typically definite,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/518.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.123ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_518.svg"> is wholly definite; if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_34">
is typically ambiguous, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/518.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.123ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_518.svg_1"> has the same
kind of indefiniteness as belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_7">. The most
important case is when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_35"> is typically definite and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_45"> has
an assigned relation of type to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_36">. We then put, as observed above,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \mu ^{(1)} &amp;= \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻ\mu &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \mu ^{(2)} &amp;= \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap t^{2}ʻ\mu &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/519.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.474ex; width: 34.933ex; height: 6.078ex;" id="img_images_519.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_37"> is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg_1">
is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{C}\)" src="images/520.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 2.041ex;" id="img_images_520.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(2)}\)" src="images/521.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_521.svg"> is an
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{2}\text{C}\)" src="images/522.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 2.041ex;" id="img_images_522.svg"> and so on. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.7ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_511.svg_1">
will consist of all numbers which are of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{(1)}\)" src="images/523.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_523.svg"> for
some <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_38"> which is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg_6">;
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}^{1}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha) = \hat{\nu}\{(\exists \mu). \mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha) . \nu = \mu^{(1)}\}. \]" src="images/524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.671ex; height: 2.7ex;" id="img_images_524.svg"></span></p>

<p>The second kind of non-homogeneous cardinals to be considered is called
the class of "descending cardinals." These are such as go into a lower
type; <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\beta\)" src="images/265.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.548ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_265.svg_1"> is a descending cardinal
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_46"> is of a lower type than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_31">. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{1}ʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}_{2}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{2}ʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}.\\ \text{N}_{1}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{1}\text{C} &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}_{2}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{2}\text{C} &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}.\\ \mu_{(1)} &amp;= \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap t_{1}ʻ\mu &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \mu_{(2)} &amp;= \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap t_{2}ʻ\mu &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/525.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.153ex; width: 37.831ex; height: 17.437ex;" id="img_images_525.svg"></span></p>

<p>We have obviously <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha = \text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.522ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_526.svg">.</p>

<p>Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha) \subset\text{N}_{1}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.069ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_527.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">
Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \in \text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\delta . \supset .\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\delta = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.161ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_528.svg">,
whence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\delta . \supset .\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\delta \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.845ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_529.svg">,
whence
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{C} - \iota ʻ\Lambda \subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.147ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_530.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">
Since also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda {\sim} \in\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha)\)" src="images/531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.94ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_531.svg">, we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}_{0}\text{C} = \text{N}_{1}\text{C} - \iota ʻ\Lambda, \]" src="images/532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_532.svg"></span>
this proposition not requiring any further typical definiteness, since
it holds however such definiteness may be introduced, remembering
that such definiteness is necessarily so introduced as to secure
significance. Further, in virtue of the fact that no class contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_199.svg_1"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_2">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Lambda \in \text{N}_{1}\text{C}(\alpha). \]" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.491ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_533.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_11">[Pg 11]</span>
Consequently <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{C} = \text{N}_{0}\text{C} \cup\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.896ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_534.svg">.</p>

<p>We can prove in just the same way
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}_{2}\text{C} &amp;= \text{N}_{0}\text{C} \cup \iotaʻ\Lambda.\\ \text{Hence}\qquad \text{N}_{1}\text{C} &amp;= \text{N}_{2}\text{C}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/535.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 29.018ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_535.svg"></span>
and this result can obviously be extended to all descending cardinals.</p>

<p>The third kind of non-homogeneous cardinals to be considered may be
called "relational cardinals." They are those applicable to classes of
relations having a given relation of type to a given class. Consider
for example <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\in_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.006ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_536.svg">. (We shall take this
as the definition of the product of the numbers of the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_6">.) Suppose now that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_7"> consists of a single term: we
want to be able to say
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = \text{Nc}ʻ\breve{\iota}ʻ\kappa . \]" src="images/537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.915ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_537.svg"></span>
We have in this case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa = \iota ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.927ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_538.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \in_{\Delta }ʻ\kappa = \downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha, \]" src="images/539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.707ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_539.svg"></span>
and we know that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\alpha\)" src="images/540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.481ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_540.svg">. But if
we put simply
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha, \]" src="images/541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.211ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_541.svg"></span>
our proposition, though not mistaken, requires care in interpretation.
Just as we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.224ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_542.svg">,
so we want a notation giving typical definiteness to the proposition
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow \alpha ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/543.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.643ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_543.svg">. This is provided
as follows.</p>

<p>Using the notation of *64, put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}_{0}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{0}^{1}ʻ\alpha &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}.\\ \text{N}_{00}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{00}c &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ \text{N}_{0}^{1}\text{C} &amp;= \text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{0}^{1}c &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}.\\ \mu_{00} &amp;= \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻt_{00}ʻt_{1}ʻ\mu &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df etc}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/544.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.779ex; width: 44.766ex; height: 14.69ex;" id="img_images_544.svg"></span>
Then we have, for example,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha \subset t_{0}^{1}ʻ\alpha,\quad\textit{i.e.}\quad \downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha \in tʻt_{0}^{1}ʻ\alpha. \]" src="images/545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.594ex; width: 41.93ex; height: 2.594ex;" id="img_images_545.svg"></span>
Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha \in\text{N}_{0}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.594ex; width: 16.631ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_546.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}^{1}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}^{1}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.687ex; width: 21.138ex; height: 2.68ex;" id="img_images_547.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">
Similarly <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in tʻ\alpha . \supset . \downarrow xʻʻ\alpha \in\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.732ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_548.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">
Thus the above definitions give us what is required.</p>

<p>In order to complete our notation for types, we should need to be able
to express the type of the domain or converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_13">, or of
any relation whose domain and converse domain have respectively given
relations of type to the domain and converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_14">. Thus we
might put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} d_{0}ʻR &amp;= t_{0}ʻ\text{D}ʻR &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ b_{0}ʻR &amp;= t_{0}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df} \end{aligned} \]" src="images/549.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 25.429ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_549.svg"></span>
("b" appears here as "d" written backwards)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} d_{00}ʻR &amp;= tʻ(d_{0}ʻR \uparrow b_{0}ʻR) &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df}\\ &amp;= tʻR\\ d^{mn}ʻR &amp;= tʻ(t^{m}ʻd_{0}ʻR \uparrow t^{n}ʻb_{0}ʻR) &amp;&amp;\quad\text{Df and so on}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/550.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 53.096ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_550.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_12">[Pg 12]</span></p>

<p>This notation would enable us to deal with descending relational
cardinals. But it is not required in the present work, and is therefore
not introduced among the numbered propositions.</p>

<p>When a typically ambiguous symbol, such as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_3">" or
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_8">," occurs more than once in a given context, it must not
be assumed, unless required by the conditions of significance, that
it is to receive the same typical determination in each case. Thus
<i>e.g.</i> we shall write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\,\text{ sm }\, \beta . \supset .\beta\, \text{ sm }\, \alpha\)" src="images/551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 18.555ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_551.svg">,"
although, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_47"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_32"> are of different types, the two
symbols "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_6">" must receive different typical determinations.</p>

<p>Formulae which are typically ambiguous, or only partially definite as
to type, must not be admitted unless every significant interpretation
is true. Thus for example we may admit
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash . \alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_552.svg"></span>
because here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_9">" must mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\alpha})\)" src="images/553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.121ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_553.svg">," so that the only ambiguity remaining is as to the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_48">, and the formula holds whatever type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_49"> may belong
to, provided "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_38">" is significant, <i>i.e.</i>
provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_50"> is a class. But we must not, from "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/554.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.721ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_554.svg">,"
allow ourselves to infer
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/555.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.662ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_555.svg"></span>
For here the conditions of significance no longer demand that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_10">" should mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\alpha})\)" src="images/553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.121ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_553.svg_1">": it
might just as well mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\beta_{\alpha })\)" src="images/556.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_556.svg">." And as we
saw, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_33"> is a lower type than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_51">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_52"> is
sufficiently large of its type, we may have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}(\beta_{\alpha})ʻ\alpha = \Lambda, \]" src="images/557.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.975ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_557.svg"></span>
so that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_133.svg_5">" is not admissible without
qualification. Nevertheless, as we shall see in <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>, there are a
certain number of propositions to be made about a wholly ambiguous
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_11"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_7">.</p>
