<div class="chapter">
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_13">[Pg 13]</span>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_100">
*100. DEFINITION AND ELEMENTARY PROPERTIES
OF CARDINAL NUMBERS.</h2>
</div>

<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *100.</p>

<p>In this number we shall be concerned only with such immediate
consequences of the definition of cardinal numbers as do not require
typical definiteness, beyond what the inherent conditions of
significance may bestow. We introduce here the fundamental definitions:</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_100_01">*100·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc} = \overrightarrow{\text{ sm }} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 14.309ex; height: 3.167ex;" id="img_images_558.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_100_02">*100·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC} = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.818ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_559.svg"></p>

<p>The definition "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_12">" is required chiefly for the sake of the
descriptive function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_39">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_100_1">*100·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \hat{\beta}(\beta\,\text{ sm }\,\alpha) = \hat{\beta}(\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta)\)" src="images/560.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.794ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_560.svg"></p>

<p>This may be stated in various equivalent forms, which are given at the
beginning of this number (<a href="#_100_1" class="pginternal">*100·1</a>—<a href="#_100_16" class="pginternal">·16</a>). After a few propositions on
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_13"> as a relation, we proceed to the elementary properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_40">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_561.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\beta . \equiv . \beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha . \equiv . \alpha \text{ sm } \beta\)" src="images/562.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.927ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_562.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·321.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta . \supset . \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/563.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.667ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_563.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta . \supset . \alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta\)" src="images/564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.051ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_564.svg"></p>

<p>We proceed next to the elementary properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_8">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \mu \in \text{NC} . \equiv . (\exists \alpha ) . \mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/565.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.233ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_565.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \mu ,\nu \in \text{NC} . \exists !\mu \cap \nu . \supset . \mu =\nu\)" src="images/566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.629ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_566.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \mu \in \text{NC} . \alpha \in \mu . \supset . \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \mu \)" src="images/567.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 30.345ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_567.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \mu \in \text{NC} . \alpha \in \mu . \supset . \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/568.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 36.967ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_568.svg"></p>

<p>Observe that when we have such a hypothesis as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/569.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.461ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_569.svg">,"
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_39">, though it may be of any type, must be of <i>some</i> type;
hence the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_40"> cannot have the typical ambiguity which belongs
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_41">. If we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.888ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_570.svg">, this
will hold only in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_41">; but "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_9">" is
a typically ambiguous symbol, which<span class="pagenum" id="Page_14">[Pg 14]</span> will represent in any type the
"same" number as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_42">. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/571.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 16.51ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_571.svg">"
is an equation which is applicable to all possible typical
determinations of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_7">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_14">."</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\mu .\supset .\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 32.212ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_572.svg"></p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\mu\)" src="images/573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.251ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_573.svg"> is unnecessary, but we cannot prove
this till later (<a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a>).</p>

<p>We end the number with some propositions (<a href="#_100_6" class="pginternal">*100·6</a>—<a href="#_100_64" class="pginternal">·64</a>) stating that
various classes (such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/574.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.964ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_574.svg">), which have already been
proved to be similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_53">, have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_42"> members.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*100·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}=\overrightarrow{\text{ sm }} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/575.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 14.309ex; height: 3.167ex;" id="img_images_575.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}=\text{D}ʻ\text{Nc} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/576.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.818ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_576.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\hat{\beta}(\beta\, \text{ sm }\,\alpha)=\hat{\beta}(\alpha\, \text{ sm }\,\beta) \quad[*32·13.*73·31.(*100·01)]\)" src="images/577.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.341ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_577.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\hat{\beta}\{(\exists R).R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻR=\alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\beta\} \quad[*100·1.*73·1]\)" src="images/578.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.699ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_578.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\hat{\beta}\{(\exists R).R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\alpha \subset \text{D}ʻR.\beta =\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha\} \quad[*100·1.*73·11]\)" src="images/579.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.279ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_579.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(1\rightarrow 1\cap \overleftarrow{\text{D}}ʻ\alpha )=\text{D}ʻʻ(1\rightarrow 1\cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.694ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_580.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·11.*33·6. \supset \vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha &amp;=\hat{\beta} \{(\exists R).R\in 1\rightarrow 1.R\in \overleftarrow{\text{D}}ʻ\alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\beta\}\\ [*22·33.*37·6] &amp;=\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(1\rightarrow 1\cap \overleftarrow{\text{D}}ʻ\alpha) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*100·1.*73·1.*33·61. \supset \vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha &amp;=\hat{\beta} \{(\exists R).R\in 1\rightarrow 1.R\in \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\alpha .\text{D}ʻR=\beta\}\\ [*22·33.*37·6] &amp;=\text{D}ʻʻ(1\rightarrow 1\cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\alpha) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/581.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.038ex; width: 91.477ex; height: 21.208ex;" id="img_images_581.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta \quad[*32·18.*73·31.(*100·01)]\)" src="images/592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 67.229ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_592.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_100_321">*100·321</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/594.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.667ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_594.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*73·37.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :\gamma\,\text{ sm }\,\alpha .\equiv _{\gamma }.\gamma \text{ sm }\beta :\\ [*100·1] &amp;\supset :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta \colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/595.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.209ex; width: 49.795ex; height: 5.549ex;" id="img_images_595.svg"></span></p>

<p>Note that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\supset .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\,\beta\)" src="images/596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.027ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_596.svg">
is not always true. We might be tempted to prove it as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·1.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv :\gamma \,\text{ sm }\,\alpha .&amp;\equiv _{\gamma }.\gamma \,\text{ sm }\,\beta :\\ [*10·1] &amp;\supset :\alpha \,\text{ sm }\,\alpha .\equiv .\alpha \,\text{ sm }\,\beta :\\ [*73·3] &amp;\supset :\alpha \,\text{ sm }\,\beta \end{array} \]" src="images/597.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.793ex; width: 67.206ex; height: 8.717ex;" id="img_images_597.svg"></span></p>

<p>But the use of *10·1 here is only legitimate when the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_4">"
concerned is a homogeneous relation. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_43">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_18"> are descending cardinals, we may have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\Lambda = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/598.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.45ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_598.svg"> without having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\text{ sm }\beta\)" src="images/599.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.636ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_599.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_100_33">*100·33</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\supset .\alpha \,\text{ sm }\,\beta\)" src="images/600.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.051ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_600.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·1.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset .(\exists \gamma ).\gamma\,\text{ sm }\, \alpha .\gamma \,\text{ sm }\, \beta.\\ [*73·31] &amp;\supset .(\exists \gamma ).\alpha\, \text{ sm }\, \gamma .\gamma \text{ sm } \beta.\\ [*73·32] &amp;\supset .\alpha\,\text{ sm }\, \beta :\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/601.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 45.348ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_601.svg"></span></p>

<p>Note that we do not always have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \,\text{ sm }\, \beta .\supset .\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta. \]" src="images/602.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.04ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_602.svg"></span></p>

<p>For if the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_15"> concerned is a descending <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_16">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_54"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_34"> are sufficiently great, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_44">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_19"> may both be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_5">. For example, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha)\,\text{ sm }\, \text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha). \]" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.393ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_603.svg"></span></p>

<p>But <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha) = \Lambda\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.405ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_604.svg">,
so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\sim}\exists !\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha ) \cap \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ(\alpha \cup - \alpha). \]" src="images/605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.426ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_605.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_16">[Pg 16]</span></p>

<p>Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\, \text{ sm }\,\beta . \supset . \exists ! \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.411ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_606.svg">" is not always true when it is
significant.</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*22·5. \supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp} . \supset : \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta . &amp;\supset . \exists ! \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta.\\ [*100·33] &amp;\supset . \alpha \, \text{ sm }\, \beta &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*100·321. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp} . \supset : \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta . \equiv . \alpha \,\text{ sm }\, \beta &amp;\qquad\text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(2).*100·31. &amp;\supset \vdash . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/609.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 85.531ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_609.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus the only case in which the implications in <a href="#_100_321" class="pginternal">*100·321</a><a href="#_100_33" class="pginternal">·33</a><a href="#_100_34" class="pginternal">·34</a> cannot

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_19">[Pg 19]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_101">
*101. ON 0 AND 1 AND 2.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *101.</p>

<p>In the present number, we have to show that 0 and 1 and 2 as previously
defined are cardinal numbers in the sense defined in <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>, and to add a
few elementary propositions to those already given concerning them. We
prove (<a href="#_101_12" class="pginternal">*101·12</a><a href="#_101_241" class="pginternal">·241</a>) that 0 and 1 are not null, which cannot be proved,
with our axioms, for any other cardinal, except (in the case of finite
cardinals) when the type is specified as a sufficiently high one. Thus
we prove (<a href="#_101_42" class="pginternal">*101·42</a><a href="#_101_43" class="pginternal">·43</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{\text{Cls}}\)" src="images/638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.373ex; width: 3.549ex; height: 1.88ex;" id="img_images_638.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{\text{Rel}}\)" src="images/639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 3.651ex; height: 1.881ex;" id="img_images_639.svg">
exist; this follows from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \neq \text{V}\)" src="images/640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 6.284ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_640.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\neq \dot{\text{V}}\)" src="images/641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 6.284ex; height: 2.842ex;" id="img_images_641.svg">.
We prove (<a href="#_101_22" class="pginternal">*101·22</a><a href="#_101_34" class="pginternal">·34</a>) that 0 and 1 and 2 are all different from
each other. We prove (<a href="#_101_15" class="pginternal">*101·15</a><a href="#_101_28" class="pginternal">·28</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ0 = 0\)" src="images/642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.902ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_642.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ1 = 1\)" src="images/643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.902ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_643.svg">, but we cannot prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ2 = 2\)" src="images/644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.902ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_644.svg"> unless
we assume the existence of at least two individuals, or define the
first 2 in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ2 = 2\)" src="images/644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.902ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_644.svg_1">" as a 2 of some type other than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{\text{Indiv}}\)" src="images/645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 4.965ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_645.svg">, where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/64.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_64.svg_13">" stands for the type of
individuals.</p>

<p>It should be observed that, since 0 and 1 and 2 are typically
ambiguous, their properties are analogous to those of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_46">" rather than to those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_43">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in\text{NC}\)" src="images/646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.461ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_646.svg">.
For example, we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*100·511.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \exists ! \text{Nc}ʻ\beta . \supset . \text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{Nc}ʻ\beta = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/622.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.956ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_622.svg_1"></p>

<p>but we shall not have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC} . \exists ! \mu . \supset. \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu =\mu\)" src="images/647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 27.858ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_647.svg">
unless the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_8">" concerned is homogeneous, since in other
cases the symbols do not express a significant proposition. But in
<a href="#_100_511" class="pginternal">*100·511</a> we may substitute 0 or 1 or 2, and the proposition remains
significant and true. In fact we have (<a href="#_101_1" class="pginternal">*101·1</a><a href="#_101_2" class="pginternal">·2</a><a href="#_101_31" class="pginternal">·31</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . 0 = \text{Nc}ʻ\Lambda . 1 = \text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻx . 2 = \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\iota ʻx \cup \iota ʻ\Lambda ), \]" src="images/648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.288ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_648.svg"></span>
where 0 and 1 and 2 have an ambiguity corresponding to that of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_17">."</p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_102">
*102. ON CARDINAL NUMBERS OF ASSIGNED TYPES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *102.</p>

<p>In this number, we shall consider a typically definite relation
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_18">," <i>i.e.</i> we shall consider the relation, to a
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_2"> which is given as of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_35">, of
the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_44"> of those classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_8"> which are similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_3"> and of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_57">. We shall then put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \mu  &amp;= \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\delta ,\\ \gamma  &amp;\in  \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\delta ,\\ \gamma  &amp;\,\text{ sm }_{(\alpha ,\beta )}\delta , \end{aligned} \]" src="images/704.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.708ex; width: 14.375ex; height: 8.547ex;" id="img_images_704.svg"></span>
and the class of all such numbers as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_45"> for a given <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_58"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_36"> we shall call <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^{\beta }(\alpha)\)" src="images/473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_473.svg_1">, so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC}^{\beta }(\alpha ) = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta }). \]" src="images/705.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 21.367ex; height: 2.755ex;" id="img_images_705.svg"></span></p>

<p>The notations here introduced for giving typical definiteness to
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_5">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_19">" are those defined in *65 for any
typically ambiguous relation.</p>

<p>By *63·01·02 we have, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_59"> is a typically ambiguous symbol,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash .\alpha _{x} = \alpha \cap tʻx,\\ &amp;\vdash .\alpha (x) = \alpha \cap tʻ\iota ʻx. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/706.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 20.754ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_706.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\alpha (x) = \alpha _{\iota ʻx}\)" src="images/707.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.72ex; width: 13.985ex; height: 2.417ex;" id="img_images_707.svg">. If we apply the
definitions to 1, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{x}\)" src="images/708.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.234ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_708.svg">" is meaningless unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_12"> is a class;
we therefore write a Greek letter in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_13">, and we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .1_{\beta } = 1\cap tʻ\beta  = 1\cap (\iota ʻ\beta \cup -\iota ʻ\beta ). \]" src="images/709.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 35.187ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_709.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \beta\)" src="images/710.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.341ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_710.svg">, we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx = \beta .\lor.\iota ʻx\neq\beta\)" src="images/711.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 19.021ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_711.svg">. Hence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :x\in \beta .\supset .\iota ʻx\in 1_{\beta }.\\ \text{Similarly}\qquad &amp;\vdash :x{\sim}\in \beta .\supset .\iota ʻx\in 1_{\beta }.\\ \text{Thus}\qquad &amp;\vdash :x\in t_{0}ʻ\beta .\supset .\iota ʻx\in 1_{\beta }. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/712.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.633ex; width: 38.011ex; height: 8.397ex;" id="img_images_712.svg"></span></p>

<p>The converse implication also holds, so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :x\in t_{0}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\iota ʻx\in 1_{\beta }. \]" src="images/713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 23.986ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_713.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{\beta}\)" src="images/714.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 2.224ex; height: 2.157ex;" id="img_images_714.svg"> consists of all unit classes whose sole members
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_14"> either are or are not members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_37">, <i>i.e.</i> for which
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \beta\)" src="images/710.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.341ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_710.svg_1">" is significant.</p>

<p>In "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in t_{0}ʻ\beta .\supset .\iota ʻx\in 1_{\beta }\)" src="images/715.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 20.718ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_715.svg">," the
hypothesis renders explicit the condition of significance; thus
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\in 1_{\beta }\)" src="images/716.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.443ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_716.svg">" is always true when significant, and
always significant when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in t_{0}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/717.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.503ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_717.svg">. On the interpretation of
negative statements concerning types, see the note at the end of this
number.</p>

<p>It should be noted that all the constant relations introduced in this
work are typically ambiguous. Consider <i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}\)" src="images/719.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_719.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/720.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_720.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/721.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_721.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_722.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\)" src="images/723.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_723.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/724.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_724.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/725.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_725.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}\)" src="images/116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_116.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}\)" src="images/117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.294ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_117.svg_1">. These<span class="pagenum" id="Page_25">[Pg 25]</span> all have more or
less typical ambiguity, though all of them have what we will call
<i>relative</i> typical definiteness, <i>i.e.</i> when the type
of the relatum is given, that of the referent is given also. (In
regard to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/720.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_720.svg_1">, it is not true that, conversely, when the
type of the referent is given, that of the relatum is also given.)
But "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_6">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_20">" have not even relative
definiteness. When the type of the relatum is given, that of the
referent becomes no more definite than before; the only restrictions
are that the relatum for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_7">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_21">" must be
a class, that the referent for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_8">" must be a class, and
that the referent for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_22">" must be a class of classes. When
a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_15"> has relative definiteness, it is enough to fix the
type of the relatum; and if further <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/726.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_726.svg">,
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_16"> leads to a descriptive function, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/727.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_727.svg">" has complete
typical definiteness as soon as the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_2"> is given. Now
the constant relations hitherto introduced, with the exception of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_9">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\text{V}}\)" src="images/728.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 2.33ex;" id="img_images_728.svg">," have all been one-many
relations, and have been used almost exclusively in the form of
descriptive functions. Hence no special notation has been required to
give typical definiteness, since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/727.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_727.svg_1">" in these circumstances,
has typical definiteness as soon as <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_3"> is assigned. But with the
consideration of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_10">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_23">," which do not
have even relative definiteness, an explicit means of giving typical
definiteness becomes necessary. It should be observed, however, that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\delta\)" src="images/729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.063ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_729.svg">" has typical definiteness, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_4"> is
known, as soon as the <i>domain</i> of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_24">" has typical
definiteness, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_5"> must belong to the converse domain.
It is for the sake of this and similar cases that we introduced the
two definitions in *65, which only give typical definiteness to the
<i>domain</i>.</p>

<p>In virtue of the definitions in *65, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_17"> is a typically ambiguous
relation, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_15"> is a referent, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_18"> becomes <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{x}\)" src="images/730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.82ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_730.svg">; if,
further, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_4"> is a relatum, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_19"> becomes <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{(x,y)}\)" src="images/731.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 5.293ex; height: 2.345ex;" id="img_images_731.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_16"> is a
referent for <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_20">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists y).x\in \overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/732.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.376ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_732.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\in \text{D}ʻ\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/733.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.752ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_733.svg">. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_734.svg"> has a member of the type next above
that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_17">, <i>i.e.</i> of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg_3">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash .\text{sg}ʻ(R_{x}) = (\overrightarrow{R})(x)\\ \text{and}\qquad &amp;\vdash .\text{sg}ʻ{R_{(x,y)}} = (\overrightarrow{R})(x_{y}) \end{aligned} \]" src="images/735.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.647ex; width: 30.383ex; height: 8.424ex;" id="img_images_735.svg"></span>
as was proved in *65. Hence in particular
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\text{sg}ʻ{\text{ sm }_{(\alpha ,\beta )}} = \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta }). \]" src="images/736.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 24.131ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_736.svg"></span></p>

<p>It is chiefly for this reason that it is worth while to introduce the
definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x_{y})\)" src="images/737.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 5.743ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_737.svg">.</p>

<p>We have, in virtue of the above, as will be proved in <a href="#_102_46" class="pginternal">*102·46</a>,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash : \gamma \in tʻ\alpha .\delta \in tʻ\beta .\gamma\,\text{ sm }\,\delta . \equiv  .\gamma \in \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\delta . \]" src="images/738.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 44.15ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_738.svg"></span></p>

<p>With regard to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_4">," which is to be interpreted by
*65·04, some caution is necessary. This will mean <i>some one</i> of
those typically different relations called "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_25">" which have
their domains composed of terms of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_60">. But
it will not mean the logical sum of all such relations, because these
relations are of different types according as their converse<span class="pagenum" id="Page_26">[Pg 26]</span> domains
differ in type, and therefore their logical sum is meaningless. Thus
for example if the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_38"> is lower than or equal to that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_61">, we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\exists !\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\beta , \]" src="images/739.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.452ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_739.svg"></span>
whence, if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_5">" has its converse domain composed of
terms of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_39">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\Lambda {\sim}\in  \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha ). \]" src="images/740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.109ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_740.svg"></span>
But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_40"> is of higher type than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_62">, we shall find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\Lambda  \in  \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha). \]" src="images/741.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.349ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_741.svg"></span>
Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_6">" is indeterminate in a way that makes a
practical difference.</p>

<p>Exactly similar remarks apply to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_8">. We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\text{NC}(\alpha ) = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha ); \]" src="images/742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.568ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_742.svg"></span>
thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_9">" shares the ambiguity of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_7">." The question whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \in\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.875ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_743.svg">
depends upon the decision of this ambiguity. The
difficulty is that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_10">" stands for the domain of
any one determination of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_26">" which has its domain composed
of objects of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_744.svg">; but it is the domain
of <i>only one</i> such determination of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_27">," because
different determinations are of different types, and therefore cannot
be taken together, even when their domains are all of the same type.
In consequence of this ambiguity, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_11">" is a symbol
which is as a rule better avoided, and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha)\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.91ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg_8">" is
not often useful except as a descriptive function, in which case the
relatum supplies the requisite typical definiteness.</p>

<p>The peculiarity of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_12">" is that it is
<i>typically</i> definite, and yet is capable of different meanings:
it is not <i>wholly</i> definite, being defined as the domain of a
relation whose converse domain is typically ambiguous. It results
that we cannot profitably make "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_10">" half-definite, as
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg_13">" does, but must make it completely definite,
as we do by taking <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\beta})\)" src="images/745.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 10.089ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_745.svg">. For this
we adopt the notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta (\alpha)\)" src="images/746.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_746.svg">. We cannot adopt
the notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha_{\beta})\)" src="images/747.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_747.svg">, because that would
conflict with *65·11, nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha)_{\beta}\)" src="images/748.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_748.svg">, because that
would conflict with *65·01, nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}_{\beta}(\alpha)\)" src="images/749.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_749.svg">, for
the same reason. But <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta(\alpha)\)" src="images/750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_750.svg"> has no previously
defined meaning. We may if we like regard "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta\)" src="images/751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.424ex; height: 2.153ex;" id="img_images_751.svg">" as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(\text{Nc}\upharpoonright tʻ\beta)\)" src="images/752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.203ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_752.svg">. Then the required
meaning of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta(\alpha)\)" src="images/750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_750.svg_1">" would result from *65·04. But
as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta\)" src="images/751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.424ex; height: 2.153ex;" id="img_images_751.svg_1">" so defined is not required, it is simpler to
regard "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta(\alpha)\)" src="images/750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_750.svg_2">" as a single symbol. We therefore
put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta (\alpha ) = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta }) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.421ex; height: 2.755ex;" id="img_images_753.svg"></p>

<p>The present number begins with various propositions (<a href="#_102_2" class="pginternal">*102·2</a>—<a href="#_102_27" class="pginternal">·27</a>)
on a typically definite relation of similarity, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }_{(\alpha,\beta)}\)" src="images/754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 7.714ex; height: 1.813ex;" id="img_images_754.svg">. We then have a set of propositions
(<a href="#_102_3" class="pginternal">*102·3</a>-<a href="#_102" class="pginternal">·46</a>) on "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\alpha_{\beta})ʻ\delta\)" src="images/755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.365ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_755.svg">." This is only
significant if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_41"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_6"> are of the same type; it then
denotes the class of those classes which are similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_7"> and
of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_63">. We then have a set of propositions
(<a href="#_102_5" class="pginternal">*102·5</a>-<a href="#_102_64" class="pginternal">·64</a>) on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta(\alpha)\)" src="images/750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_750.svg_3">, <i>i.e.</i> on cardinals
consisting of classes of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_64"> which are similar
to classes of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_42">. We next prove<span class="pagenum" id="Page_27">[Pg 27]</span> (<a href="#_102_71" class="pginternal">*102·71</a>—<a href="#_102_75" class="pginternal">·75</a>)
that no sub-class of \alpha is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.068ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_468.svg_2">, and
therefore (substituting <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_199.svg_2"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_65">) no class of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_66"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_3">, and therefore</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102*74.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \Lambda  \in  \text{NC}^{tʻ\alpha }(\alpha)\)" src="images/756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.012ex; height: 2.743ex;" id="img_images_756.svg"></p>

<p>This proves that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_8"> is a cardinal, which is a proposition
constantly required. The remaining propositions of <a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a> are concerned
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_10"> where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_46"> is a typically definite cardinal.</p>

<p>The most useful propositions in this number (apart from <a href="#_102_74" class="pginternal">*102·74</a>) are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\gamma\,\text{ sm }_{(\alpha,\beta)}\delta . \equiv  .\gamma  \in  \text{Nc}(\alpha_{\beta})ʻ\delta\)" src="images/757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 30.096ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_757.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·46.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\gamma  \in  \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\delta .\equiv .\delta  \in  \text{Nc}(\beta _{\alpha })ʻ\gamma     . \equiv  .\gamma\,\text{ sm }\,\delta .\gamma  \in  tʻ\alpha .\delta  \in  tʻ\beta \)" src="images/758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 60.604ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_758.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu  \in  \text{NC}^\beta (\alpha ). \equiv  .(\exists \delta ).\mu  = \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\delta \)" src="images/759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 36.949ex; height: 2.755ex;" id="img_images_759.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\beta  = \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\beta      = \hat{\gamma} (\gamma\,\text{ sm }\,\beta .\gamma  \in  tʻ\alpha ) = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta \cap tʻ\alpha \)" src="images/760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 59.887ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_760.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·72.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\beta \subset \alpha .\supset .{\sim}(\beta  \text{ sm } \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_761.svg"></p>

<p>This is used in proving <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC}.\supset .2^\mu &gt;\mu\)" src="images/762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 18.149ex; height: 2.085ex;" id="img_images_762.svg">,
which is the proposition from which Cantor deduced that there is
no greatest cardinal. (If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.888ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_570.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^\mu =\text{Nc}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.427ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_763.svg">,
and thus there is a rise of type.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·84.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :(\exists \gamma ).\gamma  \in  tʻ\alpha .\gamma  \text{ sm } \alpha .\delta  \text{ sm } \gamma . \equiv  .\delta  \text{ sm } \alpha\)" src="images/764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.377ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_764.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·85.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu  \cap  tʻ\beta  = \text{ sm }_{\beta }ʻʻ\mu \)" src="images/765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 28.441ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_765.svg"></p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*102·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta (\alpha ) = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta }) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.421ex; height: 2.755ex;" id="img_images_753.svg_1"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*102·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :R \in  1\rightarrow 1.\supset .R_{(x,y)} \in  1(x)\rightarrow 1(y)\)" src="images/766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 36.693ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_766.svg"></p>

<p>Here, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_21"> is a real variable, the conditions of significance
require <img alt="" data-tex="\(R = R_{(x,y)}\)" src="images/767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 10.028ex; height: 2.345ex;" id="img_images_767.svg">. But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_22"> is a typically ambiguous
constant, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/724.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_724.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}\)" src="images/719.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_719.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{(x,y)}\)" src="images/731.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 5.293ex; height: 2.345ex;" id="img_images_731.svg_1"> is a typically definite constant. It is chiefly for such
cases that propositions such as the above are useful.</p>

may hold only for <i>some</i> of the possible
determinations of the ambiguity of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_28">."</p>

<p>In using propositions, such as those of <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>, in which we have a
typically ambiguous "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_29">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_11">," any significant
typical definiteness may be added, since, when a typically ambiguous
proposition is asserted, that includes the assertion of every possible
proposition resulting from determining the ambiguity.</p>

<p>The above proposition shows that, if every class of the same type as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_43"> is similar to some class of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_68">,
then, given a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_9"> of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_69">, there
is a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_9">, of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_44">, such that the
classes similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_10"> and of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_70"> are
the same as the classes similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_10"> and of the same type
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_71">; and conversely, given any class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_11">, of the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_45">, and similar to some class of the same type
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_72">, then there is a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_11">, of the same type
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_73">, such that the classes similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_12"> and of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_74"> are the same as the classes similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_12"> and of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_75">. We may express this by
saying that, if the cardinals which go from the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_76">
to the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_46"> are never null, then those that go from the
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_47"> to the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_77">, with the exception of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_9"> (if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_10"> is one of them), are the same as those
that begin and end within the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_78">. The latter are
what we call "homogeneous" cardinals. Thus our proposition is a step
towards reducing the general study of cardinals to that of homogeneous
cardinals.</p>

<p>The following propositions are part of Cantor's proof that there
is no greatest cardinal. They are inserted here in order to enable
us to prove that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_11"> is a cardinal, namely what we call
a "descending" cardinal, <i>i.e.</i> one whose corresponding
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_9">" goes from a higher to a lower type.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_102_71">*102·71</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : R \in  \text{Cls} \rightarrow  1 . \text{D}ʻR\subset \alpha  . \text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  . \supset  . \exists ! \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  - \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/825.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 56.65ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_825.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*20·33.*4·73 . \supset \\ \vdash  \colon\colon  \text{Hp} . \varpi  = &amp;\hat{x}  (x \in  \text{D}ʻR . x {\sim}\in  \breve{R}ʻx) . \supset \colon\ldotp \\ x \in  \text{D}ʻR . &amp;\supset _{x} : x \in  \varpi  . \equiv  . x {\sim} \in  \breve{R}ʻx:\\ [*5·18] &amp;\supset _{x} : {\sim}\{x \in  \varpi  . \equiv  . x \in  \breve{R}ʻx\}:\\ [*20·43.\text{Transp}.*71·164] &amp;\supset _{x} : \varpi  \neq  \breve{R}ʻx\colon\ldotp \\ [*71·411.\text{Transp}] &amp;\supset  \colon\ldotp  \varpi  {\sim}\in  \text{ᗡ}ʻR &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*20·33.*3·26 . \supset \vdash  : \text{Hp}(1) . &amp;\supset  . \varpi  \subset  \text{D}ʻR.\\ [\text{Hp}] &amp;\supset  . \varpi  \subset  \alpha  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).*13·191 . \supset \\ \vdash  : \text{Hp} . \supset  . \hat{x} (x \in  \text{D}ʻR . x {\sim}\in  \breve{R}ʻx) \in  \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  - \text{ᗡ}ʻR : \supset \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/826.svg" style="vertical-align: -16.612ex; width: 97.21ex; height: 34.355ex;" id="img_images_826.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_102_72">*102·72</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \beta \subset \alpha  . \supset  .{\sim}(\beta  \text{ sm } \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha )\)" src="images/827.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_827.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*102·71. \supset \vdash  \colon\ldotp  \text{Hp} . &amp;\supset  : R \in  1 \rightarrow  1 . \text{D}ʻR = \beta  . \text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset  \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  . \supset _{R}     . \exists ! \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  - \text{ᗡ}ʻR:\\ [*24·55.*22·41] &amp;\supset  : R \in  1 \rightarrow  1 . \text{D}ʻR = \beta  . \supset _{R}. \text{ᗡ}ʻR \neq  \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha :\\ [*10·51] &amp;\supset  : {\sim}(\exists R) . <p class="nind"><b><a id="_102_73">*102·73</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻtʻ\alpha  = \Lambda\)" src="images/829.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.865ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_829.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*102·6 . \supset \vdash  . \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻtʻ\alpha  &amp;= \hat{\gamma}  (\gamma  \text{ sm } tʻ\alpha  . \gamma  \in  tʻ\alpha )\\ [*63·65] &amp;= \hat{\gamma}  (\gamma  \text{ sm } \text{Cl}ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha  . \gamma  \subset  t_{0}ʻ\alpha )\\ [*102·72] &amp;= \Lambda  . \supset \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/830.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.869ex; width: 56.589ex; height: 8.869ex;" id="img_images_830.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition proves that no class of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_79">
is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_4">. Now <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_5"> is the greatest class
of its type; thus there are classes of the type next above that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_80"> which are too great to be similar to any class of the type
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_81">. Thus (as will be explicitly proved later) the maximum
cardinal in one type is less than that in the next higher type.
Cantor's proposition that there is no maximum cardinal only holds when
we are allowed to rise to continually higher types: in each type, there
is a maximum for that type, namely the number of members of the type.</p>
