(1) . (2) . (3) . \supset \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/855.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.586ex; width: 90.292ex; height: 18.303ex;" id="img_images_855.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Note on negative statements concerning types</i>. Statements
such as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x {\sim} \in tʻy\)" src="images/856.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.103ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_856.svg">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x {\sim} \in t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/857.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.43ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_857.svg">"
are always false when they are significant. Hence when an object
belongs to one type, there is no significant way of expressing what
we mean when we say that it does not belong to some other type. The
reason is that, when, for example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\( t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/858.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_858.svg">
are said to be different, the statement is only significant if
interpreted as applying to the symbols, <i>i.e.</i> as meaning to
deny that the two symbols denote the same class. We cannot assert
that they denote <i>different</i> classes, since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha \neq t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/859.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 11.249ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_859.svg">"
is not significant, but we can deny that they denote
the same class. Owing to this peculiarity, propositions dealing
with types acquire their importance largely from the fact that they
can be interpreted as dealing with the symbols rather than directly
with the objects denoted by the symbols. Another reason for the
importance of typically definite propositions is that, when they
are implications of which the hypothesis can be asserted, they can
be used for <i>inference</i>, <i>i.e.</i> for the assertion of the
conclusion. Where typically ambiguous symbols occur in implications,
on the contrary, the conditions of significance may be different
for the hypothesis and the conclusion, so that fallacies may arise
from the use of such implications in inference. <i>E.g.</i> it is
a fallacy to infer "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/860.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.782ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_860.svg">" from
the (true) propositions "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\supset . \exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/861.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.526ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_861.svg">"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/862.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_862.svg">." (The truth of the first
of these two requires that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_47">" should receive the
same typical determination in both its occurrences.) For these two
reasons hypothetical concerning types are often useful, in spite of the
fact that their hypotheses are always true when they are significant.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_36">[Pg 36]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_103">
*103. HOMOGENEOUS CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *103.</p>

<p>In this number, we shall consider cardinals generated by a
homogeneous relation of similarity. A "homogeneous" cardinal is
to mean all the classes similar to some class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_82"> and
of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_83">. The "homogeneous cardinal of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_84">" will be defined as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/863.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.644ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_863.svg">;
we shall denote it by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg">."
Then the class of homogeneous cardinals is the class of
all such cardinals as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_1">,"
<i>i.e.</i> it is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}\)" src="images/865.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.775ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_865.svg">; this
we shall denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_6">." The symbol
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_2">" is typically definite as soon
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_85"> is assigned; "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_7">," on the
contrary, is typically ambiguous: it must be a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{3}\)" src="images/866.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.142ex; height: 2.089ex;" id="img_images_866.svg">, but
otherwise its type may vary indefinitely. Homogeneous cardinals have,
however, many properties which do not require that the ambiguity of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_8">" should be determined, and few which do
require this. They are important also as being the simplest kind of
cardinals, and as being a kind to which other kinds can usually be
reduced.</p>

<p>The chief advantage of homogeneous cardinals is that they are never
null (<a href="#_103_13" class="pginternal">*103·13</a><a href="#_103_22" class="pginternal">·22</a>). This enables us to avoid by their means the explicit
exclusion of exceptional cases; thus throughout Section B we shall use
homogeneous cardinals in defining the arithmetical operations: the
arithmetical sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_48"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_22">, for
example, will be defined by means of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_3">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_867.svg">, in order to exclude such a
determination of the typical ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_49"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_23"> as would make either of them null. It is true that
not only homogeneous cardinals, but also ascending cardinals (cf.
<a href="#_104" class="pginternal">*104</a>), are never null. But homogeneous cardinals are much the simplest
kind of cardinals that are never null, and are therefore the most
convenient.</p>

<p>The fact that no homogeneous cardinal is null is derived from</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \alpha  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/868.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_868.svg"></p>

<p>Other important propositions in this number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \mu  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C}     . \equiv  . (\exists  \alpha ) . \mu  = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \cap  tʻ\alpha  . \equiv  . (\exists \alpha ) . \mu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/869.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.477ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_869.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  \colon\ldotp  \mu  \in  \text{NC} . \supset  : \alpha  \in  \mu  . \equiv  . \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  = \mu\)" src="images/870.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 35.105ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_870.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition is used constantly.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_37">[Pg 37]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·27.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\mu \in \text{NC}.\alpha \in \mu \)" src="images/871.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 31.333ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_871.svg"></p>

<p>Thus to say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_47"> is the homogeneous cardinal of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_86"> is
equivalent to saying that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_48"> is a cardinal of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_87"> is
a member.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·301.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{NC}^\alpha (\alpha )=\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha )\)" src="images/872.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.682ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_872.svg"></p>

write (cf. <a href="#_103_33" class="pginternal">*103·33</a>, below)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\text{NC}(\alpha )-\iota ʻ\Lambda \subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha ). \]" src="images/911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.593ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_911.svg"></span></p>

<p>For the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_49"> is wholly arbitrary, so that any possible
determination of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}(\alpha )\)" src="images/904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_904.svg_1"> makes the above proposition
true. We may proceed a step further, and write (<a href="#_103_34" class="pginternal">*103·34</a>, below)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .\text{NC}-\iota ʻ\Lambda \subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}. \]" src="images/912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.177ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_912.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_40">[Pg 40]</span></p>

<p>But although we also have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\subset \text{NC}-\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/913.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.16ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_913.svg">,
provided the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_12">" on the right is suitably determined,
we do not have this always. For example, if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_13">"
is determined as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\alpha (tʻ\alpha )\)" src="images/914.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.924ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_914.svg">, and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_9">" as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}(tʻ\alpha )\)" src="images/915.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.7ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_915.svg">, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻtʻ\alpha \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}-\text{NC}\)" src="images/916.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.849ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_916.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_103_33">*103·33</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{NC}(\alpha ) - \iota ʻ\Lambda  \subset  \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha )\)" src="images/917.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.964ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_917.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *4·2 . (*65·02) . \supset \\ \vdash  \colon\ldotp  \mu  \in  \text{NC}(\alpha ) - \iota ʻ\Lambda  . \equiv  : \mu  \in  \text{NC} . \mu  \in  t^{2}ʻ\alpha  . \exists  ! \mu  :\\ [*100·4 . *63·5] \equiv  : (\exists \beta ) . \mu  = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  : \mu  \subset  tʻ\alpha  . \exists  ! \mu  :\\ [*65·13] \equiv  : (\exists \beta ) . \mu  = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  \cap  tʻ\alpha  : \exists  ! \mu  :\\ [*102·6] \equiv  : (\exists \beta ) . \mu  = \text{Nc}(\alpha _{\beta })ʻ\beta  . \exists  ! \mu  :\\ [*103·31] \supset  : \mu  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha ) \colon\ldotp  \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/918.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.621ex; width: 49.789ex; height: 18.374ex;" id="img_images_918.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_103_34">*103·34</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{NC} - \iota ʻ\Lambda  \subset  \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/919.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.548ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_919.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *100·31·321 . *63·5 . \supset \\ \vdash  : \mu  = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  . \beta  \in  \mu  . \supset  . \mu  = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  \cap  tʻ\beta \\ [(*103·01)] = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  .\\ [*103·2] \supset  . \mu  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash  . (1) . *100·4 . *11·11·35·54 . \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/920.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 49.317ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_920.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus every cardinal except <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_12"> is a homogeneous cardinal
in the appropriate type. Note that although of course every
homogeneous cardinal is a cardinal, yet "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\subset \text{NC}\)" src="images/921.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 10.665ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_921.svg">"
must not be asserted, because it is possible
to determine the ambiguity of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_14">" in such a way as to
make this false. Hence we do not get <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC} - \iota ʻ\Lambda =\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.16ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_922.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \Lambda  {\sim} \in  \text{NC}^\alpha (\beta ) . \supset  . \text{NC}^\beta (\alpha ) - \iota ʻ\Lambda  = \text{N}_{0}\text{C}(\alpha     ) \quad[*102·55 . *103·301]\)" src="images/923.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 67.261ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_923.svg"></p>

<p>The hypothesis of this proposition is satisfied, as will appear later,
if the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_50"> is in what we may call the direct ascent from
that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_90">, <i>i.e.</i> if it can be reached from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_91"> by
a finite number of steps each of which takes us from a type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_114.svg_20">
to either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\tau\)" src="images/297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.79ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_297.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}ʻ(\tau \uparrow \tau)\)" src="images/924.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.139ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_924.svg">.
Thus in such a case the cardinals (other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_13">) which go
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\beta\)" src="images/925.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.455ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_925.svg"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_7"> are the same as those which begin
and end within <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_8">. It will also appear that in such a case
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_14"> always is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}^\beta (\alpha )\)" src="images/926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.632ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_926.svg">.
<i>If</i> two cardinals which are not equal must always be one greater
and the other less, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \in \text{NC}^\beta (\alpha )\)" src="images/927.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.968ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_927.svg"> is
the condition for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻtʻ\beta \gt \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻtʻ\alpha\)" src="images/928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.24ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_928.svg">. In that case, we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \in \text{NC}^\beta (\alpha ). \supset . \Lambda {\sim} \in \text{NC}^\alpha(\beta )\)" src="images/929.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.419ex; height: 2.671ex;" id="img_images_929.svg">. But
there is no known proof that of two different cardinals one must be the
greater, except by assuming the multiplicative axiom and proving thence
(by Zermelo's theorem) that every class can be well-ordered (cf. *258).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*103·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/930.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.029ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_930.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *37·1 . \supset \\ \vdash  : \delta  \in  \text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  . &amp;\equiv  . (\exists \gamma ) . \gamma  \text{ sm } \alpha  . \gamma  \in  tʻ\alpha  . \delta  \text{ sm } \gamma  .\\ [*102·84] &amp;\equiv  . \delta  \text{ sm } \alpha  : \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/931.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 53.419ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_931.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *103·4 . \supset  \vdash  .\\ \text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \cap  tʻ\beta  &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \cap  tʻ\beta \\ [*102·6] &amp;= \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\alpha  . \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/933.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 42.256ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_933.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·321.\supset \vdash :\beta  \text{ sm } \alpha .&amp;\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\\ [*22·481] &amp;\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻ\beta  = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta \cap tʻ\beta .\\ [*102·6.(*103·01)] &amp;\supset .\text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\alpha  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*103·12.\supset \vdash :\text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\alpha  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta .&amp;\supset .\beta \in \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\alpha .\\ [*100·31] &amp;\supset .\beta  \text{ sm } \alpha  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/935.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 76.126ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_935.svg"></span></p>

<p>0 and 1 are the only cardinals of which the above property can be
proved universally with our assumptions. If (as is possible so far as
our assumptions go) the lowest type is a unit class, we shall have <i>in
that type</i> (though in no other) <img alt="" data-tex="\(2 = \Lambda\)" src="images/944.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.718ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_944.svg">, so that in that
type <img alt="" data-tex="\(2 {\sim} \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/945.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 9.975ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_945.svg">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_42">[Pg 42]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_104">
*104. ASCENDING CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *104.</p>

<p>In this number we have to consider cardinals derived from a relation
of similarity which goes from the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_92"> to that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_448.svg_9">, or to that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{2}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_491.svg_1">. The propositions to
be proved can be extended, by a mere repetition of the proofs, to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{3}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.338ex;" id="img_images_492.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{4}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/946.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.357ex;" id="img_images_946.svg">, etc. This extension must, however,
be made afresh in each instance; we cannot prove that it can be made
generally, because mathematical induction cannot be applied to the
series
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ t_{0}ʻ\alpha,\quad tʻ\alpha,\quad t^{2}ʻ\alpha,\quad t^{3}ʻ\alpha ,\ldotp\ldots \]" src="images/947.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.921ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_947.svg"></span></p>

<p>Ascending cardinals, though less important than homogeneous
cardinals, yet have considerable importance in arithmetic, because
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \times \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/948.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.612ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_948.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha)^{\text{Nc}ʻ\beta }\)" src="images/949.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.23ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_949.svg">
are defined as the cardinals of classes of higher types than those of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_93"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_51">, and the same applies to the product of the
cardinals of members of a class of classes. In these cases, however, we
also need cardinals of relational types, which will be dealt with in
<a href="#_106" class="pginternal">*106</a>.</p>

<p>We have to deal, in this number, with three different sets of notions,
namely</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*104·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻtʻ\alpha   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/950.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.013ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_950.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*104·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{C}=\text{D}ʻ\text{N}^{1}\text{c} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/951.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.793ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_951.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*104·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}=\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap tʻ\mu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/952.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.336ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_952.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
with similar definitions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{2}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/953.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_953.svg">, etc.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/954.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_954.svg"> consists of all classes
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_94"> but of the next higher type, <i>i.e.</i> it
is the cardinal number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_95"> in the type next above that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_5">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{C}\)" src="images/520.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 2.041ex;" id="img_images_520.svg_1"> is the class
of all such cardinals as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/954.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_954.svg_1">, and is a
typically ambiguous symbol, though <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/954.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_954.svg_2">
is typically definite when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_96"> is given; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg_2"> (if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_49"> is a cardinal which is not null) is the "same" cardinal in the
next higher type, so that, <i>e.g.</i>, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_50"> is 1 determined
as consisting of unit classes of <i>individuals</i>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg_3">
will be 1 determined as consisting of unit classes of classes of
individuals. (When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_51"> is not an existent cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg_4">
is unimportant.)</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu ^{(1)} = \text{Nc}(tʻ\alpha )ʻt^{2}ʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/992.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.294ex; height: 2.7ex;" id="img_images_992.svg"></span>

whose cardinal in one type is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_55">, but whose cardinal in the next

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the proof that, given
any two cardinals <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_56"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_27">, of the same type, we can find
two mutually exclusive classes one of which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_57"> terms while
the other has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_28"> terms. The proof requires that we should raise
the types of both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_58"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_29"> one degree above<span class="pagenum" id="Page_49">[Pg 49]</span> that in which
they were originally given, <i>i.e.</i> that we should turn <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_59">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_30"> into <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/1042.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.549ex; height: 2.021ex;" id="img_images_1042.svg">. Thus, for example,
suppose the total number of individuals in the universe were finite (a
supposition which is consistent with our primitive propositions), and
suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_60"> were this number. Then unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu =0\)" src="images/1043.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.347ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_1043.svg">, a class of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_31"> individuals will be an existent sub-class of the only class
which consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_61"> individuals, and therefore we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \in \mu .\beta \in \nu .\supset _{\alpha ,\beta }.\exists !\alpha \cap \beta . \]" src="images/1044.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.923ex; height: 2.27ex;" id="img_images_1044.svg"></span></p>

<p>But if we consider classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_62"> classes and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_32"> classes, we
shall always be able to find a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_13"> and a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_13"> such that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \gamma \in \mu ^{(1)}.\delta \in \nu^{(1)}.\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda . \]" src="images/1045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 26.886ex; height: 2.623ex;" id="img_images_1045.svg"></span></p>

<p>The existence of such a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_14"> is important in
connection with the arithmetical operations, and is therefore proved
here.</p>

<p>This proposition proves the desired conclusions provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\alpha\)" src="images/1050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.335ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_1050.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_199.svg_3"> consists of at least three terms. The
following propositions deal with the cases in which this hypothesis is
not verified.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*104·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :tʻ\alpha =tʻ\beta .\supset .(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\delta \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda \)" src="images/1058.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.703ex; height: 2.559ex;" id="img_images_1058.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*54·56.\supset \\ \vdash :\text{Hp}.\alpha {\sim}\in 0\cup 1\cup 2.&amp;\supset .(\exists x,y,z).x,y,z \in \alpha .x\neq y.x\neq z.y\neq z.\\ [*104·41] &amp;\supset .(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\delta \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\beta .\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*104·42.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1059.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.465ex; width: 78.834ex; height: 12.061ex;" id="img_images_1059.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition gives the desired result. The following
propositions re-state this result in other forms.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*104·44.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}&amp;\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{N}^{1}\text{C}.tʻ\mu     =tʻ\nu .\supset .(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \in \mu .\delta \in \nu .\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda\\ &amp;[*104·13·43]\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1060.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.188ex; width: 57.567ex; height: 5.507ex;" id="img_images_1060.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_52">[Pg 52]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_105">
*105. DESCENDING CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *105.</p>

<p>In this number, we consider cardinals generated by a relation of
similarity which goes from a higher to a lower type, <i>i.e.</i> given
any class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_8">, we consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.362ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1063.svg">
in the type of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_9"> (which we shall call
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1064.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.35ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1064.svg">) or in some lower type. Thus
<i>e.g.</i> we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa =\iotaʻʻ\alpha .\supset .\alpha \in \text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\kappa , \]" src="images/1065.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.249ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1065.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1064.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.35ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1064.svg_1">" means "classes similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_10"> but of the next lower type." Similarly
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa =\iotaʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha .\supset .\alpha \in \text{N}_{2}\text{c}ʻ\kappa , \]" src="images/1066.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.765ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1066.svg"></span>
and so on. We shall have generally
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \beta \in \text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .&amp;\equiv \alpha \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\beta ,\\ \beta \in \text{N}_{2}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .&amp;\equiv \alpha \in \text{N}^{2}\text{c}ʻ\beta , \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1067.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.339ex; width: 25.357ex; height: 5.81ex;" id="img_images_1067.svg"></span>
and so on. The chief difference between ascending and descending
cardinals is that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_15"> is one of the latter, but not one of the
former. Otherwise the propositions of the present number are mostly
analogous to corresponding propositions of <a href="#_104" class="pginternal">*104</a>.</p>

<p>On the analogy of the definitions in *104, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}_{1}\text{C}=\text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{1}\text{c}  \quad\text{Df},\\ \mu _{(1)}=\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \cap t_{1}ʻ\mu  \quad\text{Df}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1068.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.153ex; width: 26.953ex; height: 5.438ex;" id="img_images_1068.svg"></span>
with similar definitions for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{2}\text{C}\)" src="images/1069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_1069.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu_(2)\)" src="images/1070.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 4.186ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_1070.svg">.</p>

<p>No proposition of the present number is ever referred to in the sequel,
and the reader who is not interested in the subject may therefore omit
it without detriment to what follows. The principal propositions proved
are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{N}_{0}\text{C}=\text{N}_{1}\text{C}-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/1071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.536ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1071.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·251.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{N}_{0}\text{C}=\text{N}_{2}\text{C}-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/1072.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.536ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1072.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻtʻ\alpha =\Lambda\)" src="images/1073.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.644ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1073.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_53">[Pg 53]</span></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{C}\)" src="images/1074.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_1074.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{2}\text{C}\)" src="images/1069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_1069.svg_1">, in any given
type, only differs from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.318ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_11"> in that type by the
addition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_16">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\supset .\mu _{(1)}=\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1075.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 30.396ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_1075.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·322.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\supset :\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha     =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1076.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 51.249ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1076.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\mu _{(1)}.\supset :\mu _{(1)}=\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha     .\equiv .\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1077.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 49.124ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_1077.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \in \text{NC}.\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\supset :\mu =\nu ^{(1)}.\equiv .\mu _{(1)}=\nu\)" src="images/1078.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 43.683ex; height: 2.821ex;" id="img_images_1078.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*105·38.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\{\mu _{(1)}\}_{(1)}=\mu _{(2)}\)" src="images/1079.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 17.093ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_1079.svg"></p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_105_01">*105·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{1}ʻ\alpha   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1080.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1080.svg"></p>

<p>We might write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap t_{0}ʻ\alpha    \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/1081.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.455ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1081.svg"></span>
which would be equivalent to the above. But we choose the above form
for the sake of uniformity. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/721.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_721.svg_1"> is any suffix, we put, provided
<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{s}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1082.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.56ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1082.svg"> has been defined,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}_{s}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{s}ʻ\alpha     \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/1083.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.53ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1083.svg"></span>
and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(i\)" src="images/1084.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.781ex; height: 1.52ex;" id="img_images_1084.svg"> is any index for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{i}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1085.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.362ex; height: 2.331ex;" id="img_images_1085.svg"> has been defined, we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}^{i}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt^{i}ʻ\alpha    \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1086.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.133ex; height: 2.444ex;" id="img_images_1086.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus for the sake of uniformity it is better, in the above definition
<a href="#_105_01" class="pginternal">*105·01</a>, to write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻt_{1}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.784ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1087.svg">" rather than "<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_199.svg_4">."</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_60">[Pg 60]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_106">
*106. CARDINALS OF RELATIONAL TYPES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *106.</p>

<p>In this number we have to consider the cardinals whose members are
classes of relations which have a given relation of type to some given
class. For example, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha \text{ sm }\alpha\)" src="images/1191.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.572ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1191.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.217ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1192.svg"> has a given relation of type to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_101">
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_18"> is given. Thus we want a notation for
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻ\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha \]" src="images/1193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.041ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1193.svg"></span>
and all the associated ideas. In this number, we shall deal only with
relations in which the referent and relatum have a relation, as to
type, which can be expressed by the notations of *63, <i>i.e.</i>
roughly speaking, when, for suitable values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_102">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/1194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1194.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg_1">, our relations are contained in
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ t^{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t^{n}ʻ\alpha\,\,\, \text{or}\,\,\, t_{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{n}ʻ\alpha\,\,\, \text{or}\,\,\, t^{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{n}ʻ\alpha\,\,\,     \text{or}\,\,\, t_{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t^{n}ʻ\alpha. \]" src="images/1195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 62.974ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1195.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{\mu \nu }ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 5.623ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_1196.svg"> has been defined, we shall put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{N}_{\mu \nu }\text{c}ʻ\alpha &amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \cap tʻt_{\mu \nu }ʻ\alpha  &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ \text{N}_{\mu \nu }\text{C}&amp;=\text{D}ʻ\text{N}_{\mu \nu }\text{c} &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ \xi _{\mu \nu }&amp;=\text{ sm }ʻʻ\xi \cap tʻt_{\mu \nu }ʻt_{1}ʻ\xi  &amp;\quad\text{Df}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1197.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.686ex; width: 40.991ex; height: 8.503ex;" id="img_images_1197.svg"></span>
with analogous definitions for <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{\mu \nu }ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.623ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1198.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^\mu _{\nu}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.775ex; height: 2.305ex;" id="img_images_1199.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(^\mu t_{\nu }ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.81ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1200.svg">.</p>

<p>Much the most important case is that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{00}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.41ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1201.svg">. For this
case we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·1.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}\vdash :\beta \in \text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\beta \in tʻt_{00}ʻ\alpha     .&amp;\equiv .\beta \text{ sm }\alpha .\beta \in tʻtʻ(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\alpha ).\\ &amp;\equiv  .\beta \text{ sm }\alpha .\beta \subset tʻ(\alpha \uparrow \alpha )\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1202.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 74ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1202.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.294ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1203.svg"> will be the number of a class of
relations whose fields are of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_103">, provided
this class of relations is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_104">. <i>E.g.</i> the
number of terms such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \alpha\)" src="images/1205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1205.svg">, will
be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.294ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1203.svg_1">.</p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\exists !\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/1206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.954ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1206.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·22.</b><img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\lambda \in \text{N}_{0}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\text{Cnv}ʻʻ\lambda \in ^{1}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha \)" src="images/1207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.594ex; width: 35.359ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_1207.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\beta \in \text{N}^{1}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\supset .\text{N}^{11}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 34.391ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_1208.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :t_{0}ʻ\alpha =t_{0}ʻ\beta .\supset .(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \in \text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\delta \in \text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda\)" src="images/1209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.278ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1209.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_61">[Pg 61]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·4·41·411.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\supset .\mu _{(00)}=\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\mu ^{(11)}=\text{N}^{11}\text{c}ʻ\alpha     .\mu _{(11)}=\text{N}_{11}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 63.424ex; height: 2.821ex;" id="img_images_1210.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻt_{00}ʻ\alpha  = \Lambda\)" src="images/1211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.652ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1211.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence it follows that</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·54.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻt_{00}ʻ\alpha  {\sim} \in \text{N}_{00}\text{C}\)" src="images/1212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.489ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1212.svg"></p>

<p>The propositions of this number, except <a href="#_106_21" class="pginternal">*106·21</a>, are never referred
to again (except in <a href="#_154_25" class="pginternal">*154·25</a><a href="#_154_251" class="pginternal">·251</a><a href="#_154_262" class="pginternal">·262</a>, which are themselves never
used again), but they have a somewhat greater importance than the
propositions of <a href="#_105" class="pginternal">*105</a>, owing to the fact that the arithmetical
operations are defined by means of classes of relations, <i>i.e.</i>
the sum of two cardinals (for instance) is defined as the cardinal
number of a certain class of relations (cf. <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>).</p>

<p>The proof requires, in addition to <a href="#_106_12" class="pginternal">*106·12</a>, its analogue for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(^{1}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1250.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.482ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_1250.svg">. Such analogues will be assumed as
required.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·221.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\lambda \in \text{N}_{0}^{2}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\text{Cnv}ʻʻ\lambda \in ^{2}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1251.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.594ex; width: 35.359ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_1251.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·222.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Lambda {\sim}\in ^{1}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}.^{1}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.^{1}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\in     \text{Cls ex}^{2}\,\text{excl} \quad[*106·22·212]\)" src="images/1252.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 64.602ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_1252.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*106·223.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Lambda {\sim}\in ^{2}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}.^{2}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.^{2}\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\in     \text{Cls ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/1253.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 47.631ex; height: 2.418ex;" id="img_images_1253.svg"></p>

<p>Other propositions of the same kind as the above may be proved by
observing that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/1194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1194.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg_2"> are indices for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{m}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.215ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1254.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1255.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.77ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1255.svg"> have been defined, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \gamma \subset t^{n}ʻ\alpha .\beta \in \text{N}^{m}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\supset .\downarrow \beta ʻʻ\gamma \in \text{N}^{m}\text{c}ʻ\alpha , \]" src="images/1256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 42.417ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1256.svg"></span>
of which the proof is direct and simple. Hence, since we always have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{N}^{m}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1257.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.986ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1257.svg">, we also always have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\exists !\text{N}^{m}\text{c}ʻ\alpha ,\\ \text{whence}\qquad \text{N}^{mm}\text{C}\subset \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.&amp;\text{N}^{mm}\text{C}\in \text{Cls ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1258.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.209ex; width: 46.818ex; height: 5.55ex;" id="img_images_1258.svg"></span>
We have in like manner
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !\text{N}_{0}^{m}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\exists !^{m}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha. \]" src="images/1259.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.594ex; width: 20.595ex; height: 2.291ex;" id="img_images_1259.svg"></span>
But we do not always have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !\text{N}_{mn}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \,\,\text{or}\,\, \exists !\text{N}_{n}^{m}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \,\,\text{or}\,\, \exists !^{m}\text{N}_{n}\text{c}ʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/1260.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.576ex; width: 36.754ex; height: 2.273ex;" id="img_images_1260.svg"></span></p>

<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_66">[Pg 66]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_B">SECTION B.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">ADDITION, MULTIPLICATION AND EXPONENTIATION.</span></h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of Section B.</i></p>

<p>In the present section, we have to consider the arithmetical operations
as applied to cardinals, as well as the relation of greater and less
between cardinals. Thus the topics to be dealt with in this section are
the first that can properly be said to belong to Arithmetic.</p>

<p>The treatment of addition, multiplication and exponentiation to be
given in what follows is guided by the desire to secure the greatest
possible generality. In the first place, everything to be said
generally about the arithmetical operations must apply equally to
finite and infinite classes or cardinals. In the second place, we
desire such definitions as shall allow the number of summands in a sum
or of factors in a product to be infinite. In the third place, we wish
to be able to add or multiply two numbers which are not necessarily
of the same type. In the fourth place, we wish our definitions to
be such that the sum of the cardinal numbers of two or more classes
shall depend only upon the cardinal numbers of those classes, and
shall be the same when the classes overlap as when they are mutually
exclusive; with similar conditions for the product. The desire to
obtain definitions fulfilling all these conditions leads to somewhat
more complicated definitions than would otherwise be required; but in
the outcome, the result is simpler than if we started with simpler
definitions, since we avoid vexatious exceptions.</p>

<p>The above observations will become clearer through their applications.
Let us begin with the case of arithmetical addition of two classes.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_105"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_52"> are mutually exclusive classes, the sum
of their cardinal numbers will be the cardinal number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/1294.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1294.svg">. But in order that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_106"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_53"> may be
mutually exclusive, they must have no common members, and this is
only significant when they are of the same type. Hence, given two
perfectly general classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_107"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_54">, we require to
find two classes which are mutually exclusive and are respectively
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_108"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_55">; if these two classes are called
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha'\)" src="images/1295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.076ex; height: 1.742ex;" id="img_images_1295.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta'\)" src="images/1296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.908ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_1296.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha' \cup \beta')\)" src="images/1297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.318ex; height: 2.283ex;" id="img_images_1297.svg">
will be the sum of the cardinal numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_109"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_56">. We
note that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \cap \alpha\)" src="images/59.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 5.533ex; height: 1.67ex;" id="img_images_59.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \cap \beta\)" src="images/60.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.365ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_60.svg_1"> indicate
respectively the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_17">'s of the same types as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_110"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_57">, and accordingly we take as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha'\)" src="images/1295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.076ex; height: 1.742ex;" id="img_images_1295.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta'\)" src="images/1296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.908ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_1296.svg_1"> the
two classes
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \downarrow (\Lambda \cap \beta )ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha\,\,\text{and}\,\,(\Lambda \cap \alpha )\downarrow ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\beta ; \]" src="images/1298.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.543ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1298.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_67">[Pg 67]</span>
these two classes are always of the same type, always mutually
exclusive, and always similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_111"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_58"> respectively.
Hence we define
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha +\beta =\downarrow (\Lambda \cap \beta )ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha \cup (\Lambda \cap \alpha )\downarrow ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\beta  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1299.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.466ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1299.svg"></span></p>

<p>The sum of the cardinal numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_112"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_59"> will
then be the cardinal number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg">; hence we may call
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_1"> the <i>arithmetical</i> class-sum of two classes, in
contradistinction to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/1301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1301.svg">, which is the <i>logical</i>
sum. It will be noted that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_2">, unlike <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/1302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1302.svg">, does not require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_113"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_60"> should be
of the same type. Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \alpha\)" src="images/1303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.662ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1303.svg"> is not identical with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_114">, but when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \Lambda\)" src="images/1304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.035ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_1304.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \alpha\)" src="images/1303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.662ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1303.svg_1"> is also
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_18">, though in a different type. Thus the law of tautology does
not hold of the arithmetical class-sum of two classes.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_63"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_33"> are two cardinals of assigned types, we denote
their arithmetical sum by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg">. (As many kinds
of arithmetical addition occur in our work, and as it is essential
to our purpose to distinguish them, we effect the distinction by
suffixes to the sign of addition. It is, of course, only in dealing
with principles that these different symbols are needed: we do not
wish to suggest that they should be adopted in ordinary mathematics.)
Now if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg_1"> is to have the properties which we
commonly associate with the sum of two cardinals, it must be typically
ambiguous, and must be the cardinal number of any class which can
be divided into two mutually exclusive parts having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_64"> terms
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_34"> terms respectively. Hence we are led to the following
definition:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta )\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.152ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1306.svg"></span></p>

<p>In this definition, various points should be noted. In the first
place, it does not require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_65"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_35"> should be of the
same type; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg_2"> is significant whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_66">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_36"> are classes of classes. Thus it is not necessary for
significance that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_67"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_37"> should be cardinals, though if
they are not both cardinals, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu = \Lambda\)" src="images/1307.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.814ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_1307.svg">. If
they are both cardinals, we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\alpha \in \mu .\beta \in \nu .\xi \text{ sm } (\alpha +\beta )\}. \]" src="images/1308.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.874ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1308.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus in this case <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \mu .\beta \in \nu .\supset .\alpha+\beta \in \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1309.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 30.089ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1309.svg">.</p>

<p>Hence if neither <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_68"> nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_38"> is null, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_115"> has
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_69"> terms and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_61"> has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_39"> terms, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_3"> is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg_3">. It easily follows that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta .\supset .\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta ). \]" src="images/1310.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.024ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1310.svg"></span></p>

<p>Hence when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_70"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_40"> are homogeneous cardinals (<i>i.e.</i>
when they are cardinals other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_19">), their sum is the
number of the arithmetical class-sum of any two classes having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_71">
terms and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_41"> terms respectively.</p>

<p>A few words are necessary to explain why, in the definition,
we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha . \nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 22.425ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1311.svg">
rather than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\nu = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1312.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 20.45ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1312.svg">.
The reason is this. Suppose either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_72">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_42">, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_73">, is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_20">. Then, by <a href="#_102_73" class="pginternal">*102·73</a>,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \text{Nc}(\zeta)ʻtʻ\zeta\)" src="images/1313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.506ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1313.svg">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\zeta\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.066ex; height: 2.054ex;" id="img_images_329.svg_1"> is of the appropriate
type. Hence if we had put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha , \beta ).\mu =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta )\} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/1314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.177ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1314.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_68">[Pg 68]</span>
where the ambiguities of type involved in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_50"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_24"> may be determined as we please, we should have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \nu &amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\supset .tʻ\zeta +\beta \in \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu ,\\ \textit{i.e.}\qquad \nu &amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\supset .tʻ\zeta +\beta \in \Lambda +_{\text{c}} \nu . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1315.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 38.191ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1315.svg"></span>
We should also have <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻ\zeta +\beta \in \Lambda +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 18.659ex; height: 2.158ex;" id="img_images_1316.svg">
and so on. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1317.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.433ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_1317.svg"> would not have a definite
value, <i>i.e.</i> it would not merely have typical ambiguity, which
it ought to have, but it would not have a definite value even when
its type was assigned. Thus such a definition would be unsuitable.
For the above reasons, we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha . \nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1318.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 22.425ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1318.svg"> in the definition, and obtain the
typical ambiguity which we desire by means of the typical ambiguity
of the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_11">" in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta)\)" src="images/1319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.153ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1319.svg">." It is
always essential to right symbolism that the values of typically
ambiguous symbols should be unique as soon as their type is assigned.
The scope of these definitions and of the corresponding definitions for
multiplication and exponentiation (<a href="#_113_04" class="pginternal">*113·04</a><a href="#_113_05" class="pginternal">·05</a>.<a href="#_116_03" class="pginternal">*116·03</a><a href="#_116_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>) is extended
by convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_18"> of the prefatory statement.</p>

<p>The above definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg"> is designed
for the case in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_74"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_43"> are typically
definite. But we must be able to speak of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma+_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\delta\)" src="images/1321.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.014ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1321.svg">,"
and this must be a definite cardinal, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\gamma +\delta)\)" src="images/1322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.818ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1322.svg">.
If we simply write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma , \text{Nc}ʻ\delta\)" src="images/1323.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.357ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1323.svg">
in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_75">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_44"> in the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_1">,
we find
