<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\delta =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\text{Nc}ʻ\delta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta )\}. \]" src="images/1324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.044ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1324.svg"></span>
But this will not always have a definite value when the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\delta\)" src="images/1325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.014ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1325.svg"> is assigned. To
take a simple case, write <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\zeta\)" src="images/1326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 3.24ex; height: 2.158ex;" id="img_images_1326.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_15"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻy\)" src="images/1327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.283ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1327.svg"> for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_15">. Then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻtʻy=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\text{Nc}ʻtʻy=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta )\}. \]" src="images/1328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 80.623ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1328.svg"></span>
whence we easily obtain
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻtʻy=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ).\text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\iota ʻy)\}. \]" src="images/1329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.631ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1329.svg"></span>
If we determine the ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta\)" src="images/1330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 7.299ex; height: 2.158ex;" id="img_images_1330.svg"> to be
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{1}\text{c}ʻtʻ\zeta\)" src="images/1331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 8.286ex; height: 2.158ex;" id="img_images_1331.svg">, we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻy=\Lambda \]" src="images/1332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 22.875ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1332.svg"></span>
in all types; but if we determine the ambiguity to be
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻtʻ\zeta\)" src="images/1333.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 8.286ex; height: 2.158ex;" id="img_images_1333.svg">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻy=\text{Nc}ʻ(tʻ\zeta +\iota ʻy), \]" src="images/1334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.026ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1334.svg"></span>
and this exists in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\zeta +\iota ʻy\)" src="images/1335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.272ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1335.svg">, if
not in lower types. Hence the value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta+_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻy\)" src="images/1336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 18.288ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1336.svg">
depends upon the determination of the ambiguity of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻtʻ\zeta\)" src="images/1330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 7.299ex; height: 2.158ex;" id="img_images_1330.svg_1">. It is obvious that we want our definition to
yield
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\delta =\text{Nc}ʻ(\gamma +\delta ) \]" src="images/1337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.849ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1337.svg"></span>
in all types; but in order to insure that this shall hold even when,
for some values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\zeta\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.066ex; height: 2.054ex;" id="img_images_329.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\gamma =\Lambda\)" src="images/1338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.7ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1338.svg">, we
must introduce two new definitions, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\mu &amp;=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\mu  \quad\text{Df},\\ \mu +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha &amp;=\mu +_{\text{c}}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \quad\text{Df},\\ \text{whence}\qquad \vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta &amp;=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     =\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta ). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1339.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 63.928ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_1339.svg"></span>
This definition is to be applied when "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_283.svg_4">" and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\delta\)" src="images/729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.063ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_729.svg_1">" occur without any<span class="pagenum" id="Page_69">[Pg 69]</span> determination of type. On the
other hand, if we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\zeta)ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/1340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.113ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1340.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\eta)ʻ\delta\)" src="images/1341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.948ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1341.svg">,
we apply the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_2">.
We shall find that whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/1342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.113ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1342.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\delta\)" src="images/1343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.948ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1343.svg"> both exist,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\gamma  +_{\text{c}} \text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\delta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\gamma  +_{\text{c}} \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\delta . \]" src="images/1344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.361ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1344.svg"></span>
Thus the above definition is only required in order to exclude values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\zeta\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.066ex; height: 2.054ex;" id="img_images_329.svg_3"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta\)" src="images/1345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.124ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_1345.svg"> for which either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/1342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.113ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1342.svg_1">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\delta\)" src="images/1343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.948ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1343.svg_1"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_21">.</p>

<p>The commutative and associative laws of arithmetical addition are easily
deduced from the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_1">. We shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \vdash .\alpha &amp;+\beta =\text{Cnv}ʻʻ(\beta +a),\\ \text{whence}\qquad \vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha &amp;+_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha , \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1346.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 47.371ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1346.svg"></span>
because each = <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta)\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.313ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_1">. A similar though slightly
longer proof shows that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \vdash .(\alpha +\beta )&amp;+\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha +(\beta +\gamma ),\\ \text{whence}\qquad \vdash .(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta )&amp;+_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta     +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1347.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 68.793ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1347.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_2"> enables us to proceed to the
sum of any finite number of classes, and allows any one class to recur
in the summation. But it does not enable us to define the sum of an
infinite number of classes. For this we need a new definition. Since
an infinite number of classes cannot be given by enumeration, but only
by intension, we shall have to take a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_11">, and
define the arithmetical sum of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_12">. Thus now the
classes which are the summands must all be of the same type (since
they are all members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_13">), and no one class can occur more
than once, since each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_14"> only counts once. (In order
to deal with repetition, we must advance to multiplication, which will
be explained shortly.) Thus in removing the limitation to a finite
number of summands, we introduce certain other limitations. This is the
reason which makes it worth while to introduce the above definition of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_3"> in addition to the definition now to be given.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_15"> is a class of classes, the sum of the cardinal numbers of
the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_16"> will evidently be obtained by constructing
a class of mutually exclusive classes whose members have a one-one
relation to the members of corresponding members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_17">. Suppose
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_116">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_62"> are two different members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_18">, and
suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_19"> is a member both of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_117"> and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_63">. Then we
wish to count <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_20"> twice over, once as a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_118"> and once
as a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_64">. The simplest way to do this is to form the
ordinal couples <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow \alpha\)" src="images/1348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.13ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1348.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow \beta\)" src="images/1349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.963ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1349.svg">, which
are not identical except when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_119"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_65"> are identical.
Thus if we take all such ordinal couples, <i>i.e.</i> if we take the
class
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{R} \{(\exists x).x\in \alpha .R=x\downarrow \alpha\}, \]" src="images/1350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.305ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_1350.svg"></span>
for every <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_120"> which is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_19">, we get a class of
mutually exclusive classes, namely the classes of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow\alpha ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.371ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1351.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \kappa\)" src="images/1352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.517ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1352.svg">, each of these is
similar to the corresponding member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_20">. Hence the logical sum
of this class of classes, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{R} \{(\exists \alpha ,x).\alpha \in \kappa .x\in \alpha .R=x\downarrow \alpha\}, \]" src="images/1353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.283ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_1353.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_70">[Pg 70]</span>
has the required number of terms. Now, by *85·601,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \downarrow \alpha ʻʻ\alpha =\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/1354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.689ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1354.svg"></span>
Hence the class whose logical sum we are taking is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1355.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.513ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1355.svg">. Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Sigma ʻ\kappa =sʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.184ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1356.svg"></span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.294ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1357.svg"> may be called the <i>arithmetical</i> sum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_21">, in contradistinction to <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg">, which is the logical
sum. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.294ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1357.svg_1"> bears to <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_1"> a relation analogous
to that which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_4"> bears to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/1301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1301.svg_1">.</p>

<p>We put further <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa =\text{Nc}ʻsʻ\in\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa \quad\text{Df}.\)" src="images/1359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.944ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1359.svg"></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_1"> is the sum of the numbers of members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_22">.</p>

<p>It is to be observed that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_2"> is not in
general a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1360.svg">. For, if two members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_23"> have the same cardinal number, this will only count
once in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1360.svg_1">, whereas it counts twice in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1361.svg">.</p>

<p>We shall find that, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \beta\)" src="images/1362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_1362.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup \iota ʻ\beta )=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta . \]" src="images/1363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.168ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1363.svg"></span>
Thus where a finite number of summands are concerned, the two
definitions of addition agree, except that the first allows one class
to count several times over, while the second does not.</p>

<p>In dealing with multiplication, our procedure is closely analogous
to the procedure for addition. We first define the <i>arithmetical
class-product</i> of two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_121"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_66">, which is
a certain class whose cardinal number is the product of the cardinal
numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_122"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_67">. We write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg">
for the arithmetical class-product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_68"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_123">, and
define it as the class of all ordinal couples of which the referent
is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_124"> and the relatum a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_69">,
<i>i.e.</i> as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{R} \{(\exists x,y).x\in \alpha .y\in \beta .R=x\downarrow y\}. \]" src="images/1365.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.242ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_1365.svg"></span>
By *40·7, this class is <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 11.327ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1366.svg">. Hence we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \beta \times \alpha =sʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.151ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1367.svg"></span>
The class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_70">, and each member of it is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_125">; hence if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha =\mu\)" src="images/1369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.876ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1369.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta=\nu\)" src="images/1370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.543ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1370.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 11.327ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1366.svg_1"> consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_45">
classes having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_76"> members each. The class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1371.svg"> is important also in connection with
exponentiation.</p>

<p>The product of two cardinals is defined as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha \times \beta )\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.152ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1372.svg"></span>
In regard to types, this definition calls for analogous remarks to
those which were made on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_3">. Also, as before, we
need definitions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1373.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.535ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1373.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \times _{\text{c}}\mu\)" src="images/1374.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.535ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1374.svg">, whence we obtain
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \times _{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha \times _{\text{c}}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1375.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 39.325ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1375.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_71">[Pg 71]</span>By means of these definitions, we can define the product of any finite
number of cardinals; but in order to define products which have an
infinite number of factors, we need a new definition.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_24"> is a class of classes, we take <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg">
as its arithmetical product. In simple cases, it is easy to see the
justification of this decision. <i>E.g.</i> let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_25"> consist of
the three classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{1}\)" src="images/1377.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1377.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{2}\)" src="images/1378.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1378.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{3}\)" src="images/1379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.375ex;" id="img_images_1379.svg">,
and let the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{1}\)" src="images/1377.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1377.svg_1"> be <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/1380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1380.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg">; those
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{2}\)" src="images/1378.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1378.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{1}\)" src="images/1382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.096ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1382.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{2}\)" src="images/1383.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.096ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1383.svg">; those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{3}\)" src="images/1379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.375ex;" id="img_images_1379.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z_{1}\)" src="images/1384.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.04ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1384.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z_{2}\)" src="images/1385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.04ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1385.svg">. Then the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_1"> are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;x_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{1}\unicode{x228d} y_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{2}\unicode{x228d} z_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{3},\\ &amp;x_{2}\downarrow \alpha _{1}\unicode{x228d} y_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{2}\unicode{x228d} z_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{3},\\ &amp;x_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{1}\unicode{x228d} y_{2}\downarrow \alpha _{2}\unicode{x228d} z_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{3},\\ &amp;x_{2}\downarrow \alpha _{1}\unicode{x228d} y_{2}\downarrow \alpha _{2}\unicode{x228d} z_{1}\downarrow \alpha _{3},\\ \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1386.svg" style="vertical-align: -4.977ex; width: 24.233ex; height: 11.086ex;" id="img_images_1386.svg"></span>
with four more obtained by substituting <img alt="" data-tex="\(z_{2}\)" src="images/1385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.04ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1385.svg_1"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(z_{1}\)" src="images/1384.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.04ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1384.svg_1"> in the
above. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = 8 = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha_{1} \times _{\text{c}} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha _{2} \times _{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha _{3}\)" src="images/1387.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 43.725ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1387.svg">.
In general, however, the existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_2"> is
doubtful, owing to the doubt as to the validity of the multiplicative
axiom. (We shall return to this point shortly.) Hence there is no proof
that the product of an infinite number of factors cannot be zero unless
one of the factors is zero.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_26"> is a class of mutually exclusive
classes, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_3"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1388.svg">. On account of its lower type,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1388.svg_1"> is often more convenient than
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_4">. Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Prod}ʻ\kappa =\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa  \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/1389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.94ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1389.svg"></span>
or (what comes to the same thing)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Prod}=\text{D}_{\in }\mid {\in}_{\Delta} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 21.045ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_1390.svg"></span>
For the product of the cardinal numbers of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_27">, we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa =\text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1391.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.137ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1391.svg"></span>
As in the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_161.svg_2">
is not in general a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1360.svg_2">. We shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\alpha \neq \beta .\supset .\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup \iota ʻ\beta )=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \times _{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta . \]" src="images/1392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.389ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1392.svg"></span>
Thus for products of a finite number of different factors, the two
definitions of multiplication agree.</p>

<p>It remains to define exponentiation. Since this is not a commutative
operation, it essentially involves an order as between the base and the
exponent; hence we do not obtain a definition of the exponentiation of
a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_28">, analogous to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_4"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_271.svg_1">, but only a definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_172.svg_2">,
which may be extended to any finite number of exponentiations. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha\,\text{exp}\,\beta =\text{Prod}ʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 30.354ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1393.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_1"> has the meaning explained
above, resulting from *38·03. It will be observed that, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha = \mu\)" src="images/1394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.876ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1394.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta= \nu\)" src="images/1395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.543ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1395.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_2"> is a class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_46">
mutually exclusive classes each of which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_77"> terms; hence
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \text{exp}\beta\)" src="images/1396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.186ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1396.svg"> may suitably be used to define <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_172.svg_3">.
Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu ^\nu =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha \,\text{exp}\,\,\beta )\} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/1397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.15ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1397.svg"></span>
and for the same reasons as before, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha ^{\text{N}_{c}\text{c}ʻ\beta} = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha ^{\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.578ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_1398.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_72">[Pg 72]</span></p>

<p>The above definition of exponentiation gives the same value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^\nu\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_2"> as results from Cantor's definition by means of
"Belegungen." The class of Cantor's "Belegungen" is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \hat{R} \{R\in 1\rightarrow &amp;\text{Cls}.\text{D}ʻR\subset \alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\beta \},\\ \textit{i.e.}\qquad &amp;(\alpha \uparrow \beta )_{\Delta }ʻ\beta, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1399.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.377ex; width: 36.278ex; height: 5.885ex;" id="img_images_1399.svg"></span>
and it is easily proved that this is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \,\text{exp}\,\beta\)" src="images/1400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.941ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1400.svg">.</p>

<p>The usual formal properties of exponentiation result without much
difficulty from the above definitions.</p>

<p>The above definition of exponentiation is so framed as to make
propositions on exponentiation independent of the multiplicative axiom,
except when exponentiation is to be connected with multiplication,
<i>i.e.</i> when it is to be shown that the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_47"> factors,
each of which is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_78">, is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_172.svg_4">. This proposition cannot be
proved generally without the multiplicative axiom. Similarly, in the
theory of multiplication, the proposition that the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \mu\)" src="images/1401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.563ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_1401.svg">'s
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_1402.svg"> requires the multiplicative axiom (as
does also the proposition that a product is zero when and only when
one of its factors is zero). Otherwise, the theory of multiplication
proceeds without the need for employing the multiplicative axiom.</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 1234px;" id="i_072">
<img alt="Mathematical diagram showing a 4x2 grid with rows labeled κ₁-κ₄ (left) and λ₁-λ₄ (right). Each row contains arrows s₁-s₄ connecting dots. Curved arrows labeled S at top and bottom suggest cyclic relationships, typical of formal logic or category theory diagrams." height="1870" src="images/i_072.jpg" width="1234" id="img_images_i_072.jpg">
</figure>

<p>To take first the connection of addition and multiplication: this
connection, in the form in which we naturally suppose it to hold, is
affirmed in the proposition:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\kappa \in \nu \cap \text{Cls excl}ʻ\mu .&amp;\supset .sʻ\kappa \in \mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu  &amp;\qquad \text{(A)}\\ \textit{or}\qquad \mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\kappa \in \nu \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\mu .&amp;\supset .\Sigma ʻ\kappa \in \mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1403.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 60.528ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1403.svg"></span>
We will take the first of these as being simpler. It affirms that
the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \mu\)" src="images/1401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.563ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_1401.svg_1">'s is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_1404.svg">. This
can be proved when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_48"> is finite, whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_79"> is finite or
not; but when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_49"> is infinite, it cannot be proved without the
multiplicative axiom. This may be seen as follows. We know that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \vdash :&amp;\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\alpha \in \mu .\beta \in \nu .\supset .\\ &amp;\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta \in \nu \cap \text{Cls excl}ʻ\mu .sʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta \in \mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu   &amp;\qquad \text{(A)}\\ \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1405.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.078ex; width: 61.507ex; height: 5.288ex;" id="img_images_1405.svg"></span>
Thus (A) above will result if we can prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa ,\lambda \in \nu \cap \text{Cls excl}ʻ\mu .\supset .sʻ\kappa \text{ sm }sʻ\lambda , \]" src="images/1406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 36.149ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1406.svg"></span>
since we shall put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_3"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg">,
and use (B).</p>

<p>Since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_29">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \in \nu\)" src="images/1408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.284ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_1408.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\text{ sm }\lambda\)" src="images/1409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 6.529ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1409.svg">.
Assume
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda . \]" src="images/1410.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.647ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1410.svg"></span>
Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa _{1}\)" src="images/1411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.291ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1411.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa _{2}\)" src="images/1412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.291ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1412.svg">, ... be members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_30">,
and let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda _{1}\)" src="images/1413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.307ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_1413.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda _{2}\)" src="images/1414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.307ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_1414.svg">, ... be the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_1"> which are correlated with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa _{1}\)" src="images/1411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.291ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1411.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa_{2}\)" src="images/1415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.291ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1415.svg">,
... by <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_2">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda _{1}=\breve{S}ʻ\kappa _{1} . \lambda _{2}=\breve{S} ʻ\kappa _{2}.\text{etc}\)" src="images/1416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.764ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_1416.svg">.
We have, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_31">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \in \text{Cl}ʻ\mu\)" src="images/1417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.069ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1417.svg">,
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_73">[Pg 73]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa _{1}\text{ sm }\lambda _{1}.\kappa _{2}\text{ sm }\lambda_{2}.\text{etc}\)" src="images/1418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 21.911ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_1418.svg">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha S\beta .\supset _{\alpha ,\beta}.\alpha \text{ sm }\beta\)" src="images/1419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 17.158ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_1419.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }\)" src="images/1420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.48ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1420.svg">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_32"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_2"> are finite, we can pick out arbitrarily
a correlation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{1}\)" src="images/1421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.375ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_1421.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa _{1}\)" src="images/1411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.291ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1411.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda _{1}\)" src="images/1413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.307ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_1413.svg_1">,
another <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{2}\)" src="images/1422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.375ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_1422.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa _{2}\)" src="images/1412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.291ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1412.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda _{2}\)" src="images/1414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.307ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_1414.svg_1">, and so
on; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{1}\unicode{x228d} S_{2}\unicode{x228d}\)" src="images/1423.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.464ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1423.svg"> ... correlates
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg">, and therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa \text{ sm }sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.367ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1425.svg">.
But when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_33"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_3"> are infinite, this
method is impracticable. In this case, we proceed as follows.</p>

<p>By *73·01, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \overline{\text{ sm }} \beta =(1\rightarrow 1)\cap\overleftarrow{\text{D}}ʻ\alpha \cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\beta\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.876ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_1426.svg">.</p>

<p>Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \overline{\text{ sm }} \alpha\)" src="images/1427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.803ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_1427.svg">" will stand for all the
permutations of a class into itself; "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \overline{\text{ sm }}\beta\)" src="images/1428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.636ex; height: 2.17ex;" id="img_images_1428.svg">"
stands for all the permutations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_126"> into <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_71">,
<i>i.e.</i> all the <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg">'s whose domain is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_127"> and
whose converse domain is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_72">. It is obvious that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\exists !\alpha \overline{\text{ sm }} \beta \cap \gamma \overline{\text{ sm }} \delta .\supset .\alpha =\gamma .\beta =\delta . \]" src="images/1430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 36.22ex; height: 2.219ex;" id="img_images_1430.svg"></span>
In the case of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_34"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_4"> above, we know that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \text{ sm }\beta\)" src="images/1431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.636ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1431.svg"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha S\beta\)" src="images/1432.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.188ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1432.svg">; thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha \in \kappa .\supset _{\alpha }.\exists !\alpha \overline{\text{ sm }} (\breve{S} ʻ\alpha )\\ \text{or}\qquad\qquad\quad \beta \in \lambda .\supset _{\beta }.\exists !(Sʻ\beta )\overline{\text{ sm }} \beta .\\ \text{Put}\qquad \text{Crp}(S)ʻ\beta =(Sʻ\beta )\overline{\text{ sm }} \beta  \qquad\text{Df}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1433.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.966ex; width: 39.476ex; height: 9.064ex;" id="img_images_1433.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}\)" src="images/1434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.778ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1434.svg">" stands for "correspondence." Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}(S)ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.636ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1435.svg"> is the class of all correspondences of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_73">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.032ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1437.svg"> is the class of all
such classes of correspondences. If we extract one member out of each
of these classes of correspondences, we get a class of relations whose
sum is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_1">; <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \varpi \in \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda .\supset .\dot{s} ʻ\varpi \in (sʻ\kappa )\overline{\text{ sm }} (sʻ\lambda ). \]" src="images/1438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.847ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_1438.svg"></span>
Thus the desired result follows whenever
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !{\in}_{\Delta }ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda . \]" src="images/1439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1439.svg"></span>
Now we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\supset .\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/1440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.66ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_1440.svg">.</p>

<p>Consequently
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Mult ax}.\supset :S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda .\kappa ,\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}. \supset .sʻ\kappa \text{ sm }sʻ\lambda , \]" src="images/1441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 80.402ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_1441.svg"></span>
whence, by what was said previously,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Mult ax}.\supset :\kappa \in \nu \cap \text{Cls excl}ʻ\mu .\supset .sʻ\kappa \in \mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa =\mu \times _{\text{c}}\nu . \]" src="images/1442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 64.175ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1442.svg"></span></p>

<p>The consideration of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta }ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.419ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1443.svg"> leads
similarly to the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\kappa \in \nu \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\mu .\supset .{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \in \mu ^\nu .\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa =\mu ^\nu. \]" src="images/1444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 67.329ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1444.svg"></span>
The proof is closely analogous to that for the connection of addition
and multiplication.</p>

<p>It will be seen that, in the above use of the multiplicative axiom, we
have two classes of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_35"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_5"> concerning which
we assume
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda , \]" src="images/1445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.616ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1445.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> we assume that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_36"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_6"> are similar
classes of similar classes. A slightly modified hypothesis concerning
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_37"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_7"> will enable us to obtain many results,
without the multiplicative axiom, which otherwise might be expected to
require this axiom. This is effected as follows.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_74">[Pg 74]</span></p>

<p>Put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda .\equiv .(\exists T).T\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻT=sʻ\lambda .\kappa =T_{\in }ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.594ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1446.svg">,
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\text{ sm }\)" src="images/1447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.814ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_1447.svg">" is a single symbol representing a relation.</p>

<p>When this relation holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_38"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_8">, we shall
say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_39"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_9"> have "double similarity." In this
case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg"> correlates <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_2">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in}\)" src="images/1449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.576ex; height: 1.935ex;" id="img_images_1449.svg">
correlates <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_40"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_10">, so that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_74"> is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_11">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.214ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1450.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Tʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.588ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1451.svg">, is
its correlate in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_41">. We shall then have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda .\supset .sʻ\kappa  \text{ sm } sʻ\lambda ,\\ &amp;\vdash :\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda .\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa =\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\lambda ,\\ &amp;\vdash :\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda .\supset .\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa =\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\lambda . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1452.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 35.257ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_1452.svg"></span></p>

<p>Also we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda .\supset .(\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda . \]" src="images/1453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.465ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1453.svg"></span>
Conversely,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :\kappa ,\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda .\\ &amp;\varpi \in \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda .T=\dot{s} ʻ\varpi .\supset .T\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻT=sʻ\lambda .\kappa =T_{\in }ʻʻ\lambda , \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1454.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.228ex; width: 72.578ex; height: 5.588ex;" id="img_images_1454.svg"></span>
whence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \vdash \colon\colon \text{Mult ax}.\supset \colon\ldotp \kappa ,\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2}     \text{excl}:&amp;(\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda :\\ &amp;\supset .\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1455.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.209ex; width: 75.776ex; height: 5.55ex;" id="img_images_1455.svg"></span>
Hence the multiplicative axiom is only required in order to pass from
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{ sm }.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda \]" src="images/1456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.987ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1456.svg"></span>
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda\)" src="images/1457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 10.437ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1457.svg">. It is this fact, and the
consequent possibility of diminishing the use of the multiplicative
axiom, which has led us to the employment of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm} \,\text{sm}\)" src="images/1458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.93ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_1458.svg">"
in the present section.</p>

<p>We treat also, in this section, the relation of greater and less
between cardinals. We say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1459.svg">
when there is a part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_128"> which is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_75">, but
no part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_76"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_129">. The principal proposition
in this subject is the Schröder-Bernstein theorem, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\mu \geq \nu .\nu \geq \mu .\supset .\mu =\nu . \]" src="images/1460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 24.788ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1460.svg"></span>
This is an immediate consequence of *73·88. It cannot be shown, without
assuming the multiplicative axiom, that of any two cardinals one must
be the greater, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\mu \neq \nu .\supset :\mu &gt;\nu .\lor.\nu &gt;\mu. \]" src="images/1461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 35.587ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_1461.svg"></span>
If we assume the multiplicative axiom, this results from Zermelo's
proof that on that assumption, every class can be well-ordered,
together with Cantor's proof that of any two well-ordered series which
are not similar, one must be similar to a part of the other. But these
propositions cannot be proved till a much later stage (*258).</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_75">[Pg 75]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_110">
*110. THE ARITHMETICAL SUM OF TWO CLASSES AND OF
TWO CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *110.</p>

<p>In this number, we start from the definition:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta =\downarrow (\Lambda \cap \beta )ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha \cup (\Lambda \cap \alpha )\downarrow ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\beta  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.837ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1462.svg"></p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_5"> is called the "arithmetical class-sum" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_130">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_77">. The definition is framed so as to give two mutually
exclusive classes respectively similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_131"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_78">, so
that the number of terms in the logical sum of these two classes is the
arithmetical sum of the numbers of terms in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_132"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_79">
respectively. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_6"> is significant whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_133"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_80"> are classes, whatever their types may be.</p>

<p>By means of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_7">, we define the arithmetical sum of two
cardinals as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta )\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.523ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1463.svg"></p>

<p>This defines the "arithmetical sum of two cardinals." (It is not
necessary to <i>significance</i> that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_80"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_50"> should
be cardinals, but only that they should be classes of classes. If,
however, either is not a cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\Lambda\)" src="images/1464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.814ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_1464.svg">).
It will be observed that, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_81"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_51"> are typically
definite, so are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_134"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_81"> in the above definition;
but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_3"> is typically ambiguous, on account of the ambiguity of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_10">." Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_4"> is also typically
ambiguous.</p>

<p>It will be shown that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_5"> is always a cardinal, and
that, if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta, \quad\text{then}\quad \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta ). \]" src="images/1465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.543ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1465.svg"></span>
Hence whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_82"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_52"> are cardinals other than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_22">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_6"> is an existent cardinal in some
types, though it may be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_23"> in others.</p>

<p>Two more definitions are required in this number, namely:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\mu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.758ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1466.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\mu +_{\text{c}}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1467.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.758ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1467.svg"></p>

<p>These definitions are needed in order to apply the definition of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_7"> to the case in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_83"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_53"> are
replaced by typically ambiguous symbols <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_51"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_25">. It does not make any difference to the value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1468.svg"> how the ambiguities of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_52"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_26"> are determined, so long as
they are determined in a way that insures <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha.\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.626ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1469.svg">;
but if there are types in which either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_53"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_27"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_24">, we get <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\Lambda\)" src="images/1470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1470.svg">
in all types if we determine the ambiguities so that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha=\Lambda\)" src="images/1471.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.094ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1471.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\Lambda\)" src="images/1472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.927ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1472.svg">. It is in
order to<span class="pagenum" id="Page_76">[Pg 76]</span> exclude such determinations of the ambiguity that the above
definitions are required. Also in connection with these definitions and
the corresponding definitions <a href="#_113_04" class="pginternal">*113·04</a><a href="#_113_05" class="pginternal">·05</a> and <a href="#_116_03" class="pginternal">*116·03</a><a href="#_116_04" class="pginternal">·04</a> and <a href="#_117_02" class="pginternal">*117·02</a><a href="#_117_03" class="pginternal">·03</a>,
the convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_19"> of the prefatory statement must be noted.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number begin with the properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_4">. We show (<a href="#_110_11" class="pginternal">*110·11</a><a href="#_110_12" class="pginternal">·12</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_5">
consists of two mutually exclusive parts, which are respectively
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_135"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_82">; we show (<a href="#_110_14" class="pginternal">*110·14</a>) that if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_136"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_83"> are mutually exclusive, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/1301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1301.svg_2">
is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_6">, and (<a href="#_110_15" class="pginternal">*110·15</a>) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_16"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_16"> are respectively similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_137"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_84">, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma + \delta\)" src="images/1473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.999ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_1473.svg"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_7">. We show (<a href="#_110_16" class="pginternal">*110·16</a>)
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha + \beta)\)" src="images/1474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.313ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1474.svg"> consists of all classes which can
be divided into two mutually exclusive parts which are respectively
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_138"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_85">.</p>

<p>We then proceed (<a href="#_110_2" class="pginternal">*110·2</a>—<a href="#_110_252" class="pginternal">·252</a>) to the consideration of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg_4">.
Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_84"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_54"> are typically definite, and the definition
<a href="#_110_02" class="pginternal">*110·02</a> applies to any typically definite symbols, such as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_7"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.391ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1475.svg">. We
