prove (<a href="#_110_21" class="pginternal">*110·21</a>) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_85"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_55"> are cardinals, their
sum consists of all classes similar to some class of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha + \beta\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg_8">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \mu .\beta \in \nu\)" src="images/1476.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.83ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1476.svg">; we
prove (<a href="#_110_22" class="pginternal">*110·22</a>) that the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_8"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_867.svg_1"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha + \beta)\)" src="images/1474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.313ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1474.svg_1">, and
(<a href="#_110_25" class="pginternal">*110·25</a>) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_86"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_56"> are cardinals, their sum is equal
to the sum of the "same" cardinals in any other types in which they are
not null, <i>i.e.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu .\supset .\mu  +_{\text{c}}\nu  = \text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu      +_{\text{c}}\text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu \)" src="images/1477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 70.235ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_1477.svg"></p>

<p>We then (<a href="#_110_3" class="pginternal">*110·3</a>—<a href="#_110_351" class="pginternal">·351</a>) consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1468.svg_1">,
to which we apply the definitions *110·03·04. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta      = \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha  + \beta)\)" src="images/1478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.731ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1478.svg">
whence the other properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1468.svg_2">
follow from previous propositions.</p>

<p>We then have (<a href="#_110_4" class="pginternal">*110·4</a>—<a href="#_110_44" class="pginternal">·44</a>) various propositions on the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_8"> and
its existence and kindred matters. The chief of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\mu  +_{\text{c}}\nu .\supset .\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC} - \iota ʻ\Lambda .\mu ,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/1479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 42.345ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1479.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\mu  +_{\text{c}}\nu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/1480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.712ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1480.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition requires no hypothesis, because, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_87"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_57"> are not both cardinals, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu = \Lambda\)" src="images/1481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.814ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_1481.svg">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_25"> is a cardinal, by <a href="#_102_74" class="pginternal">*102·74</a>.</p>

<p>Our next set of propositions (<a href="#_110_5" class="pginternal">*110·5</a>—<a href="#_110_57" class="pginternal">·57</a>) are concerned with the
permutative and associative laws, which are <a href="#_110_51" class="pginternal">*110·51</a> and <a href="#_110_56" class="pginternal">*110·56</a>
respectively.</p>

<p>We then (<a href="#_110_6" class="pginternal">*110·6</a>—<a href="#_110_643" class="pginternal">·643</a>) consider the addition of 0 or 1, proving
(<a href="#_110_61" class="pginternal">*110·61</a>) that a cardinal is unchanged by the addition of 0, and
(<a href="#_110_643" class="pginternal">*110·643</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 +_{\text{c}}1 = 2\)" src="images/1482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 10.075ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_1482.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_14">*110·14</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \cap \beta  = \Lambda .\supset .\alpha \cup \beta \text{ sm }(\alpha +\beta )   \quad[*110·13.*73·3]\)" src="images/1495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.383ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1495.svg"></p>

<p>Thus whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_140"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_87"> are mutually exclusive, their

their cardinal numbers.</p>

<p>Thus when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_141"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_88"> are of the same type,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta )\)" src="images/1505.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.313ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1505.svg"> exists at least in the type next above
that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_142"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_89">. We cannot prove that it exists in
the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_143"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_90">. <i>E.g.</i> suppose the lowest
type contained only one member; then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_21"> were that one member,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻx+\iota ʻx)\)" src="images/1506.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.49ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1506.svg"> would not exist in the type to which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg_4"> belongs, but would exist in the next type, <i>i.e.</i>
there would not be two individuals, but there would be two classes,
namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_26"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg_5">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\Lambda \cup \iota ʻ\iota ʻx\in \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻx+\iota ʻx)\)" src="images/1507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.11ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1507.svg">.</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash *110·25.*104·265.\supset \\ \vdash :\text{Hp}.\exists !\mu ^{(1)}.\exists !\nu ^{(1)}.&amp;\supset .\mu ^{(1)}+_{\text{c}}\nu ^{(1)} = \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*110·202.&amp;\supset \vdash :{\sim}(\exists !\mu ^{(1)}.\exists !\nu ^{(1)}).\supset .\mu ^{(1)}+_{\text{c}}\nu ^{(1)}     = \Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*104·264.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}(2).&amp;\supset .{\sim}(\exists !\mu .\exists !\nu ).\\ [*110·202] &amp;\supset .\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu  = \Lambda .\\ [(2)] &amp;\supset .\mu ^{(1)}+_{\text{c}}\nu ^{(1)} = \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(3).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1531.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.554ex; width: 75.593ex; height: 22.24ex;" id="img_images_1531.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_252">*110·252</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\supset .\mu _{(00)}+_{\text{c}}\nu _{(00)} = \mu +_{\text{c}}\nu   \quad[\text{Proof as in *110·251}]\)" src="images/1532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 60.589ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_1532.svg"></p>

<p>A similar proof applies to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(2)}\)" src="images/521.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_521.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu ^{(2)}\)" src="images/1533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.549ex; height: 2.021ex;" id="img_images_1533.svg">, etc.,
and to any such derived cardinals whose existence follows from that
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_88"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_58">. The proposition does not hold generally for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu _{(1)}\)" src="images/1534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 1.8ex;" id="img_images_1534.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{(1)}\)" src="images/1535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 3.35ex; height: 1.8ex;" id="img_images_1535.svg"> and other descending derived cardinals,
because they may be null when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_89"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_59"> exist.</p>

<p>The following proposition (*110·3) is more often used than any other in
this number except <a href="#_110_4" class="pginternal">*110·4</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_3">*110·3</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta      = \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha +\beta ) \quad[*110·22.(*110·03·04)]\)" src="images/1536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 77.381ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1536.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_31">*110·31</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\gamma  \text{ sm } \alpha .\delta  \text{ sm } \beta .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\delta  = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta      \quad[*110·24·3]\)" src="images/1537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 66.443ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1537.svg"></p>

<p>The following proposition is frequently used.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_32">*110·32</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \cap \beta  = \Lambda .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta  = \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha \cup \beta )  \quad[*110·3·14]\)" src="images/1538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.539ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1538.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·33.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}&amp;\vdash :\xi \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta     . \equiv  .(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma  \text{ sm } \alpha .\delta  \text{ sm } \beta .\gamma \cap \delta  = \Lambda .\xi  = \gamma \cup \delta \\ &amp;[*110·3·16]\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1539.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 66.455ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1539.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is used in <a href="#_110_63" class="pginternal">*110·63</a>. We might have used the above
to define arithmetical addition, but this method would have been less
convenient than the method adopted in this number, both because there
would<span class="pagenum" id="Page_81">[Pg 81]</span> have been more difficulty in dealing with types, and because the
existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1540.svg"> (in the
types in which it does exist) is less evident with the above definition
than with the definitions given in <a href="#_110_01" class="pginternal">*110·01</a><a href="#_110_02" class="pginternal">·02</a><a href="#_110_03" class="pginternal">·03</a><a href="#_110_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_331">*110·331</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\xi -\gamma \text{ sm }\beta .\gamma \subset \xi\}\)" src="images/1541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.427ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1541.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash . *110·33.*24·47.&amp;\supset \\ \vdash :\xi \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{\text{c}}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .&amp;\equiv .(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\delta \text{ sm }\beta .\gamma \subset \xi .\delta =\xi -\gamma .\\ [*13·195]  &amp;\equiv .(\exists \gamma ).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\xi -\gamma \text{ sm }\beta .\gamma \subset \xi :\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1542.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 66.045ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1542.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_34">*110·34</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}&amp;\vdash :\exists !\text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\alpha .\exists !\text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\beta .\supset .\text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}}     \text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\beta =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta \\ &amp;[*110·23·3]\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1543.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 66.124ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1543.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_351">*110·351</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} \text{N}_{00}\text{c}ʻ\beta =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}}     \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  \quad[*106·21.*110·34]\)" src="images/1545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.999ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1545.svg"></p>

<p>Similar propositions will hold generally for <i>ascending</i> cardinals.</p>

<p>The following proposition (*110·4) is the most used of the propositions
in this number. It is useful both in the form given, and in the form
resulting from transposition, in which it shows that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu =\Lambda\)" src="images/1464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.814ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_1464.svg_1">
unless both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_90"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_60"> are existent cardinals.
It is chiefly useful in avoiding the necessity of the hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_91">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/1546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.295ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_1546.svg"> in such propositions as the commutative
and associative laws.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_4">*110·4</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu .\supset .\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\mu ,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C} \quad[*110·201·202·2]\)" src="images/1547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.213ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1547.svg"></p>

<p>The following propositions, down to <a href="#_110_411" class="pginternal">*110·411</a> inclusive, are concerned
with types. They are not referred to in the sequel.</p>

no hypothesis. This is owing to <a href="#_110_4" class="pginternal">*110·4</a> and <a href="#_102_74" class="pginternal">*102·74</a>.</p>

<p>The above proposition depends upon the fact that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}}\nu\)" src="images/1320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1320.svg_9">
is typically ambiguous, even when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_92"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_61"> are typically
definite. It is used in the theory of inductive cardinals
(<a href="#_120_32" class="pginternal">*120·32</a><a href="#_120_41" class="pginternal">·41</a><a href="#_120_424" class="pginternal">·424</a>).</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the commutative and
associative laws for arithmetical addition of cardinals.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_5">*110·5</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\beta +\alpha  = \text{Cnv}ʻʻ(\alpha +\beta)\)" src="images/1562.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.955ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1562.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*55·14.\supset \vdash .\text{Cnv}ʻʻ(\alpha +\beta ) &amp;= \Lambda _{\beta }\downarrow ʻʻ\iota ʻʻ\alpha \cup \downarrow \Lambda _{\alpha }ʻʻ\iota ʻʻ\beta \\ [(*110·01)] &amp;= \beta +\alpha .\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1563.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.191ex; width: 60.712ex; height: 5.514ex;" id="img_images_1563.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_83">[Pg 83]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·501.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\beta  + \alpha \text{ sm }\alpha  + \beta    \quad[*110·5.*73·4]\)" src="images/1564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.889ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1564.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_51">*110·51</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu =\nu  +_{\text{c}} \mu   \quad[*110·2·501.*73·37]\)" src="images/1565.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.624ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1565.svg"></p>

<p>It is not necessary to the truth of the above proposition that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_93">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_62"> should be cardinals. If either is not a cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} \nu\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg_5">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{\text{c}} \mu\)" src="images/1566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.227ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_1566.svg"> are both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_27">.</p>

<p>The following propositions lead to the associative law (<a href="#_110_56" class="pginternal">*110·56</a>).</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*110·551.*103·2.\supset \\ \vdash :\mu ,\nu ,\varpi  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.&amp;\supset .(\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu ) +_{\text{c}} \varpi =\mu  +_{\text{c}} (\nu  +_{\text{c}}     \varpi ) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*110·4.\text{Transp}.&amp;\supset \\ \vdash :{\sim}(\mu ,\nu ,\varpi \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}).&amp;\supset .(\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu ) +_{\text{c}} \varpi =\Lambda .\mu  +_{\text{c}} (\nu  +_{\text{c}}     \varpi )=\Lambda .\\ [*13.171]   &amp;\supset .(\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu ) +_{\text{c}} \varpi =\mu  +_{\text{c}} (\nu  +_{\text{c}} \varpi )&amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1579.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 76.45ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_1579.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_84">[Pg 84]</span></p>

<p>This is the associative law for arithmetical addition. It will be seen
that, like the commutative law, it does not require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_94">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_63">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varpi\)" src="images/274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.873ex; height: 0.998ex;" id="img_images_274.svg_2"> should be cardinals.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·561.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu  +_{\text{c}} \varpi  = (\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu ) +_{\text{c}} \varpi  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.989ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1580.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_57">*110·57</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu ) +_{\text{c}} (\varpi  +_{\text{c}} \rho ) = \mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu  +_{\text{c}} \varpi  +_{\text{c}}     \rho  \quad[*110·56.(*110·561)]\)" src="images/1581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 66.006ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1581.svg"></p>

<p>The following propositions, concerning the addition of 0 or 1, are used
frequently in dealing with inductive cardinals (<a href="#_120" class="pginternal">*120</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_6">*110·6</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\supset .\mu  +_{\text{c}} 0 = \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/1582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 31.035ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1582.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*101·11.*110·21.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :\xi \in \mu  +_{\text{c}} 0.&amp;\equiv .(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\alpha \in \mu .\beta \in 0.\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha  + \beta ).\\ [*54·102] &amp;\equiv .(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in \mu .\xi \text{ sm }(\alpha  + \Lambda ).\\ [*110·152] &amp; \equiv .(\exists \alpha ,\gamma ,\delta ).\alpha \in \mu .\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\delta \text{ sm }\Lambda .\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\xi =\gamma \cup \delta .\\ [*73·47] &amp;\equiv .(\exists \alpha ,\gamma ).\alpha \in \mu .\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\xi =\gamma .\\ [*13·195] &amp;\equiv .(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in \mu .\xi \text{ sm }\alpha .\\ [*37·1]  &amp;\equiv .\xi \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu \colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1583.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.068ex; width: 80.017ex; height: 21.267ex;" id="img_images_1583.svg"></span></p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_95"> is a typically definite cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_11"> is
the same cardinal rendered typically ambiguous; when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_96"> is a
typically ambiguous cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_12">, is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_97">. In place
of the above proposition, we might write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC}.\supset.\mu +_{\text{c}} 0 = \mu\)" src="images/1584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 21.773ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1584.svg">;
this would be true whenever the ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} 0\)" src="images/1585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.159ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_1585.svg"> was
so determined as to make it significant. But the above form gives more
information.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_61">*110·61</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} 0=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.214ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1586.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*101·1.\supset \vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} 0&amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} \text{Nc}ʻ\Lambda \\ [*110·32] &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha \cup \Lambda )\\ [*24·24] &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1587.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 45.516ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1587.svg"></span></p>

<p>In this proposition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_55"> is typically ambiguous; hence
we escape the necessity of putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1588.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.129ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1588.svg">
on the right, as we should have to do if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_56"> were
typically definite. We can deduce <a href="#_110_61" class="pginternal">*110·61</a> from <a href="#_110_6" class="pginternal">*110·6</a> as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*110·3.\supset \vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} 0&amp;=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} 0\\ [*110·6] &amp;=\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha \\ [*103·4] &amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \end{array} \]" src="images/1589.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 43.154ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1589.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_85">[Pg 85]</span></p>

<p>We have to travel via <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_9"> in this
proof, in order to avoid the possibility of a typical determination
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_57"> which would make <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha=\Lambda\)" src="images/1471.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.094ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1471.svg_1">.
It is for the same reason that we cannot put
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1590.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.653ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1590.svg">"; for if the
first <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_58"> is determined to a type in which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\Lambda\)" src="images/1591.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.094ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1591.svg">, while the second is not, this equation
becomes false.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·62.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu =0.\equiv .\mu =0.\nu =0\)" src="images/1592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 28.528ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1592.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*103·27.*101·11·13.&amp;\supset \vdash .0=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\Lambda  &amp;\quad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*110·43.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu =0.&amp;\equiv :\Lambda \in \mu  +_{\text{c}} \nu :\\ [*110·202] &amp;\equiv :\exists !\mu .\exists !\nu :(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\mu =\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma .\nu =\text{Nc}ʻ\delta .\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\gamma \cup \delta =\Lambda :\\ [*24·32.*13·22] &amp;\equiv :\exists !\mu .\exists !\nu :\mu =\text{Nc}ʻ\Lambda .\nu =\text{Nc}ʻ\Lambda :\\ [*101·1·12] &amp;\equiv :\mu =0.\nu =0\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1593.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 96.474ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_1593.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_110_63">*110·63</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} 1=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,y).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .y{\sim}\in \gamma .\xi =\gamma \cup \iota ʻy\}\)" src="images/1594.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.805ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1594.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*101·2.\supset \\ \vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} 1&amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{\text{c}} \text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻx\\ [*110·33] &amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\delta \text{ sm }\iota ʻx.\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\xi =\gamma \cup \delta\}\\ [*73·45] &amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\delta \in 1.\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\xi =\gamma \cup \delta\}\\ [*52·1] &amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,\delta ,y).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .\delta =\iota ʻy.\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\xi =\gamma \cup \delta\}\\ [*13·195.*51·211] &amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,y).\gamma \text{ sm }\alpha .y{\sim}\in \gamma .\xi =\gamma \cup \iota ʻy\}.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1595.svg" style="vertical-align: -9.941ex; width: 71.999ex; height: 21.014ex;" id="img_images_1595.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is much used in the theory of finite and
infinite, both cardinal and ordinal. It connects mathematical induction
for inductive cardinals with mathematical induction for inductive
classes (cf. <a href="#_120" class="pginternal">*120</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*110·631.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\supset \mu  +_{\text{c}}1=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,y).\gamma \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu .y{\sim}\in \gamma .\xi =\gamma \cup \iota ʻy\}\)" src="images/1596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.166ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1596.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*110·211.*101·21.\supset \\ \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\mu  +_{\text{c}}     1&amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu .\delta \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ1.\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\xi =\gamma \cup \delta\}\\ [*101·28] &amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,\delta ).\gamma \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu .\delta \in 1.\gamma \cap \delta =\Lambda .\xi =\gamma \cup \delta\}\\ [*52·1.*51·211] &amp;=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,y).\gamma \in \text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu .y{\sim}\in \gamma .\xi =\gamma \cup \iota ʻy\}:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1597.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.41ex; width: 84.419ex; height: 13.95ex;" id="img_images_1597.svg"></span></p>

<p>The proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu \in \text{NC}.\supset .\mu  +_{\text{c}} 1=\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,y).\gamma \in \mu .y{\sim}\in \gamma .\xi \text{ sm }\gamma \cup \iota ʻy\} \]" src="images/1598.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.172ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1598.svg"></span>
which might at first sight seem demonstrable, will only be true
universally if the total number of objects in any one type
is not finite. For suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_144"> is a type, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1599.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.876ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1599.svg">.
Then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_145"> is a finite class, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu =\iota ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1600.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.988ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1600.svg">. Hence
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \in \mu . \supset _{\gamma ,y}. y\in \gamma\)" src="images/1601.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 16.519ex; height: 1.907ex;" id="img_images_1601.svg">. Hence
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\xi} \{(\exists \gamma ,y).\gamma \in \mu .y{\sim}\in \gamma.\xi \text{ sm }(\gamma \cup \iota ʻy)\}=\Lambda\)" src="images/1602.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.11ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1602.svg">
in all types. But <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{\text{c}} 1\)" src="images/1603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.159ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_1603.svg"> will exist in all types higher
than that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_17">. If on the other hand the number of entities in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_146"> is infinite, we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ y\in \alpha .\supset .\alpha -\iota ʻy\in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .y{\sim}\in \alpha -\iota ʻy. \]" src="images/1604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 39.599ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1604.svg"></span>
Hence in this case the above proposition will be true universally.</p>

less.</p>

<p>The above proof depends upon the fact that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_59">"

and therefore, when they are asserted to be equal, this must
hold in any type, and therefore, in particular, in that type for
which we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/798.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.721ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_798.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i> for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_864.svg_10">. This is why the use of <a href="#_100_3" class="pginternal">*100·3</a> is
legitimate.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_88">[Pg 88]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_111">
*111. DOUBLE SIMILARITY.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *111.</p>

<p>The arithmetical properties of a class, so far as these do not require
or assume that it is a class of classes, are the same for any similar
class. But a class of classes has many arithmetical properties
which it does not share with all similar classes of classes. For
example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_42"> is a class of classes, the number of members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_5"> is an arithmetical property of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_43">, but it
is obvious that this is not determined by the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_44">, but requires also a knowledge of the numbers of members
of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_45">. For example, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_46"> consist of the
two members <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_147"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_91">, and let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_12"> consist
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_18"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_17">. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \text{ sm } \lambda\)" src="images/1619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 6.529ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1619.svg">;
but in order to be able to infer <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa \text{ sm } sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1620.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.367ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1620.svg">,
we require <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_47">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/1621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.059ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_1621.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \text{ sm } \gamma .\beta \text{ sm } \delta\)" src="images/1622.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 13.782ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_1622.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \text{ sm } \delta .\beta \text{ sm } \gamma\)" src="images/1623.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 13.782ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_1623.svg"> or some such further
datum. The relation of "double similarity," to be defined in the
present number, is a relation between classes of classes, which,
when it holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_48"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_13">, insures that all
the arithmetical properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_49"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_14"> are the
same, <i>e.g.</i> we have (in particular) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻsʻ\kappa =\text{Nc}ʻsʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1624.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.594ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1624.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta }ʻ\kappa=\text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta }ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.531ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1625.svg">.
This relation we denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\, \text{sm}\)" src="images/1626.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.93ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_1626.svg">," which is to be
read as one symbol. It is defined as follows: We define first the class
of "double correlators" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_50"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_15">, which we denote
by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \overline{\text{ sm }}\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda\)" src="images/1627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 11.192ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_1627.svg">,"
and of which the definition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*111·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \overline{\text{ sm }}\, \overline{\text{ sm }} \lambda =(1\rightarrow 1)\cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻsʻ\lambda \cap \hat{T} (\kappa =T_{\in }ʻʻ\lambda     ) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.727ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_1628.svg"></p>

<p>so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :T\in \kappa \overline{\text{ sm }}\, \overline{\text{ sm }} \lambda .\equiv .T\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻT=sʻ\lambda .\kappa =T_{\in }ʻʻ\lambda . \]" src="images/1629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 55.982ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1629.svg"></span></p>

<p>We then define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda\)" src="images/1457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 10.437ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1457.svg_1">" as meaning
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \overline{\text{ sm }}\, \overline{\text{ sm }} \lambda\)" src="images/1630.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 10.814ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_1630.svg"> is
not null, <i>i.e.</i> that there is at least one double correlator of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_51"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_16">.</p>

<p>To illustrate the nature of a double correlator, let us suppose that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_52"> consists of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{1}\)" src="images/1377.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1377.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha_{2}\)" src="images/1631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1631.svg">,
and that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{1}\)" src="images/1377.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1377.svg_3"> consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{11}\)" src="images/1632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 3.082ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1632.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{12}\)" src="images/1633.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 3.082ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1633.svg">,
while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha _{2}\)" src="images/1378.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1378.svg_2"> consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{21}\)" src="images/1634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 3.082ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1634.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{22}\)" src="images/1635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 3.082ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1635.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{23}\)" src="images/1636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 3.082ex; height: 1.375ex;" id="img_images_1636.svg">.
Similarly let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_17"> consist of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta _{1}\)" src="images/1637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.268ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1637.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta _{2}\)" src="images/1638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.268ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1638.svg">
while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta _{1}\)" src="images/1637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.268ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1637.svg_1"> consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{11}\)" src="images/1639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.896ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1639.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{12}\)" src="images/1640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.896ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1640.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta_{2}\)" src="images/1641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.268ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1641.svg">
consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{21}\)" src="images/1642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.896ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1642.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{22}\)" src="images/1643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.896ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1643.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y_{23}\)" src="images/1644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.896ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1644.svg">. Now let <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_1">
correlate each <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_22"> with the <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_5"> having the same two suffixes.
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_2"> is a one-one, and its converse domain is <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_3">.
Moreover <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }ʻ\beta _{1}\)" src="images/1645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.202ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1645.svg"> (which is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Tʻʻ\beta _{1}\)" src="images/1646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.576ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1646.svg">) = <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha_{1}\)" src="images/1647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.436ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1647.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }ʻ\beta _{2}=\alpha _{2}\)" src="images/1648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.655ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1648.svg">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in}ʻʻ\lambda =\kappa\)" src="images/1649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.93ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1649.svg">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_3"> is a double correlator according to
the definition.</p>

<p>The essential characteristic of a double correlator <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_4"> is that
(1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_5"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_4">, (2)
<img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/1650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.095ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1650.svg"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_53"> and
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_89">[Pg 89]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_18">. If we write <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_3"> in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/1651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.095ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1651.svg">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in \lambda\)" src="images/1652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1652.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta \in \kappa\)" src="images/1653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.166ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1653.svg">; moreover <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/1654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.074ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1654.svg"> is a correlator of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_92">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_54"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_19"> are similar
classes of similar classes. They are not merely this, however, for
we not only know that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg_2"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_93">, but we
know a particular correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_94">, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(T\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/1654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.074ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1654.svg_1">. This is essential to the use of double
similarity, as will appear shortly.</p>

<p>Let us consider the relation between <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_55"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_20"> which
consists in their being similar classes of similar classes. This means
that there is a correlator <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_4"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_56"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_21">, such
that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in \lambda\)" src="images/1652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1652.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg_4"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_95">.
That is to say, we are to consider the hypothesis
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻS=\kappa .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\lambda .S \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  \text{ sm } \]" src="images/1655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.987ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1655.svg"></span>
or, as it may be more briefly expressed,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !\kappa \overline{\text{ sm }} \lambda \cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{ sm }. \]" src="images/1656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.119ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1656.svg"></span>
Let us assume <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in \kappa \overline{\text{ sm }} \lambda \cap\text{ᗡ}ʻʻʻ\text{ sm }\)" src="images/1657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.606ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1657.svg">.
If we attempt to prove (say) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_7"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_5">, we find that we are forced to assume the multiplicative
axiom, unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_57"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_22"> are finite. This necessity
arises as follows. Let us put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Crp}(S)ʻ\beta =(Sʻ\beta )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \beta , \]" src="images/1658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.083ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1658.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}\)" src="images/1434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.778ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1434.svg_1">" stands for "correspondence." Then we know that
whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in \lambda\)" src="images/1652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1652.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}(S)ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.636ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1435.svg_1"> is not null.
Further it is easy to prove that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_58"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_23"> are
classes of mutually exclusive classes, and if we can pick out one
representative member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}(S)ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.636ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1435.svg_2"> for each value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_96"> which is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_24">, then the relational sum
of all these representative correlations gives us a correlator of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_6">. That is, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\kappa ,\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.S\in \kappa \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻʻʻ\text{ sm }.R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda     .\supset .\dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻR\in (sʻ\kappa )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (sʻ\lambda ). \]" src="images/1659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 92.315ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_1659.svg"></span></p>

<p>But in order to infer hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa \text{ sm } sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1620.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.367ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1620.svg_1">, we need
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.305ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1660.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> we need
to be able to pick out a particular correlator for each pair of similar
classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg_5"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_97">. This, however, cannot be done in
general without assuming the multiplicative axiom. It follows that we
must not define two classes as having double similarity when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\kappa \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda \cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{ sm }\)" src="images/1661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.245ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1661.svg">,
but must give a definition which enables us to specify a particular
correlator for each pair of similar classes. This is what is effected
by the above definition of double correlators, where our <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_5"> is given
as of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/1650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.095ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1650.svg_1">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(T\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻT =sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.832ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1662.svg">. If the multiplicative
axiom is assumed, but in general not otherwise, we have (<a href="#_111_5" class="pginternal">*111·5</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa ,\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset :\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda .\equiv .\exists !\kappa \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda \cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{ sm }. \]" src="images/1663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.475ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_1663.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the present number, we shall begin with various properties of
double correlators. We prove (<a href="#_111_11" class="pginternal">*111·11</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_6"> is a double
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_59"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_25"> when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_7">
is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_7">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in}\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/1664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.095ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1664.svg">
is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_60"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_26">. We prove (<a href="#_111_112" class="pginternal">*111·112</a>)
that in the same hypothesis, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }\upharpoonright \lambda \in\kappa \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda \cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{ sm }\)" src="images/1665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.22ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1665.svg">.
We prove (<a href="#_111_13" class="pginternal">*111·13</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\upharpoonright sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.069ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1666.svg"> is a double
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_27"> with itself; that (<a href="#_111_131" class="pginternal">*111·131</a>) if <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_8"> is a
double correlator of<span class="pagenum" id="Page_90">[Pg 90]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_61"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_28">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{T}\)" src="images/1667.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 2.4ex;" id="img_images_1667.svg"> is a
double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_29"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_62">; that (<a href="#_111_132" class="pginternal">*111·132</a>) if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_9"> are double correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_63"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_30">
and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_31"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_98"> respectively, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid T\)" src="images/1668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.938ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_1668.svg"> is a
double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_64"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_99">. Hence it follows
(<a href="#_111_45" class="pginternal">*111·45</a><a href="#_111_451" class="pginternal">·451</a><a href="#_111_452" class="pginternal">·452</a>) that double similarity is reflexive, symmetrical, and
transitive.</p>

<p>We then proceed (<a href="#_111_2" class="pginternal">*111·2</a>—<a href="#_111_34" class="pginternal">·34</a>) to consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.032ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1437.svg_1">,
where it is to be supposed that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_7"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.493ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1669.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_32">, and that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg_6"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_98"> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in \lambda\)" src="images/1652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1652.svg_3">. We prove</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*111·32.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}\vdash :\lambda ,Sʻʻ\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.&amp;S\in 1\rightarrow 1.R\in {\in}_{\Delta }ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda     .M = \dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻR.\supset .\\ &amp;M\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻM = sʻ\lambda .Sʻʻ\lambda  = M_{\in }ʻʻ\lambda .S\upharpoonright \lambda  = M_{\in }\upharpoonright \lambda\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1670.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.209ex; width: 78.199ex; height: 5.55ex;" id="img_images_1670.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus in the case supposed, <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg"> is a double correlator of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.493ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1669.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_33">. Thus</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*111·322.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}\vdash :\kappa ,\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.S\in \kappa  \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\,  \lambda .R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Crp}(S)ʻʻ\lambda     .&amp;M = \dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻR.\supset .\\ &amp;M\in \kappa  \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\,  \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\,  \lambda .S = M_{\in }\upharpoonright \lambda\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1672.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.226ex; width: 80.604ex; height: 5.584ex;" id="img_images_1672.svg"></span></p>

<p>We then proceed (<a href="#_111_4" class="pginternal">*111·4</a>—<a href="#_111_47" class="pginternal">·47</a>) to various propositions on "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\,\text{ sm }\)" src="images/1673.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 8.192ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_1673.svg">,"
and finally (<a href="#_111_5" class="pginternal">*111·5</a><a href="#_111_51" class="pginternal">·51</a><a href="#_111_53" class="pginternal">·53</a>) state three propositions which
assume the multiplicative axiom, namely</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*111·5.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_65">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/1621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.059ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_1621.svg_1">,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda . \equiv  .\exists !\kappa  \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\,  \lambda \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻʻʻ\text{ sm }\)" src="images/1674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.233ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1674.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*111·51.</b> In the same case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\kappa\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda \cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{ sm }.\supset .sʻ\kappa\text{ sm } sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1675.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 34.384ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_1675.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_66"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_34"> are similar classes of
mutually exclusive similar classes, their sums are similar.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*111·53.</b> In the same case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_67">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/1621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.059ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_1621.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \lambda\)" src="images/1457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 10.437ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1457.svg_2">. Hence the multiplicative axiom
implies that two classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_100"> mutually exclusive classes each of
which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_64"> terms, have the same number of terms in their sum.</p>

<p>The class <img alt="" data-tex="\((\alpha \uparrow \beta )_{\Delta }ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1704.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.035ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1704.svg"> is important,
being the class of Cantor's "Belegungen," used by him to define
exponentiation; we have in fact
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha  \uparrow  \beta )_{\Delta }ʻ\beta  = (\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\beta }. \]" src="images/1705.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.97ex; height: 2.7ex;" id="img_images_1705.svg"></span>
Thus the above proposition shows that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \beta )\)" src="images/1706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.21ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1706.svg">
is less than or equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\beta}\)" src="images/1707.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.23ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_1707.svg">; and
since, whenever it is not zero, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1708.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1708.svg">,
it is less than or equal to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha }. \]" src="images/1709.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.978ex; height: 2.7ex;" id="img_images_1709.svg"></span></p>
