<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_97">[Pg 97]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_112">
*112. THE ARITHMETICAL SUM OF A CLASS OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *112.</p>

<p>In this number, we return to the arithmetical operations. The
definition of addition in <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a> was only applicable to a finite number
of summands, because the summands had to be enumerated. In the present
number, we define the arithmetical sum of a class of classes, so that
the summands are given as the members of a class, and do not require to
be enumerated. Hence the definition in this number is as applicable to
an infinite number of summands as to a finite number.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_68"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes, the number of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_10"> will be the sum of the numbers of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_69">;
<i>i.e.</i> if we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_5">" for the sum of
the numbers of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_70">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset .\text{Nc}ʻsʻ\kappa =\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa . \]" src="images/1756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 34.238ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_1756.svg"></span>
But when the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_71"> are not mutually exclusive, a
term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_23"> which is a member of two members (say <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_148"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_99">) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_72"> has to be counted twice over in obtaining
the arithmetical sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_73">, whereas in the logical sum <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_24"> is
only counted once. Thus we need a construction which shall duplicate
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_25">, taking it first as a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_149">, and then as a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_100">. This is effected if we replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_26"> first by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow \alpha\)" src="images/1348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.13ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1348.svg_1">, and then by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow \beta\)" src="images/1349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.963ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1349.svg_1">. In fact,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow \alpha\)" src="images/1348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.13ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1348.svg_2"> has the kind of arithmetical properties which
we mean to secure when we speak of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_27"> considered as a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_150">"—a phrase which, as it stands, does not serve our purpose,
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_28"> is simply <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_29"> however we may choose to consider it. Thus we
replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_151"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow \alphaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.371ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1757.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_101"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow \betaʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.036ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1758.svg"> and so on; <i>i.e.</i> (using *85·5), we
replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_152"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in \unicode{x21A7}\alpha\)" src="images/1759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.943ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1759.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_102"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\in \unicode{x21A7}\beta\)" src="images/1760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1760.svg"> and so on. These new classes are similar
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_153"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_103"> and so on, and are mutually exclusive.
Hence their <i>logical</i> sum has the number of terms which is wanted
for the <i>arithmetical</i> sum of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_74">. Thus we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \Sigma ʻ\kappa &amp;=sʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa   &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa &amp;=\text{Nc}ʻ\Sigma ʻ\kappa   &amp;\quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1761.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 30.41ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1761.svg"></span></p>

<p>With regard to the second of these definitions, it is to be
observed that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_6"> is not a function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1360.svg_3">, unless no two members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_75"> are similar;
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.719ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1360.svg_4"> cannot contain the same number twice over.
For the same reason, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_35"> is a class of cardinals, and we
define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Sum}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1762.svg">," we do not get what<span class="pagenum" id="Page_98">[Pg 98]</span> is wanted for
arithmetical addition, because our definition will not enable us to
deal with summations in which there are numbers that are repeated.
We could, if it were worth while, define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Sum}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1762.svg_1">" as
follows: Take a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_76">, consisting of one class
having each number which is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_36">, <i>i.e.</i> let
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_77"> be a selection from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_37">; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.294ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1357.svg_2">
will have the required number of terms. <i>i.e.</i> we might put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Sum}ʻ\lambda  = \hat{\xi} \{(\exists \kappa ).\kappa \in \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda .\xi \text{ sm }\Sigma ʻ\kappa\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.404ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1763.svg"></span>
But since this definition is only available for sums in which no number
is repeated, it is not worth while to introduce it.</p>

<p>In this number we prove the following propositions among others.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset .sʻ\kappa \in \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.938ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_1764.svg"></p>

<p>This is an extension of <a href="#_110_32" class="pginternal">*110·32</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\kappa \text{ sm }\text{ sm }\lambda .\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa  = \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\lambda .\Sigma ʻ\kappa \text{ sm }\Sigma ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 47.39ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1765.svg"></p>

<p>The chief point in the above proposition is that it does not require
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_78">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/1621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.059ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_1621.svg_3">.</p>

<p><a href="#_112_2" class="pginternal">*112·2</a>—<a href="#_112_24" class="pginternal">·24</a> are concerned with the use of the multiplicative axiom and
the propositions of <a href="#_111" class="pginternal">*111</a> in which it appears as hypothesis. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·22.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  \text{Mult ax}.\supset :\exists !(\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\lambda )\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{ sm }.\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa  = \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.133ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1766.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence we derive the proposition</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\kappa ,\lambda \in \mu \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\nu .\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa  = \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 61.711ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1767.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> assuming the multiplicative axiom, two classes which
each consist of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_101"> classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_65"> terms each have the same
number of terms in their sum. This number would naturally be defined
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_102"> multiplied by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_66">, but owing to the necessity of the
multiplicative axiom in this proposition, we have selected a different
definition of multiplication (<a href="#_113" class="pginternal">*113</a>) which does not depend upon the
multiplicative axiom. The reader should observe that the similarity
of two classes, each of which consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_103"> mutually exclusive
sets of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_67"> terms, cannot be proved in general without the
multiplicative axiom.</p>

<p>The remaining propositions of this number give properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg">
in special cases. We prove that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻ\Lambda = \Lambda\)" src="images/1769.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.148ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1769.svg"> (<a href="#_112_3" class="pginternal">*112·3</a>),
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻ\alpha = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.823ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1770.svg"> (<a href="#_112_321" class="pginternal">*112·321</a>),
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \beta .\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup\iota ʻ\beta ) = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha +_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1771.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.04ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1771.svg"> (<a href="#_112_34" class="pginternal">*112·34</a>),
which connects the definition of addition in this number with that in
<a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>. Finally we prove the general associative law for addition, in the
following two forms:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .sʻ\Sigma ʻʻ\lambda  = \Sigma ʻsʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.22ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1772.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\Sigma ʻ\Sigma ʻʻ\lambda  = \text{Nc}ʻ\Sigma ʻsʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.993ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_1773.svg"></p>

<p>The following proposition is a lemma for <a href="#_112_153" class="pginternal">*112·153</a>, which is required
for <a href="#_112_16" class="pginternal">*112·16</a>. *112·16 in turn is used in <a href="#_112_17" class="pginternal">*112·17</a>, which is a fundamental
proposition in the theory of addition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_112_152">*112·152</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :T\in 1\rightarrow Cls.\beta \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻT.\supset .(T\parallel \breve{T} _{\in })ʻʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}\beta  = \in \unicode{x21A7}(Tʻʻ\beta )\)" src="images/1789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.156ex; height: 2.966ex;" id="img_images_1789.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *37·6.*85·601.&amp;\supset \vdash .(T\parallel \breve{T} _{\in })ʻʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}\beta  = \hat{R} \{(\exists y).y\in \beta .R = (T\parallel \breve{T} _{\in })ʻ(y\downarrow     \beta )\} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*55·61.\supset \\ \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .(T\parallel \breve{T} _{\in })ʻʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}\beta  &amp;= \hat{R} \{(\exists y).y\in \beta .R = (Tʻy)\downarrow (T_{\in }ʻ\beta )\}\\ [*37·11] &amp;= \hat{R} \{(\exists y).y\in \beta .R = (Tʻy)\downarrow (Tʻʻ\beta )\}\\ [*38·131] &amp;= \downarrow (Tʻʻ\beta )ʻʻ(Tʻʻ\beta )\\ [*85·601] &amp;= \in \unicode{x21A7}(Tʻʻ\beta ):\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1790.svg" style="vertical-align: -9.528ex; width: 97.566ex; height: 20.188ex;" id="img_images_1790.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the following proposition, we have a double correlator of a sort
which will frequently occur in cardinal arithmetic, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\parallel\breve{T}_{\in }\)" src="images/1791.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.557ex; height: 2.966ex;" id="img_images_1791.svg">
with its converse domain limited, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_11"> is a given double
correlator (or single correlator, on other occasions). As appears from
the propositions used in the above proof of <a href="#_112_152" class="pginternal">*112·152</a>, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_12"> is a
correlator whose converse domain includes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_104"> and has <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_6"> as
a member, <img alt="" data-tex="\((T\parallel \breve{T} _{\in })ʻ(y\downarrow \beta ) =(Tʻy)\downarrow (Tʻʻ\beta )\)" src="images/1792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.785ex; height: 2.966ex;" id="img_images_1792.svg">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\parallel \breve{T}_{\in }\)" src="images/1793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.557ex; height: 2.966ex;" id="img_images_1793.svg"> is an operation which, when
operating on suitable relations of individuals to classes (including
selectors), turns the individuals into their correlates and the classes
into the classes of their members' correlates. This is why it is a
useful relation.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_112_153">*112·153</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\in \kappa \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \lambda .\supset .(T\parallel \breve{T} _{\in })\upharpoonright     sʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\lambda \in (\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\lambda )\)" src="images/1794.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.826ex; height: 2.966ex;" id="img_images_1794.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition establishes the agreement of the two definitions of
addition, namely that in <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a> and that in <a href="#_112" class="pginternal">*112</a>. It will be seen that
the definition of *112 is inapplicable to the addition of a class to
itself, if this is to give the double of the class, instead of (like
logical addition) simply reproducing the class. Hence the need of the
condition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\neq \beta\)" src="images/1831.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_1831.svg"> in the above proposition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·341.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \beta  {\sim} \in  \kappa  . \supset  . \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ(\kappa  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta ) = \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa  +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1832.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.229ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1832.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *51·211 . \supset  \vdash  : \text{Hp} . &amp;\supset  . \kappa  \cap  \iota ʻ\beta  = \Lambda  .\\ [*112·311] \supset  . \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ(\kappa  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta ) &amp;= \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa  +_{c} \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻ\beta \\ [*112·321] &amp;= \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa  +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  : \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1833.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 59.77ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1833.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·35.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \alpha  \neq  \beta  . \alpha  \neq  \gamma  . \beta  \neq  \gamma  . \supset  . \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta  \cup  \iota ʻ\gamma ) = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/1834.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 74.746ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1834.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *51·231 . *112·311 . \supset \\ \vdash  : \text{Hp} . \supset  . \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta  \cup  \iota ʻ\gamma ) &amp;= \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta ) +_{c}     \Sigma  \text{Nc}ʻ\iota ʻ\gamma \\ [*112·34·321] &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  +_{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma  : \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1835.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 70.58ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1835.svg"></span></p>

<p>Similar propositions can obviously be proved for any finite number of
summands.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_104">[Pg 104]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :sʻ\kappa ,sʻʻ\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻsʻ\kappa  = \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻsʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1836.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 50.162ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_1836.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*112·15.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻsʻ\kappa  &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻsʻsʻ\kappa \\ [*42·1] &amp;= \text{Nc}ʻsʻsʻʻ\kappa \\ [*112·15] &amp;= \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻsʻʻ\kappa :\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1837.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 58.254ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1837.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*112·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .sʻ\Sigma ʻʻ\lambda  = \Sigma ʻsʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.22ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1772.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*112·1.\supset \vdash .sʻ\Sigma ʻʻ\lambda  &amp;= sʻsʻʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻʻ\lambda \\ [*42·1] &amp;= sʻsʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻʻ\lambda \\ [*40·38] &amp;= sʻ\in \unicode{x21A7}ʻʻsʻ\lambda\\ [*112·1] &amp;= \Sigma ʻsʻ\lambda .\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1838.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 44.522ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_1838.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above is the associative law for arithmetical addition.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_105">[Pg 105]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_113">
*113. ON THE ARITHMETICAL PRODUCT OF TWO CLASSES OR OF
TWO CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *113.</p>

<p>In this number, we give a definition of multiplication which can be
extended to any finite number of factors, but not to an infinite
number of factors. We define first the arithmetical class-product of
two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_154"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_105">, and thence the product of two
cardinals <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_104"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_68"> as the number of terms in the product
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_155"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_106"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_156"> has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_105"> terms and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_107"> has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_69"> terms. In <a href="#_114" class="pginternal">*114</a>, we shall give a definition of
multiplication which is not restricted to a finite number of factors.
The advantages of the definition to be given in this number are, that
it does not require the factors to be of the same type, and that
it enables us to multiply a class by itself without (as in logical
addition and multiplication) simply reproducing the class in question.
The disadvantage of the definition in this number is the impossibility
of extending it to an infinite number of factors.</p>

<p>The arithmetical class-product of two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_157"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_108">,
which we denote by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_1"><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_5" id="FNanchor_5">[5]</a>, is the class of all
ordinal couples which take their referent from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_158"> and their
relatum from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_109">, <i>i.e.</i> it is the class of all such
relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1842.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \alpha\)" src="images/1205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1205.svg_1"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\beta\)" src="images/1843.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1843.svg">. For a given <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_7">, the class of couples we obtain is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1844.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.031ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1844.svg">, which is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_159">; and the
number of such classes, for varying <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_8">, is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_29">. Thus
we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_30"> classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_60"> couples,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_2"> is the logical sum of these classes of
couples. The class of such classes as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1844.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.031ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_1844.svg_1">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in \beta\)" src="images/1845.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1845.svg">, is important again in connection with exponentiation;
we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\alpha =\alpha \downarrow_{,,}y\)" src="images/1846.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 16.07ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1846.svg">, whence the
class of such classes, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_9"> is varied among the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_110">'s, is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_4">, and
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \beta \times \alpha =sʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta   \quad(\text{cf}. *40·7), \]" src="images/1847.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 33.353ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1847.svg"></span>
which we take as the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_3">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_106">[Pg 106]</span></p>

<p>We represent the arithmetical product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_106"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_70"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c}\nu\)" src="images/162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_162.svg_1">. This, as well as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \times_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/1848.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.492ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1848.svg">,
is defined in terms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \times \beta\)" src="images/1849.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1849.svg"> exactly as, in <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>, the
sum was defined in terms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +\beta\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_8">.</p>

<p>The present number contains many propositions which belong to the
theory of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_5"> rather than (specially)
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_4">; and many propositions are rather logical
than arithmetical in their nature, <i>i.e.</i> they might have
been given in *55. The line is, however, so hard to draw that it
has seemed better to deal simultaneously with all propositions on
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_6"> or on its sum, which is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\times \alpha\)" src="images/1850.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1850.svg">.
Thus in the present number, the early propositions,
down to <a href="#_113_118" class="pginternal">*113·118</a>, deal mainly with logical properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1371.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_5">; the following
propositions, down to <a href="#_113_13" class="pginternal">*113·13</a>, deal mainly with arithmetical properties
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_7">; the propositions <a href="#_113_14" class="pginternal">*113·14</a>—<a href="#_113_191" class="pginternal">·191</a>
are concerned mainly with arithmetical properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times\alpha\)" src="images/1851.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1851.svg">;
<a href="#_113_2" class="pginternal">*113·2</a>—<a href="#_113_27" class="pginternal">·27</a> deal with the simpler properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times_{c}\nu\)" src="images/1852.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_1852.svg">;
<a href="#_113_3" class="pginternal">*113·3</a>—<a href="#_113_34" class="pginternal">·34</a> give propositions involving the multiplicative
axiom, and exhibiting the connection (assuming this axiom) of addition
and multiplication; <a href="#_113_4" class="pginternal">*113·4</a>—<a href="#_113_491" class="pginternal">·491</a> are concerned with various forms of
the distributive law; <a href="#_113_5" class="pginternal">*113·5</a>—<a href="#_113_541" class="pginternal">*113·541</a> deal with the associative law of
multiplication, and the remaining propositions deal with multiplication
by 0 or 1 or 2.</p>

<p>The most important propositions in the present number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :R\in \beta \times \alpha .\equiv .(\exists x,y).x\in \alpha .y\in \beta .R=x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1853.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.023ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1853.svg"></p>

<p>This merely embodies the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_6">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·105.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\alpha .\supset .\alpha \downarrow_{,,}.\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/1854.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.957ex; height: 2.27ex;" id="img_images_1854.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is especially useful in dealing with exponentiation
(<a href="#_116" class="pginternal">*116</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·114.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha =\Lambda .\lor.\beta =\Lambda :\equiv .\beta \times \alpha =\Lambda\)" src="images/1855.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 32.924ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1855.svg"></p>

<p>It is in virtue of this proposition that a product of a finite number of
factors only vanishes when one of its factors vanishes.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·118.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ(\beta \times \alpha )\subset \alpha .sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(\beta \times \alpha )\subset \beta\)" src="images/1856.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.019ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1856.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is chiefly useful in the analogous theory of ordinal
products (<a href="#_165" class="pginternal">*165</a>, <a href="#_166" class="pginternal">*166</a>), where it enables us to apply *74·773. Unless
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\Lambda\)" src="images/1857.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.868ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1857.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ(\beta \times \alpha)=\alpha\)" src="images/1858.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.581ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1858.svg">,
and unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =\Lambda ,sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(\beta \times \alpha )=\beta\)" src="images/1859.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.084ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1859.svg"> (<a href="#_113_116" class="pginternal">*113·116</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\alpha .\supset .\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\beta \cap \text{Cl excl}ʻ\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1860.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 42.8ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1860.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_160"> is null, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1371.svg_2">
consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_31"> mutually
exclusive classes each having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_61"> members.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·127.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{aligned}\vdash :R\upharpoonright y\in \alpha \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \gamma .S\upharpoonright \delta \in \beta &amp;\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \delta .\supset .\\ &amp;(R\parallel \breve{S} )\upharpoonright (\delta \times \gamma )\in (\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (\gamma \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\delta     )\end{aligned}\]" src="images/1861.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.479ex; width: 76.706ex; height: 6.089ex;" id="img_images_1861.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_107">[Pg 107]</span></p>

<p>This is an important proposition, since it gives a double
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_8"> with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\delta\)" src="images/1862.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.413ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1862.svg"> whenever simple correlators of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_161"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_19"> and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_111"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_18"> are given.
It leads at once to</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \alpha  \text{ sm } \gamma  . \beta  \text{ sm } \delta  . \supset  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } \gamma  \downarrow_{,,}     ʻʻ\delta  . (\beta  \times  \alpha ) \text{ sm } (\delta  \times  \gamma )\)" src="images/1863.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 64.257ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1863.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is fundamental in the theory of multiplication, since
it shows that the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \times \alpha\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg_7"> depends
only upon the numbers of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_162"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_112">. It is
also fundamental in the theory of exponentiation, as will appear in
<a href="#_116" class="pginternal">*116</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha  \times  \beta ) = \text{Nc}ʻ(\beta  \times  \alpha )\)" src="images/1864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.032ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1864.svg"></p>

<p>This is the source of the commutative law of multiplication (<a href="#_113_27" class="pginternal">*113·27</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·146.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \alpha  \neq  \beta  . \supset  . \alpha  \times  \beta  \text{ sm } {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta )\)" src="images/1865.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.266ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1865.svg"></p>

<p>This connects our present theory of multiplication with the theory of
selections.</p>

<p>We come next to propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} \nu\)" src="images/171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_171.svg_1">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·204.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  \colon\ldotp  \mu  = \Lambda  . \lor . \nu  = \Lambda  . \lor . {\sim} (\mu , \nu  \in  \text{NC}) : \supset  . \mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \Lambda\)" src="images/1866.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.181ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1866.svg"></p>

<p>The use of this proposition, like that of <a href="#_110_4" class="pginternal">*110·4</a>, is for avoiding
trivial exceptions.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \mu  \times _{c} \nu  \in  \text{NC}\)" src="images/1867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.694ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1867.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma  \times _{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\delta  = \text{Nc}ʻ(\gamma  \times  \delta )\)" src="images/1868.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.22ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1868.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition enables us to infer propositions on products of
cardinals from propositions on products of classes, and is therefore
constantly used.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·27.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \nu  \times _{c} \mu\)" src="images/1869.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 17.825ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1869.svg"></p>

<p>This is the commutative law of cardinal multiplication.</p>

<p>The chief proposition using the multiplicative axiom is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  \colon\ldotp  \text{Mult ax} . \supset  : \mu , \nu  \in  \text{NC} . \kappa  \in  \nu  \cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\mu  . \supset  . \Sigma ʻ\kappa  \in  \mu  \times _{c}     \nu\)" src="images/1870.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 55.632ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1870.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> assuming the multiplicative axiom, the sum of the numbers
of members in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_71"> classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_107"> terms is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c}\nu\)" src="images/162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_162.svg_2">.
If we had taken this sum as <i>defining</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c}\nu\)" src="images/162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_162.svg_3">,
almost all propositions on multiplication would have required
the multiplicative axiom. The advantage of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_9">
is that, given <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \text{ sm } \gamma\)" src="images/1871.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.584ex; height: 1.502ex;" id="img_images_1871.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\text{ sm } \delta\)" src="images/1872.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.192ex; height: 2.061ex;" id="img_images_1872.svg">,
we can construct a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1873.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1873.svg">
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\delta \)" src="images/1874.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.413ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1874.svg">, without using the
multiplicative axiom. This is proved in <a href="#_113_127" class="pginternal">*113·127</a> (mentioned above).</p>

<p>The distributive law, which is next considered, has various forms. We
have, to begin with,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . (\beta  \cup  \gamma ) \times  \alpha  = (\beta  \times  \alpha ) \cup  (\gamma  \times  \alpha )\)" src="images/1875.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.374ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1875.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence, using also the commutative law, we easily deduce</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . (\nu  +_{c} \varpi ) \times _{c} \mu  = \mu  \times _{c} (\nu  +_{c} \varpi ) = (\mu  \times _{c} \nu ) +_{c}     (\mu  \times _{c} \varpi )\)" src="images/1876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.661ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1876.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_108">[Pg 108]</span></p>

<p>But the distributive law also holds when, instead of enumerated
summands <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_113">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_20"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_72">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varpi\)" src="images/274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.873ex; height: 0.998ex;" id="img_images_274.svg_3">, the summands are
given as the members of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_79">, which may be infinite. We
have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·48.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . sʻ\alpha  \times  ʻʻ\kappa  = \alpha  \times  sʻ\kappa  = \text{Cnv}ʻʻ(sʻ\kappa  \times  \alpha )\)" src="images/1877.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.505ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1877.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence, using the definitions of <a href="#_112" class="pginternal">*112</a>, we find</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·491.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \kappa  \in  \text{Cls}^{2}     \text{excl} . \supset  . \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \times  ʻʻ\kappa  = \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha  \times  \Sigma ʻ\kappa ) = \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \times _{c} \Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.889ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_1878.svg"></p>

<p>This is an extension of the distributive law to the case where the
number of summands may be infinite.</p>

<p>The associative law</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·54.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . (\mu  \times _{c} \nu ) x_{c} \varpi  = \mu  \times _{c} (\nu  \times _{c} \varpi )\)" src="images/1879.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.912ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1879.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">is proved without any difficulty.</p>

<p>We prove next that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} \nu = 0\)" src="images/1880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.358ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_1880.svg"> when, and only when,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = 0\)" src="images/1881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.513ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_1881.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu = 0\)" src="images/1882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.347ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_1882.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_108">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_73"> being existent cardinals
(<a href="#_113_602" class="pginternal">*113·602</a>); that a cardinal is unchanged when it is multiplied by 1
(<a href="#_113_62" class="pginternal">*113·62</a><a href="#_113_621" class="pginternal">·621</a>); that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} 2 = \mu +_{c} \mu\)" src="images/1883.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.533ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_1883.svg"> (<a href="#_113_66" class="pginternal">*113·66</a>) and
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times _{c} (\nu + 1) = (\mu \times _{c} \nu ) +_{c} \mu\)" src="images/1884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.864ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1884.svg"> (<a href="#_113_671" class="pginternal">*113·671</a>).</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*113·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta  \times  \alpha  = sʻ\alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 24.522ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1885.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_113_03">*113·03</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \hat{\xi}  \{(\exists \alpha , \beta ) . \mu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  . \nu  \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta      . \xi  \text{ sm } (\alpha  \times  \beta )\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1886.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.489ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_1886.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_113_04">*113·04</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta  \times _{c} \mu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  \times _{c} \mu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1887.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.388ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1887.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_113_05">*113·05</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  \times _{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  = \mu  \times _{c} \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.723ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_1888.svg"></p>

<p>In relation to types, <a href="#_113_03" class="pginternal">*113·03</a><a href="#_113_04" class="pginternal">·04</a><a href="#_113_05" class="pginternal">·05</a> call for similar remarks to those
made in <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a> for addition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \beta  \times  \alpha  = sʻ\alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta  \quad[(*113·02)]\)" src="images/1889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 35.929ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1889.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : R \in  \beta  \times  \alpha  . \equiv  . (\exists x, y) . x \in \alpha  . y \in  \beta  . R = x\downarrow y \quad[*40·7 . *113·1]\)" src="images/1890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.999ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1890.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·102.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : y \in  \beta  . \supset  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} y = (\alpha  \uparrow  \beta )_{\Delta }ʻ\iota ʻy\)" src="images/1891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 33.628ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1891.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *35·103 . \supset \\ \vdash  \colon\ldotp  \text{Hp} . \supset  : x (\alpha  \uparrow  \beta ) y . \equiv  . x \in  \alpha  :\\ [*85·51] \supset  : (\alpha  \uparrow  \beta )_{\Delta }ʻ\iota ʻy = \downarrow  yʻʻ\alpha \\ [(*38·03)] = \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} y : \supset  \vdash  . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1892.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.359ex; width: 34.636ex; height: 11.849ex;" id="img_images_1892.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_113_103">*113·103</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta  = (\alpha  \uparrow  \beta )_{\Delta }ʻʻ\iotaʻʻ\beta      = (\alpha  \uparrow  \beta ) \unicode{x21A7} ʻʻ\beta  \quad[*113·102 . *85·52]\)" src="images/1893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 66.84ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1893.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_109">[Pg 109]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·104.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{E}! \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻy \quad[*38·12]\)" src="images/1894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.748ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1894.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·105.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \exists  ! \alpha  . \supset  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} \in  1 \rightarrow  1\)" src="images/1895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 21.951ex; height: 2.27ex;" id="img_images_1895.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *113·104. *71·166 . &amp;\supset  \vdash  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls}  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash  . *38·131. \supset  \vdash  : \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻy = \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻz . x \in  \alpha  . &amp;\supset  . x \downarrow  y \in  \alpha  \downarrow_{,,}     ʻz .\\ [*38·131]  &amp;\supset  . (\exists xʻ) . xʻ \in  \alpha  . x \downarrow  y = xʻ \downarrow  z.\\ [*55·202] &amp;\supset  . y = z  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash  .(2). *10·11·23·35. &amp;\supset  \vdash  : \exists  ! \alpha .\alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻy = \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻz . \supset  . y = z  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash  .(1).(3). *71·54. \supset  \vdash . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1896.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.61ex; width: 88.681ex; height: 18.352ex;" id="img_images_1896.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·106.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : x \in  \alpha  . y \in  \beta  . \supset  . x \downarrow  y \in  \beta  \times  \alpha       \quad[*113·101]\)" src="images/1897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.206ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1897.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·107.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \exists  ! \alpha  . \exists  ! \beta  . \supset  . \exists  ! \beta  \times  \alpha  \quad [*113·106]\)" src="images/1898.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.375ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1898.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \exists  ! \alpha  . \supset  . \alpha   \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta  \in  \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  : (y) . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} y \in  \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 46.816ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1899.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash  . *113·105·104 . *73·26 . &amp;\supset  \vdash  : \exists  ! \alpha  . \supset  . \alpha   \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta  \text{ sm } \beta  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash  . *38·2. *73·611. &amp; \supset  \vdash  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} y \text{ sm } \alpha  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash  . (1) . (2) . &amp;\supset  \vdash  .  \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1900.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.817ex; width: 63.44ex; height: 8.766ex;" id="img_images_1900.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·111.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \alpha  \downarrow_{,,} ʻʻ\beta  \in  \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}  \quad[*113·103 . *85·55]\)" src="images/1901.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 43.407ex; height: 2.693ex;" id="img_images_1901.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_112">[Pg 112]</span></p>

<p><i>Note to</i> <a href="#_113_144" class="pginternal">*113·144</a>. In virtue of <a href="#_113_143" class="pginternal">*113·143</a> and *55·61 we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash  \colon\ldotp  \text{Hp} *113·144.\supset :PTR. \equiv  .R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup \iota ʻ\beta ).P = (R\parallel \breve{R} )ʻ(\alpha  \downarrow  \beta ). \]" src="images/1931.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.322ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_1931.svg"></span></p>

<p>At a later stage (in <a href="#_150" class="pginternal">*150</a>) we shall put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\dagger S = (R\parallel \breve{R} )ʻS \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1932.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.915ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_1932.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus we shall have, anticipating this notation,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash  : \text{Hp} *113·144.\supset .T = \{\dagger(\alpha \downarrow \beta )\}\upharpoonright {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta ). \]" src="images/1933.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.467ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1933.svg"></span></p>

<p>Hence we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\alpha  \neq  \beta .\supset .\{\dagger(\alpha \downarrow \beta )\}\upharpoonright {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\iota     ʻ\alpha  \cup  \iota ʻ\beta )\in (\beta  \times  \alpha )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup \iota ʻ\beta ). \]" src="images/1934.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.228ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1934.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_117">[Pg 117]</span></p>

<p>This proposition constitutes part of the reason for our definitions. It
is obvious that such definitions ought, if possible, to be chosen as
will yield this proposition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·251.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\gamma  \times  \delta \in \text{Nc}ʻ\gamma  \times _{c} \text{Nc}ʻ\delta  \quad[*113·25.*100·3]\)" src="images/1986.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.017ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1986.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_113_26">*113·26</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\exists !\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu .\supset .\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu      \times _{c} \text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu\)" src="images/1987.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 70.2ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_1987.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*37·29. \text{Transp}.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset .\exists !\mu .\exists !\nu .\\ [*102·64] &amp;\supset .(\exists \alpha ,\beta ,\gamma ,\delta ).\mu  = \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\gamma .\nu  = \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\delta &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*102·88.&amp;\supset \vdash :\mu  = \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\gamma .\nu  = \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\delta .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu .\supset .\\ &amp;\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu  = \text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\gamma .\text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu  = \text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\delta .\exists !\text{Nc}(\eta )ʻ\gamma .\exists !\text{Nc}(\zeta )ʻ\delta  .\\ [*113·221]&amp;\supset .\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu  \times _{c} \text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu  = \text{Nc}ʻ(\gamma  \times  \delta ) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*37·29.\text{Transp}.*113·221.\supset \\ \vdash :\mu  &amp;= \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\gamma .\nu  = \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\delta .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\zeta }ʻʻ\nu .\supset .\mu  \times _{c}     \nu  = \text{Nc}ʻ(\gamma  \times  \delta ) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(2).(3).\supset \vdash :\mu  &amp;= \text{Nc}(\alpha )ʻ\gamma .\nu  = \text{Nc}(\beta )ʻ\delta .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\varsigma }ʻʻ\nu     .\supset .\\&amp;\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\mu  \times _{c} \text{ sm }_{\varsigma }ʻʻ\nu  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .(4).*11·11·35·45.(1).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1988.svg" style="vertical-align: -15.177ex; width: 118.348ex; height: 31.485ex;" id="img_images_1988.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*113·261.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\supset .\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \mu ^{(1)} \times _{c} \nu ^{(1)} = \mu _{(00)} \times _{c}     \nu _{(00}) = \text{etc}.\)" src="images/1989.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 58.098ex; height: 2.821ex;" id="img_images_1989.svg"></p>

<p>Here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{etc}\)" src="images/1990.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.889ex; height: 1.416ex;" id="img_images_1990.svg">." includes all ascending derivatives of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_110">.
We shall only prove the result for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.597ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_514.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu ^{(1)}\)" src="images/1042.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.549ex; height: 2.021ex;" id="img_images_1042.svg_1">,
since it is proved in just the same way for the other cases.
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{(1)} \times _{c} \nu ^{(2)}\)" src="images/1991.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.791ex; height: 2.51ex;" id="img_images_1991.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^{(1)} \times _{c} \nu_{(00)}\)" src="images/1992.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 11.393ex; height: 2.821ex;" id="img_images_1992.svg">
or etc. will serve equally well; <i>i.e.</i> it is not necessary to
take the same derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_111"> as of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_74">.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*104·264·265.\supset \\ \vdash :\text{Hp}.\exists !\mu .\exists !\nu .\supset .\mu ^{(1)} = \text{ sm }_{\mu }ʻʻ\mu .\nu ^{(1)} = \text{ sm }_{\nu }ʻʻ\mu .\exists !\mu ^{(1)}.\exists     !\nu ^{(1)}.\\ [*113·26] \supset :\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \mu ^{(1)} \times _{c} \nu ^{(1)} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*104·264.*113·204.\supset\\ \vdash :{\sim}(\exists !\mu .\exists !\nu ).\supset .\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \Lambda .\mu ^{(1)} \times _{c} \nu ^{(1)} = \Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1993.svg" style="vertical-align: -9.03ex; width: 73.301ex; height: 19.192ex;" id="img_images_1993.svg"></span></p>

<p>As appears in the above proof, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{i}\)" src="images/1994.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.104ex; height: 2.367ex;" id="img_images_1994.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota^{j}\)" src="images/1995.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.648ex; height: 1.901ex;" id="img_images_1995.svg"> are any
derivatives of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_112"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_75">, the above proposition holds
provided we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !\mu .\exists !\nu .\supset .\exists !\mu^{i}.\exists !\nu^{j} . \]" src="images/1996.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 20.791ex; height: 2.481ex;" id="img_images_1996.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus it holds for all ascending derivatives, but not always for
descending derivatives.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_113_27">*113·27</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \nu  \times _{c} \mu\)" src="images/1997.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 17.825ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1997.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*113·2·141.\supset \\ \vdash :\xi \in \mu  \times _{c} \nu . &amp;\equiv  .(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\xi \text{ sm }(\beta  \times  \alpha ).\\ [*113·2] &amp;\equiv .\xi \in \nu  \times _{c} \mu :\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1998.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 66.725ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1998.svg"></span></p>

<p>Note that this proposition is not confined to the case in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_113">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_76"> are cardinals. When either or both are not cardinals,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu  \times _{c} \nu  = \Lambda  = \nu  \times _{c} \mu . \]" src="images/1999.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 20.652ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_1999.svg"></span></p>

distributive law, when the summands are not enumerated, but given as

arithmetical class-multiplication and logical addition of classes.</p>
