<p>After the proposition (<a href="#_116_36" class="pginternal">*116·36</a>) already quoted, on the connection of
exponentiation and multiplication, we proceed to a set of propositions
on the case where a number of classes are all given as similar (by
assignable correlations) to a given class. In <a href="#_116_411" class="pginternal">*116·411</a>, we prove that
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_95"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes, each of which
is similar to a given class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_26">, and if, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in\kappa\)" src="images/2353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.517ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2353.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻ\alpha\)" src="images/2354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.183ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2354.svg"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_177"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_27">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_15"> is the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/2355.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.396ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2355.svg">, then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{T}ʻʻ\gamma  = \text{Nc}ʻT_{\Delta }ʻ\gamma  = \text{Nc}ʻ(\kappa  \,\text{exp}\,\, \gamma ) = (\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma }. \]" src="images/2356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.138ex; height: 3.742ex;" id="img_images_2356.svg"></span>
This is a further connection of multiplication and exponentiation. (On
the purport of this and following propositions, see the explanation
preceding <a href="#_116_4" class="pginternal">*116·4</a>.) In <a href="#_116_43" class="pginternal">*116·43</a>, the hypothesis is somewhat modified.
We still have a set <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_96"> of classes which are all similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_28">, but the correlator for a given class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_178"> is not
given as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻ\alpha\)" src="images/2354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.183ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2354.svg_1">, but is given as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻw\)" src="images/2357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.355ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2357.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/2358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2358.svg"> is a member
of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_20"> which is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_97">. Then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa =\text{D}ʻʻMʻʻ\delta\)" src="images/2359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.861ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2359.svg">. We assume that <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\upharpoonright \delta\)" src="images/2360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.583ex; height: 2.061ex;" id="img_images_2360.svg"> is a
one-one, and that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻw\)" src="images/2357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.355ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2357.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻv\)" src="images/2361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.833ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2361.svg"> have domains which overlap,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(w = v\)" src="images/2362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.734ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_2362.svg">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_98"> is a class of mutually exclusive
classes, each of which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_283.svg_5"> terms, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_99">
has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\delta\)" src="images/729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.063ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_729.svg_2"> terms. Then it is proved in *116·43 that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Prod}ʻ\text{D}ʻʻMʻʻ\delta  \text{ sm } \text{ sm } (\gamma  \,\text{exp}\,\, \delta ).\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\text{D}ʻʻMʻʻ\delta  = (\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\delta }. \]" src="images/2363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 64.877ex; height: 2.7ex;" id="img_images_2363.svg"></span>
This proposition and another (<a href="#_116_45" class="pginternal">*116·45</a>) which follows from it are useful
in proving the formal laws of exponentiation. The proof of these
occupies the following propositions from <a href="#_116_5" class="pginternal">*116·5</a> to <a href="#_116_68" class="pginternal">*116·68</a>. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*116·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\mu ^\nu  \times _{c} \mu ^{\varpi } = \mu ^{\nu  +_{c} \varpi }\)" src="images/2364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 19.92ex; height: 2.243ex;" id="img_images_2364.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*116·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\mu ^{\varpi } x_{c} \nu ^{\varpi } = (\mu  \times _{c} \nu )^{\varpi }\)" src="images/2365.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.768ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2365.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*116·63.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\mu ^{\nu  \times _{c} \varpi } = (\mu ^\nu )^{\varpi }\)" src="images/2366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.67ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2366.svg"></p>

<p>An extension of the first of these is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*116·661.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ(\alpha  \,\text{exp}\,)ʻʻ\kappa  = (\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha )^{\Sigma \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa }\)" src="images/2367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.001ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_2367.svg"></p>

<p>Here the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_100"> need not be finite. The
purport of the proposition is as follows: Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_128">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_29">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_21">, ... be the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_101">; form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\,\,\text{exp}\,\,\beta\)" src="images/2368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.697ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2368.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \, \,\text{exp}\,\, \gamma\)" src="images/2369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.645ex; height: 1.502ex;" id="img_images_2369.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \,\,\text{exp}\,\, \delta\)" src="images/2370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.421ex; height: 2.061ex;" id="img_images_2370.svg">, ...,
and take the product of the numbers of all these; then the resulting
number is the same as if we first took the sum of the numbers of all
the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_102">, thus obtaining (say) a number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_123">, and
raised <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_64"> to the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_124">th power.</p>

<p>An extension of <a href="#_116_55" class="pginternal">*116·55</a> is given by <a href="#_116_68" class="pginternal">*116·68</a>, where we prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset .\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\,\text{exp}\,\gamma ʻʻ\kappa  = (\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma }. \]" src="images/2371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.062ex; height: 2.7ex;" id="img_images_2371.svg"></span></p>

<p>There is no analogous extension of <a href="#_116_63" class="pginternal">*116·63</a>.</p>

<p>We prove next Cantor's proposition (which is very useful)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*116·72.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  = 2^{\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha }\)" src="images/2372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.745ex; height: 2.474ex;" id="img_images_2372.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the number of combinations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_125"> things any number
at a time is <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^\mu\)" src="images/2373.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.284ex; height: 1.528ex;" id="img_images_2373.svg">. (Observe that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_126"> need not be finite.)
The remainder of the number is concerned with consequences of this
proposition.</p>

<p>This proposition shows that we may raise or lower the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_127">

provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_128"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_83">, or rather <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_15"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\nu\)" src="images/2427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.821ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2427.svg">, exist in the new types.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_152">[Pg 152]</span></p>

<p>In the above proposition, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \in \text{NC}\)" src="images/1546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.295ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_1546.svg_1">" is sufficient
hypothesis as to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_86">, since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \neq \Lambda\)" src="images/2460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.786ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2460.svg">" is implied by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \nu \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\mu\)" src="images/2461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.767ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2461.svg">. But <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \neq \Lambda\)" src="images/2462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.951ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_2462.svg"> is
essential, since if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \Lambda\)" src="images/625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.951ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_625.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu = \Lambda\)" src="images/2463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.987ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_2463.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa= \Lambda\)" src="images/2464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.89ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2464.svg">
(provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu = 0)\)" src="images/2465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.228ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2465.svg">, whence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa = 1\)" src="images/2466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.207ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2466.svg">.</p>

<p>The above proposition connects exponentiation with multiplication.</p>

</figure>

<p>The following propositions, which illustrate certain generalizations
of the relations of rows and columns, may be made clearer by the
accompanying figure, in which, for the sake of simplicity, all the
classes concerned are taken to be finite.</p>

<p>Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_103"> be a set of classes, constituted by four rows of
five dots in the figure, which are each given as similar to a given
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_30">, represented by the top row of five dots in the
figure, namely the row enclosed in an oval. We assume that an actual
correlating relation is given correlating each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_104">
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_31">. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_44"> be the class of these relations, and
assume that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_45"> consists of one correlator for each member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_105">, and that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/2207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.043ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_2207.svg_1">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda = \kappa\)" src="images/2469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.083ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2469.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \lambda . \supset. \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \gamma\)" src="images/2470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 18.252ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2470.svg">.
Put <img alt="" data-tex="\(T = \dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/2471.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.347ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_2471.svg">. Then, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\in \gamma\)" src="images/2472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.047ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2472.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_16">
relates to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_3"> every member of the column below <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_4">, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{T}ʻz\)" src="images/2473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.002ex; height: 3.629ex;" id="img_images_2473.svg"> consists of the four dots which are
vertically below <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_5">; assuming, what in the circumstances is
possible, that each dot is placed below its correlate in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_32">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{T}ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.536ex; height: 3.665ex;" id="img_images_2474.svg"> represents the columns, while
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/2475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.762ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2475.svg"> represents the rows.</p>

<p>We prove, in <a href="#_116_41" class="pginternal">*116·41</a>, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{T}ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.536ex; height: 3.665ex;" id="img_images_2474.svg_1">,
the class of rows, has double similarity with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2476.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.728ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2476.svg">,
or, what comes to the same thing, with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.712ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2477.svg">.
Hence it follows that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Tʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.536ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2478.svg">,
which is the whole class of dots, is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\times \lambda\)" src="images/2479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.313ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_2479.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \times \kappa\)" src="images/2480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.297ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_2480.svg">, and that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{T}ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 13.982ex; height: 3.665ex;" id="img_images_2481.svg">, which is the product of
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_153">[Pg 153]</span>the numbers of the columns, is equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\lambda)^{\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma}\)" src="images/2482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.064ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_2482.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma}\)" src="images/2483.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.049ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_2483.svg">.
The correlator which is used for proving these propositions is <img alt="" data-tex="\(W\)" src="images/2484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.371ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2484.svg">,
where, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_25"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_46"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_6"> is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_33">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(W\)" src="images/2484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.371ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2484.svg_1"> correlates <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻz\)" src="images/2485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.127ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2485.svg"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\downarrow z\)" src="images/2486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.157ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2486.svg">.</p>

<p>Similarly, by correlating <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻz\)" src="images/2485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.127ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2485.svg_1"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\downarrow R\)" src="images/2487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.157ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2487.svg">, calling the
correlator <img alt="" data-tex="\(U\)" src="images/2488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.735ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2488.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(Uʻʻ\downarrow Rʻʻ\gamma =Rʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/2489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 21.177ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2489.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(U_{\in }ʻ\gamma \downarrow_{,,}R=\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 18.389ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2490.svg">, whence
<img alt="" data-tex="\(U_{\in }ʻʻ\gamma \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\lambda =\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/2491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 23.022ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2491.svg">.
Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/2475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.762ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2475.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i> the class of rows, has
double similarity with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/2492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.728ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2492.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/2493.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.712ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2493.svg">, whence the product of the numbers
of the rows is <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma)^{\text{Nc}ʻ\lambda}\)" src="images/2494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.038ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_2494.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{Nc}ʻ\gamma )^{\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa}\)" src="images/2495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.027ex; height: 2.587ex;" id="img_images_2495.svg">.</p>

<p>Finally, we take a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_22"> similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_106"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_47"> (illustrated in the figure by the column of dots enclosed
in an oval), and calling <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_1"> a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_48"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_23">, we replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_49"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻʻ\delta\)" src="images/2496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.097ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2496.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_107">
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻMʻʻ\delta\)" src="images/2497.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.541ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2497.svg">. We thus find that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\upharpoonright\delta\)" src="images/2498.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.583ex; height: 2.061ex;" id="img_images_2498.svg">
correlates with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_24"> a class of relations whose domains
are mutually exclusive, and which each correlate their domains with
a given class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_34">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻMʻʻ\delta\)" src="images/2497.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.541ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2497.svg_1"> has double
similarity with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\delta\)" src="images/2499.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.413ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2499.svg">, whence the same
results as before with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_302.svg_25"> in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_108"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_50">.</p>

<p>The following propositions are useful in connecting multiplication with
exponentiation, and in proving the formal laws of exponentiation.</p>

<p><a href="#_116_4" class="pginternal">*116·4</a><a href="#_116_401" class="pginternal">·401</a> are lemmas for <a href="#_116_41" class="pginternal">*116·41</a>.</p>

<p>We have now to prove the three formal laws of exponentiation, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \mu ^\nu  \times _{c} \mu ^{\varpi } &amp;= \mu ^{\nu  +_{c} \varpi },\\ \mu ^{\varpi } \times _{c} \nu ^{\varpi } &amp;= (\mu  \times _{c} \nu )^{\varpi },\\ \text{and}\qquad (\mu ^\nu )^{\varpi } &amp;= \mu ^{\nu  \times _{c} \varpi }. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/2332.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.603ex; width: 26.973ex; height: 8.338ex;" id="img_images_2332.svg_1"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_157">[Pg 157]</span>
Of these the first is an immediate consequence of the distributive law,
while the second and third result from forms of the associative law of
multiplication.</p>

<p>The following propositions are lemmas for
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu ^{\varpi } \times _{c} \nu ^{\varpi } = (\mu  \times _{c} \nu )^{\varpi }. \]" src="images/2526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.48ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2526.svg"></span>
The principal previous propositions used in the proof are <a href="#_115_6" class="pginternal">*115·6</a> and
<a href="#_116_43" class="pginternal">*116·43</a>. The proof proceeds as follows.
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\alpha \,\,\text{exp}\,\,\gamma ) \times  (\beta \,\,\text{exp}\,\,\gamma )\,\text{is}\,\text{Prod}ʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\gamma  \times  \text{Prod}ʻ\beta \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\gamma. \]" src="images/2527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 56.974ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2527.svg"></span>
This, using *115·6, and putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}\)" src="images/2528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.285ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_2528.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \downarrow_{,,}\)" src="images/2529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.117ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_2529.svg"> in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_26"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_10"> of that proposition, is
similar to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\hat{\mu} \{\exists z).z\in \gamma .\mu  = \alpha \downarrow_{,,}z \times  \beta \downarrow_{,,}z\},\, \textit{i.e.}\, \text{to}\, {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\hat{\mu}     \{(\exists z).z\in \gamma .\mu  = \downarrow zʻʻ\alpha  \times  \downarrow zʻʻ\beta\}. \]" src="images/2530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 84.242ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_2530.svg"></span>
Now by <a href="#_113_65" class="pginternal">*113·65</a>, putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\dagger = R\parallel \breve{R}\quad\text{Dft}\)" src="images/2531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.125ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_2531.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow zʻʻ\alpha \times \downarrow zʻʻ\beta =(\downarrow z)\dagger ʻʻ(\alpha \times \beta)\)" src="images/2532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.739ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2532.svg">.
We now apply <a href="#_116_43" class="pginternal">*116·43</a>, taking <img alt="" data-tex="\((\downarrow z)\dagger\)" src="images/2533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.576ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2533.svg"> as the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻz\)" src="images/2534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.787ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2534.svg">
of that proposition, or rather, taking <img alt="" data-tex="\((\downarrow z)\dagger\upharpoonright (\alpha \times \beta)\)" src="images/2535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.031ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2535.svg">.
Thus we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\hat{\mu} \{(\exists z).z\in \gamma .\mu  = \downarrow zʻʻ\alpha  \times  \downarrow zʻʻ\beta \}\text{ sm }(\alpha  \times  \beta )\,\,\text{exp}\,\,\gamma . \]" src="images/2536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.053ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2536.svg"></span>
Hence our proposition follows.</p>

which is awkward.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_171">[Pg 171]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_117">
*117. GREATER AND LESS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *117.</p>

<p>A cardinal <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_131"> is said to be greater than another cardinal <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_87">
when there is a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_181"> which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_132"> terms and has
a part which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_88"> terms, while there is no class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_131">
which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_89"> terms and has a part which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_133"> terms. The
relation "greater than" is transitive and asymmetrical; and by the
Schröder-Bernstein theorem, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_134"> is greater than or equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_90">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_91"> is greater than or equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_135">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \nu\)" src="images/2638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_2638.svg">. But we cannot prove that of any two cardinals one must be the
greater, unless we assume the multiplicative axiom. The proof then
follows from Zermelo's theorem that on that assumption every class can
be well-ordered. This subject will be dealt with at a later stage.</p>

<p>The form of the definitions is so arranged as to allow of the
inequality of two cardinals in different types. The relevant
considerations are the same as for the definitions of addition,
multiplication and exponentiation.</p>

<p>Our definition of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \nu\)" src="images/2639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2639.svg">" is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·01.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\mu \gt \nu .=.(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =&amp;\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta .\\ &amp;\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .{\sim}\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ\beta \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \quad\text{Df}\end{align}\]" src="images/2640.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 69.648ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_2640.svg"></span></p>

<p>We also define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/2641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.888ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2641.svg">" as meaning "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/2642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.876ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2642.svg">,"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \gt \nu\)" src="images/2643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.723ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2643.svg">" as meaning
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha \gt \nu\)" src="images/2644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.711ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2644.svg">," for the reasons explained in
<a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>. It then easily follows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \nu\)" src="images/2639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2639.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_136"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_92">
must be homogeneous cardinals (this is part of <a href="#_117_15" class="pginternal">*117·15</a>); that if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_137"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_93"> are homogeneous cardinals, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \nu\)" src="images/2639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2639.svg_2">, the
same holds if we substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_17"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\nu\)" src="images/2427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.821ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2427.svg_1">
for one or both of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_138"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_94"> (<a href="#_117_16" class="pginternal">*117·16</a>); that</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .{\sim}\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ\beta \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/2645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.659ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2645.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">and that</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \gt \nu .\equiv .(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.045ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2646.svg"></p>

<p>We cannot define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \geq \nu\)" src="images/2647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.928ex;" id="img_images_2647.svg">" as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \nu .\lor.\mu =\nu\)" src="images/2648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 14.682ex; height: 1.842ex;" id="img_images_2648.svg">,"
because "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu =\nu\)" src="images/2649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_2649.svg">" restricts <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_139"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_95"> too much by
requiring that they should be of the same type, and restricts them too
little by not requiring that they should both be existent cardinals. To
avoid both these inconveniences, we put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \geq \nu .=:\mu \gt \nu .\lor.\mu ,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\mu =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\nu   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 47.251ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2650.svg"></p>

<p>The use of this definition is chiefly through the propositions</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·108.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\lor.\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.529ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2651.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_172">[Pg 172]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \geq \nu .\equiv .(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.045ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2652.svg"></p>

<p>In <a href="#_117_2" class="pginternal">*117·2</a>, we repeat the Schröder-Bernstein theorem (*73·88), which is
required in most of the remaining propositions of this number. It leads
at once to the propositions</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha \cap \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.084ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2653.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">(which practically supersedes the definition of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq\)" src="images/2654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2654.svg">")</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·221.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .(\exists \rho ).\rho \subset \alpha .\rho \text{ sm }\beta\)" src="images/2655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.467ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2655.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·222.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\beta \subset \alpha .\supset .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.021ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2656.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\text{Nc}ʻ\beta \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 49.008ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2657.svg"></p>

<p>This last proposition may be called the Schröder-Bernstein theorem with
as much propriety as *73·88; the two are scarcely different.</p>

<p>If we now revert to the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \gt \nu\)" src="images/2639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2639.svg_3">, or to <a href="#_117_13" class="pginternal">*117·13</a>,
and apply <a href="#_117_22" class="pginternal">*117·22</a>, we see (<a href="#_117_26" class="pginternal">*117·26</a>) that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha&gt;\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/2658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2658.svg">"
may be conveniently regarded as asserting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .{\sim}(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/2659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.253ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2659.svg">;
in fact, the best ideas to work with are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq\)" src="images/2654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2654.svg_1"> and its converse
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\leq\)" src="images/2660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2660.svg">, which for practical purposes we regard as defined by
*117·22, and from which we derive <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gt\)" src="images/2661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2661.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lt\)" src="images/2662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2662.svg"> . The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gt\)" src="images/2661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2661.svg_1"> will be the
product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq\)" src="images/2654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2654.svg_2"> into the negation of its converse; this holds for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_140"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_96"> (<a href="#_117_281" class="pginternal">*117·281</a>) as well as for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_65"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_157.svg_33">.</p>

<p><a href="#_117_3" class="pginternal">*117·3</a><a href="#_117_31" class="pginternal">·31</a> constitute an important use of <a href="#_110_72" class="pginternal">*110·72</a>, namely to prove that
one existent cardinal is greater than another or equal to it when the
first can be obtained by adding to the second (where what is added must
be a cardinal). That is to say, we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha \geq \text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .(\exists \varpi ).\varpi \in \text{NC}.\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha =\text{Nc}ʻ\beta +_{c}\varpi\)" src="images/2663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.531ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2663.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \geq \nu .\equiv :\mu ,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}:(\exists \varpi ).\varpi \in \text{NC}.\mu =\nu +_{c}\varpi\)" src="images/2664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.511ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2664.svg"></p>

<p><a href="#_117_4" class="pginternal">*117·4</a>—<a href="#_117_471" class="pginternal">·471</a> are concerned in proving that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gt\)" src="images/2661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2661.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq\)" src="images/2654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2654.svg_3"> are
transitive, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gt\)" src="images/2661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2661.svg_3"> is asymmetrical (<a href="#_117_42" class="pginternal">*117·42</a>), and allied propositions.</p>

<p>Our next set of propositions is concerned with 0 and 1 and 2. We prove
that a homogeneous cardinal is whatever is greater than or equal to
0 (<a href="#_117_501" class="pginternal">*117·501</a>); that a homogeneous cardinal other than 0 is whatever
is greater than 0 (<a href="#_117_511" class="pginternal">*117·511</a>); that a homogeneous cardinal other than
0 is whatever is greater than or equal to 1 (<a href="#_117_531" class="pginternal">*117·531</a>); and that a
homogeneous cardinal other than 0 and 1 is whatever is greater than 1
(<a href="#_117_55" class="pginternal">*117·55</a>), and is whatever is greater than or equal to 2 (<a href="#_117_551" class="pginternal">*117·551</a>).</p>

<p>We next prove a set of propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq\)" src="images/2654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2654.svg_4"> which have no
analogues for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gt\)" src="images/2661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2661.svg_4">, except when the cardinals concerned are finite. Thus
<i>e.g.</i> we prove</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·561.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \geq \nu .\varpi \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\supset .\mu +_{c}\varpi \geq \nu +_{c}\varpi\)" src="images/2665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 38.575ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2665.svg"></p>

<p>If we substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gt\)" src="images/2661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2661.svg_5"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\geq\)" src="images/2654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.312ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.751ex;" id="img_images_2654.svg_5">, this no longer holds. Thus <i>e.g.</i>
put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu =2\)" src="images/2666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.513ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_2666.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu =1\)" src="images/2667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.347ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_2667.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varpi =\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/2668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 7.26ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_2668.svg"> (cf. <a href="#_123" class="pginternal">*123</a>); then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu &gt;\nu\)" src="images/2669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.58ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2669.svg">, but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}\varpi =\nu +_{c}\varpi =\varpi\)" src="images/2670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 21.51ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_2670.svg">. Similar
remarks apply to the analogous propositions (<a href="#_117_571" class="pginternal">*117·571</a><a href="#_117_581" class="pginternal">·581</a><a href="#_117_591" class="pginternal">·591</a>) on
multiplication and exponentiation.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_173">[Pg 173]</span></p>

<p>We prove next that a sum is greater than or equal to either of its
summands (<a href="#_117_6" class="pginternal">*117·6</a>); that a product neither of whose factors vanishes
is greater than or equal to either of its factors (<a href="#_117_62" class="pginternal">*117·62</a>); that,
assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_141"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_97"> are existent cardinals, then if they are
neither 0 nor 1, their product is greater than or equal to their sum
(<a href="#_117_631" class="pginternal">*117·631</a>), and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_142"> is neither 0 nor 1, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu \geq \mu\times _{c} \nu\)" src="images/2671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.627ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_2671.svg"> (<a href="#_117_652" class="pginternal">*117·652</a>).</p>

<p>The last important proposition in this number is Cantor's theorem</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·661.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \mu  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C} . \supset  . 2^\mu  &gt; \mu\)" src="images/2672.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 21.525ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2672.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which follows immediately from <a href="#_102_72" class="pginternal">*102·72</a> and <a href="#_116_72" class="pginternal">*116·72</a>.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are much used in the following section,
on finite and infinite.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_01">*117·01</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\mu  \gt \nu  . = . <p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_02">*117·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  . = . \mu  \gt \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.219ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2674.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_03">*117·03</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \gt \nu  . = . \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  \gt \nu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2675.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.889ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2675.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_04">*117·04</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  \lt \nu  . = . \nu  \gt \mu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2676.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 19.616ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2676.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_05">*117·05</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  \geq  \nu  . = : \mu  \gt \nu  . \lor . \mu , \nu  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C} .\mu  = \text{ sm }ʻʻ\nu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2677.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 47.251ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_2677.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_06">*117·06</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu  \leq  \nu  . = . \nu  \geq  \mu  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2678.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 19.616ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2678.svg"></p>

<p>The analogues of <a href="#_117_02" class="pginternal">*117·02</a><a href="#_117_03" class="pginternal">·03</a> are to be applied also to <a href="#_117_04" class="pginternal">*117·04</a><a href="#_117_05" class="pginternal">·05</a><a href="#_117_06" class="pginternal">·06</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·1.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash  : \mu  \gt \nu  . &amp;\equiv  . (\exists \alpha , \beta ) . \mu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  . \nu  = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  .\\ &amp;\exists  ! \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha  \cap  \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  . {\sim} \exists  ! \text{Cl}ʻ\beta  \cap  \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  \quad[(*117·01)]\end{align}\]" src="images/2679.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 54.935ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_2679.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \mu  \gt \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  . \equiv  . \mu  \gt \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  \quad[(*117·02)]\)" src="images/2680.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.543ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2680.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·102.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  &gt; \nu  . \equiv  . \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  &gt; \nu  \quad[(*117·03)]\)" src="images/2681.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.548ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2681.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·103.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \mu  &lt; \nu  . \equiv  . \nu  &gt; \mu  \quad[(*117·04)]\)" src="images/2682.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.275ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2682.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_117_104">*117·104</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  \colon\ldotp  \mu  \geq  \nu  . \equiv  : \mu  &gt; \nu  . \lor . \mu , \nu  \in  \text{N}_{0}\text{C} . \mu  = \text{ sm }ʻʻ\nu  \quad[(*117·05)]\)" src="images/2683.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.664ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2683.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·105.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \mu  \leq  \nu  . \equiv  . \nu  \geq  \mu  \quad[(*117·06)]\)" src="images/2684.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.275ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2684.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*117·106.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha  &gt; \text{Nc}ʻ\beta  . \equiv  . \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha  &gt; \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta \quad [*117·101·102]\)" src="images/2685.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.215ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2685.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition (which is the Schröder-Bernstein theorem) is
fundamental in the theory of greater and less.</p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="GENERAL_NOTE_ON_CARDINAL_CORRELATORS">
GENERAL NOTE ON CARDINAL CORRELATORS.</h2>
</div>

<p>The correlators established at various stages throughout Section B
present certain analogies to each other, and they or others closely
resembling them will be found to be the correlators required in
relation-arithmetic (Part IV). We shall therefore here collect together
the most important propositions hitherto proved on correlators.</p>

<p>When we have to deal with correlators of two different functions
of a single class, as <i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_13"> and

the converse domain. Sometimes it is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota} \mid \text{D}\)" src="images/2809.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.415ex; height: 2.432ex;" id="img_images_2809.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\in}\mid \text{D}\)" src="images/2810.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.123ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_2810.svg">. Thus for example the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/2811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.885ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2811.svg">, by means of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.294ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1357.svg_3"> is
defined (<a href="#_112" class="pginternal">*112</a>), has double similarity with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_110"> if

the correlator is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/720.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_720.svg_4">, <i>i.e.</i>
