<p class="nind"><b>*73·63.</b>
    <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :S\in \alpha \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \beta .T\upharpoonright \alpha ,T\upharpoonright \beta \in 1\rightarrow 1.\alpha \cup &amp;\beta \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻT.\supset .\\ &amp;T\mid S\mid \breve{T} \in (Tʻʻ\alpha )\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (Tʻʻ\beta )\end{align}\]" src="images/2840.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.405ex; width: 69.427ex; height: 5.941ex;" id="img_images_2840.svg"></span></p>

<p>By means of the above correlators, most correlators that are required
can be calculated. Thus it will be seen that <a href="#_116_192" class="pginternal">*116·192</a> in the above list
is an immediate consequence of <a href="#_113_127" class="pginternal">*113·127</a> and <a href="#_115_502" class="pginternal">*115·502</a>, since
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \,\,\text{exp}\,\,\beta =\text{Prod}ʻ\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\,\text{and}\,sʻ\text{Prod}ʻ\gamma \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\delta =\delta \times \gamma . \]" src="images/2841.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 55.851ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2841.svg"></span></p>

<p>In order to develop the subject, it is almost always necessary,
not merely to prove that two classes are similar, but actually to
construct a correlator of the two classes. This applies equally to
relation-arithmetic, in which analogous correlators are used to prove
ordinal similarity.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_187">[Pg 187]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_C">SECTION C.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">FINITE AND INFINITE.</span></h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section C.</i></p>

<p>The distinction of finite and infinite is not required, as appears from
Section B, for the definition of the arithmetical operations or for the
proof of their formal laws. There are, however, many important respects
in which finite cardinals and classes differ respectively from infinite
cardinals and classes, and these differences must now be investigated.</p>

<p>There are two different ways in which we may define the finite and the
infinite, and these two ways cannot (so far as is known at present)
be shown to be equivalent except by assuming the multiplicative
axiom. As there seems no good reason for regarding one of these ways
as giving more exactly than the other what is usually meant by the
words "finite" and "infinite," we shall, to avoid confusion, give
other names than these to each of the two ways of dividing classes and
cardinals. The division effected by the first method of definition we
shall call the division into <i>inductive</i> and <i>non-inductive</i>;
that effected by the second method we shall call the division into
<i>non-reflexive</i> and <i>reflexive</i>.</p>

<p>The division into inductive and non-inductive, which is treated in
*120, is defined as follows. An inductive cardinal is one which can
be reached from 0 by successive additions of 1; that is, an inductive
cardinal is one which has to 0 the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\((+_{c}1)_{*}\)" src="images/2842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.52ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2842.svg">, where (by
*38·02) <img alt="" data-tex="\(+_{c}1\)" src="images/2843.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.772ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2843.svg"> is the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +_{c}1\)" src="images/2844.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.225ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2844.svg"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_184">, and the
subscript asterisk has the meaning defined in *90. Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC induct}=\hat{\alpha}\{\alpha (+_{c}1)_{*}0\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2845.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.322ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2845.svg"></span>
By applying the definition of *90, this gives
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\colon \alpha _{\in }\text{NC induct}.\equiv \colon\ldotp \xi \in \mu .\supset _{\xi }.\xi +_{c}1\in \mu :0\in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\alpha \in \mu . \]" src="images/2846.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 59.27ex; height: 2.28ex;" id="img_images_2846.svg"></span>
This proposition may be regarded as stating that an inductive cardinal
is one which obeys mathematical induction starting from 0, <i>i.e.</i>
it is one which possesses every property possessed by 0 and by the
numbers obtained by adding 1 to numbers possessing the property.
In elementary mathematics, it is customary to regard mathematical
induction, as applied to the series of natural numbers, as a principle
rather than a definition, but according to<span class="pagenum" id="Page_188">[Pg 188]</span> the above procedure it
becomes a definition rather than a principle. This procedure is
unavoidable as soon as it is perceived that there are cardinals which
do not obey mathematical induction starting from 0. (This only holds
on the assumption that the total number of objects in any one type is
not one of the inductive cardinals. This assumption, in a slightly
different form, is introduced below as the "axiom of infinity.")
Thus for example <img alt="" data-tex="\(0\neq 1\)" src="images/2847.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.28ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2847.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi \neq \xi +_{c}1.\supset .\xi+_{c}1\neq \xi +_{c}2\)" src="images/2848.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 28.354ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2848.svg">.
Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_185"> is any inductive cardinal,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \alpha +_{c}1\)" src="images/2849.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 10.69ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2849.svg">. But we know that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_1">,
the first of Cantor's transfinite cardinals<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_6" id="FNanchor_6">[6]</a>, satisfies
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}=\aleph _{0}+_{c}1\)" src="images/2850.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 12.535ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_2850.svg">. Thus mathematical induction starting from 0
cannot be validly applied to prove properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_2">. It
follows that the inductive cardinals as above defined are only some
among cardinals; nor does it appear that there is any way of defining
them except as those that obey mathematical induction starting from 0.
It follows that mathematical induction is not a principle, to be either
proved or assumed as an axiom, but is merely a characteristic defining
a certain class of cardinals, namely the class of inductive cardinals.</p>

<p>By a syllogism in Barbara, it is evident that 0 is an inductive
cardinal; hence by the definition 1 is an inductive cardinal, and
hence 2, 3, ... are inductive cardinals. Thus any given cardinal
in the series of natural numbers can be shown to be an inductive
cardinal. The usual elementary properties of inductive cardinals, such
as the uniqueness of subtraction and division, are easily proved by
mathematical induction.</p>

<p>We define an inductive class as a class the number of whose terms is
an inductive cardinal. More simply, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cls induct}=sʻ\text{NC induct}   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2851.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.938ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2851.svg"></span>
It is then easily shown that an inductive class is one which can be
reached from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_32"> by successive additions of single members.
That is, if we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} M=\hat{\eta} \hat{\zeta} \{(\exists y).\zeta =\eta \cup \iota ʻy\},\\ \text{then}\quad \text{Cls induct}=\overleftarrow{M}_{*}ʻ\Lambda . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/2852.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.147ex; width: 26.877ex; height: 7.425ex;" id="img_images_2852.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\colon \rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv \colon\ldotp \eta \in \mu .\supset _{\eta ,y}.\eta \cup \iota ʻy\in \mu :\Lambda \in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\rho \in \mu . \]" src="images/2853.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 63.081ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_2853.svg"></span>
We might equally well have begun by defining inductive classes, and
proceeded to define inductive cardinals as the cardinals of inductive
classes; in that case, we should have used the above relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_2"> to
define inductive classes.</p>

<p>Some of the properties which we expect inductive cardinals to possess,
such for example as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \alpha +_{c}1\)" src="images/2849.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 10.69ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2849.svg_1">, can only be proved
by assuming that no inductive cardinal is null, <i>i.e.</i> that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\alpha }.\exists !\alpha . \]" src="images/2854.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 23.345ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2854.svg"></span>
This amounts to the assumption that, in any fixed type, a class
can be found<span class="pagenum" id="Page_189">[Pg 189]</span> having any assigned inductive number of terms. If
this were false, there would have to be some definite member of the
series of natural numbers which gave the total number of objects of
the type in question. Thus suppose there were exactly n individuals
in the universe, and no more, where n is an inductive cardinal. We
should then have <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{n}\)" src="images/2855.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.279ex; height: 1.528ex;" id="img_images_2855.svg"> classes, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{2^{n}}\)" src="images/2856.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.93ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_2856.svg"> classes of classes,
and so on. In that case, in the type of individuals we should have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(n+_{c}1=\Lambda\)" src="images/2857.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 10.722ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2857.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(n+_{c}2=\Lambda\)" src="images/2858.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 10.722ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2858.svg">, etc. Hence we should have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ n+_{c}1=(n+_{c}1)+_{c}1,\,\text{etc}. \]" src="images/2859.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.726ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2859.svg"></span>
In the type of classes, we should get similar results for <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{n}\)" src="images/2855.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.279ex; height: 1.528ex;" id="img_images_2855.svg_1">, and
so on. It is plain (though not demonstrable except in each particular
case) that if the assumption <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset_{\alpha }.\exists !\alpha\)" src="images/2860.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 22.716ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2860.svg">
fails in any one type, it fails in any other type in the same
hierarchy, and if it holds in any one, it holds in any other; for if
n be the total number of individuals, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg_3"> is an inductive
cardinal, the total number of any other type is an inductive cardinal,
while if <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg_4"> is not an inductive cardinal, no more is the total
number of any other type. Hence the assumption <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\alpha }.\exists !\alpha\)" src="images/2861.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 22.716ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2861.svg">
is either true in any type or false in any type in one hierarchy. We
shall call it the "axiom of infinity," putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Infin ax}.=:\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\alpha }.\exists !\alpha   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2862.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 39.597ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2862.svg"></span>
This assumption, like the multiplicative axiom, will be adduced as
a hypothesis whenever it is relevant. It seems plain that there is
nothing in logic to necessitate its truth or falsehood, and that it can
only be legitimately believed or disbelieved on empirical grounds. When
we wish to use a typically definite form of the axiom, we shall employ
the definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Infin ax}(x).=:\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\alpha }.\exists !\alpha (x)  \quad\text{Df} \]" src="images/2863.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.077ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2863.svg"></span>
which asserts that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_186"> is any inductive cardinal, there are
at least <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_187"> terms of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_36">.</p>

<p>It is important to observe that, although the axiom of infinity cannot
(so far as appears) be proved a priori, we can prove that any given
inductive cardinal exists in a sufficiently high type. For if the total
number of individuals be <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg_5">, the numbers of objects in succeeding
types are <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{n}\)" src="images/2855.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.279ex; height: 1.528ex;" id="img_images_2855.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{2^{n}}\)" src="images/2856.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.93ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_2856.svg_1">, etc., and these numbers grow beyond
any assigned inductive cardinal. Owing, however, to the fact that we
cannot add together an infinite number of classes whose types increase
without limit, we cannot hence show that there is a type in which
every inductive cardinal exists, though we can show of every inductive
cardinal that there is a type in which it exists. <i>i.e.</i> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_188"> is any inductive cardinal, there must be a type for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_37">
such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\alpha (x)\)" src="images/2864.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.389ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2864.svg"> is true; but there need not be a type
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_38"> such that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_189"> is any inductive cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\alpha (x)\)" src="images/2865.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.389ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2865.svg">
is true.</p>

<p>The axiom of infinity suffices to prove the existence, in appropriate
types, of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{\aleph _{0}}\)" src="images/292.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.995ex; height: 1.932ex;" id="img_images_292.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{2^{{}\aleph_{0}}}\)" src="images/2866.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.602ex; height: 2.187ex;" id="img_images_2866.svg">,
... <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{1}\)" src="images/2867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_2867.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{2}\)" src="images/2868.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_2868.svg">, ...<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_7" id="FNanchor_7">[7]</a>. It does not
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_190">[Pg 190]</span>suffice, so far as we know, to prove the existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{\omega}\)" src="images/2869.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.565ex; height: 1.927ex;" id="img_images_2869.svg">
or any Aleph with a greater suffix than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\omega\)" src="images/2870.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.407ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2870.svg">, because
the existences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{1}\)" src="images/2867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_2867.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{2}\)" src="images/2868.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.91ex;" id="img_images_2868.svg_1">, ... are proved in
successively rising types, and no meaning can be found for a type whose
order is infinite.</p>

<p>The other definition of finite and infinite is of less importance
in practice than the definition by induction. It is dealt with in
<a href="#_124" class="pginternal">*124</a>. According to this definition, we call a class reflexive when it
contains a proper part similar to itself, <i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cls refl}=\hat{\alpha} \{(\exists R).R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻR=\alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset \alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻR\neq \alpha\} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/2871.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 64.682ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2871.svg"></span>
or, what comes to the same thing,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cls refl}=\hat{\alpha}\{(\exists R).R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset \text{D}ʻR.\exists !\overrightarrow{B}ʻR.\alpha =\text{D}ʻR\}  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2872.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.819ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_2872.svg"></span>
We call a cardinal reflexive when it is the homogeneous cardinal of a
reflexive class, <i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC refl} = N_{0}ʻʻ\text{Cls refl}  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2873.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.889ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2873.svg"></span>
It is easy to show that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC refl} =\hat{\alpha} \{\exists !\alpha .\alpha =\alpha +_{c}1\}. \]" src="images/2874.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.496ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2874.svg"></span>
We find that inductive classes and cardinals are non-reflexive, and
reflexive classes and cardinals are non-inductive. We find also that
reflexive cardinals are those that are equal to or greater than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_4">, while inductive cardinals are those that are less than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_5">. By assuming the multiplicative axiom, we can show
that every cardinal is equal to, greater than, or less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_7">,
whence it follows that every cardinal is either reflexive or
inductive, thus identifying the two definitions of finite and infinite.
But so long as we refrain from assuming either the multiplicative axiom
or some special axiom <i>ad hoc</i>, it remains possible (so far as is
known at present) that there may be cardinals neither greater than,
nor equal to, nor less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_6">. Such cardinals, if they
exist, are neither inductive nor reflexive: they are infinite if we
define infinity by the negation of induction, but finite if we define
infinity by reflexiveness. It is possible that further investigation
may either prove or disprove the existence of such cardinals; for the
present, their existence must remain an open question, except for those
who regard the multiplicative axiom as a self-evident truth.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_121" class="pginternal">*121</a> we shall consider <i>intervals</i> in a discrete series;
<i>i.e.</i> in a series generated by a one-one relation between
consecutive terms. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_4"> be the generating relation of such a
series, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_39"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_16"> be two members of the series, of which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_17"> is the later, the terms which lie between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_40"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_18"> are the
terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_7"> for which we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xP_{\text{po}}z.zP_{\text{po}}y, \]" src="images/2875.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 12.801ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2875.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg"> has the meaning defined in *91. Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P(x-y)=\overleftarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻy  \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/2877.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 32.432ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_2877.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x-y)\)" src="images/2878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.628ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2878.svg">" means "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_5">-interval between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_41"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_19">."
We want<span class="pagenum" id="Page_191">[Pg 191]</span> also symbols for the interval together with one or both of its
end-points. For these we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} P(x\unicode{x22A3} y)&amp;=\overleftarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻy   &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ P(x\unicode{x27dd}y)&amp;=\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻy   &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ P(x\vdash\dashv y)&amp;=\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻy   &amp;\quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/2879.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.831ex; width: 37.323ex; height: 12.793ex;" id="img_images_2879.svg"></span>
<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_8" id="FNanchor_8">[8]</a>
Thus, for example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_42"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_20"> be inductive cardinals, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_6"> be the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/88.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_88.svg_6"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(n+_{c}1\)" src="images/2880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.135ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2880.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x &lt; y\)" src="images/2881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_2881.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x-y)\)" src="images/2878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.628ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2878.svg_1"> will be the numbers greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_43"> and less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_21">,
while <img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\unicode{x27dd} y)\)" src="images/2882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.219ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2882.svg"> will be these numbers together with <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_22">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\unicode{x22A2}y)\)" src="images/2883.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.244ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2883.svg"> will be these numbers together with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_44">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\vdash\dashv y)\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg"> will be these numbers together with both <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_45"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_23">. By means of intervals, we define a class of relations
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu}\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_99"> is any inductive cardinal), where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\nu }z\)" src="images/2886.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 4.834ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2886.svg">"
means that we can pass from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_46"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_8"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_100"> steps. In order
to fit the case in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_47"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_9"> are identical, and to insure
that no relation such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu}\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg_1"> shall hold between terms which do
not both belong to the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_7">, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\nu }=\hat{x} \hat{y} \{\text{Nc}ʻP(x\vdash\dashv y)=\nu +_{c}1\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2887.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.419ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2887.svg"></span>
Then, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{0}=I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/2889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.574ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2889.svg">,
and if further <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/2890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 10.247ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_2890.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}= P\)" src="images/2891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 7.156ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2891.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{2}=P^{2}\)" src="images/2892.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 8.269ex; height: 2.226ex;" id="img_images_2892.svg">, etc. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_8"> is a transitive serial relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg">
is the relation "immediately preceding," which has great importance
in well-ordered series. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}=P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/2894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 11.729ex; height: 2.394ex;" id="img_images_2894.svg">. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_9"> is a transitive serial relation generating a finite series or
a progression or a series of the type of the negative and positive
integers in order of magnitude, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P=(P_{1})_{\text{po}}. \]" src="images/2895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 11.423ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2895.svg"></span></p>

<p>In <a href="#_121" class="pginternal">*121</a> we shall only consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu}\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg_2"> in the case where
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in (1\rightarrow \text{Cls})\cup (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1), \]" src="images/2896.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.738ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2896.svg"></span>
and generally we shall have the further hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_1">. We can then prove that the interval
between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_48"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_24"> is always an inductive class (it will be null
unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{*}y\)" src="images/2897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.843ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2897.svg">); this proposition is useful in its application to
the number-series and to progressions generally.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in (1\rightarrow \text{Cls})\cup (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1).P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2898.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 33.99ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2898.svg">,
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_192">[Pg 192]</span>the class of such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_101"> is an
inductive cardinal) is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Potid}ʻP\)" src="images/2900.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.495ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2900.svg">, the class
of powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_10"> (cf. *91 <i>seq.</i>). This identification (which
does not hold in general without the above hypothesis) leads to many
useful propositions. In *91 <i>seq.</i>, we treated powers of a
relation without the use of numbers, <i>i.e.</i> without defining the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_102">th power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_11">. When the powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_12"> are the class of
such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_1">, we can of course take <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_2"> as
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_103">th power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_13">. The general definition of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_104">th
power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_14"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_105"> is an inductive cardinal) will be given
later, in *301; we shall denote it by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^\nu\)" src="images/2901.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2901.svg">, thereby including the
notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}\)" src="images/2902.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.812ex; height: 1.887ex;" id="img_images_2902.svg"> already defined.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_122" class="pginternal">*122</a> we shall deal with progressions, <i>i.e.</i> with series of the
type of the series of natural numbers. In this number, we shall deal
with such series as generated by one-one relations; they will be dealt
with at a later stage (*263) as generated by transitive relations.
We define a progression as a one-one relation whose domain is the
posterity of its first term, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Prog} = (1 \rightarrow  1) \cap  \hat{R} (\text{D}ʻR = \overleftarrow{R}_{*}ʻBʻR) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2903.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.961ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_2903.svg"></span>
According to this definition, there must be a first term <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻR\)" src="images/2904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.792ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2904.svg">;
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/2905.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2905.svg"> will be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R} ʻʻ\overleftarrow{R}_{*}ʻBʻR\)" src="images/2906.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.02ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_2906.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\text{po}}ʻBʻR\)" src="images/2907.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 10.477ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_2907.svg">, which is contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{*}ʻBʻR\)" src="images/2908.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.588ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_2908.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg">;
since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2910.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.252ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2910.svg">, every term of the field of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_29"> has a successor, so that there is no end to the series; since
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR = \text{D}ʻR = \overleftarrow{R}_{*}ʻBʻR\)" src="images/2911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.219ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_2911.svg">, every term of the
series can be reached from the beginning by successive steps. These
characteristics suffice to define progressions.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_123" class="pginternal">*123</a> we proceed to the definition and discussion of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_7">,
the smallest of reflexive cardinals. This is the cardinal number of any
class whose terms can be arranged in a progression; hence it is the
class of domains of progressions, <i>i.e.</i> we may put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \aleph _{0} = \text{D}ʻʻ\text{Prog} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/2912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 19.833ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_2912.svg"></span>
With this definition, remembering that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_33"> is a cardinal,
we can prove that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_8"> is a cardinal; but to prove that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_9"> is an <i>existent</i> cardinal, we need the axiom of
infinity. The existence-theorem for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_10"> is then derived
from the inductive cardinals, which, if no one of them is null, form a
progression when arranged in order of magnitude. It should be observed
that this existence-theorem is for a higher type than that for which
the axiom of infinity is assumed. In order to get an existence-theorem
for the same type, we need the multiplicative axiom as well.</p>

<p>After a number on reflexive classes and cardinals (<a href="#_124" class="pginternal">*124</a>) and a number
on the axiom of infinity (<a href="#_125" class="pginternal">*125</a>), the Section ends with a number (<a href="#_126" class="pginternal">*126</a>)
on "typically indefinite inductive cardinals." The constant inductive
cardinals are the typically ambiguous symbols 0, 1, 2, ...; thus we
want to define the class of inductive cardinals in such a way that a
variable member of the class shall be typically ambiguous. This is not
possible without a sacrifice of rigour, but in *126 it is shown how
to minimize the sacrifice of rigour, and how to obviate the resulting
logical dangers. A variable whose values are typically ambiguous is
said to be "typically indefinite."</p>

<p>A proof that all inductive cardinals exist has often been derived from
<a href="#_120_57" class="pginternal">*120·57</a> (below). But according to the doctrine of types, this proof is
invalid, since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{0} 1\)" src="images/2913.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.249ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_2913.svg">" in *120·57 is necessarily of higher
type than "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_145">."</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_193">[Pg 193]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_118">
*118. ARITHMETICAL SUBSTITUTION AND UNIFORM
FORMAL NUMBERS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *118.</p>

<p>A difficulty arises respecting substitution in arithmetic. For
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_146"> is a formal number and its occurrence in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\mu\)" src="images/2914.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.609ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2914.svg"> is
arithmetical, then by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_21"> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_147"> is always to be taken
in an existential type. Hence we can only substitute a real variable
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_4"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_148"> under the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\xi\)" src="images/2915.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.878ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2915.svg">, and we can
only substitute another formal number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_35"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_149"> provided
that the equation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu = \sigma\)" src="images/2916.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.673ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_2916.svg">, which justifies the substitution,
is arithmetical, <i>i.e.</i> provided that in this equation the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_150"> is such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\mu\)" src="images/573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.251ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_573.svg_2">.</p>

<p>The result is that the application of *20·18 is apt to lead to
fallacies owing to the different meanings which a formal number may
possess in different occurrences. Hitherto we have considered each case
in detail, <i>e.g.</i> note on <a href="#_110_61" class="pginternal">*110·61</a>, and proof of <a href="#_110_56" class="pginternal">*110·56</a>.</p>

<p>The condition for the safe application of *20·18 is given in *118·01,
namely</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\mu .\mu =\sigma .\supset :f\mu .\equiv .f\sigma  \quad[*20·18]\)" src="images/2917.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.076ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2917.svg"></p>

<p>This question is more fully discussed in the prefatory statement of
this volume. The first reference to *118·01 is in <a href="#_120_222" class="pginternal">*120·222</a>. Another
way of evading the difficulty is to work with formal numbers which,
together with all their components, are of the same type. This leads to
the consideration of Uniform Formal Numbers, which with the exception
of *118·01 occupies the rest of the number.</p>

<p>The <i>dominant type</i> of a formal number as used in any context
is the type of the formal number itself in that context, and the
<i>subordinate types</i> of the formal number are the dominant types of
its component formal numbers.</p>

<p>When the dominant types of some of the formal numbers are not expressly
indicated by an explicit notation (cf. *65), the rules according to
which the dominant types thus left ambiguous are to be related, so far
as they are related, including the rules governing the relation of
subordinate types, if left ambiguous, to dominant types, are given by
conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_18">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_22">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_24"> of the
prefatory statement in this volume.</p>

<p>We have now to consider an important special case which arises when
types are explicitly indicated by the use of *65·01·03. A formal
number,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_194">[Pg 194]</span> whose subordinate types are the same as its dominant type, is
called <i>uniform</i>; and if some of its subordinate types are the
same as its dominant type, it is called <i>partially uniform</i>. A
formal number can only be partially uniform, or at least so designated
as to be necessarily partially uniform, when the dominant type and
those subordinate types identical with it are expressly indicated by
*65·01·03. For otherwise the conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_19">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_23">,
and perhaps also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_25">, apply; and these do not secure
uniformity, and may perhaps in some contexts be inconsistent with it.</p>

<p>Common sense in its consideration of arithmetic habitually disregards
the possibility of a formal number representing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_34">. In other
words, it always applies conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_24"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_26">.
But also, owing to its disregard of types, it assumes that the formal
numbers are all uniform. The assumption which is really essential to
this common sense reasoning, so far as the form of its arithmetical
conclusions are concerned, is the assumption that none of the numerical
symbols represent <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_35">. This assumption is secured here, when
no types are expressly indicated, by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_25"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_27">.
We have now to consider the effect on arithmetical operations of the
other assumption, that the formal numbers are uniform, or partially
uniform. There is no difficulty arising from any change of convention
for symbolism, since, as stated above, partial or complete uniformity
is secured by express indication of type. Accordingly conventions
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_20">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_26"> continue, as always, to apply when the
types of formal numbers are left ambiguous.</p>

<p>Convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_28"> will not be applied either in <a href="#_118" class="pginternal">*118</a> or <a href="#_119" class="pginternal">*119</a> or
<a href="#_120" class="pginternal">*120</a>: in *118 the fact is entirely unimportant since the dominant types
of equational occurrences are always indicated, so that no case arises
when it could apply.</p>

<p>Apart from its intrinsic interest and its bearing on substitution,
the arithmetic of uniform formal numbers is necessary for *120, where
the fundamental arithmetical properties of inductive numbers are
investigated.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are proved by the use of the results of
<a href="#_117" class="pginternal">*117</a>. The basis of the reasoning is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \leq \nu .\supset :\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu .\supset .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/2918.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 38.129ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2918.svg"></p>

<p>In *118·2·3·4 the meaning of the symbolism for dominant types is
stated, namely</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(\mu +_{c}\nu )_{\xi }=\hat{\eta} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\eta \text{ sm }_{\xi }(\alpha +\beta )\}\)" src="images/2919.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 62.015ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_2919.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(\mu \times _{c}\nu )_{\xi }=\hat{\eta} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\eta \text{ sm }_{\xi }(\alpha \times \beta )\}\)" src="images/2920.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 62.015ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_2920.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(\mu ^\nu )_{\xi }=\hat{\eta} \{(\exists \alpha ,\beta ).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha .\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta     .\eta \text{ sm }_{\xi }(\alpha \,\,\text{exp}\,\,\beta )\}\)" src="images/2921.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 60.408ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_2921.svg"></p>

<p>The important propositions which are finally reached for addition are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}.\supset .(\mu +_{c}\nu )_{\xi }=(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu +_{c}\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu)_{\xi }\)" src="images/2922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 51.833ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2922.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_195">[Pg 195]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{NC}.\supset .(\mu +_{c}\nu )_{\xi }=(\mu +_{c}\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu )_{\xi }\)" src="images/2923.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 41.952ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2923.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·241.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\supset .(\mu +_{c}\nu )_{\xi }=(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu +_{c}\nu )_{\xi }\)" src="images/2924.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 42.117ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2924.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(\mu +_{c}\nu +_{c}\varpi )_{\xi }=\{(\mu +_{c}\nu )_{\xi }+_{c}\varpi\}_{\xi }=\{\mu +_{c}(\nu +_{c}\varpi     )_{\xi }\}_{\xi }\)" src="images/2925.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 57.858ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2925.svg"></p>

<p>The important propositions for multiplication are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}-\iota ʻ0.\supset .(\mu \times _{c}\nu )_{\xi }=(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu \times _{c}\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu     )_{\xi }\)" src="images/2926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 58.139ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2926.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{NC}.\mu \neq 0.\supset .(\mu \times _{c}\nu )_{\xi }=(\mu \times _{c}\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu )_{\xi }\)" src="images/2927.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 48.722ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2927.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·341.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{NC}.\nu \neq 0.\supset .(\mu \times _{c}\nu )_{\xi }=(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu \times _{c}\nu )_{\xi }\)" src="images/2928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 48.722ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2928.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·351.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \neq 0.\supset .(\mu \times _{c}\nu \times _{c}\varpi )_{\xi }=\{\mu \times _{c}(\nu \times _{c}\varpi     )_{\xi }\}_{\xi}\)" src="images/2930.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 47.099ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2930.svg"></p>

<p>The important propositions for exponentiation are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC}-\iota ʻ0.\mu \neq 1.\supset .(\mu ^\nu )_{\xi }=\{(\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu )^{\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu     }\}_{\xi}\)" src="images/2931.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 56.724ex; height: 2.688ex;" id="img_images_2931.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·46.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \neq 0.\mu \neq 1.\supset .(\mu ^{\nu +_{c}\varpi })_{\xi }=\{\mu ^{(\nu +_{c}\varpi )_{\xi }}\}_{\xi }\)" src="images/2936.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 40.191ex; height: 2.688ex;" id="img_images_2936.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·461.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(\mu ^{\nu +_{c}\varpi })_{\xi }=\{(\mu ^\nu )_{\xi }\times _{c}(\mu     ^{\varpi })_{\xi }\}_{\xi }\)" src="images/2937.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 31.017ex; height: 2.421ex;" id="img_images_2937.svg"></p>

<p>with two analogous propositions *118·462·463,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·47.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\varpi \neq 0.\supset .{(\mu \times _{c}\nu )^{\varpi }}_{\xi }=[\{(\mu \times _{c}\nu     )_{\xi }\}^{\varpi }]_{\xi }\)" src="images/2938.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.974ex; width: 40.852ex; height: 2.67ex;" id="img_images_2938.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*118·471.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \neq 0.\nu \neq 0.\lor.\varpi =0.\lor.{\sim}&amp;(\mu ,\nu ,\varpi \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}):\supset .\\ &amp;\{(\mu \times _{c}\nu )^{\varpi }\}_{\xi }=\{(\mu ^{\varpi })_{\xi }\times _{c}(\nu     ^{\varpi })_{\xi }\}_{\xi }\end{align}\]" src="images/2939.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.087ex; width: 62.403ex; height: 5.305ex;" id="img_images_2939.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">with two analogous propositions <a href="#_118_472" class="pginternal">*118·472</a><a href="#_118_473" class="pginternal">·473</a>.</p>

<p>It is thus seen that, apart from some exceptional cases connected with
0 and 1, in all arithmetical operations uniform, or partially uniform,
formal numbers can replace those constructed in obedience to convention
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_27">.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_118_01">*118·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\mu .\mu =\sigma .\supset :f\mu .\equiv .f\sigma   \quad[*20·18]\)" src="images/2940.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.076ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2940.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_196">[Pg 196]</span></p>

<p>As far as the symbolism is concerned, this proposition with the
omission of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\mu\)" src="images/573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.251ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_573.svg_3"> from the hypothesis is a transcript
of *20·18. But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_151"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_36"> (not excluding both) is a
formal number, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\mu\)" src="images/573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.251ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_573.svg_4"> is required in case the occurrence of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_152"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\mu\)" src="images/2914.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.609ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2914.svg_1"> is arithmetical. In fact this proposition embodies
the three fundamental propositions of the Principle of Arithmetical
Substitution arrived at in the Prefatory Explanations on Types. Its
necessity arises from the convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_28"> which is explained
there.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_201">[Pg 201]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_119">*119. SUBTRACTION.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *119.</p>

<p>The treatment of subtraction follows the same general lines as that of
addition, and is simplified by the results in <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>. A difficulty arises
from the fact that subtraction (in any ordinary sense of the term)
is not always possible; and also from the fact that the result, when
possible, is not always a cardinal number.</p>

<p>We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma -_{c}\nu =\hat{\xi} \{\text{Nc}ʻ\xi  +_{c}\nu =\gamma .\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu\}      \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2997.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.956ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_2997.svg"></p>

<p>Thus when subtraction (in the ordinary sense of the term) is not
possible,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \gamma -_{c}\nu =\Lambda  . \]" src="images/2998.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.29ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_2998.svg"></span></p>

<p>The question of existential adjustment of types is dealt with by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_31"> of the prefatory statement combined with the following
definitions:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\nu   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2999.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.392ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2999.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma -_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\gamma -_{c}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3000.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.116ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3000.svg"></p>

<p>We then proceed to deduce the elementary properties derivable from
these definitions.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\gamma -_{c}\nu .\supset .\gamma ,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/3001.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 24.89ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_3001.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·12</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\xi \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\alpha \text{ sm }\xi +\beta\)" src="images/3002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 35.054ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3002.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\xi \in \gamma -_{c}\nu .\supset .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\xi \subset \gamma -_{c}\nu\)" src="images/3003.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 31.371ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3003.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\gamma \geq \nu .\supset .\exists !(\gamma -_{c}\nu )\cap t_{0}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3004.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.483ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3004.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\gamma -_{c}\nu .\supset .\gamma \geq \nu\)" src="images/3005.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 19.817ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_3005.svg"></p>

<p>The next group of propositions is concerned with some simple results of
subtraction.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :(\gamma +_{c}\nu )-_{c}\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\supset .\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma =(\gamma +_{c}\nu )-_{c}\nu\)" src="images/3006.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.722ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3006.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\gamma -_{c}\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\supset .(\gamma -_{c}\nu )+_{c}\nu =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3007.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.117ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3007.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\gamma -_{c}\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\supset .\alpha +_{c}\gamma =(\alpha +_{c}\nu )+_{c}(\gamma -_{c}\nu )\)" src="images/3008.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.443ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3008.svg"></p>

<p>Associative laws are then considered.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu +_{c}(\nu -_{c}\varpi )\subset (\mu +_{c}\nu )-_{c}\varpi\)" src="images/3009.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.635ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3009.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :(\mu +_{c}\nu )-_{c}\varpi \in \text{NC}.\exists !\{\mu +_{c}(\nu -_{c}\varpi )\}.\supset .\mu +_{c}(\nu -_{c}\varpi     )=(\mu +_{c}\nu )-_{c}\varpi\)" src="images/3010.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 74.638ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3010.svg"></p>

<p>The question of types is then dealt with:</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_202">[Pg 202]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{ sm }_{\delta ,\gamma }ʻʻ(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\gamma }=(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\delta }\cap     \text{D}ʻ\text{ sm }_{\delta ,\gamma }\)" src="images/3011.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.693ex; width: 44.104ex; height: 2.389ex;" id="img_images_3011.svg"></p>

<p>A difficulty arises from the fact that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau _{1}\)" src="images/3012.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 1.976ex; height: 1.314ex;" id="img_images_3012.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau_{2}\)" src="images/3013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 1.976ex; height: 1.314ex;" id="img_images_3013.svg">
are two complete types whose members are classes, we cannot
prove that, either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau _{1} = \text{ sm }ʻʻ\tau _{2}\)" src="images/3014.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.592ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3014.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau _{2}= \text{ sm }ʻʻ\tau _{1}\)" src="images/3015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.592ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3015.svg">. We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·54.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{SM}(\delta ,\gamma ).=:tʻ\delta =\text{D}ʻ\text{ sm }_{\delta ,\gamma }.\lor.tʻ\gamma =\text{D}ʻ\text{ sm }_{\gamma ,\delta }    \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3016.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.693ex; width: 51.585ex; height: 2.389ex;" id="img_images_3016.svg"></p>

<p>Then we obtain</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·541.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :\text{SM}(\delta ,\gamma ).(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\gamma }&amp;\in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\delta }\in     \text{NC}.\supset .\\ &amp;\text{ sm }_{\delta ,\gamma }ʻʻ(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\gamma }=(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\delta }\end{align}\]" src="images/3017.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.159ex; width: 50.749ex; height: 5.45ex;" id="img_images_3017.svg"></span></p>

<p>Finally we show that any existential adjustment of types will suffice
for the components:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu .\supset .\mu -_{c}\nu =\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu -_{c}\nu\)" src="images/3018.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 49.575ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3018.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·62.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}.\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu .\supset .\mu -_{c}\nu =\mu -_{c}\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\nu\)" src="images/3019.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 49.245ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3019.svg"></p>

<p>Also <a href="#_119_25" class="pginternal">*119·25</a><a href="#_119_26" class="pginternal">·26</a> are now extended to</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu .\supset :\mu \geq \nu .\equiv .\exists !(\mu -_{c}\nu )_{\xi }\)" src="images/3020.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 38.278ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3020.svg"></p>

<p>The only applications of the propositions of this number are in
connection with Inductive Cardinals (cf. <a href="#_120" class="pginternal">*120</a>).</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*119·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma -_{c}\nu =\hat{\xi} \{\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu =\gamma .\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu\}    \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3021.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.956ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_3021.svg"></p>

<p>Here the suffix to the sign of subtraction is introduced to show that
we are concerned with cardinal subtraction. It will be found that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma -_{c}\nu\)" src="images/3022.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.074ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_3022.svg"> is not an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_15"> except under hypotheses for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_36"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_106">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_119_02">*119·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\nu \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3023.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.392ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3023.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_119_03">*119·03</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma -_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\gamma -_{c}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3000.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.116ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3000.svg_1"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\beta  \quad[*119·02·03]\)" src="images/3024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.205ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3024.svg"></p>

<p>Note that the occurrence of a formal number in the place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_37">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_107"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma -_{c}\nu\)" src="images/3022.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.074ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_3022.svg_1"> is an arithmetic occurrence, and
accordingly <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_32"> applies to it.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\xi \in \gamma -_{c}\nu .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu =\gamma .\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu    \quad [(*119·01)]\)" src="images/3025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.874ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3025.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\xi \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\nu .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha    \quad[(*119·02).*103·13]\)" src="images/3026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.058ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3026.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·102.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :\xi \in \gamma -_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta     =\gamma .\exists !\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta\\ &amp;[(*119·03).*110·3]\end{align}\]" src="images/3027.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 56.221ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3027.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·103.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :\xi \in \text{Nc}ʻ\alpha -_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta .\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\text{Nc}ʻ\beta =\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\alpha\\ &amp;[*119·04.*110·3.*103·13]\end{align}\]" src="images/3028.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 48.837ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3028.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*119·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\gamma -_{c}\nu .\supset .\gamma ,\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}      \quad[*110·4·42.*103·34]\)" src="images/3029.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.654ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3029.svg"></p>

<p>The penultimate step in the proof employs the principle, explained in
the prefatory statement, that, since in the previous line the equation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\xi +_{c}\nu =\gamma +_{c}\nu \]" src="images/3048.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 18.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3048.svg"></span>
has its sides undetermined in type by the conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_21"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_33">, any convenient type can be chosen for them. The type
chosen in this line is such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\gamma +_{c}\nu\)" src="images/3049.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_3049.svg">, and the
references indicate the existence of at least one such type.</p>
