<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_207">[Pg 207]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_120">
*120. INDUCTIVE CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *120.</p>

<p>Inductive Cardinals are those that obey mathematical induction starting
from 0, <i>i.e.</i> in the language of Part II, Section E, they are
the posterity of 0 with respect to the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_109"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu+_{c}1\)" src="images/3085.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.977ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3085.svg">,
or, in more popular language, they are those that can be
reached from 0 by successive additions of 1. In former days, these
were supposed to be all the cardinals, and mathematical induction was
treated as a kind of self-evident axiom. We now know that only certain
cardinals obey mathematical induction starting from 0. It is these
cardinals which are to be considered in this number. They embrace 0, 1,
2, ... and generally all those cardinals which would be commonly called
finite, all those which can be expressed in the usual Arabic system of
numeration, and no others. The propositions to be proved concerning
them in this number are elementary and familiar; the interest lies
entirely in the definition and method of proof, not in the propositions
themselves.</p>

<p>Put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct} = \hat{\alpha} \{\alpha (+_{c}1)_{*}0\}\quad\text{Df}.\)" src="images/3086.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.322ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3086.svg"></p>

<p>Since <img alt="" data-tex="\((+_{c}1)_{*}\)" src="images/2842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.52ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2842.svg_1"> has necessarily its domain and converse domain
of the same type, it is important to be careful in noting the relations
of type. Accordingly we also put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct} = \hat{\alpha} \{\alpha (+_{c}1)_{*}0_{\xi }\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.099ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_3087.svg"></span></p>

<p>We begin by applying the propositions of *90. Thus we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}:\phi \xi .\supset _{\xi }.\phi (\xi +_{c}1):\phi 0_{\eta }:\supset     .\phi \alpha\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 48.706ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .0\in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3089.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 16.72ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3089.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·121.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct}.\supset .(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }\in \text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct}\)" src="images/3090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 44.409ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3090.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}:\xi \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi \xi .\supset _{\xi }.\phi (\xi +_{c}1):\phi     0_{\eta }:\supset .\phi \alpha \)" src="images/3091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 64.635ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3091.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha .\supset .\text{ sm }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.169ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha .\supset .a+_{c}1\in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3093.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 44.074ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_3093.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·152.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC}.\text{ sm }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\alpha \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/3094.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 63.367ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3094.svg"></p>

<p>We then proceed to deduce the elementary properties of inductive
<i>classes</i>, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cls induct} = sʻ\text{NC induct}. \]" src="images/3095.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.255ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3095.svg"></span></p>

<p>We have</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_208">[Pg 208]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3096.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 39.52ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3096.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·211.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\rho \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\rho \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3097.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 45.026ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3097.svg"></p>

<p>(We do not have an equivalence here, because, for aught we know, it
might be possible to determine the ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3098.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.229ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3098.svg">
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\rho = \Lambda\)" src="images/3099.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.816ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3099.svg">, even when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 13.942ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3100.svg">.
his will not be possible, however, if the axiom of infinity
is assumed.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·212·213.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Lambda ,\iota ʻx\in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.19ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3101.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·214.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \rho \text{ sm }\sigma .\supset :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\sigma \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3102.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 45.566ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3102.svg"></p>

<p>We have a set of propositions applying induction to classes directly,
and not through the intermediary of cardinals. Thus we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·251.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\eta \in \text{Cls induct}.\supset .\eta \cup \iota ʻy\in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3103.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 39.988ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3103.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \rho \in \text{Cls induct}:\phi\eta .\supset _{\eta ,x}.\phi(\eta \cup \iota ʻx):\phi\Lambda :\supset .\phi\rho\)" src="images/3104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 49.357ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3104.svg"></p>

<p>We then state the axiom of infinity, and prove (<a href="#_120_33" class="pginternal">*120·33</a>) that it
is equivalent to the assumption that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_190"> is an inductive
cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \alpha +_{c}1\)" src="images/2849.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 10.69ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2849.svg_2">. To prove this, we first
prove various propositions about <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +_{c}1\)" src="images/2844.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.225ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2844.svg_1">, among others the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·311.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\alpha +_{c}1.a+_{c}1=\beta +_{c}1.\supset .\alpha =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta .\exists !\alpha\)" src="images/3105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 47.163ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3105.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·322.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset :\exists !\alpha .\equiv .\alpha \neq \alpha +_{c}1\)" src="images/3106.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 39.613ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3106.svg"></p>

<p>We then proceed to consider subtraction (<a href="#_120_41" class="pginternal">*120·41</a>—<a href="#_120_418" class="pginternal">·418</a>), which only gives
a cardinal number when the subtrahend is an inductive cardinal. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \nu \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha +_{c}\nu .\supset :\alpha +_{c}\nu =\beta +_{c}\nu .\supset .\alpha =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 62.329ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3107.svg"></p>

<p>We might validly put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \beta\)" src="images/2262.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2262.svg_1"> instead of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3108.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.368ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3108.svg">,
since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \beta\)" src="images/2262.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2262.svg_2"> will be true whenever it
is significant.</p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·411.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \nu \in &amp;\text{NC induct}.\supset :\\ &amp;\exists !\gamma -_{c}\nu .\supset .\gamma -_{c}\nu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}:\gamma \geq \nu .\equiv .(\gamma -_{c}\nu )\cap t_{0}ʻ\gamma     \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\end{align}\]" src="images/3109.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 64.547ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3109.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·4111.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \nu \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\gamma .\supset :\gamma \geq \nu .\equiv .(\gamma -_{c}\nu )_{\xi }\in     \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/3110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 58.222ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3110.svg"></p>

<p>Hence we arrive at the conditions requisite for the usual point of view
of subtraction; namely,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·412.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{NC induct}.\gamma \geq \nu .\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\gamma .\supset .(\gamma -_{c}\nu )_\xi =\{(\iota \alpha )(\alpha +_{c}\nu     =\gamma )\}_{\xi }\)" src="images/3111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 69.842ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3111.svg"></p>

<p>Also from <a href="#_120_4111" class="pginternal">*120·4111</a> we deduce</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·414.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}-\iota ʻ0.\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\mu .\supset .(\mu -_{c}1)_{\xi }\in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}\)" src="images/3112.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 48.181ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3112.svg"></p>

<p>And from <a href="#_120_411" class="pginternal">*120·411</a>.<a href="#_119_34" class="pginternal">*119·34</a>, we find</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·416.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\gamma -_{c}\nu .\supset .(\gamma -_{c}\nu )+_{c}\nu =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3113.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.074ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3113.svg"></p>

<p>We prove next that no proper part of an inductive class is similar
to the whole (<a href="#_120_426" class="pginternal">*120·426</a>), <i>i.e.</i> that inductive classes are
non-reflexive, and various connected propositions, <i>e.g.</i></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_209">[Pg 209]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·423.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct} -\iota ʻ0.\equiv .(\exists \beta ).\beta \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C  induct}.\alpha =(\beta +_{c}1)_{\eta }\)" src="images/3114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 65.603ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3114.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·4232.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct} -\iota ʻ0.\equiv .(\exists \beta ).\beta \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C   induct} -\iota ʻ\Lambda .\alpha =(\beta +_{c}1)_{\eta }\)" src="images/3115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 72.663ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3115.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·428.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha +_{c}\nu .\alpha \neq 0.\supset .\alpha +_{c}\nu &gt;\nu\)" src="images/3116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 47.11ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3116.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·429.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \nu \in \text{NC induct}.\supset :\mu &gt;\nu .\equiv .\mu \geq \nu +_{c}1\)" src="images/3117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 41.277ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3117.svg"></p>

<p>The last two of the above propositions do not hold in general when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_110"> is a cardinal which is not inductive.</p>

<p>We prove next that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_191"> is an existent inductive cardinal,
then any existent cardinal is greater than, equal to, or less than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_192"> (<a href="#_120_441" class="pginternal">*120·441</a>); that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_193">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_134"> are inductive
cardinals, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +_{c}\beta\)" src="images/3118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.375ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3118.svg"> (<a href="#_120_45" class="pginternal">*120·45</a><a href="#_120_4501" class="pginternal">·4501</a>), and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha+_{c}\beta\)" src="images/3119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.375ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3119.svg">
is an inductive cardinal other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_36">, so are
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_194"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_135"> (<a href="#_120_452" class="pginternal">*120·452</a>). We then have some propositions
dealing with mathematical induction starting from 1 or 2, <i>e.g.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·4622.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{NC}.\beta \in &amp;\text{NC}(\eta ).\exists !\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\beta .\supset :\\ &amp;\beta (+_{c} 1)_{*}\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha .\equiv .\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\beta (+_{c}1)_{*}\text{ sm }_{\xi }ʻʻ\alpha\end{align}\]" src="images/3120.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.147ex; width: 60.258ex; height: 5.425ex;" id="img_images_3120.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·47.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\colon \beta \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct} -\iota ʻ0.\equiv \colon\ldotp \xi \in \mu .\supset _{\xi }.(\xi +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in     \mu :1_{\eta }\in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\beta \in \mu\)" src="images/3121.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 70.833ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3121.svg"></p>

<p>From <a href="#_120_452" class="pginternal">*120·452</a> we deduce</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·48.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\beta \geq  \alpha .\supset .\alpha \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/3122.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 48.285ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3122.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">so that any number less than an inductive number is inductive. Hence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·481.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\eta \in \text{Cls induct}.\xi \subset \eta .\supset .\xi \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3123.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 40.211ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3123.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which is a proposition constantly used, and</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·491.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv :\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\beta }.\exists !\beta \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi\)" src="images/3124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 52.33ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3124.svg"></p>

<p>We then prove that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_195">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_136"> are inductive cardinals,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \times _{c}\beta\)" src="images/3125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.375ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3125.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\beta\)" src="images/253.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.541ex; height: 1.974ex;" id="img_images_253.svg_5"> are either inductive
cardinals or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_37"> (<a href="#_120_5" class="pginternal">*120·5</a><a href="#_120_52" class="pginternal">*120·52</a>), while conversely if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\times _{c} \beta\)" src="images/3126.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.375ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3126.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ^\beta\)" src="images/253.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.541ex; height: 1.974ex;" id="img_images_253.svg_6"> is an existent inductive cardinal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_196"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_137"> are so also, with exceptions for 0 and 1 (<a href="#_120_512" class="pginternal">*120·512</a><a href="#_120_56" class="pginternal">·56</a><a href="#_120_561" class="pginternal">·561</a>).
Hence we infer the uniqueness of division and the taking of roots
(<a href="#_120_51" class="pginternal">*120·51</a><a href="#_120_53" class="pginternal">·53</a><a href="#_120_55" class="pginternal">·55</a>) so long as inductive numbers are concerned.</p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions on the axiom of infinity and the
multiplicative axiom. We prove (<a href="#_120_61" class="pginternal">*120·61</a>) that if there is any existent
cardinal which is not inductive, the axiom of infinity is true. From
*83·9·904, we infer by induction that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_112"> is an inductive
class of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_38"> is not a number, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_16">
exists (<a href="#_120_62" class="pginternal">*120·62</a>), whence it follows that either the multiplicative
axiom or the axiom of infinity must be true (<a href="#_120_64" class="pginternal">*120·64</a>).</p>

<p>Finally, we have a set of propositions on inductive classes. We prove</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\rho ,\sigma \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\rho \cup \sigma \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\rho +\sigma \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3127.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 62.173ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3127.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·74.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 37.917ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3128.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·75.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :sʻ\kappa \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\kappa \in \text{Cls induct}.\kappa \subset \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.315ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3129.svg"></p>

<p>with analogous propositions (involving however a hypothesis as to
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_210">[Pg 210]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_113">) on the subject of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_17">.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are essential to the ordinary
arithmetic of finite numbers. In the present work, however, they are
not much used after the present section until we reach Part V, Section
E, where we deal with the ordinal theory of finite and infinite.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*120·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct} = \hat{\alpha}\{\alpha (+_{c}1)_{*}0\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.693ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3130.svg"></p>

<p>Note that in virtue of our general conventions for descriptive
functions of two arguments (*38),
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ +_{c}1=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} (a=\beta +_{c}1). \]" src="images/3131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.179ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_3131.svg"></span>
That is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(+_{c}1\)" src="images/2843.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.772ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2843.svg_1"> is the relation of a cardinal to its immediate
predecessor. It is the number written in the usual mathematical
notation as +1 in the series of positive and negative integers, just as
its converse is the number -1. (It should be observed that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_111">
is any cardinal, +<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_112"> is not identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_113">, since +<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_114">
is a relation, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_115"> is a class of classes.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·011.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct} =\hat{\alpha} \{\alpha (+_{c}1)_{*}0_{\xi }\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 32.47ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_3132.svg"></p>

<p>All members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct}\)" src="images/3133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 11.072ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3133.svg"> belong to the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{\xi }\)" src="images/3134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 2.02ex; height: 2.174ex;" id="img_images_3134.svg">, so that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_197"> is any member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct}\)" src="images/3133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 11.072ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3133.svg_1">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi \in \alpha\)" src="images/3135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.205ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_3135.svg">" is significant.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls induct} = sʻ\text{NC induct} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3136.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·021.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}_{\xi }\text{induct} = sʻ\text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3137.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 31.52ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3137.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of these definitions an inductive class is one whose cardinal
is an inductive cardinal.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_03">*120·03</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}.=:\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{a}.\exists !\alpha  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 38.79ex; height: 1.975ex;" id="img_images_3138.svg"></p>

<p>"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.545ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_380.svg_2">," like "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Mult ax}\)" src="images/3139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.733ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_3139.svg">," is an arithmetical
hypothesis which some will consider self-evident, but which we prefer
to keep as a hypothesis, and to adduce in that form whenever it is
relevant. Like "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Mult ax}\)" src="images/3139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.733ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_3139.svg_1">," it states an existence-theorem.
In the above form, it states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_198"> is any inductive
cardinal, there is at least one class (of the type in question)
which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_199"> terms. An equivalent assumption would be that,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_6"> is any inductive class, there are objects which are not
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_7">. For in that case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_49"> be such an object,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ(\rho \cup \iota ʻx)=\text{Nc}ʻ\rho +_{c}1\)" src="images/3140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.979ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3140.svg">. Hence by
induction, every inductive cardinal must exist. Another equivalent
assumption would be that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_208.svg_3"> (the class of all objects of
the type in question) is not an inductive class. The assumption that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_12"> exists in the type in question is, as we shall see, a
stronger assumption than the above, unless we assume the multiplicative
axiom.</p>

<p>If the axiom of infinity is true, the inductive cardinals are all
different one from another, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +_{c}\beta\)" src="images/3118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.375ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3118.svg_1">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_200"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_138"> are inductive cardinals, is not equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_201"> unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = 0\)" src="images/3141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.429ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3141.svg">. But if the axiom of infinity is false,
then, in any assigned type, all the cardinals after a certain one are
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_39">. (Except in the lowest type, the last existent cardinal
must be a power of 2.) That is, if (say) 8 were the largest existent
cardinal in the type in question, we should<span class="pagenum" id="Page_211">[Pg 211]</span> have, in that type,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(9 = \Lambda\)" src="images/3142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.718ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_3142.svg">, and the same would hold of 10, 11, .... This
possibility has to be taken account of in what follows.</p>

<p>In order to give typical definiteness to the axiom of infinity, we write</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_04">*120·04</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}(x).=:\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{a}.\exists !\alpha (x) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.899ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3143.svg"></p>

<p>Then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax} (x)\)" src="images/3144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.6ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3144.svg">" states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_202"> is any
inductive cardinal, there are at least <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_203"> objects of the same
type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_50">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_1">*120·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\equiv .\alpha (+_{c}1)_{*}0 \quad[(*120·01)]\)" src="images/3145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.611ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3145.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_101">*120·101</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\colon \alpha \in \text{NC induct}. \equiv \colon\ldotp \xi \in \mu .\supset _{\xi }.\xi +_{c}1\in     \mu :0\in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\alpha \in \mu \\ &amp;[*120·1.*90·131.*38·12]\end{align}\]" src="images/3146.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.096ex; width: 60.78ex; height: 5.323ex;" id="img_images_3146.svg"></span></p>

<p>The right-hand side of the above equivalence gives the usual formula
for mathematical induction. Observe that the conditions of significance
require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi +_{c}1\)" src="images/3147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.768ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_3147.svg"> should be taken in the same type as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_5">. This fact is specially relevant in the proof of <a href="#_120_15" class="pginternal">*120·15</a>.</p>

<p>The symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct}\)" src="images/371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 10.183ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_371.svg_3">" is of ambiguous type not necessarily
the same in different occurrences; also, according to the convention
explained in the prefatory statement as holding for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_18"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC induct}\)" src="images/371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 10.183ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_371.svg_4">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha ,\beta \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 16.684ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3148.svg">" will not
imply that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_204"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_139"> are of the same type. Accordingly
to avoid error in connection with <a href="#_120_1" class="pginternal">*120·1</a><a href="#_120_101" class="pginternal">·101</a> typical definiteness is
required as in the three following propositions.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·102.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}. \equiv  .\alpha (+_{c} 1)_{*}0_{\eta } \quad[(*120·011)]\)" src="images/3149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 46.707ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3149.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·103.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash  \colon\colon \alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}. \equiv \colon\ldotp \xi \in \mu .\supset _{\xi }.(\xi     +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \mu :0_{\eta }\in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\alpha \in \mu \\ &amp;[*120·101]\end{align}\]" src="images/3150.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.096ex; width: 65.489ex; height: 5.323ex;" id="img_images_3150.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_11">*120·11</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}:\phi\xi .\supset _{\xi }.\phi (\xi +_{c}1):\phi 0_{\eta }:\supset     .\phi \alpha \\ &amp;[*120·102.*90·112]\end{align}\]" src="images/3151.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.096ex; width: 49.334ex; height: 5.323ex;" id="img_images_3151.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_12">*120·12</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  .0\in \text{NC induct} \quad\left[*120·101 \frac{0}{\alpha}\right]\)" src="images/3152.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.798ex; width: 32.819ex; height: 2.755ex;" id="img_images_3152.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_121">*120·121</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct}.\supset .(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }\in \text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct} \quad[*90·172.*120·102]\)" src="images/3153.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 67.539ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3153.svg"></p>

<p>By means of this proposition and <a href="#_120_12" class="pginternal">*120·12</a>, any assigned cardinal in the
series of natural numbers can be shown to be an inductive cardinal;
thus <i>e.g.</i> to show that 27 is an inductive cardinal, we shall
only have to use <a href="#_120_121" class="pginternal">*120·121</a> twenty-seven times in succession.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·122.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .1\in \text{NC induct} \quad[*120·12·121.*110·641]\)" src="images/3154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.878ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3154.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_123">*120·123</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .2\in \text{NC induct}. \text{etc}. \quad[*120·122·121.*110·643]\)" src="images/3155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.911ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3155.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·124.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\alpha +_{c}1\neq 0\)" src="images/3156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 12.762ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3156.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*110·4. \text{Transp}.&amp;\supset \vdash :\alpha {\sim}\in \text{NC}.\supset .\alpha +_{c}1=\Lambda .\\ [*101·12]  &amp;\supset .\alpha +_{c}1\neq 0  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*110·632. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{NC}.\supset :\xi \in \alpha +_{c}1.\supset .\exists !\xi :\\ [*24·63] &amp;\supset :\Lambda {\sim}\in \alpha +_{c}1:\\ [*54·102]  &amp;\supset :\alpha +_{c}1\neq 0  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3157.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 65.953ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_3157.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_212">[Pg 212]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}:\xi \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi \xi .\supset _{\xi }.\phi (\xi +_{c}1):\phi     0_{\eta }:\supset .\phi \alpha\)" src="images/3158.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 64.635ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3158.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*120·121. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \xi \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi \xi .\supset _{\xi }.\phi (\xi +_{c}1):\supset :\\ &amp;\xi \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi \xi .\supset _{\xi }.(\xi +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi (\xi +_{c}1)      &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*120·12. &amp;\supset \vdash :\phi 0_{\eta }.\supset .0_{\eta }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi 0_{\eta }  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2). &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :\\ \xi \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi \xi .&amp;\supset _{\xi }.(\xi +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi (\xi +_{c}1):0_{\eta }\in     \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi 0_{\eta }:\\ \left[*120·11 \frac{\xi \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\phi \xi}{\phi \xi }\right]&amp;\supset :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C     induct}.\phi \alpha \colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3159.svg" style="vertical-align: -9.627ex; width: 94.896ex; height: 20.384ex;" id="img_images_3159.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is often convenient for inductive proofs.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{NC induct} \subset \text{NC}\)" src="images/3160.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 18.919ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3160.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash . *110·42. \text{Simp}.\supset \vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC}.\supset .\alpha +_{c}1\in \text{NC}   &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*101·11. *120·11 \frac{\alpha \in \text{NC}}{\phi \alpha} .\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3161.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.582ex; width: 55.191ex; height: 6.295ex;" id="img_images_3161.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition does not show that every inductive cardinal is an
<i>existent</i> cardinal; to obtain this, we require the axiom of
infinity.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_15">*120·15</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha .\supset .\text{ sm }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.169ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>i.e.</i> a cardinal which is not null and is inductive in any one
type is also inductive in any other type.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*101·15.*120·12.&amp;\supset \vdash .\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ0_{\xi }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*110·4. &amp;\supset \vdash .\alpha =\Lambda _{\xi }.\supset .(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi } = \Lambda _{\xi } &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*118·201. &amp;\supset \vdash :\exists !(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }.\supset .\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }=(\alpha     +_{c}1)_{\eta }\\ [*118·241.*110·4] &amp;= (\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha +_{c} 1)_{\eta }  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .*120·121. &amp;\supset \vdash :\exists !(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }.\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\supset .(\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha     +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\\ [(3)]    &amp;\supset .\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }\in 1\,\text{N}_{C}\text{induct}   &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .(4).*2·2.   &amp; \supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\supset :\\\\ &amp;(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }=\Lambda _{\xi }.\lor.\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C  induct} &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash .(2).(5).*3·48.&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha =\Lambda _{\xi }.\lor.\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}:\supset :\\ &amp;(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }=\Lambda _{\xi }.\lor.\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\xi }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C  induct} &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ \vdash .(1).(6).*120·11.*4·6.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3162.svg" style="vertical-align: -18.574ex; width: 121.49ex; height: 38.28ex;" id="img_images_3162.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha .\supset .\alpha +_{c}1\in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 44.325ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_3163.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*120·15. \supset \vdash :\alpha \in \text{N}_{\xi }\text{C induct}.\exists !\alpha .&amp;\supset .\text{ sm }_\eta ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\\ [*120·121]    &amp;\supset .(\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\\ [*118·241.*120·14]   &amp; \supset .(\alpha +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3164.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.912ex; width: 74.875ex; height: 8.955ex;" id="img_images_3164.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·152.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC}.\text{ sm }ʻʻ\alpha \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\alpha \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/3094.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 63.367ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3094.svg_1"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·521. \supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset .\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{ sm }ʻʻ\alpha =\alpha .\\ [*120·15]    &amp;\supset .\alpha \in \text{NC induct}  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*37·29. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\exists !\alpha &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3165.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 55.676ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_3165.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_213">[Pg 213]</span></p>

<p>The following propositions, giving alternative forms for the definition
of inductive <i>classes</i>, are inserted in order to show that the
theory of inductive classes might be treated in a less arithmetical
manner than we have adopted.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\rho \in \alpha  \quad[(*120·02)]\)" src="images/3166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.316ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3166.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·201.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \rho \text{ sm }\sigma .\supset :\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho \in \text{NC induct}.\equiv .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\sigma \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 56.012ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3167.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·35.*103·13.*100·511.\supset \\ \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\sigma .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\sigma =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho :\\ [*120·152.*103·13] \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3168.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 56.018ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_3168.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho \in  \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 39.52ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3169.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*120·14·2. \supset \vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.&amp;\equiv .(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in  \text{NC induct}.\alpha \in \text{NC}.\rho \in \alpha .\\ [*103·27]  &amp;\equiv .(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in  \text{NC induct}. \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho =\alpha .\\ [*13·195] &amp;\equiv .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho \in  \text{NC induct}:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3170.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 74.271ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_3170.svg"></span></p>

<p>Note that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\text{Nc}ʻ\rho \in\text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 35.892ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3171.svg">"
is not proved above. The proof encounters the
difficulty that we may have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\rho = \Lambda\)" src="images/3099.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.816ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3099.svg_1">; in order
to establish our proposition in this case, we have to show that if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 14.519ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_3172.svg">, then <i>every</i> class is an
inductive class. We can however prove the following implication.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·211.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Nc}ʻ\rho \in \text{NC induct} - \iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\rho \in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 45.026ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3173.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·511.&amp;\supset  \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset.\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{Nc}ʻp=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho .\\ [*120·15] &amp;\supset . \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho \in \text{NC induct}.\\ [*120·21] &amp;\supset .\rho \in  \text{Cls induct}:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3174.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 47.641ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_3174.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·212.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Lambda \in \text{Cls induct}  \quad[*120·211·12]\)" src="images/3175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.702ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3175.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·213.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\iota ʻ\alpha \in  \text{Cls induct} \quad [*120·211·122]\)" src="images/3176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.869ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3176.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition might be used to define inductive classes. It gives
a form of mathematical induction applicable to classes instead of
to numbers. Virtually it states that an inductive class is one
which can be formed by adding members one at a time, starting from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_40">. This is made more explicit in <a href="#_120_25" class="pginternal">*120·25</a>. Instead of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta\in \mu .\supset _{\eta ,y}.\mu \cup \iota ʻy\in \mu\)" src="images/3188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 22.514ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3188.svg">,
in the above propositions, as well as in those that follow, we may
plainly substitute
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \eta \in \mu .y{\sim}\in \eta .\supset _{\eta ,y}.\eta \cup \iota ʻy\in \mu . \]" src="images/3189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 30.669ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3189.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_217">[Pg 217]</span></p>

<p>The above proposition establishes (with the natural limitations) the
uniqueness (within each type) of subtraction (conceived as in <a href="#_120_412" class="pginternal">*120·412</a>)
when the subtrahend is an inductive cardinal. (When the subtrahend is
a non-inductive cardinal, subtraction ceases to give a unique result.)
Hence we are led to the following extensions of <a href="#_118" class="pginternal">*118</a> for the case of
inductive cardinals:</p>

<p>The above proposition shows that no reflexive class is inductive.</p>

<p>The following definition, in which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{spec}\)" src="images/3238.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.158ex; height: 1.452ex;" id="img_images_3238.svg">" stands for
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(species\)" src="images/3239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.129ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_3239.svg">," defines the "species" of a cardinal <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_140"> as all
cardinals which are less than, equal to, or greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_141">.
We cannot prove, unless by assuming the multiplicative axiom, that
all cardinals belong to the species of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_142">, except in the case
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_143"> is an inductive cardinal. In all other cases there may,
so far as is known at present, be other cardinals which are neither
greater nor less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_144">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_223">[Pg 223]</span></p>

<p>It is on this proposition that the irrelevance of types in the
consideration of inductive cardinals depends.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·463.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\colon .\alpha \in \text{NC}.\supset \colon\colon &amp;(\exists \gamma ).\gamma \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}.\beta =(\alpha +_{c}\gamma     )_{\eta }.\equiv \colon\ldotp \\ &amp;\xi \in \mu .\supset _{\xi }.(\xi +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \mu :\text{ sm }_{\eta }ʻʻ\alpha \in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\beta \in \mu \\ [*120·462.*90·11]\end{align}\]" src="images/3273.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.626ex; width: 67.816ex; height: 8.383ex;" id="img_images_3273.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_47">*120·47</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\colon \beta \in \text{N}_{\eta }\text{C induct}-\iota ʻ0.\equiv \colon\ldotp \xi \in \mu .\supset _{\xi }.(\xi     +_{c}1)_{\eta }\in \mu :1_{\eta }\in \mu :\supset _{\mu }.\beta \in \mu \\ &amp;[*120·423·463]\end{align}\]" src="images/3274.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.096ex; width: 71.461ex; height: 5.323ex;" id="img_images_3274.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus mathematical induction starting from 1 will apply to all inductive
cardinals except 0. Similar propositions can be similarly proved for 2,
3, ....</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·48.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\beta \geq \alpha .\supset .\alpha \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda \\ &amp;[*120·452.*117·31]\end{align}\]" src="images/3281.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 48.913ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3281.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus every cardinal which is not greater than every inductive cardinal
is an inductive cardinal.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·481.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\eta \in \text{Cls induct}.\xi \subset \eta .\supset .\xi \in \text{Cls induct} \quad[*117·222.*120·21·48]\)" src="images/3282.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 67.238ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3282.svg"></p>

<p>Thus if any inductive class can be found which contains a given class,
the given class is also inductive.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·49.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC}-\text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\beta \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\alpha &gt;\beta\)" src="images/3283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 60.875ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3283.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*120·48.\text{Transp}.&amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .{\sim}(\beta \geq \alpha ) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*120·441. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :\alpha &gt;\beta .\lor.\beta \geq \alpha  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3284.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 58.235ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_3284.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus every non-inductive cardinal (except <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_41">) is greater than
every inductive cardinal (except <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_42">).</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_491">*120·491</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv :\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\beta }.\exists !\beta \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi\)" src="images/3124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 52.33ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3124.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*120·49.&amp;\supset \vdash :\xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\beta \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\xi &gt;\beta .\\ [*120·429.*117·12]&amp;\supset .\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\xi \geq \beta +_{c}1.\exists !\beta \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*117·104·12.*103·13.&amp;\supset \vdash :\xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\beta \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\beta +_{c}1\neq \Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(2).*101·12.*102·13.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.&amp;\supset :\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\supset .\beta \neq \Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(3).&amp;\supset \vdash :\xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\supset .\exists !\beta \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .*120·121.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \beta \in \text{NC induct}.&amp;\supset _{\beta }.\exists !\beta \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi :\supset :\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\supset _{\beta }.\exists !(\beta +_{c}1)\cap     \text{Cl}ʻ\xi .\\ [*117·242.*120·429] &amp;\supset _{\beta }.\text{Nc}ʻ\xi  &gt; \beta .\\ [*117·42.(*117·03)] &amp;\supset _{\beta }.\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\xi \neq \beta :\\ [*13·196] &amp;\supset :\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\xi {\sim}\in \text{NC induct}:\\ [*120·21] &amp;\supset :\xi {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct} &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash .(4).(5).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3285.svg" style="vertical-align: -19.696ex; width: 98.752ex; height: 40.524ex;" id="img_images_3285.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·492.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC}-\text{NC induct}.\beta \geq \alpha .\supset .\beta \in \text{NC}-\text{NC induct}\\ &amp;[*120·48.\text{Transp}]\end{align}\]" src="images/3286.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 54.611ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3286.svg"></span></p>

<p>In virtue of <a href="#_120_491" class="pginternal">*120·491</a>, a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_6"> which is not inductive contains
sub-classes having 0, 1, 2, 3, ... terms. If we take the successive
classes of sub-classes
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 0\cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi , 1\cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi , 2\cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi , ..., \]" src="images/3287.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 31.435ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3287.svg"></span>
these are mutually exclusive, and all exist provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_43">
is not an inductive<span class="pagenum" id="Page_225">[Pg 225]</span> cardinal, <i>i.e.</i> provided the axiom of
infinity holds. Thus if the axiom of infinity holds, we get <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_8">
classes of sub-classes contained in any non-inductive class.
It follows, as we shall see later, that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_7"> is a non-inductive
class, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\xi\)" src="images/3288.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.231ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3288.svg"> is a reflexive class. This seems to
be the nearest approach possible to identifying the two definitions of
finite and infinite when the multiplicative axiom is not assumed. When
the multiplicative axiom is assumed as well as the axiom of infinity,
we pick out one class from <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\cap \text{Cl}ʻ\xi\)" src="images/3289.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.257ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3289.svg">, one from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(2\cap\text{Cl}ʻ\xi\)" src="images/3290.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.257ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3290.svg">, and so on; then, forming the logical sum of
all these classes, we get <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_13"> terms which are members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_8">. Hence it follows that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_9"> is a reflexive class; for, as we
shall see later, a reflexive class is one which contains sub-classes of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_14"> terms. Thus with the help of the multiplicative axiom,
the two definitions of finite and infinite can be identified.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_5">*120·5</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha ,\beta \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha \times _{c}\beta .\supset .\alpha \times _{c}\beta \in \text{NC induct}\)" src="images/3293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 51.687ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3293.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*113·203.&amp;\supset \vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\exists !\alpha \times _{c}0.\supset .\alpha \in \text{NC}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\\ [*113·601] &amp;\supset .\alpha \times _{c}0=0.\\ [*120·12] &amp;\supset .\alpha \times _{c}0\in \text{NC induct} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*113·671. &amp;\supset \vdash .\alpha \times _{c}(\beta +_{c}1)=(\alpha \times _{c}\beta )+_{c}\alpha .\\ [*120·4501.*113·203] &amp;\supset \vdash :\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\alpha \times _{c}\beta \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .\\ &amp;\alpha \times _{c}(\beta +_{c}1)\in \text{NC induct} &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).*120·13.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3294.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.068ex; width: 89.785ex; height: 21.267ex;" id="img_images_3294.svg"></span></p>

<p>The restriction involved in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\alpha \times _{c}\beta\)" src="images/3295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.262ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3295.svg"> in
the hypothesis of the above proposition is not necessary if we assume
that the axiom of infinity must fail in any one type if it fails in any
other, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Lambda \cap tʻ\alpha \in \text{NC induct}.\supset .\Lambda \cap tʻ\beta \in \text{NC induct}, \]" src="images/3296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 45.546ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3296.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_226">[Pg 226]</span>where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_205"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_145"> are any two objects of any two
types. To prove this proposition would require assumptions, as to
the interrelation of various types, which have not been made in our
previous proofs.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_51">*120·51</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma ,\in \text{NC induct}.\alpha \neq 0.\exists !\alpha \times _{c}\beta .\alpha\times _{c}\beta =\alpha \times _{c}\gamma     .\supset .\beta =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 70.07ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3297.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition establishes the uniqueness of division among inductive
cardinals.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash . *120·44·436. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :(\exists \delta ):\beta =\gamma +_{c}\delta .\lor.\gamma =\beta +_{c}\delta   &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash . *113·43. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\beta =\gamma +_{c}\delta .\supset .\alpha \times _{c}\gamma =(\alpha \times _{c}\gamma )+_{c}(\alpha \times _{c}\delta     ).\\ [*120·42.\text{Transp}]    &amp;\supset .\alpha \times _{c}\delta =0.\\ [*113·602]    &amp;\supset .\delta =0.\\ [*110·6]    &amp;\supset .\beta  = \text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma   &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \text{Similarly}\quad    &amp;\vdash :\text{Hp}.\gamma =\beta +_{c}\delta .\supset .\gamma =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta .\\ [*100·53.*113·203]    &amp;\supset .\beta =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma   &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).(3).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3298.svg" style="vertical-align: -11.652ex; width: 86.854ex; height: 24.434ex;" id="img_images_3298.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_146">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_40"> in the above are typically ambiguous symbols,
such as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 0, 1, 2, ... \text{Nc}ʻ\rho , \text{Nc}ʻ\sigma , ..., \]" src="images/3299.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.668ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3299.svg"></span>
we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta = \gamma\)" src="images/3300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.526ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3300.svg">; for in this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\beta.\gamma =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.303ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3301.svg">.
Also if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_147"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_41"> are of the same type, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta=\gamma\)" src="images/3302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.526ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3302.svg">,
in virtue of <a href="#_103_43" class="pginternal">*103·43</a>. Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\gamma\)" src="images/3303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.526ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_3303.svg">" may, with
truth, be substituted for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\text{ sm }ʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.148ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3304.svg">" in the above
proposition, since the result is true whenever significant. But in this
form the proposition gives less information, since it tells us nothing
as to what happens when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_148"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_42"> are not of the same
type.</p>

<p>The above proposition may also be deduced from <a href="#_120_611" class="pginternal">*120·611</a>, by *62·231.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*120·63.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Cls induct} - \overleftarrow{{\in}}ʻ\Lambda \subset \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{mult} \quad[*120·62.*88·2]\)" src="images/3335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.275ex; height: 3.432ex;" id="img_images_3335.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition the multiplicative axiom is not required
in dealing with a finite number of factors, even when some or all of
the factors are themselves infinite.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_120_64">*120·64</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \text{Infin ax}.\lor.\text{Mult ax}\)" src="images/3336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 21.439ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_3336.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*120·61.\text{Transp}.&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp {\sim}\text{Infin ax}.\supset :\text{N}_{0}\text{C}\subset \text{NC induct}:\\ [*120·21]  &amp;\supset :(\kappa ).\kappa \in \text{Cls induct}:\\ [*120·62]  &amp;\supset :(\kappa ):\Lambda {\sim}\in \kappa .\supset .\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa :\\ [*88·37]    &amp;\supset :\text{Mult ax}\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3337.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 58.649ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_3337.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus of our two arithmetical axioms, the multiplicative axiom and the
axiom of infinity, at least one must be true.</p>
