<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_233">[Pg 233]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_121">*121. INTERVALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *121.</p>

<p>The present number is concerned with the class of terms between
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_51"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_25"> with respect to some relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_15">, <i>i.e.</i>
those terms which lie on a road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_52"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_26"> on which any two
consecutive terms have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_16">. Such a road may be called
a <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_17">-road, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(zPw\)" src="images/3363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.371ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_3363.svg">, the step from <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_10"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/2358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2358.svg_1"> may be
called a <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_18">-step. In order that a <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_19">-road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_53"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_27">
should exist, it is necessary and sufficient that we should have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\text{po}}y\)" src="images/3364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.732ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3364.svg">. When this condition is fulfilled, there will
in general be many <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_20">-roads from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_54"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_28">. But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.{\sim}(yP_{\text{po}}y)\)" src="images/3365.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 21.966ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3365.svg">, or if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.{\sim}(xP_{\text{po}}x)\)" src="images/3366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.714ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3366.svg">,then at most one
road leads from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_55"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_29">. This follows from the propositions of
*96. In virtue of those propositions, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.{\sim}(yP_{\text{po}}y).xP_{\text{po}}y\)" src="images/3367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 28.704ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3367.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_21"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_3368.svg"> throughout the road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_56"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_30">, and this road forms an
open series. The two other possibilities with a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3369.svg">
are (assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\text{po}}y\)" src="images/3364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.732ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3364.svg_1">)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;(1)\quad xP_{\text{po}}x,\\ &amp;(2) \quad yP_{\text{po}}y.{\sim}(xP_{\text{po}}x). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/3370.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.12ex; width: 21.774ex; height: 5.372ex;" id="img_images_3370.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the first case, there is a cyclic road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_57"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_58">, and
there are two roads from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_59"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_31">, one consisting of that part
of the cycle which is required to reach <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_32">, the other consisting of
this part together with the whole cycle required to travel from <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_33">
back to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_34">. Thus the class of terms which can be reached in some
journey from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_60"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_35"> is the whole class of descendants of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_61">,
<i>i.e.</i> the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{*}ʻx\)" src="images/3371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3371.svg">, which is the cycle
composing the road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_62"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_63">.</p>

<p>In the second case, the descendants of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_64"> form a <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_36"> is
in the circular part of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_1">. Here, as before, there are two roads
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_65"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_37">, of which the first stops as soon as it reaches
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_38">, while the second proceeds to travel round the circle until it
comes to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_39"> again. Thus here again, all the descendants of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_66"> lie
on some road between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_67"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_40">.</p>

<p>The interval between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_68"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_41"> is defined as the class of terms
lying on some road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_69"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_42">. There will be four kinds of
interval, according as we do or do not include the end-points as such.
We denote the kind including both end-points by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P(x\vdash\dashv y), \]" src="images/3373.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.513ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3373.svg"></span>
that excluding both by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P(x\unicode{x2013} y) \]" src="images/3374.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.993ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3374.svg"></span>
and the other two respectively by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P(x\dashv y), P(x \unicode{x27dd} y). \]" src="images/3375.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.356ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3375.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_234">[Pg 234]</span></p>

<p>The definitions are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻy, \quad\overleftarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻy, \quad\overleftarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻx\cap     \overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻy, \quad\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}_{\text{po}}ʻy. \]" src="images/3376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 68.776ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_3376.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_22"> is either one-many or many-one, it will be one-one
throughout the interval <img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\vdash\dashv y)\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_1">, except at most at one
exceptional point, namely the junction of the tail and circle of the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_2">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\text{po}}x\)" src="images/3377.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.918ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3377.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(yP_{\text{po}}y)\)" src="images/3378.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.067ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3378.svg">, the
interval between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_70"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_43"> cannot be <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_3">-shaped, but must
be either open or cyclic; in either case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_23"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg_2">
throughout <img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\vdash\dashv y)\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_2">, with no exceptions; for
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3379.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_24"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg_3">
throughout the interval because the interval is contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\)" src="images/3380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.275ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3380.svg">, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/3381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3381.svg">,
because the interval is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻy\)" src="images/3382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.906ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_3382.svg">. Thus
throughout this number we shall constantly have the hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in(\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1)\cup (1\rightarrow \text{Cls})\)" src="images/3383.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.109ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3383.svg">; if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3384.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3384.svg">, the interval is to be supposed traversed
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_71"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_44">, while if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/3381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3381.svg_1">, it
is to be supposed traversed from <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_45"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_72">. In either case the
interval between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_73"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_46"> must be an inductive class. This is
proved in <a href="#_121_47" class="pginternal">*121·47</a>. If, however, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_25"> is serial (cf. <a href="#_204" class="pginternal">*204</a>), and thus
neither many-one nor one-many, the interval between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_74"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_47">
is the stretch of the series between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_75"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_48">, with or without
end-points according to the definition chosen, and need not be an
inductive class.</p>

<p>If the interval between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_76"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_49"> (both included) has
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu +_{c}1\)" src="images/386.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.977ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_386.svg_2"> members, we say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\nu }y\)" src="images/3385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.891ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3385.svg">. Thus if
there is only one road from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_77"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_50">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\nu }y\)" src="images/3385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.891ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3385.svg_1">"
means that it requires <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_116"> steps to get from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_78"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_51">.
Assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3379.svg_1">, if we also have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_2"> (<i>i.e.</i> if none of the families
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_26"> are cyclic), then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\nu }y\)" src="images/3385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.891ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3385.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(yPz\)" src="images/3386.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.86ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3386.svg">, we shall have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{\nu +_{c}1}z\)" src="images/3387.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.592ex; width: 7.501ex; height: 2.137ex;" id="img_images_3387.svg">. On this basis an inductive theory of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu}\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg_3">
is built up, and it is shown that the class of such relations
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_3"> for different inductive values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_117"> is the
same as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Potid}ʻP\)" src="images/2900.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.495ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2900.svg_1">, the class of powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_27"> including
<img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/3388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3388.svg"> (<a href="#_121_5" class="pginternal">*121·5</a>). The definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_4"> is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\nu } = \hat{x} \hat{y} \{\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻP(x\vdash\dashv y)=v+_{c}1\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.305ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3389.svg"></span></p>

<p>The whole class of such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu}\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg_4"> for different
inductive values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_118"> is called <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{finid}ʻP\)" src="images/3390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3390.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{finid}ʻP=\hat{R} \{(\exists \nu ).\nu \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda .R=P_{\nu }\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3391.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.926ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_3391.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg"> exists, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3379.svg_2">, then the
descendants of <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_1">, so long as we do not reach a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_52"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(yP_{\text{po}}y\)" src="images/3393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.547ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3393.svg">, may be unambiguously described as the 2nd, 3rd,
... <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_119">th, ... terms of the posterity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_3"> itself
being the 1st term. The correlation thus effected with the inductive
cardinals is the logical essence of the process of counting; the last
cardinal used in the correlation is the cardinal number of terms
counted. We will call these terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{P}\)" src="images/3394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3394.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{P}\)" src="images/3395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3395.svg">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu_{P}\)" src="images/3396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3396.svg">,
..., defining <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg"> as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \nu _{P} = \breve{P} _{\nu -_{c}1}ʻBʻP \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/3398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.592ex; width: 22.123ex; height: 3.006ex;" id="img_images_3398.svg"></span></p>

<p>This notation does not conflict with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{\xi }\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 2.006ex; height: 1.667ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg"> as defined in
*65.01. There <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_10"> must be a class if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_120"> is a cardinal, here
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_121"> must be a cardinal and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_28"> a relation.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_235">[Pg 235]</span></p>

<p>Hence whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_1"> exists, the number of terms from the
beginning to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_2"> (both included) is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_122">. This is
the fact upon which counting relies. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_29"> is a many-one and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_1"> is contained in diversity, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_123"> is any
inductive cardinal other than 0, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_3"> exists when and
only when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻBʻP\)" src="images/3400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.755ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3400.svg"> has at least <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_124"> members;
<i>i.e.</i> roughly speaking, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_4"> exists whenever it could
possibly be expected to exist. In this case the whole posterity of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_4"> is contained in the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{P}\)" src="images/3394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3394.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{P}\)" src="images/3395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3395.svg_1">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu_{P}\)" src="images/3396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3396.svg_1">,
... (<a href="#_121_62" class="pginternal">*121·62</a>). If the posterity is an inductive class, this
series stops; if not, it forms a <i>progression</i> (cf. <a href="#_122" class="pginternal">*122</a>).</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are very useful, not only in
this section, but in the ordinal theory of finite and infinite and in
parts of the book subsequent to that theory.</p>

<p>After some propositions which merely repeat definitions and give
immediate consequences, we proceed (<a href="#_121_3" class="pginternal">*121·3</a> ff.) to the theory of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_5">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·302.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P_{0}=I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/3401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 26.861ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3401.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·305.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P_{1}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P\)" src="images/3402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 19.539ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3402.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in (l\rightarrow \text{Cls})\cup (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1).P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P_{1}=P\)" src="images/3403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 47.101ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3403.svg"></p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_30"> is a transitive serial relation, we shall have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}=P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/2894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 11.729ex; height: 2.394ex;" id="img_images_2894.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·321.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu &gt;0.\supset .P_{\nu }\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 19.942ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3404.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·333.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P_{\nu +_{c}1}=P\mid P_{\nu }\)" src="images/3405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 40.431ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3405.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·35·351·352.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in (1\rightarrow \text{Cls})\cup (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1).&amp;P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\mu ,\nu \in \text{NC induct}.\supset .\\ &amp;P_{\mu }\mid P_{\nu }=P_{\nu }\mid P_{\mu }=P_{\mu +_{c}\nu }\end{align}\]" src="images/3406.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.138ex; width: 57.172ex; height: 5.407ex;" id="img_images_3406.svg"></span></p>

<p>A similar result holds for <img alt="" data-tex="\((P_{\mu })_{\nu }\)" src="images/3407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 5.401ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3407.svg">, which = <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\mu x_{c}\nu }\)" src="images/3408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 4.991ex; height: 2.23ex;" id="img_images_3408.svg">
n the same circumstances.</p>

<p>We next proceed to the proof that an interval (under a similar
hypothesis) is always an inductive class. This occupies <a href="#_121_4" class="pginternal">*121·4</a>—<a href="#_121_47" class="pginternal">·47</a>,
being summed up in the proposition</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·47.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :R\in (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1)\cup (1\rightarrow \text{Cls}).\supset .R(x \vdash\dashv  z)\in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.157ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3409.svg"></p>

<p>This is an important proposition. It leads to</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*121·481.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset :\text{Nc}ʻR(x\vdash\dashv  y)\leq \text{Nc}ʻ&amp;R(x \vdash\dashv  z).\equiv .\\ &amp;R(x \vdash\dashv  y)\subset R(x \vdash\dashv  z)\end{align}\]" src="images/3410.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 63.757ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3410.svg"></span></p>

<p>with a similar proposition if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/726.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_726.svg_1">.</p>

<p>The next set of propositions (<a href="#_121_5" class="pginternal">*121·5</a>—<a href="#_121_52" class="pginternal">·52</a>) is concerned with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{finid}ʻP\)" src="images/3390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3390.svg_1">. Assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1)\cup (1\rightarrow \text{Cls}).P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/3411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 33.99ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3411.svg">, we prove
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{finid}ʻP=\text{Potid}ʻP\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.035ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{finid}ʻP-\iotaʻP_{0}\subset \text{Pot}ʻP\)" src="images/3413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.513ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3413.svg">
(<a href="#_121_5" class="pginternal">*121·5</a>); that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_31"> is not null,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{finid}ʻP-\iota ʻP_{0}=\text{Pot}ʻP\)" src="images/3414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.513ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3414.svg"> (<a href="#_121_501" class="pginternal">*121·501</a>); that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ\text{finid}ʻP=P_{*}\)" src="images/3415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.398ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3415.svg">
(<a href="#_121_52" class="pginternal">*121·52</a>) and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ(\text{finid}ʻP-\iotaʻP_{0})=P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.412ex; height: 2.385ex;" id="img_images_3416.svg">
(<a href="#_121_502" class="pginternal">*121·502</a>); and that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{2}=P^{2}.P_{3}=P^{3}\)" src="images/3417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 17.545ex; height: 2.261ex;" id="img_images_3417.svg">
etc. (<a href="#_121_51" class="pginternal">*121·51</a>).</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} P&amp;(x\unicode{x2013}y)=P(x\dashv Pʻy).\supset .\text{E}!Pʻy,\\ \text{whereas}\qquad &amp;z\in P(x\unicode{x2013}y).\equiv _{z}.z\in P(x\dashv Pʻy) \end{aligned} \]" src="images/3503.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 43.226ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3503.svg"></span>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*96·302. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.xR_{*}y.xR_{*}z.\supset :yR_{*}z.\lor.zR_{*}y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*121·37. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.xR_{*}y.yR_{*}z.\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv y)\subset R(x\vdash\dashv z) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*121·37. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.xR_{*}z.zR_{*}y.\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv z)\subset R(x\vdash\dashv y) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).(3). &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.xR_{*}y.xR_{*}z.\supset :\\ &amp;R(x\vdash\dashv y)\subset R(x\vdash\dashv z).\lor.R(x\vdash\dashv z)\subset R(x\vdash\dashv y) &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .*121·23. &amp;\supset \vdash :{\sim}(xR_{*}y).\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv y)=\Lambda .\\ [*24·12] &amp;\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv y)\subset R(x\vdash\dashv z) &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash .(5)\frac{z,\,y}{y,\,z}. &amp;\supset \vdash :{\sim}(xR_{*}z).\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv z)\subset R(x\vdash\dashv y) &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ \vdash .(4).(5).(6).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3533.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.56ex; width: 84.036ex; height: 28.252ex;" id="img_images_3533.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following series of propositions are concerned with proving
<a href="#_121_47" class="pginternal">*121·47</a>, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1)\cup (1\rightarrow \text{Cls}).\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv z)\in \text{Cls induct}. \]" src="images/3534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.146ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3534.svg"></span>
The proof for <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/726.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_726.svg_2"> follows from that for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3535.svg"> by <a href="#_121_143" class="pginternal">*121·143</a>. Confining ourselves,
therefore, to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3535.svg_1">, we proceed as follows.</p>

<p>We prove first that, starting from z and going backwards, each new
step adds only one term (which may not be distinct from all its
predecessors); <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.xRy.yR_{*}z.\supset .R(x\vdash\dashv z)=\iota ʻx\cup R(y\vdash\dashv z). \]" src="images/3536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.798ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3536.svg"></span>
From this it follows by induction that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg"> is an
inductive class, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.845ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3538.svg">. Thus we only have to
prove that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_1"> is an inductive class. Here we must
distinguish two cases, according as <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(zR_{\text{po}}z)\)" src="images/3539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.219ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3539.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(zR_{\text{po}}z\)" src="images/3540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.698ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3540.svg">. In the former case, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !R(z\vdash\dashv z).\supset .R(z\vdash\dashv z)=\iota ʻz, \]" src="images/3541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.722ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3541.svg"></span>
whence <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_2"> is an inductive class, and therefore so
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.845ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3538.svg_1">.</p>

<p>But in the latter case, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(zR_{\text{po}}z\)" src="images/3540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.698ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3540.svg_1">, the matter is more
difficult. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_11"> is a member of a cycle, the cycle being
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_3">. We have to prove that this cycle must be an
inductive class. Given <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR_{*}z\)" src="images/3542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 5.051ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_3542.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_79"> will be a member of this
cycle if <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR_{\text{po}}x\)" src="images/3543.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.183ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3543.svg">, and may be at the end of the tail of a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_4">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(xR_{\text{po}}x)\)" src="images/3544.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.703ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3544.svg">. (Cf. *96.)</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 1200px;" id="i_243">
<img alt="Mathematical diagram showing a sequence and cycle. Left side: linear progression from x to R with arrows. Right side: circular cycle with arrows connecting points labeled a and z, with R marking entry point. An incoming arrow from above enters the cycle at top. Illustrates relation R connecting linear and cyclical structures." height="668" src="images/i_243.jpg" width="1200" id="img_images_i_243.jpg">
</figure>

<p>By *96·453, we know that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_30"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg_4"> when confined to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_4">. Hence<span class="pagenum" id="Page_244">[Pg 244]</span> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_12"> has
a unique predecessor, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg">. Assume <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\neq z\)" src="images/3546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.266ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3546.svg">. We then imagine
a barrier placed between <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_13">, <i>i.e.</i> we construct a
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_14"> which is to hold between any two consecutive members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_6"> except <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_14">. Putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha=R(z\vdash\dashv z)-\iota ʻa\)" src="images/3547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.189ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3547.svg">,
we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(S=\alpha \upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/3548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.842ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3548.svg">. Then the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_15"> generates an open series consisting of all the terms of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_7">; <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\sim}(aS_{\text{po}}a).S(z\vdash\dashv a)=R(z\vdash\dashv z). \]" src="images/3549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 32.923ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3549.svg"></span>
Hence, by our previous case, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(S(z\vdash\dashv a)\)" src="images/3550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.49ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3550.svg"> is an
inductive class, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_8">.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(a = z\)" src="images/3551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.266ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_3551.svg">, then by *96·33 the cycle reduces to the single term
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_15">, and therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_9"> is still an inductive class.</p>

<p>Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3537.svg_10">, and therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x\vdash\dashv z)\)" src="images/3538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.845ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3538.svg_2">, is
always an inductive class when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3535.svg_2">, which
was to be proved.</p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, we have only to prove
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)\in \text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3556.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.376ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3556.svg">. This is obvious when
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(zR_{\text{po}}z)\)" src="images/3539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.219ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3539.svg_1">, for then either <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z)=\iotaʻz\)" src="images/3557.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.831ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3557.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(z\vdash\dashv z=\Lambda\)" src="images/3558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.31ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3558.svg">. But when <img alt="" data-tex="\(zR_{\text{po}}z\)" src="images/3540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.698ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3540.svg_2">, it
is more difficult.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_247">[Pg 247]</span></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the identification of
such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_6"> with powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_32"> in the sense of *91.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_121_52">*121·52</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :P\in (\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1)\cup (1\rightarrow \text{Cls}).P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .\dot{s} ʻ\text{finid}ʻP=P_{*}\\ &amp;[*121·5.*91·55]\end{align}\]" src="images/3589.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.097ex; width: 56.429ex; height: 5.326ex;" id="img_images_3589.svg"></span></p>

<p>We shall at a later stage (*301) give a general definition of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P^\nu\)" src="images/2901.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2901.svg_1">. When this definition has been introduced, we shall be able
to prove, with the hypothesis of *121·51,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \nu \in \text{NC induct}.\supset .P_{\nu }=P^\nu . \]" src="images/3590.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 26.915ex; height: 1.981ex;" id="img_images_3590.svg"></span>
The definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^\nu\)" src="images/2901.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2901.svg_2"> is postponed on account of various
complications which render a general definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^\nu\)" src="images/2901.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2901.svg_3"> difficult.
The chief difficulty arises when<span class="pagenum" id="Page_248">[Pg 248]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists} !P\dot{\cap} I\)" src="images/3591.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 6.235ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_3591.svg">.
Thus suppose we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(yPy\)" src="images/3592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.916ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3592.svg">; we shall also have <img alt="" data-tex="\(yP^{2}y\)" src="images/3593.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.029ex; height: 2.351ex;" id="img_images_3593.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(yP^{3}y\)" src="images/3594.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.029ex; height: 2.349ex;" id="img_images_3594.svg">,
etc. Hence if we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \nu \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ0.\supset _{\nu }.xP^\nu y. \]" src="images/3596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 31.155ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3596.svg"></span>
Again, suppose this case excluded, but suppose
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \mu ,y).\mu \in \text{NC induct}.y\in P(x\vdash\dashv z).yP^\mu y . \]" src="images/3597.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.353ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3597.svg"></span>
Then we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \nu \in \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ0-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\supset .yP^{\mu  \times _{c}\nu }y. \]" src="images/3598.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 39.008ex; height: 2.184ex;" id="img_images_3598.svg"></span>
Thus the general definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^\nu\)" src="images/2901.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2901.svg_4"> has to be complicated, except
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_3">.</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the series of relations
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_7"> and the series of terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_6">. The relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_8"> holds between two terms (roughly speaking) when it
requires <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_126"> steps to get from the first to the second; the term
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_7"> is the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_127">th term starting from <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_5">, which, when
it exists, is <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{P}\)" src="images/3394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3394.svg_2">. In order that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_8"> should exist, it is
necessary that <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_6"> should exist, and that there should be just one
term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_80"> in the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_33"> such that the interval from <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_7"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_81"> (both included) consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_128"> terms. When this is the case
for all inductive cardinals from 1 to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_129">, we can say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_34">
generates a series starting from <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_8"> and having at least <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_130">
terms, each correlated with one of the cardinals in the interval from
1 to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_131">, both included; <i>i.e.</i> the series has a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_155">th
term, whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\leq \mu \leq \nu\)" src="images/3599.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.729ex; height: 1.995ex;" id="img_images_3599.svg">. If this holds for all inductive
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_132">, the family of <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_9"> is a progression<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_9" id="FNanchor_9">[9]</a>. (It will
be observed that all such terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{P}\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.507ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg_9"> belong to the family of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_10">, which need not form the whole field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_35">.)</p>
