<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_278">[Pg 278]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_124">
*124. REFLEXIVE CLASSES AND CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *124.</p>

<p>In this number, we have to take up the second definition of
infinity mentioned in the introduction to this Section. A class
which is infinite according to this definition we propose to call a
reflexive class, because a class which is of this kind is capable
of <i>reflexion</i> into a part of itself. A class is called
<i>reflexive</i> when there is a one-one relation which correlates the
class with a proper part of itself. (A <i>proper part</i> is a part
not the whole.) A reflexive cardinal is the homogeneous cardinal of a
reflexive class.</p>

<p>We prove easily that reflexive classes are not inductive (<a href="#_124_271" class="pginternal">*124·271</a>),
that reflexive cardinals are such as are greater than or equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_24"> (<a href="#_124_23" class="pginternal">*124·23</a>), and such as are unchanged by adding 1
(excepting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_48">) (<a href="#_124_25" class="pginternal">*124·25</a>). To prove that classes which are
not inductive must be reflexive has not hitherto been found possible
without assuming the multiplicative axiom. We do not need, however,
to assume the axiom generally, but only as applied to products of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_25"> factors. With this assumption, the result follows by a
series of propositions explained below. Thus if a product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_9">
factors, no one of which is zero, is never zero, then the two
definitions of the finite and the infinite coincide (<a href="#_124_56" class="pginternal">*124·56</a>).</p>

<p>We will call a cardinal <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_143"> a "multiplicative cardinal" if a
product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_144"> factors none of which are zero is never zero.
Thus all inductive cardinals are multiplicative cardinals; and the
assumption needed for identifying the two definitions of finite and
infinite is that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_26"> should be a multiplicative cardinal.</p>

<p>For a reflexive class we use the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/3908.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 6.932ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3908.svg">," and
for a reflexive cardinal we use "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC refl}\)" src="images/3909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.109ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3909.svg">." We define a
reflexive cardinal as the <i>homogeneous</i> cardinal of a reflexive
class, <i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC refl} = \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻʻ\text{Cls refl} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3910.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3910.svg"></span>
The only effect of this is to exclude <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_49"> from reflexive
cardinals, which is convenient. We then need (on the analogy of
<a href="#_110_03" class="pginternal">*110·03</a><a href="#_110_04" class="pginternal">*110·04</a>) a definition of what is meant when an ambiguous symbol such
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_66"> is said to be reflexive, and we therefore put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nc}ʻ\rho  \in  \text{NC refl} . = . \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻ\rho  \in  \text{NC refl} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 40.278ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3911.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_279">[Pg 279]</span></p>

<p>For the class of multiplicative cardinals we use the notation
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC mult}\)" src="images/3912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.548ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3912.svg">." Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NC mult} = \text{NC} \cap  \hat{\alpha}  \{\kappa  \in  \alpha  \cap  \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}. \supset _{\kappa } . \exists  ! {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa     \} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/3913.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.896ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_3913.svg"></span>
whence it follows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \text{NC mult}\)" src="images/3914.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.761ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3914.svg">, a product of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_218"> factors, none of which is zero, will never be zero.</p>

<p>We begin, in this number, with the more obvious properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/3908.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 6.932ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3908.svg_1">, proving that a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/3908.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 6.932ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3908.svg_2"> is one which
contains sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_27"> terms (<a href="#_124_15" class="pginternal">*124·15</a>), that it is one
whose number is unchanged when a single term is taken away (<a href="#_124_17" class="pginternal">*124·17</a>),
and that it remains reflexive if any inductive class is taken away from
it (<a href="#_124_182" class="pginternal">*124·182</a>).</p>

<p>We then give corresponding propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC refl}\)" src="images/3909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.109ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3909.svg_1">
(<a href="#_124_23" class="pginternal">*124·23</a><a href="#_124_25" class="pginternal">·25</a><a href="#_124_252" class="pginternal">·252</a>), proving, in addition to propositions already mentioned,
that a reflexive cardinal is greater than every inductive cardinal
(<a href="#_124_26" class="pginternal">*124·26</a>), and that a class which is neither inductive nor reflexive
(if there be such) is one which neither contains nor is contained in
any progression (<a href="#_124_34" class="pginternal">*124·34</a>). On such classes, see the remarks at the end
of this number.</p>

<p>We then (<a href="#_124_4" class="pginternal">*124·4</a><a href="#_124_41" class="pginternal">·41</a>) give a proposition merely embodying the definition
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC mult}\)" src="images/3912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.548ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_3912.svg_1">, and show that all inductive cardinals are
multiplicative, which follows immediately from <a href="#_120_62" class="pginternal">*120·62</a>.</p>

<p>The following series of propositions (<a href="#_124_51" class="pginternal">*124·51</a> ff.) are concerned with
the proof that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_28"> is a multiplicative cardinal, then
the two definitions of finite and infinite coalesce. The proof, which
is somewhat complicated, proceeds as follows.</p>

<p>To begin with, we know that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_8"> is a class which is not
inductive, it contains classes having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_145"> terms, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_146"> is any
inductive cardinal. Thus we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists  ! 0 \cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\rho , \exists  ! 1 \cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\rho , ... \exists  ! \nu  \cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\rho , .... \]" src="images/3915.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 40.718ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3915.svg"></span>
The classes of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(0 \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3916.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 8.435ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3916.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \cap\text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3917.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 8.435ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3917.svg">,
... <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3918.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 8.503ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3918.svg">, ... thus form a progression, which is
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3919.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 8.41ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3919.svg">. Hence (<a href="#_124_511" class="pginternal">*124·511</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash  : \rho  {\sim} \in  \text{Cls induct} . \supset  . \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho  \in  \text{Cls refl}. \]" src="images/3920.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 40.851ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3920.svg"></span>
So far, the multiplicative axiom is not required.</p>

<p>The above progression of classes of classes is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\rho )ʻʻ\text{NC induct}. \]" src="images/3921.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.586ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3921.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_45"> is a selective relation for this class of classes,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg_1"> is a progression contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.79ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3922.svg">. Hence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*124·513.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \exists  ! {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\rho )ʻʻ\text{NC induct} . \supset  . \text{Cl}ʻ\rho  \in  \text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/3923.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.131ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3923.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*124·514.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  \colon\ldotp  \aleph _{0} \in  \text{NC mult} . \supset  : \rho  {\sim} \in  \text{Cls induct} . \supset  . \text{Cl}ʻ\rho  \in  \text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/3924.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 55.064ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3924.svg"></p>

<p>To prove the next step, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \aleph _{0} \in  \text{NC mult} . \exists  ! \aleph _{0} \cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho  . \supset  . \exists  ! \aleph _{0} \cap  \text{Cl}ʻ\rho , \]" src="images/3925.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 45.833ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3925.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_280">[Pg 280]</span>
we make a fresh start. We have, by hypothesis, a progression <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_39">
whose domain is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.79ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3922.svg_1">; hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{D}ʻR\subset \rho\)" src="images/3926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.408ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3926.svg">.
Thus it will suffice to prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \aleph _{0} \in  \text{NC mult} . R \in  \text{Prog} . \text{D}ʻR \subset  \text{Cls induct} . \supset  . \exists  ! \aleph _{0} \cap  sʻ\text{D}ʻR, \]" src="images/3927.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 61.09ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_3927.svg"></span>
where the conditions of significance require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg_8"> should
consist of classes.</p>

<p>For this purpose, we prove that no member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg_9"> can be the
last that has new members which have not occurred before. The proof
proceeds by showing that if this were not so, <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/3928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.222ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3928.svg"> would
be an inductive class, and therefore, by <a href="#_120_75" class="pginternal">*120·75</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg_10"> would
be an inductive class. Hence (<a href="#_124_534" class="pginternal">*124·534</a>) the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg_11">
which introduce new terms form an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_29">, by <a href="#_123_19" class="pginternal">*123·19</a>;
and so therefore do the classes of new terms which they introduce
(<a href="#_124_535" class="pginternal">*124·535</a>). Hence (<a href="#_124_536" class="pginternal">*124·536</a>) a selection from these classes of new
terms, which is a sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/3928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.222ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3928.svg_1">, is also an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/1.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_1.svg_10">,
and therefore (<a href="#_124_54" class="pginternal">*124·54</a>) there is a progression contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/3928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.222ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3928.svg_2"> if the selection in question exists. This completes
the proof.</p>

<p>In virtue of <a href="#_124_511" class="pginternal">*124·511</a> and <a href="#_120_74" class="pginternal">*120·74</a>, we have, without the multiplicative
axiom,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*124·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \rho  {\sim} \in  \text{Cls induct} . \equiv  . \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho  \in  \text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/3929.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 40.222ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3929.svg"></p>

<p>Hence if it could be shown that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\rho\)" src="images/3922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.79ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3922.svg_2"> cannot be reflexive
unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\rho\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_164.svg_9"> is reflexive, a double application of this would enable
us, by means of <a href="#_124_6" class="pginternal">*124·6</a>, to identify the two definitions of the finite
without the multiplicative axiom.</p>

<p>In virtue of the above proposition, if there are any numbers which are
neither inductive nor reflexive, they are such as are neither greater
than, less than, nor equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_30">. (The existence of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_31"> in a suitable type can be deduced from the existence
of numbers which are neither inductive nor reflexive; cf. <a href="#_124_6" class="pginternal">*124·6</a>.) Two
further propositions (<a href="#_124_33" class="pginternal">*124·33</a><a href="#_124_34" class="pginternal">·34</a>) are given below on non-inductive
non-reflexive classes and cardinals. The subject is resumed in the
remarks at the end of the number.</p>

propositions subsequently used are not it, but the lemmas which lead to
it.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_124_513">*124·513</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\cap \text{Cl}ʻ\rho )ʻʻ\text{NC induct}.\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl} \quad[*124·512·15]\)" src="images/3989.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.101ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3989.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_124_514">*124·514</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \aleph _{0}\in \text{NC mult}.\supset :\rho {\sim}\in &amp;\text{Cls induct}.\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}\\ &amp;[*124·511·513·4]\end{align}\]" src="images/3990.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 54.436ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3990.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned in proving that, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_32"> is a multiplicative cardinal, then a class such as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg_2"> in <a href="#_124_512" class="pginternal">*124·512</a> must be such that a progression is contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3991.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.204ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3991.svg">. The characteristics of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg_3"> which are
used in the proof are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\in \aleph _{0}.\text{D}ʻP\subset\text{Cls induct}\)" src="images/3992.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.736ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3992.svg">.
Since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\in \aleph _{0}\)" src="images/3993.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.921ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3993.svg">, we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists R).R\in \text{Prog}.\text{D}ʻP = \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/3994.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.526ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3994.svg">. Hence the
hypothesis with which the following series of propositions is concerned
is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in  \text{Prog}.\text{D}ʻR\subset \text{Cls induct}, \]" src="images/3995.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 28.635ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_3995.svg"></span>
but the earlier propositions do not need the full hypothesis.</p>

<p>In what follows, note that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \in \text{D}ʻR,\gamma-sʻ\overrightarrow{R}_{\text{po}}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3996.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.397ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_3996.svg">
is the class of those terms which occur in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_45"> and have never
occurred before in any earlier member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg_12">. We prove that,
with our hypothesis, members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg_13"> for which this class
of new terms is not null form a class which has no last member, and
therefore form a progression.</p>

<p>The above proposition identifies the two definitions of the finite, on
the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\in \text{NC mult}\)" src="images/4020.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 13.684ex; height: 1.97ex;" id="img_images_4020.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*124·57.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}-\text{NC induct}.\supset .2^{2^\mu }\in \text{NC refl} \quad[*124·511.*116·72]\)" src="images/4021.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.999ex; height: 2.536ex;" id="img_images_4021.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*124·58.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp 2^\mu \in \text{NC refl}.\supset _{\mu }.\mu \in \text{NC refl}:\supset .\text{N}_{0}\text{C}-\text{NC induct}=\text{NC refl}\)" src="images/4022.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 63.132ex; height: 2.28ex;" id="img_images_4022.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*124·57.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :\mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{C}-\text{NC induct}.\supset .2^\mu \in \text{NC refl}.\\ [\text{Hp}] &amp;\supset .\mu \in \text{NC refl} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*124·2·27.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4023.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 80.863ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_4023.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition gives another hypothesis which would enable us to
identify the two definitions of the finite if it could be proved, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 2^\mu \in \text{NC refl}.\supset _{\mu }.\mu \in \text{NC refl}, \]" src="images/4024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 28.951ex; height: 2.326ex;" id="img_images_4024.svg"></span>
or, what comes to the same thing,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}.\supset .\rho \in \text{Cls refl}. \]" src="images/4025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 29.757ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4025.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_124_6">*124·6</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\rho {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\equiv .\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/4026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 40.222ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4026.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*124·511.&amp;\supset \vdash :\rho {\sim}\in \text{Cls induct}.\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*120·74. &amp;\supset \vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls induct}.\\ [*124·271] &amp;\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho {\sim}\in \text{Cls refl} &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4027.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 75.016ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_4027.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*124·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \aleph _{0}\in     \text{NC mult}.\supset :\rho \in \text{Cls refl}.\equiv .\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}.\equiv .\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}\)" src="images/4028.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 72.109ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4028.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*124·6·271.&amp;\supset \vdash :\rho \in \text{Cls refl}.\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}.\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*124·6·56. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \aleph _{0}\in     \text{NC mult}.\supset :\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl}.\supset .\rho \in \text{Cls refl}. &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ [(1)] &amp;\supset .\text{Cl}ʻ\rho \in \text{Cls refl} &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).(3).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4029.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 91.225ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_4029.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following properties of cardinals which are neither inductive nor
reflexive (supposing there are such) are easily proved. Let us put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{NC med}&amp;=\text{N}_{0}\text{C}-\text{NC induct}-\text{NC refl} \quad\text{Df},\\ \text{Cls med}&amp;=-\text{Cls induct}-\text{Cls refl} \quad\text{Df}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4030.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 43.514ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_4030.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{med}\)" src="images/4031.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.147ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_4031.svg">" stands for "mediate." Then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu \in \text{NC med}.\supset .\mu +_{c}1\in \text{NC med}.\mu -_{c}1\in \text{NC med}.\mu \neq \mu +_{c}1.\mu \neq \mu -_{c}1. \]" src="images/4032.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 74.163ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_4032.svg"></span>
Hence mediate cardinals have no maximum or minimum.
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \mu ,\nu \in &amp;\text{NC med}.\supset .\mu +_{c}\nu \in &amp;\quad\text{NC med},\\ \mu \in &amp;\text{NC med}.\nu \in \text{NC med}\cup \text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ0.\supset .\mu \times _{c}\nu \in &amp;\quad\text{NC med}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4033.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 73.347ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_4033.svg"></span>
whence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\mu \in \text{NC med}.\supset .\mu ^{2},\mu ^{3},...\in \text{NC med},\\ &amp;\mu ^\nu \in \text{NC med}.\supset :\mu \in \text{NC med}.\lor.\nu \in \text{NC med},\\ &amp;\mu \in \text{NC med}.\supset .2^{2^\mu }\in \text{NC refl},\\ &amp;\text{whence}\qquad \exists !\text{NC med}.\supset .(\exists \nu ).\nu \in \text{NC med}.2^\nu \in \text{NC refl}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4034.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.288ex; width: 55.921ex; height: 11.707ex;" id="img_images_4034.svg"></span>
since we have either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \in \text{NC med}.2^\mu \in \text{NC refl}\)" src="images/4035.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 24.96ex; height: 2.085ex;" id="img_images_4035.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^\mu \in \text{NC med}.2^{2^\mu }\in \text{NC refl}\)" src="images/4036.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 26.53ex; height: 2.06ex;" id="img_images_4036.svg">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_289">[Pg 289]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_125">
*125. THE AXIOM OF INFINITY.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *125.</p>

<p>The present number is merely concerned to give a few equivalent
forms of the axiom of infinity, and of the kindred assumption of the
existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_295.svg_33">.</p>

<p>In virtue of <a href="#_125_24" class="pginternal">*125·24</a><a href="#_125_25" class="pginternal">·25</a> below, if the axiom of infinity holds in any
one type, then it holds in any other type which can be derived from
this one, or from any type from which this one can be derived. Hence if
we assume, as it seems natural to do, that all extensional types are
derived from a first type, namely that of individuals, then the axiom
of infinity in any such type is equivalent to the assumption that the
number of individuals is not inductive.</p>

<p>We deal, in this number, first with equivalent forms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.545ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_380.svg_4">,
then with equivalent forms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax} (x)\)" src="images/3144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.6ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3144.svg_1">, then
with equivalent forms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/4037.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.257ex; height: 1.994ex;" id="img_images_4037.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\aleph_{0}(x)\)" src="images/4038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.311ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4038.svg">.
When "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.545ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_380.svg_5">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\aleph _{0}\)" src="images/4037.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.257ex; height: 1.994ex;" id="img_images_4037.svg_1">"
occurs in this number without typical definition, it and all other
typically ambiguous symbols are to be taken in the lowest logically
possible types, or with the same relative types as if this had been
done. The propositions of this number are often not referred to in the
sequel, but are here collected together on account of their intrinsic
interest.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_293">[Pg 293]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_126">
*126. ON TYPICALLY INDEFINITE INDUCTIVE CARDINALS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nindc"><i>Recapitulation of Conventions and Summary of</i> *126.</p>

<p>We have now arrived at the stage where we can adopt the standpoint of
ordinary arithmetic, and can for the future in arithmetical operations
with cardinals ignore differences of type. In order to understand how
this is so, it will be necessary briefly to recall the line of thought
of some of the previous numbers and the conventions upon which the
symbolism is based.</p>

<p>The symbolism of <a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a>, though perfectly precise as to the typical
relations of the various symbols, is in fact too complex for use,
except in cases of absolute necessity. It is better to use the
typically ambiguous symbols <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_33"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_13">, combined
with some simple rules of interpretation of the symbolism, so as to
secure that the various occurrences of the same symbols are in their
proper relationships of type. This is the course followed in <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>,
<a href="#_101" class="pginternal">*101</a>, and in every number from <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a> onwards.</p>

<p>The important symbols which involve an explicit or implicit use of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.701ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_130.svg_34"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_129.svg_12"> are called 'formal numbers,' and it is
only necessary to make the rules of interpretation apply to them.</p>

<p>A constant formal number is any symbol representing a typically
ambiguous constant such that there is a constant <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_219"> such that,
however the ambiguities of type may be determined, the former constant
is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_67">. The variable formal numbers are
defined by enumeration. They are divided into three Sets, the Primary
Set, the Argumental Set, and the Arithmetical Set.</p>

<p>The Primary Set consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_68">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma\text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.995ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_195.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi \text{Nc}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_161.svg_5">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_220"> is a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/4071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4071.svg">
of any type and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_114"> is a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\)" src="images/4072.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.142ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_4072.svg"> of any type.
Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_221"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_115"> may themselves be complex symbols which
in some way involve variables.</p>

<p>The Argumental Set has only one member <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_18">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_158"> is a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\)" src="images/4072.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.142ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_4072.svg_1"> of any type. In its capacity
of a formal number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_19"> is only interesting when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_159"> is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_19">; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_20"> gives the
corresponding <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_20"> in another type, provided that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_160"> is
not <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_50">. Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_161"> may be a complex symbol which in some
way involves a variable, <i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/1588.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.129ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1588.svg_1">
is a formal number of the Argumental Set: <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_162"> is called the
<i>argument</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }ʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.986ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_21">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_294">[Pg 294]</span></p>

<p>The Arithmetical Set consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu +_{c}\nu\)" src="images/4073.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_4073.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times_{c}\nu\)" src="images/1852.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_1852.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu ^\nu\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.017ex;" id="img_images_172.svg_14">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu -_{c}\nu\)" src="images/4074.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.21ex; height: 1.808ex;" id="img_images_4074.svg">. These formal numbers
are only interesting when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_163"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_147"> are also members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC}\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_150.svg_21">. Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_164"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_148"> may be complex symbols, so long
as one of them at least involves a variable. For example <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{3+_{c}\nu}\)" src="images/4075.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.834ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_4075.svg">
is a formal number, and so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha +_{c}(3+_{c}\nu)\)" src="images/4076.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.831ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4076.svg">.</p>

<p>The Primary and Argumental and Arithmetical Sets of Formal Numbers are
derived from the corresponding sets of <i>variable</i> formal numbers,
by adding to them the constant formal numbers obtained by substituting
constants for the variables occurring in the expressions for the
members of the variable set in question.</p>

<p>In the formal numbers of the arithmetical set as written above, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_165">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_149"> are called the <i>first components</i>. Thus every formal
number of this set has two first components. The first components (if
any) of the first components are also called <i>components</i> of the
original formal number, and so on; so that components of components are
components of the original symbol.</p>

<p>A formal number of the arithmetical set, whose components are all
formal numbers, either constant or variable but <i>not</i> belonging to
the argumental set, is called a <i>pure arithmetical</i> formal number.
These are the formal numbers which it is important in arithmetic to
secure from assuming the value <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_51"> owing to lowness of type.</p>

<p>The logical investigation of <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a> and <a href="#_101" class="pginternal">*101</a>, where typically ambiguous
formal numbers are used, is directly concerned in investigating the
premisses necessary to secure various propositions from fluctuating
truth-values owing to the intrusion of null-values among the cardinals.
The convention, necessary to avoid determinations of type which we
never wish to consider, is as follows, where the terms used are
explained fully in the prefatory statement:</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_22">. Argumental occurrences are bound to logical and
attributive occurrences; and, if there are no argumental occurrences,
equational occurrences are bound to logical occurrences. This rule only
applies so far as meaning permits after the assignment of types to the
real variables.</p>

<p>In <a href="#_110" class="pginternal">*110</a>, <a href="#_113" class="pginternal">*113</a>, <a href="#_116" class="pginternal">*116</a>, <a href="#_119" class="pginternal">*119</a> we consider the arithmetical operations of
addition, multiplication, exponentiation, and subtraction. Also in
<a href="#_117" class="pginternal">*117</a> we consider the comparison of cardinal numbers in respect to the
relation of greater and less.</p>

<p>There is no interest in complicating our theorems by allowing for the
cases when a pure arithmetical formal number, whose components are
ambiguous as to type, becomes equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_52"> owing to the low
type of one of its <i>components</i>. Also in the theory of greater and
less the possibility of null-values in low types has no real interest.
Accordingly these are excluded from any consideration by the definitions</p>
<p class="nindc">
<a href="#_110_03" class="pginternal">*110·03</a><a href="#_110_04" class="pginternal">·04</a>, <a href="#_113_04" class="pginternal">*113·04</a><a href="#_113_05" class="pginternal">·05</a>, <a href="#_116_03" class="pginternal">*116·03</a><a href="#_116_04" class="pginternal">*116·04</a>, <a href="#_117_02" class="pginternal">*117·02</a><a href="#_117_03" class="pginternal">·03</a>,
</p><p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_295">[Pg 295]</span>
as far as members of the primary set of formal numbers are concerned;
and for other formal numbers by the following convention:</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_34">. Whenever a formal number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_37"> occurs, so that,
if it were replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_69">, the dominant type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_135.svg_70"> would by definition have to be adequate, then the
dominant type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_38"> is also to be adequate.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_39"> is a pure arithmetical formal number, this convention
secures that the type of every component is adequate.</p>

<p>But in arithmetic we also wish to avoid the intrusion of null-values
into the consideration of equations, so far as this avoidance can be
attained by the use of high types. Accordingly when we are concerned
with the purely arithmetical point of view, we add also the following
definition and convention (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_29">).</p>

<p><i>Definition</i>. An <i>arithmetical equation</i> is an equation
between pure arithmetical formal numbers whose dominant types are both
determined adequately.</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_30">. All equations involving pure arithmetical formal numbers
are to be arithmetical.</p>

<p>This convention is used in <a href="#_117" class="pginternal">*117</a> and in some earlier propositions which
are noted in the prefatory statement.</p>

<p>Its effect is to render the statement of hypotheses often unnecessary.
Examples of its application to the numbers where it is not used in the
symbolism are also considered in the prefatory statement.</p>

<p>In the case of the inductive numbers we cannot logically prove, apart
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Infin ax}\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.545ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_380.svg_6">, that one type exists which is adequate for
all the formal numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, etc. But we can prove that for any
particular inductive number, say 521, a type exists for which 521 is
not equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_53">. Accordingly for a given symbolic form, in
which the symbolism necessarily has only finite complexity, when the
types of variables which by hypothesis represent inductive classes or
inductive numbers, not <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_54">, have been settled, it is always
possible to fix on a type which will be adequate for all the pure
arithmetical formal numbers produced by the symbolism of the form, and
also at the same time (and here the peculiar properties of inductive
numbers come in) to have chosen the original types of the variables so
that any of the variables can assume the value of any assigned constant
inductive number, say 521, without being null.</p>

<p>The result is that we may assume that the symbols representing
inductive numbers are never null, and thereby obtain the stable
truth-values of propositions about them.</p>

<p>Accordingly we proceed as follows: we put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*126·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC ind}=\text{NC induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4077.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.419ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4077.svg">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_296">[Pg 296]</span></p>

<p>We make the rule that when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC ind}\)" src="images/372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.041ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_372.svg_1"> appears, convention
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_31"> is always applied. The result is that when a formal
number is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC ind}\)" src="images/372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.041ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_372.svg_2"> we need never think about its type, and
accordingly all the conventions vanish from the mind, as far as pure
arithmetical indefinite inductive cardinals are concerned. We supersede
all other conventions by the single one that, if it has been proved
or assumed that a formal number represents an inductive cardinal,
the types are so arranged that that formal number is not equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_55">. The proofs of propositions in this number consist largely
of the production of a definite type in which this result is attained.</p>

<p>The important propositions are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*126·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\nu \in \text{NC ind}.\supset .(\nu +_{c}1)\cap tʻ\nu \in \text{NC ind}\)" src="images/4078.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.849ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4078.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*126·121.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .1,2,3, ... \in \text{NC ind}\)" src="images/4079.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4079.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*126·13·14·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha ,\beta \in \text{NC ind}.\supset .\alpha +_{c}\beta ,\alpha \times _{c}\beta ,\alpha ^\beta \in \text{NC ind}\)" src="images/4080.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 47.063ex; height: 2.388ex;" id="img_images_4080.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*126·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha ,\beta \in \text{NC ind}-\iota ʻ0.\equiv .\alpha \times _{c}\beta \in \text{NC ind}-\iota ʻ0\)" src="images/4081.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 48.497ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4081.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*126·151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha ,\beta \in \text{NC ind}-\iota ʻ0.\alpha \neq 1.\equiv .\alpha ^\beta \in \text{NC ind}-\iota ʻ0-\iota ʻ1\)" src="images/4082.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 56.944ex; height: 2.436ex;" id="img_images_4082.svg"></p>

<p>Also <a href="#_126_4" class="pginternal">*126·4</a><a href="#_126_42" class="pginternal">·42</a><a href="#_126_43" class="pginternal">·43</a> give the fundamental propositions for subtraction,
division, and "inverse exponentiation"; and <a href="#_126_5" class="pginternal">*126·5</a><a href="#_126_51" class="pginternal">·51</a><a href="#_126_52" class="pginternal">·52</a><a href="#_126_53" class="pginternal">·53</a> the
fundamental propositions for the relations of greater and less.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*126·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC ind}=\text{Nc induct}-\iota ʻ\Lambda   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4083.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.79ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4083.svg"></p>

<p>Whenever the symbol <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NC ind}\)" src="images/372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.041ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_372.svg_3"> is used the <i>Rule of Indefinite
Numbers</i> is adhered to, so that all consideration of distinctions
in type among inductive cardinals can be laid aside (cf. Prefatory
Statement and also the Summary of this number).</p>

<p>This proposition, taken in connection with <a href="#_120_4232" class="pginternal">*120·4232</a>, embodies the
convention named the Rule of Indefinite Numbers and its justification.
The convention is that 1, 2, 3, ... are always in future to be used in
existential types. In other words whenever any particular inductive
number is employed, it is determined in a type in which it is not
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_56">. The justification is that by <a href="#_126_11" class="pginternal">*126·11</a><a href="#_126_12" class="pginternal">·12</a> such a type can
always be found for each particular inductive number.</p>

<p>The convention is also applied to arithmetical formal numbers in
<a href="#_126_13" class="pginternal">*126·13</a><a href="#_126_14" class="pginternal">·14</a><a href="#_126_15" class="pginternal">·15</a>.</p>

really the outcome of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_23">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_35">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_32">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<h2 class="nobreak" id="PART_IV">PART IV.<br>
<br>
RELATION-ARITHMETIC.</h2>
</div>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_301">[Pg 301]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SUMMARY_OF_PART_IV">SUMMARY OF PART IV.</h2>
</div>


<p><span class="allsmcap">The</span> subject to be treated in this Part is a general kind of
arithmetic of which ordinal arithmetic is a particular application.
The form of arithmetic to be treated in this Part is applicable to all
relations, though its chief importance is in regard to such relations
as generate series. The analogy with cardinal arithmetic is very close,
and the reader will find that what follows is much facilitated by
bearing the analogy in mind.</p>

<p>The outlines of relation-arithmetic are as follows. We first define
a relation between relations, which we shall call <i>ordinal
similarity</i> or <i>likeness</i>, and which plays the same part for
relations as similarity plays for classes. Likeness between <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_46"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_8"> is constituted by the fact that the fields of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_47"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_9">
can be so correlated by a one-one relation that if any two terms have
the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_48">, their correlates have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_10">, and vice
versa. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_49"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_11"> generate series, we may express this by
saying that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_50"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_12"> are like if their fields can be correlated
without change of order. Having defined likeness, our next step is to
define the <i>relation-number</i> of a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_51"> as the class of
relations which are like <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_52">, just as the cardinal number of a class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_222"> is the class of classes which are similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_223">. We
then proceed to addition. The ordinal sum of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_53"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_13"> is defined as the relation which holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_91"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_55">
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_92"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_56"> have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_54"> or the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_14">, or
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_93"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_57"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_55"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_15"> generate series, it will be seen that this defines
the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_56"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_16"> as the series resulting from adding the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_17">-series after the end of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_57">-series. The sum is thus not
commutative. The sum of the relation-numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_58"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_18"> is of
course the relation-number of their sum, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_1">
have no common terms.</p>

<p>The ordinal product of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_59"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_19"> is the relation
between two couples <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\downarrow x\)" src="images/4112.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.734ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4112.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\downarrow y\)" src="images/4113.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4113.svg">, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_94">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_58"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_18">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/2358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2358.svg_2"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_2"> and either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y.zQw\)" src="images/4114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.887ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_4114.svg">. Thus, for example, if the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_60">
consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{P}\)" src="images/3394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3394.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{P}\)" src="images/3395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.846ex;" id="img_images_3395.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(3_{P}\)" src="images/3667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.52ex; height: 1.844ex;" id="img_images_3667.svg_2">, and the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_20">
consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{Q}\)" src="images/4115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 2.584ex; height: 2.157ex;" id="img_images_4115.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{Q}\)" src="images/4116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 2.584ex; height: 2.157ex;" id="img_images_4116.svg">, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \times Q\)" src="images/4117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4117.svg"> will hold
from any earlier to any later term of the following series:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 1_{Q}\downarrow 1_{P},\, 2_{Q}\downarrow 1_{P},\, 1_{Q}\downarrow 2_{P},\, 2_{Q}\downarrow 2_{P},\, 1_{Q}\downarrow 3_{P},\,     2_{Q}\downarrow 3_{P}. \]" src="images/4118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 52.506ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4118.svg"></span>
It is plain that, denoting the ordinal product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_61"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_21"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \times Q\)" src="images/4117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4117.svg_1">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Cʻ(P\times Q)=CʻP\times CʻQ, \]" src="images/4119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.146ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4119.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_302">[Pg 302]</span>
where the second "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\times\)" src="images/2195.svg" style="vertical-align: 0.02ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.09ex;" id="img_images_2195.svg_2">" as standing between classes has the
meaning defined in *113·01.</p>

<p>Infinite ordinal sums and products will also be defined, but the
definitions are somewhat complicated.</p>

<p>The arithmetic which results from the above definitions satisfies all
those of the formal laws which are satisfied in ordinal arithmetic,
when this is not confined to finite ordinals; that is to say,
relation-numbers satisfy the associative law for addition and for
multiplication<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_10" id="FNanchor_10">[10]</a>, they satisfy the distributive law in the shape
(where the + and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\times\)" src="images/2195.svg" style="vertical-align: 0.02ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.09ex;" id="img_images_2195.svg_3"> are those appropriate to relation-numbers)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\beta +\gamma )\times \alpha =(\beta \times \alpha )+(\gamma \times \alpha ), \]" src="images/4120.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.117ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4120.svg"></span>
and they satisfy the exponential laws
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha ^\beta \times \alpha ^\gamma &amp;=\alpha ^{(\beta +\gamma )},\\ (\alpha ^\beta )^\gamma &amp;=\alpha ^{\beta \times \gamma }. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4121.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.438ex; width: 17.357ex; height: 6.006ex;" id="img_images_4121.svg"></span>
They do not in general satisfy the commutative law either in addition
or in multiplication, nor do they satisfy the distributive law in the
form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \times (\beta +\gamma )=(\alpha \times \beta )+(\alpha \times \gamma ), \]" src="images/4122.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.117ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4122.svg"></span>
nor the exponential law
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha ^\gamma \times \beta ^\gamma =(\alpha \times \beta )^\gamma . \]" src="images/4123.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.564ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4123.svg"></span>
But in the particular case in which the relations concerned are finite
serial relations, the corresponding relation-numbers do satisfy these
additional formal laws; hence the arithmetic of <i>finite</i> ordinals
is exactly analogous to that of inductive cardinals (cf. Part V,
Section E).</p>

<p>If the relations concerned are limited to well-ordered relations,
relation-arithmetic becomes ordinal arithmetic as developed by Cantor;
but many of Cantor's propositions, as we shall see in this Part, do not
require the limitation to well-ordered relations.</p>


<div class="footnotes"><h3>FOOTNOTES:</h3>

<div class="footnote">

<p class="nind">
<a class="label pginternal" href="#FNanchor_10" id="Footnote_10">[10]</a>
For the associative law of multiplication, a hypothesis
is required as to the kind of relation concerned. Cf. <a href="#_174_241" class="pginternal">*174·241</a><a href="#_174_25" class="pginternal">·25</a>.</p>
