<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_303">[Pg 303]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_A_II">SECTION A.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">ORDINAL SIMILARITY AND RELATION-NUMBERS.</span></h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of Section A.</i></p>

<p>Two series generated by the relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_62"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_22"> respectively
are said to be ordinally similar when their terms can be correlated
as they stand, without change of order. In the accompanying figure,
the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_17"> correlates the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_3"> in
such a way that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_2">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\((\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy)\)" src="images/4124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.346ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4124.svg">,
and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(zQw\)" src="images/4125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.462ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4125.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\((Sʻz)P(Sʻw)\)" src="images/4126.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.525ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4126.svg">. It is evident that the journey
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_95"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_59"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_3">) may, in such a case, be taken
by going first to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{S} ʻx\)" src="images/4127.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.111ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4127.svg">, thence to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{S} ʻy\)" src="images/4128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.928ex;" id="img_images_4128.svg">, and
thence back to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_60">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy.\equiv .x(S\mid Q\mid \breve{S})y\)" src="images/4129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.517ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4129.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}\)" src="images/4130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 13.196ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4130.svg">. Hence to say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_63">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_23"> are ordinally similar is equivalent to saying that there is
a one-one relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_18"> which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_4"> for its converse domain
and gives <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}\)" src="images/4130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 13.196ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4130.svg_1">. In this case we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_19"> a
<i>correlator</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_24"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_64">.</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 1200px;" id="i_303">
<img alt="Commutative diagram showing relations P, Q, S, and Š connecting elements x and y. Top row shows P:x→y extending to P=s|Q|Š. Bottom row shows Q:Š'x→Š'y extending to Q. Vertical arrows show S:x↓ and Š:y↑, demonstrating P decomposes as composition s|Q|Š in relational algebra." height="575" src="images/i_303.jpg" width="1200" id="img_images_i_303.jpg">
</figure>

<p>We denote the relation of ordinal similarity by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{smor}\)" src="images/4131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_4131.svg">,"
which is short for "similar ordinally." Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\,\text{smor}\,Q.\equiv .(\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻQ=\text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S} . \]" src="images/4132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.819ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4132.svg"></span></p>

<p>It will be found that the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}\)" src="images/4133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.48ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4133.svg"> plays the
same part in relation to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_25"> in relation-arithmetic as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.455ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4134.svg">
plays in relation to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_152"> in cardinal arithmetic. It is therefore
desirable to have a simpler notation for <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}\)" src="images/4133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.48ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4133.svg_1">. We
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S^{;}Q=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 20.807ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4135.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_304">[Pg 304]</span>
We shall find that the semi-colon so defined has the same kind of
properties in relation-arithmetic as the two inverted commas have in
cardinal arithmetic. Corresponding to the notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{\in }ʻ\beta\)" src="images/4136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.28ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4136.svg">,
we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S\dagger  Q = S\mid Q\breve{S}  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4137.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 20.182ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4137.svg"></span>
We shall thus have <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger =S\parallel\breve{S}\)" src="images/4138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.788ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4138.svg">. It will
appear that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger\)" src="images/4139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.464ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4139.svg"> has ordinal properties analogous to
the cardinal properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{\in }\)" src="images/4140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.642ex; height: 1.998ex;" id="img_images_4140.svg">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\parallel\breve{S} _{\in }\)" src="images/4141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.489ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4141.svg"> appears as a cardinal correlator,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\parallel \text{Cnv}ʻS\dagger\)" src="images/4142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.755ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4142.svg"> will appear as an ordinal correlator
(in each case with the converse domain suitably limited).</p>

<p>The elementary properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg"> will be considered in <a href="#_150" class="pginternal">*150</a>. We
shall then, in <a href="#_151" class="pginternal">*151</a>, be able to study ordinal similarity, taking as our
definition of an ordinal correlator
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q=\hat{S}\{S\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻQ=\text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S^{;}Q\} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/4144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.504ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4144.svg"></span>
and defining two relations as ordinally similar when they have at least
one ordinal correlator, <i>i.e.</i> putting (on the analogy of *73)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{smor}=\hat{P} \hat{Q}\{\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.8ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_4145.svg"></span></p>

<p>There is no need to confine the notion of ordinal similarity (or
likeness, as we shall also call it) to <i>serial</i> relations. When
two relations have ordinal similarity, their internal structures are
analogous, and they therefore have many common properties. Whenever
similarity has been proved between two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_224"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_153">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_154"> is given as the field of some relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_26">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_20"> is the correlating relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_1"> is like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_27">,
and has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_225"> for its field. Hence similar classes are the
fields of like relations. It must not be supposed, however, that like
relations are coextensive with relations whose fields are similar.
This does not hold even when we confine ourselves to serial relations,
except in the special case of <i>finite</i> serial relations.</p>

<p>The definition of relation-numbers (<a href="#_152" class="pginternal">*152</a>) is as follows: The
relation-number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_65">, which we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg">, is the class
of relations which are ordinally similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_66">; and the class of
relation-numbers, which we denote by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}R\)" src="images/4147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.414ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_4147.svg">, is the class of
all classes of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_1">. The elementary properties of
relation-numbers, treated in *152, are closely analogous to those of
cardinal numbers treated in <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>.</p>

<p>After a few propositions about the ordinal 0 and the ordinal 2, which
we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r}\)" src="images/2.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_1"> (<a href="#_153" class="pginternal">*153</a>), we pass to the consideration
of relation-numbers of various types. It will be observed that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{smor}\)" src="images/4131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_4131.svg_1">," like "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_14">," is a relation which is
ambiguous as to the type both of its domain and of its converse
domain. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \,\text{smor} \,Q\)" src="images/4148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4148.svg">" only has an unambiguous meaning
when the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_67"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_28"> are determined. <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_68"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_29"> may
or may not be of the same type; the only restriction upon the type
of either is that both must be "homogeneous" relations, <i>i.e.</i>
relations whose domain and converse domain<span class="pagenum" id="Page_305">[Pg 305]</span> are of the same type. This
restriction results from the fact that <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_5"> occurs in the definition
of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\text{smor}\,Q\)" src="images/4149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4149.svg">," and a relation does not have a field unless
it is homogeneous; hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_30"> must be homogeneous, and therefore,
whatever <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_21"> may be, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}\)" src="images/4133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.48ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_4133.svg_2"> must be homogeneous,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_69"> must be homogeneous. Thus <i>e.g.</i> such relations
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/720.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_720.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/724.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_724.svg_2">, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/725.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_725.svg_1"> are not ordinally similar either
to themselves or to anything else. Whenever "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\text{smor}\,Q\)" src="images/4149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4149.svg_1">"
is <i>significant</i> for a suitable <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_31">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\text{smor}\,P\)" src="images/4150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 8.948ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_4150.svg">;
but if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_70"> is not homogeneous, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\text{smor}\,Q\)" src="images/4149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4149.svg_2">" is never
significant. Hence throughout the theory of ordinal similarity, the
relations of which ordinal similarity is affirmed or denied must be
homogeneous. The correlators, on the contrary, need not be homogeneous.</p>

<p>Owing to the homogeneity of our relations, the types of
relation-numbers are much more easily dealt with than they otherwise
would be; for the type of a homogeneous relation is determined by that
of a single class, namely its field, whereas the type of a relation
in general depends upon the types of <i>two</i> classes, namely its
domain and its converse domain. Since, where likeness is concerned, the
type of the field determines the type of the relation, propositions
concerning the relations between different typical determinations of
a given relation-number are, for the most part, exactly analogous to
and deducible from those for cardinals. In fact, a relation ordinally
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_32"> exists in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_71"> when, and only when, a
class similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_6"> exists in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_4">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists !\text{Nr}(P)ʻQ.\equiv .\exists !\text{Nc}(CʻP)ʻCʻQ. \]" src="images/4151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.827ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4151.svg"></span>
The half of this proposition follows from the fact that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_72"> is
like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_33">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_5"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_7">. The other half follows
from the fact, mentioned above, that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =CʻQ\)" src="images/4152.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.164ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4152.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\text{ sm } \beta\)" src="images/4153.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.636ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4153.svg">,
then there is a relation like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_34"> and having
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_226"> for its field. Now if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_227"> belongs to the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_6">, any relation having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_228"> for its field is contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻCʻP\uparrow t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.264ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4154.svg">. Hence in the case supposed
there is a relation like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_35"> and contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻCʻP\uparrow t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.264ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4154.svg_1">.
But the relations contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻCʻP\uparrow t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.264ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4154.svg_2">
constitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻP\)" src="images/4155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4155.svg">. Hence there is a relation which is like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_36">
and is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻP\)" src="images/4155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4155.svg_1">, whence our proposition results. By
means of this proposition and those of <a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a>—<a href="#_106" class="pginternal">6</a>, the properties
of relation-numbers with respect to types follow easily. The
conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_24">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IIT}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.267ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_190.svg_36"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_33"> apply to
relation-numbers as to cardinals; they are to be applied in the same
way as in the analogous propositions of Part III, Section A.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_306">[Pg 306]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_150">
*150. INTERNAL TRANSFORMATION OF A RELATION.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *150.</p>

<p>In this number we introduce two notations which have uses in regard to
relations closely analogous to the uses of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4156.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}\)" src="images/2830.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_2830.svg_1"> in regard to classes. These two notations are defined as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} S^{;}Q&amp;=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}   \quad\text{Df},\\ S\dagger  Q&amp;=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}   \quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4157.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.803ex; width: 22.068ex; height: 6.738ex;" id="img_images_4157.svg"></span>
We then have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .S\dagger Q=S^{;}Q=S\mid Q\mid \breve{S}=(S\parallel \breve{S})ʻQ\)" src="images/4158.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.391ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4158.svg">.</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger Q\)" src="images/4159.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.259ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4159.svg"> is merely an alternative to <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_2">, just as <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4160.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.777ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4160.svg">
is an alternative to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4156.svg_1">. Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger =S\parallel \breve{S}\)" src="images/4161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.788ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4161.svg">, in virtue of *38·01 and *43·01.</p>

<p>The uses of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_3"> occur chiefly when <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_22"> is a one-one relation
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.058ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4162.svg">. This case is illustrated in the figure
in the introduction to this section. Here if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_37"> relates <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_96">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_61">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_4"> relates <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻx\)" src="images/4163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.111ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4163.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2835.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2835.svg_1">. Thus given a class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_229"> similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_8">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_23"> is the correlating relation,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_5"> has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_230"> for its field, and has, in very many respects,
properties analogous to those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_38">.</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_6"> is important for many special values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_24">. For example,
let <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_39"> be a relation between relations; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(C^{;}Q\)" src="images/4164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.26ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4164.svg"> will be the
corresponding relation of the fields of these relations. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_40"> be
any relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x^{;}Q\)" src="images/4165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.476ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4165.svg"> will be the corresponding relation
between ordered couples of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_97"> is the relatum; <i>i.e.</i>
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(yQz\)" src="images/4166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.95ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_4166.svg">, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x^{;}Q\)" src="images/4165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.476ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4165.svg_1"> will hold between
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow x\)" src="images/4167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4167.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\downarrow x\)" src="images/4112.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.734ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4112.svg_1">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_41"> is a relation between
classes, and we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta Q\gamma\)" src="images/4168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.299ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4168.svg">, then the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cup ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.385ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4169.svg">
will hold between <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/1301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1301.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cup \gamma\)" src="images/4170.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.191ex; height: 1.842ex;" id="img_images_4170.svg">.
In short, whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_25"> is a one-many relation, and therefore gives
rise to a descriptive function, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_7"> is the relation which
holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2835.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2835.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻz\)" src="images/4171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.869ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4171.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_42"> holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_62">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_19">.</p>

<p>We introduce one other new notation in this number, corresponding to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \unicode{x2640}_{,,}y\)" src="images/4172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 4.991ex; height: 2.54ex;" id="img_images_4172.svg"> in *38. This notation is thus defined:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q\unicode{x2640}_{.,}y=\unicode{x2640}y^{;}Q  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 18.55ex; height: 2.54ex;" id="img_images_4173.svg"></span>
The purpose of this notation is to enable us to proceed to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x2640}_{.,}^{;}P\)" src="images/4174.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 5.923ex; height: 2.636ex;" id="img_images_4174.svg"> and other similar notations; or, otherwise
stated, to enable us to treat <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x2640}y^{;}Q as\)" src="images/4175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.146ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4175.svg"> a function
of y rather than of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_43">. Take for example the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow^{;}Q\)" src="images/4176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.104ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4176.svg">.
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_307">[Pg 307]</span>We may wish to consider various relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4177.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.104ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4177.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4178.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.919ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_4178.svg">, where we are to have (say) <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_4">. To express the
relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4177.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.104ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4177.svg_1"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4178.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.919ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_4178.svg_1"> resulting from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_5">, we need the above notation. By its help, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} x\downarrow ^{;}Q&amp;=Q\downarrow_{.,} ʻx.y\downarrow ^{;}Q=Q\downarrow_{.,} ʻy.\\ \text{Hence}\qquad  xPy.&amp;\equiv .(Q\downarrow_{.,} ʻx)(Q\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}P)(Q\downarrow_{.,} ʻy). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4179.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.23ex; width: 47.11ex; height: 5.591ex;" id="img_images_4179.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}P\)" src="images/4180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4180.svg"> is the relation between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow^{;}Q\)" src="images/4176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.104ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4176.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4178.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.919ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_4178.svg_2"> corresponding to the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_73">
between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_98"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_63">. <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}P\)" src="images/4180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4180.svg_1"> plays the same part
in relation-arithmetic as is played by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1371.svg_4">
in cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p>The notations of this number are capable of occasional uses in cardinal
arithmetic<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_11" id="FNanchor_11">[11]</a>, but their chief utility is in relation-arithmetic, in
which they are fundamental.</p>

<p>In order to minimize the use of brackets, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} RʻS^{;}Q&amp;=Rʻ(S^{;}Q)  &amp;\quad\text{Df},\\ R^{;}S^{;}Q&amp;=R^{;}(S^{;}Q)  &amp;\quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4181.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 28.76ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_4181.svg"></span></p>

<p>As an immediate result of the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_8"> we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x(S^{;}Q)y.\equiv .(\exists z,w).xSz.ySw.zQw\)" src="images/4182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.742ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4182.svg"></p>

<p>We have also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Cnv}ʻS^{;}Q=S^{;}\breve{Q}\)" src="images/4183.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.845ex; height: 2.914ex;" id="img_images_4183.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .R^{;}S^{;}Q=(R\mid S)^{;}Q\)" src="images/4184.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.998ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4184.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition, which is the analogue of <img alt="" data-tex="\((P\mid Q)ʻʻ\gamma=PʻʻQʻʻy\)" src="images/4185.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.122ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4185.svg">
(*37·33), is very often used. We have also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .S^{;}(Q\unicode{x228d} R)=S^{;}Q\unicode{x228d} S^{;}R\)" src="images/4186.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.52ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4186.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .S^{;}\dot{\Lambda} =\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/4187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 10.754ex; height: 2.541ex;" id="img_images_4187.svg"></p>

<p>The remaining propositions of this number (with a few exceptions) may
be thus classified:</p>

<p>(1) Propositions concerning the domain, converse domain, and field of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_9"> (<a href="#_150_2" class="pginternal">*150·2</a>—<a href="#_150_23" class="pginternal">·23</a>). Owing to the fact that the chief applications
of this subject are to cases where <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_44"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_10"> are serial, the
<i>field</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_11"> is more important than its domain or converse
domain. Thus the chief propositions here are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset .CʻS^{;}Q=SʻʻCʻQ\)" src="images/4188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 37.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4188.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :CʻQ=\text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset .CʻS^{;}Q=\text{D}ʻS\)" src="images/4189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.107ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4189.svg"></p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.058ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4162.svg_1"> is verified in almost all
applications of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_12">. When it is not verified, the part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_9">
not contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4190.svg"> is irrelevant to the value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_13">.
The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ=\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4191.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.058ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4191.svg"> is very often verified in practice,
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_308">[Pg 308]</span>since it is verified when <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_26"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_45">.</p>

<p>(2) Propositions concerning relations with limited domains, converse
domains, or fields (<a href="#_150_32" class="pginternal">*150·32</a>—<a href="#_150_38" class="pginternal">·38</a>). Broadly speaking, a limitation
on the <i>field</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_46"> is equivalent to a limitation on the
<i>converse domain</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_27">, and both are equivalent to a
corresponding limitation on the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_15"> provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.03ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_4192.svg">.
The limitations that occur in practice are limitations on the converse
domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_28">, with consequent limitations on the fields of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_47"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_16">.</p>

<p>The chief propositions on this subject are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(S\upharpoonright CʻQ)^{;}Q=S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.112ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4193.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp y\in CʻQ.\supset _{y}.Rʻy=Sʻy:\supset .R^{;}Q=S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 43.183ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_4194.svg"></p>

<p>(This follows from *150·32 and *35·71.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·36.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(S\upharpoonright \beta )^{;}Q=S^{;}(Q\unicode{x0294f}\beta )\)" src="images/4195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.924ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4195.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·37.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset .S^{;}(Q\unicode{x0294f}\beta )=(S^{;}Q)\unicode{x0294f}Sʻʻ\beta =(S\upharpoonright \beta )^{;}Q=\{(Sʻʻ\beta     )\upharpoonleft S\}^{;}Q\)" src="images/4196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 73.393ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4196.svg"></p>

<p>(3) Propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_17"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_29"> is one-many or many-one
(<a href="#_150_4" class="pginternal">*150·4</a>—<a href="#_150_56" class="pginternal">·56</a>). We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp S\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\supset :x(S^{;}Q)y.\equiv .(\exists z,w).x=Sʻz.y=Sʻw.zQw\)" src="images/4197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.299ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4197.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is used constantly. Only slightly less useful is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp S\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset :x(S^{;}Q)y.\equiv .(\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy)\)" src="images/4198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.979ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4198.svg"></p>

<p>The remaining propositions of this set are chiefly applications of
<a href="#_150_4" class="pginternal">*150·4</a><a href="#_150_41" class="pginternal">·41</a> to special cases.</p>

<p>(4) A few propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x2640}_{.,}y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 5.333ex; height: 2.54ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg"> (<a href="#_150_6" class="pginternal">*150·6</a>—<a href="#_150_62" class="pginternal">·62</a>).
These are immediate consequences of the definition.</p>

<p>(5) A set of propositions on couples and matters connected with them
(<a href="#_150_7" class="pginternal">*150·7</a>—<a href="#_150_75" class="pginternal">·75</a>). The chief of these is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.z,w\in \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset .S^{;}(z\downarrow w)=(Sʻz)\downarrow (Sʻw)\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.326ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is very often used in relation-arithmetic. Useful also
is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·73.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .S^{;}(\alpha \uparrow \beta )=Sʻʻ\alpha \uparrow Sʻ\beta\)" src="images/4201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.598ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4201.svg"></p>

<p>(6) We next have four propositions (<a href="#_150_8" class="pginternal">*150·8</a>—<a href="#_150_83" class="pginternal">·83</a>) on <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}P\)" src="images/4202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.908ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4202.svg"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_74">
is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_48">. These belong with the propositions of *92; they
are useful in the ordinal theory of finite and infinite. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·82·83.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp S\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1:\text{D}ʻQ\subset &amp;\text{ᗡ}ʻS.\lor.\text{ᗡ}ʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS:\supset .\\ \text{Pot}ʻS^{;}Q=S\daggerʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻQ.(S^{;}Q)_{\text{po}}=S^{;}Q_{\text{po}}\end{align}\]" src="images/4203.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.078ex; width: 65.38ex; height: 5.288ex;" id="img_images_4203.svg"></span></p>

<p>It follows that, in the hypothesis supposed, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_30"> is a correlator
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_75"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_49">, it is also a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_2"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/4204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.667ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_4204.svg">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_309">[Pg 309]</span></p>

<p>(7) Propositions concerning the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger\)" src="images/4139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.464ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4139.svg_1"> (<a href="#_150_14" class="pginternal">*150·14</a>—<a href="#_150_171" class="pginternal">·171</a>
and <a href="#_150_9" class="pginternal">*150·9</a>—<a href="#_150_94" class="pginternal">·94</a>). These have uses analogous to those of propositions
concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{\in }\)" src="images/4140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.642ex; height: 1.998ex;" id="img_images_4140.svg_1">. The most important are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .R\dagger  \mid S\dagger  =(R\mid S)\dagger\)" src="images/4205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.304ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4205.svg"></p>

<p>(This follows immediately from <a href="#_150_13" class="pginternal">*150·13</a>, above.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .S\dagger  =S\parallel \breve{S} \)" src="images/4206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.176ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4206.svg"></p>

<p>(This follows immediately from the definition.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\dot{s} ʻR\dagger  ʻʻ\lambda =R\dagger  (\dot{s} ʻ\lambda )=R^{;}\dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.915ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_4207.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is analogous to <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻRʻʻʻ\kappa =Rʻʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.682ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4208.svg">
(*40·38), <i>i.e.</i> to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ sʻR_{\in }ʻʻ\kappa =R_{\in }ʻsʻ\kappa =Rʻʻsʻ\kappa , \]" src="images/4209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 32.277ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4209.svg"></span>
as appears on substituting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_722.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\dagger\)" src="images/4210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.722ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4210.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/721.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_721.svg_3"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in }\)" src="images/4211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_4211.svg"> in this variant of *40·38.</p>

<p>The remaining propositions are mainly of the nature of lemmas, to be
used once or twice each in relation-arithmetic.</p>

when placed between two letters, defines a descriptive function
of the arguments represented by those letters. Thus for example
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x2640}\)" src="images/2828.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2828.svg_2">" may represent any of the following:

<p>The two following definitions serve merely for the avoidance of
brackets.</p>

<p>The following propositions, on the domain, converse domain and field of

ever used, but is inserted in order that the general case may not
remain unconsidered.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_150_22">*150·22</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset .CʻS^{;}Q=SʻʻCʻQ  \quad[*150·21·211.*37·22]\)" src="images/4246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.498ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4246.svg"></p>

<p>In practice, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_19"> is used, we almost always have <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4247.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.058ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4247.svg">.
For the use of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_20"> is to obtain a relation analogous
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_50"> and having a different field; now <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_21"> is analogous
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x0294f}\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4248.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.321ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4248.svg">, for the part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_10"> which
lies outside <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4190.svg_1"> is unaffected by <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_31">. Hence if we
have, to start with, a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_51"> whose field is not contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4190.svg_2">, we shall usually find it profitable to limit the
field to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4190.svg_3">, and consider the transformed relation rather
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}(Q\unicode{x0294f}\text{ᗡ}ʻS)\)" src="images/4249.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.29ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4249.svg"> than as <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_22">. Thus the
hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/4162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.058ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4162.svg_2"> will be verified in almost all
useful applications of the notion of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_23">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_150_4">*150·4</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp S\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\supset :x(S^{;}Q)y.\equiv .(\exists z,w).x=Sʻz.y=Sʻw.zQw\\ &amp;[*150·11.*71·36]\end{align}\]" src="images/4268.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 62.927ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_4268.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is fundamental in the theory of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_24">, because in
most of the uses of this notion <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_32"> is one-many. The proposition
states that when <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_33"> is one-many, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_25"> is the relation between
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻs\)" src="images/4269.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.878ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4269.svg"> of terms related by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_52">. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_34"> is the relation
of wife to husband, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_53"> is the relation of brother to brother,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_26"> is the relation between wives of brothers. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_54"> is a
relation between relations, <img alt="" data-tex="\(C^{;}P\)" src="images/4270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.169ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4270.svg"> will be the corresponding relation
of their fields; and so on.</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*150·933. \supset \vdash :sʻCʻʻCʻQ&amp;\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P = S{\dagger}^{;}Q. \equiv  .\\ &amp;sʻCʻʻCʻP\subset \text{D}ʻS.sʻCʻʻCʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P = S{\dagger}^{;}Q  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*150·933 \frac{\breve{S}}{S}.\supset \vdash :sʻCʻʻCʻP&amp;\subset \text{D}ʻS.Q = \breve{S} {\dagger}^{;}P. \equiv  .\\ &amp;sʻCʻʻCʻP\subset \text{D}ʻS.sʻCʻʻCʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.Q = \breve{S} {\dagger}^{;}P &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*150·93.*5·32.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp S\in 1\rightarrow 1.&amp;\supset :sʻCʻʻCʻP\subset \text{D}ʻS.sʻCʻʻCʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P = S{\dagger}^{;}Q. \equiv  .\\ &amp;sʻCʻʻCʻP\subset \text{D}ʻS.sʻCʻʻCʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.Q = \breve{S} {\dagger}^{;}P  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).(3).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4323.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.012ex; width: 99.074ex; height: 27.155ex;" id="img_images_4323.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is the analogue of *74·61, which (with a few
trivial transformations) may be written
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\supset :sʻ\lambda \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\kappa  = S_{\in}ʻʻ\lambda . \equiv  .sʻ\kappa \subset \text{D}ʻS.\lambda  = (\breve{S} )_{\in}ʻʻ\kappa . \]" src="images/4324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 70.127ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4324.svg"></span></p>

<p>In obtaining ordinal analogues of such propositions, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{\in }\)" src="images/4140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.642ex; height: 1.998ex;" id="img_images_4140.svg_2">
will be replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger\)" src="images/4139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.464ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4139.svg_3">, and the two inverted commas will
be replaced by the semi-colon; a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_116"> will be
replaced, in most of its occurrences, by a relation of relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_77">,
but will sometimes be replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg">.</p>

<p>The above proposition (<a href="#_150_94" class="pginternal">*150·94</a>) is used in proving that the converse of
a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_78"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_56"> is a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_57">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_79"> (<a href="#_164_21" class="pginternal">*164·21</a>). The corresponding cardinal proposition (<a href="#_111_131" class="pginternal">*111·131</a>)
uses *74·6, which is practically the same proposition as *74·61, which
is the analogue of *150·94.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·95.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :CʻR\subset \text{Cl}ʻ\alpha .\supset .(S\upharpoonright \alpha )_{\in }^{;}R = S^{;}R\)" src="images/4326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.074ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_4326.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*37·421.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :\beta \in CʻR.\supset .(S\upharpoonright \alpha )ʻʻ\beta  = Sʻʻ\beta .\\ [*37·11]                \supset .(S\upharpoonright \alpha )_{\in }ʻ\beta  = S_{\in }ʻ\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*150·35.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4327.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 66.456ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_4327.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_318">[Pg 318]</span></p>

<p>The above proposition is used in the theory of "first differences"
(<a href="#_170_41" class="pginternal">*170·41</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*150·96.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{ᗡ}ʻ\dot{s} ʻ\lambda \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset .\text{D}^{;}(T\parallel \breve{S} \upharpoonright \lambda =T_{\in }\upharpoonright     \text{D}ʻʻ\lambda \)" src="images/4328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.812ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4328.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*150·51.&amp;\supset \vdash :\alpha {\text{D}^{;}(T\parallel \breve{S} )\upharpoonright \lambda }\beta .\equiv .\\ &amp;(\exists M,N).N\in \lambda .M=T\mid N\mid \breve{S} .\alpha =\text{D}ʻM.\beta =\text{D}ʻN &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*41·13.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :N\in \lambda .\supset .\text{ᗡ}ʻN\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\\ [*37·321]  &amp;\supset .\text{D}ʻ(N\mid \breve{S} )=\text{D}ʻN.\\ [*37.32]  &amp;\supset .\text{D}ʻ(T\mid N\mid \breve{S} )=Tʻʻ\text{D}ʻN  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).*37·6.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset .\alpha \{\text{D}^{;}(T\parallel \breve{S} )\upharpoonright \lambda\}\beta .&amp;\equiv .\beta \in \text{D}ʻʻ\lambda .\alpha =Tʻʻ\beta .\\ [*37·101]  &amp;\equiv .\alpha (T_{\in }\upharpoonright \text{D}ʻʻ\lambda )\beta \colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4329.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.569ex; width: 92.842ex; height: 28.269ex;" id="img_images_4329.svg"></span></p>
