<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_319">[Pg 319]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_151">
*151. ORDINAL SIMILARITY.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *151.</p>

<p>In this number, we give the definition of ordinal similarity, and
various equivalent forms; we prove that ordinal similarity is reflexive
(<a href="#_151_13" class="pginternal">*151·13</a>), symmetrical (<a href="#_151_14" class="pginternal">*151·14</a>) and transitive (<a href="#_151_15" class="pginternal">*151·15</a>), and we give
some particular cases of ordinal similarity (<a href="#_151_6" class="pginternal">*151·6</a> ff.). Propositions
in this number should be compared with those in *73, to which they are
analogous.</p>

<p>The class of ordinal correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_80"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_58"> is written
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\)" src="images/4332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.17ex;" id="img_images_4332.svg">, where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{smor}\)" src="images/4131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_4131.svg_2">" stands for
"similar ordinally." We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q=\hat{S}\{S\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻQ=\text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S^{;}Q\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4333.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.504ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4333.svg"></span></p>

<p>(We might equally well put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q=(1\rightarrow 1)\cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻCʻQ\cap \dagger \overleftarrow{Q}ʻP \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/4334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.937ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_4334.svg"></span>
which is an equivalent but more condensed form of the definition.) We
then define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_81"> is ordinally similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_59">" as meaning that there
is at least one ordinal correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_82"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_60">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{smor}=\hat{P} \hat{Q} (\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.298ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_4335.svg"></span></p>

<p>We shall find that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_83"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_61"> generate well-ordered series,
they have at most one correlator (*250·6), but this does not hold in
general for other series.</p>

<p>After giving the elementary properties of ordinal similarity, we
have three important propositions on its connection with cardinal
similarity, namely: (<a href="#_151_18" class="pginternal">*151·18</a>) if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_84"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_62">, the field
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_85"> is similar to the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_63"> (the converse does not hold
in general, but holds if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_86"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_64"> are finite serial relations);
(<a href="#_151_19" class="pginternal">*151·19</a>) if <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_7"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_11">, there is a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_40">
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_65"> and having <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_8"> for its field, and vice versa;
(<a href="#_151_191" class="pginternal">*151·191</a>) <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_36"> is an ordinal correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_87"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_66"> when,
and only when, it is a cardinal correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_12"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P=S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.714ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4336.svg">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_320">[Pg 320]</span></p>

<p>We then have a set of propositions on correlators of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\upharpoonright CʻQ\)" src="images/4257.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.526ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4257.svg_1"> (<a href="#_151_2" class="pginternal">*151·2</a>—<a href="#_151_243" class="pginternal">·243</a>). Most of the correlators
with which we shall be concerned are of this form. The most useful
proposition here is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\upharpoonright CʻQ\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S^{;}Q.\equiv .S\upharpoonright CʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\)" src="images/4337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 66.224ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_4337.svg"></p>

<p>A useful consequence of this proposition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·231.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp (y).\text{E}!Sʻy:S\upharpoonright CʻQ\in 1\rightarrow 1.P=S^{;}Q:\supset .S\upharpoonright CʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\)" src="images/4338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 66.022ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_4338.svg"></p>

<p>This consequence is useful because the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\((y).\text{E}!Sʻy\)" src="images/4339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.97ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4339.svg">
is satisfied by most of the relations which occur as correlators.</p>

<p>We have next a number of propositions on the inferribility of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q=\breve{S} ^{;}P\)" src="images/4340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.714ex; height: 2.903ex;" id="img_images_4340.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \breve{S} ^{;}P\)" src="images/4341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.81ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4341.svg"> from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P=S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.714ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4336.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.81ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4342.svg">, and connected matters
(<a href="#_151_25" class="pginternal">*151·25</a>—<a href="#_151_29" class="pginternal">·29</a>).</p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S^{;}Q.\supset .Q=\breve{S} ^{;}P\)" src="images/4343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 49.563ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4343.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·26.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp S\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset :&amp;P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, S^{;}Q.\supset .\breve{S} ^{;}P\,\unicode{x2abd}\,     Q:\\ &amp;S^{;}Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset .Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \breve{S} ^{;}P\end{align}\]" src="images/4344.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.803ex; width: 52.156ex; height: 6.738ex;" id="img_images_4344.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·29.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P\,\text{smor}\,Q.\equiv :(\exists S):&amp;xPy.\supset _{x,y}.(\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy):\\ &amp;zQw.\supset _{z,w}.(Sʻz)P(Sʻw)\end{align}\]" src="images/4345.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.513ex; width: 47ex; height: 6.156ex;" id="img_images_4345.svg"></span></p>

<p><a href="#_151_29" class="pginternal">*151·29</a> is never used, but is inserted in order to show that our
definition of "ordinal similarity" agrees with what is commonly
understood by that term. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_88"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_67"> are regarded as serial, so
that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_6">" means "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_99"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_64"> in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_89">-series," and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(zQw\)" src="images/4125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.462ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4125.svg_1">" means "<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_20"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/2358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2358.svg_3"> in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_68">-series," then our
proposition states that two series are ordinally similar when their
terms can be so correlated that predecessors in either are correlated
with predecessors in the other, and successors with successors,
<i>i.e.</i> when the two series can be correlated without change of
order.</p>

<p>We have next (<a href="#_151_31" class="pginternal">*151·31</a>—<a href="#_151_52" class="pginternal">·52</a>) a set of miscellaneous propositions, of
which the most useful are</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_151_401">*151·401</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :T\upharpoonright CʻP\in X,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P.T\upharpoonright CʻQ\in Y\overline{\text{smor}} Q.S\in &amp;P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\supset .\\ &amp;T^{;}S\in X\,\overline{\text{smor}} \,Y\end{align}\]" src="images/4346.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.07ex; width: 64.905ex; height: 5.271ex;" id="img_images_4346.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_151_5">*151·5</a>.</b>
    <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :S\upharpoonright CʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\supset .\text{D}ʻP=Sʻʻ\text{D}ʻQ.\text{ᗡ}ʻP=Sʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻQ.&amp;\overrightarrow{B}ʻP=Sʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻQ.\\ &amp;\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P} =Sʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{Q}\end{align}\]" src="images/4347.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.529ex; width: 78.798ex; height: 8.19ex;" id="img_images_4347.svg"></span></p>

<p><a href="#_151_401" class="pginternal">*151·401</a> will be useful in such cases as the following: Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_90">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_69"> be relations between relations, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}P\)" src="images/4348.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.06ex; height: 1.616ex;" id="img_images_4348.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}Q\)" src="images/4349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.151ex; height: 2.055ex;" id="img_images_4349.svg"> will be the corresponding relations of their domains.
Suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/4350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.705ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4350.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright CʻQ\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.343ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4351.svg">.
Then, by *151·401, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_37"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_91"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_70">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}S\)" src="images/4352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.82ex; height: 1.665ex;" id="img_images_4352.svg"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}P\)" src="images/4348.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.06ex; height: 1.616ex;" id="img_images_4348.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}Q\)" src="images/4349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.151ex; height: 2.055ex;" id="img_images_4349.svg_1">.</p>

<p><a href="#_151_5" class="pginternal">*151·5</a> shows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_38"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_92"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_71">, it correlates <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg_4"> with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻQ\)" src="images/4353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.876ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4353.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/4354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.414ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4354.svg"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻQ\)" src="images/4355.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4355.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/3663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3663.svg_6"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻQ\)" src="images/4356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.864ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4356.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/4357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4357.svg"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{Q}\)" src="images/4358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.864ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4358.svg">.</p>

<p>Our next set of propositions (<a href="#_151_53" class="pginternal">*151·53</a>—<a href="#_151_59" class="pginternal">·59</a>) is concerned with the
correlation of powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_93"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_72"> and kindred matters. We show
(<a href="#_151_55" class="pginternal">*151·55</a>) that a<span class="pagenum" id="Page_321">[Pg 321]</span> correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_94"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_73"> is also a correlator
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/4204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.667ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_4204.svg_2">, and therefore if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_95">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_74"> are similar, so are <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_5"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/4204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.667ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_4204.svg_3">
(<a href="#_151_56" class="pginternal">*151·56</a>); we show also (<a href="#_151_59" class="pginternal">*151·59</a>) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_96"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_75"> are similar,
so are <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\nu }\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.488ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\nu }\)" src="images/4359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.825ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4359.svg">. These propositions are used in
the theory of progressions (*263·17).</p>

<p>The remaining propositions (<a href="#_151_6" class="pginternal">*151·6</a> to the end) are concerned with
applications to particular cases. The most useful of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\iota ^{;}P\,\text{smor}\,P\)" src="images/4360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 12.77ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_4360.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which shows how to raise the type of a relation without changing its
relation-number;</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .x\downarrow ^{;}P\,\text{smor}\,P.(x\downarrow )\upharpoonright CʻP\in (x\downarrow ^{;}P)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P\)" src="images/4361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.236ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_4361.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·65.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\downarrow x^{;}P\,\text{smor}\,P.(\downarrow x)\upharpoonright CʻP\in (\downarrow x^{;}P)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P\)" src="images/4362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.979ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_4362.svg"></p>

<p>We prove also that all members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_2"> (<i>i.e.</i> all relations
of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1842.svg_2">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_411.svg_1">) are similar
<a href="#_151_63" class="pginternal">*151·63</a>), and that all relations of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg_1"> are
similar (<a href="#_151_631" class="pginternal">*151·631</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*151·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\text{smor}\,Q.\equiv .(\exists S).S\upharpoonright CʻQ\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S^{;}Q   \quad[*151·22]\)" src="images/4390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.357ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4390.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition (*151·23) is very useful. It is the analogue of
*73·15. (It should be observed that, in all propositions concerning
likeness, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.998ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4143.svg_27"> plays the same part as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.455ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4134.svg_1"> plays in
propositions concerning similarity.) By means of *151·23, we can
establish likeness in all those numerous cases in which a relation
which is not usually one-one becomes one-one when confined to a
certain converse domain, as for example if we have to deal with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4391.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.619ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4391.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/4392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.043ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_4392.svg">, or with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright P_{\Delta }ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.562ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4393.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.773ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4394.svg">. Thus
<i>e.g.</i> by the above proposition, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_76"> is any relation whose
field is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta }ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4395.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright \kappa \in\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.773ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4396.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}Q\)" src="images/4349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.151ex; height: 2.055ex;" id="img_images_4349.svg_2"> will be an ordinally similar
relation whose field is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta }ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4397.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_151_28">*151·28</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P\,\text{smor}\,Q.\equiv :(\exists S):S\in 1\rightarrow 1:&amp;xPy.\supset _{x,y}.(\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy):\\ &amp;zQw.\supset _{z,w}.(Sʻz)P(Sʻw)\end{align}\]" src="images/4422.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.513ex; width: 58.893ex; height: 6.156ex;" id="img_images_4422.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*150·41. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\colon S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\supset \colon\ldotp (\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy).\equiv .xS^{;}Qy:(Sʻz)P(Sʻw).\equiv .z\breve{S} ^{;}Pw\colon\ldotp     \\ [*23·1] &amp;\supset \colon\ldotp xPy.\supset _{x,y}.(\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy):\equiv .P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, S^{;}Q:\\ &amp;zQw.\supset _{z,w}.(Sʻz)P(Sʻw):\equiv .Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \breve{S} ^{;}P\colon\ldotp \\ [*151·27] &amp;\supset \colon\ldotp xPy.\supset _{x,y}.(\breve{S} ʻx)Q(\breve{S} ʻy):zQw.\supset _{z,w}.(Sʻz)P(Sʻw):\equiv .\\ &amp;CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S^{;}Q  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*5·32.*151·21.&amp;\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4423.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.162ex; width: 106.18ex; height: 21.455ex;" id="img_images_4423.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition shows that ordinal similarity as we have defined
it has the properties which are commonly associated with the term
"ordinal similarity," namely that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_97"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_77"> are ordinally similar
when their fields can be so correlated that two terms having the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_98"> are always correlated with two terms having the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_78">, and vice versa.</p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 10.007ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_4424.svg"> is redundant in <a href="#_151_28" class="pginternal">*151·28</a>; this is
shown in the following proposition.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_330">[Pg 330]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_152">
*152. DEFINITION AND ELEMENTARY PROPERTIES
OF RELATION-NUMBERS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *152.</p>

<p>The relation-number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_100">, which we denote by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_2">, is
defined as the class of relations which are ordinally similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_101">,
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nr}ʻP = \overrightarrow{\text{smor}}ʻP. \]" src="images/4464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.137ex; height: 3.434ex;" id="img_images_4464.svg"></span>
Hence our definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nr} = \overrightarrow{\text{smor}} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 15.707ex; height: 3.167ex;" id="img_images_4465.svg"></span>
The class of relation-numbers consists of all such classes as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_3">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{NR} = \text{D}ʻ\text{Nr} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.361ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4466.svg"></span>
These two definitions are analogous to those of <a href="#_100" class="pginternal">*100</a>, merely
substituting "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{smor}\)" src="images/4131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_4131.svg_3">" for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm}\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.776ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_427.svg_15">." They are justified
by similar considerations, and lead to similar results. With the
exception of <a href="#_152_7" class="pginternal">*152·7</a><a href="#_152_71" class="pginternal">·71</a><a href="#_152_72" class="pginternal">·72</a>, the propositions of this number are the
analogues of those of *100, and call for no remarks other than those in
the introduction to *100 (<i>mutatis mutandis</i>).</p>

<p><a href="#_152_7" class="pginternal">*152·7</a><a href="#_152_71" class="pginternal">·71</a><a href="#_152_72" class="pginternal">·72</a> give relations between relation-numbers and cardinals.
*152·7, which is constantly used, states that the cardinal number
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_13"> consists of the fields of the relation-number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_79">,
<i>i.e.</i> the classes similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_14"> are the fields of the
relations similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_80">; in symbols,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*152·7.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{Nc}ʻCʻQ = Cʻʻ\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4467.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.496ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4467.svg"></p>

<p>Hence it follows that the fields of a relation-number form a cardinal
number, <i>i.e.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*152·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : \mu  \in  \text{NR} . \supset  . Cʻʻ\mu  \in  \text{NC}\)" src="images/4468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.799ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4468.svg"></p>

<p>Hence also it follows that cardinals other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_57"> consist
of classes of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻʻ\mu\)" src="images/4469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.799ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4469.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_166"> is a relation-number
other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_58">, <i>i.e.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*152·72.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \text{NC} - \iota ʻ\Lambda  = Cʻʻʻ(\text{NR} - \iota ʻ\Lambda )\)" src="images/4470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.638ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4470.svg"></p>

<p>In <a href="#_154_9" class="pginternal">*154·9</a>, we shall show how to remove the restriction to numbers other
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_59">, thus arriving at
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash  . \text{NC} = Cʻʻʻ\text{NR}. \]" src="images/4471.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.519ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4471.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above proposition, the same remarks as to types are to be
made as in the case of <a href="#_100_35" class="pginternal">*100·35</a>. If in a certain type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_4">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.731ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4487.svg"> are both null, we have in that type
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.388ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4488.svg">, but we need not have <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\text{smor}\,Q\)" src="images/4149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4149.svg_3">.
Thus for example we shall find that, in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg_2">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nr}ʻ(t^{2}ʻx\uparrow t^{2}ʻx)=\Lambda =\text{Nr}ʻʻ(t^{3}ʻx\uparrow t^{3}ʻx). \]" src="images/4489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.594ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_4489.svg"></span>
But we do not have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (t^{2}ʻx\uparrow t^{2}ʻx)\text{smor}(t^{3}ʻx\uparrow t^{3}ʻx). \]" src="images/4490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.544ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_4490.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*152·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{NR}.\equiv .(\exists P).\mu =\text{Nr}ʻP    \quad[*37·78·79.(*152·02·01)]\)" src="images/4491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.065ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4491.svg"></p>

number, and may be subjected to the conventions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{IT}\)" src="images/262.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.45ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_262.svg_25">,

<p>The utility of <a href="#_152_6" class="pginternal">*152·6</a><a href="#_152_62" class="pginternal">·62</a><a href="#_152_63" class="pginternal">·63</a> is that they enable us to raise the type of
a relation-number to any required extent. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ^{;}P\)" src="images/4509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 3.133ex; height: 1.568ex;" id="img_images_4509.svg"> gives a
relation whose field is a class of the next type above that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_10">,
<i>i.e.</i> of the type <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{2}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.938ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4510.svg">; while <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow ^{;}P\)" src="images/4511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.014ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4511.svg"> gives
a relation whose field is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrowʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4512.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.173ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4512.svg">, which is of the type
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻ(\iota ʻx\uparrow CʻP)\)" src="images/4513.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.725ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4513.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in CʻP\)" src="images/4514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.836ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4514.svg">, or, more generally,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.998ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4515.svg">, this is the type <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{2}ʻP\)" src="images/4516.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.861ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4516.svg">. Thus if we put
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q=x\downarrow ^{;}P\)" src="images/4517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 10.821ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4517.svg">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ tʻQ=tʻ(CʻQ\uparrow CʻQ)=tʻ(tʻP\uparrow tʻP)=tʻ(P\downarrow P). \]" src="images/4518.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.489ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4518.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow ^{;}P\)" src="images/4511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.014ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4511.svg_1"> is a relation whose field consists of terms of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_102">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_152_7">*152·7</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Nc}ʻCʻQ=Cʻʻ\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4519.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.496ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4519.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_334">[Pg 334]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_153">
*153. THE RELATION-NUMBERS <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r}\)" src="images/2.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_3"> AND <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_1">.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *153.</p>

<p>The relation-numbers <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r}\)" src="images/2.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_4"> have already been defined
(in *56), though it remains for the present number to show that they
are relation-numbers. They are the ordinal 0 and 2 respectively,
<i>i.e.</i> they are the ordinal numbers of well-ordered series of no terms and
series of two terms respectively. But there is no means of introducing
an ordinal 1 which shall be analogous to the cardinal 1 as completely
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r}\)" src="images/2.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_5"> are analogous to 0 and 2. The only relations
whose fields are unit classes are relations of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg_3">. We therefore put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*153·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}=\hat{R} \{(\exists x).R=x\downarrow x\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.778ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_4524.svg"></p>

<p>The above definition gives the nearest possible approach to an
ordinal 1. <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_2"> so defined is a relation-number, and is the
relation-number corresponding to 1 in the sense that it is the
relation-number of all such relations as have a field consisting of
one term. But <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_3"> is not what is called an "ordinal number,"
because this term is confined by usage to the relation-numbers of
well-ordered series, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg_4"> is not a serial relation. It
is essential to a serial relation to be contained in diversity; and if,
by definition, we include <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg_5"> among series, we introduce
more exceptions than we avoid. Moreover <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_4"> does not have the
kind of properties which we wish 1 to have; <i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\dot{+}1_{s}\)" src="images/4525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 5.899ex; height: 2.41ex;" id="img_images_4525.svg">
is not <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_6">.</p>

<p>We do not use <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{r}\)" src="images/4526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_4526.svg">, because we shall at a later stage define
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu _{r}\)" src="images/4527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.027ex; height: 1.357ex;" id="img_images_4527.svg"> as the class of those <i>series</i> whose fields have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_150"> terms, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{r}=\Lambda\)" src="images/4528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 6.628ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_4528.svg">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r}\)" src="images/2.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2.svg_5"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_7">
have the values <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/4529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.729ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_4529.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{R} \{(\exists x,y).x\neq y.R=x\downarrow y\}\)" src="images/4530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.363ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_4530.svg">,
as already defined. On account of this general definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu_{r}\)" src="images/4531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.027ex; height: 1.357ex;" id="img_images_4531.svg">,
we choose a different symbol for the relation-number 1, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_5"> has the merit of being as like <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{r}\)" src="images/4526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_4526.svg_1"> as possible.</p>

<p>To illustrate, by anticipation, the way in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_6"> differs from
proper ordinal numbers, we may point out that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_7"> is added to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_8">, we do not obtain <img alt="" data-tex="\(3_{r}\)" src="images/4532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.861ex;" id="img_images_4532.svg">. We shall define <img alt="" data-tex="\(3_{r}\)" src="images/4532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.861ex;" id="img_images_4532.svg_1"> as the
class of series which consist of three terms, <i>i.e.</i> the class of
relations of the form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d} x\downarrow z\unicode{x228d} y\downarrow z, \]" src="images/4533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 17.418ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4533.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y.x\neq z.y\neq z\)" src="images/4534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 17.973ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_4534.svg">. We shall define the sum of two
ordinal numbers<span class="pagenum" id="Page_335">[Pg 335]</span> as the ordinal number of the sum of two relations
having these ordinal numbers (cf. <a href="#_180" class="pginternal">*180</a>), and it will appear that if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_103"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_81"> are relations whose fields have no members in common,
then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x228d} Q\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow CʻQ \]" src="images/4535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.234ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4535.svg"></span>
has a relation-number which is the sum of those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_104"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_82">.
Suppose now <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.507ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4536.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q=z\downarrow z\)" src="images/4537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.299ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4537.svg">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y.x\neq z.y\neq z\)" src="images/4534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 17.973ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_4534.svg_1">. Then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x228d} Q\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow CʻQ=x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d} x\downarrow z\unicode{x228d} y\downarrow z\unicode{x228d} z\downarrow z. \]" src="images/4538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 44.519ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4538.svg"></span>
This is not a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(3_{r}\)" src="images/4532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.861ex;" id="img_images_4532.svg_2">, because of the additional term
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\downarrow z\)" src="images/4539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.492ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4539.svg">. Thus the addition of one term to a series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_105"> does
not give the same number as results from the addition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}\)" src="images/4.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 2.069ex; height: 1.862ex;" id="img_images_4.svg_8"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_6">. Hence the addition of 1 to an ordinal number has to be
separately treated<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_12" id="FNanchor_12">[12]</a>.</p>

<p>We prove in this number that <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r} = \text{Nr}ʻ\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/4540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.569ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_4540.svg">
(<a href="#_153_11" class="pginternal">*153·11</a>), that <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}=\text{Nr}ʻ(\Lambda \downarrow \iotaʻx)\)" src="images/4541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.17ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4541.svg">
(<a href="#_153_24" class="pginternal">*153·24</a>; observe that we have to take a couple of
classes (or relations) in order to be sure of the existence
of two different objects of the class in question), and that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1_{s}=\text{Nr}ʻ(y\downarrow y\)" src="images/4542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.513ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4542.svg">) (<a href="#_153_32" class="pginternal">*153·32</a>). We prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻʻ0_{r} =0\)" src="images/4543.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.623ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4543.svg">
(<a href="#_153_18" class="pginternal">*153·18</a>), <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻʻ2_{r}=2\)" src="images/4544.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.623ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4544.svg"> (<a href="#_153_212" class="pginternal">*153·212</a>), and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻʻ1_{s}=1\)" src="images/4545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.652ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4545.svg"> (<a href="#_153_36" class="pginternal">*153·36</a>).
We have also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{C} ʻʻ0=0_{r}\)" src="images/4546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.623ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4546.svg"> (not proved) and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{C}ʻʻ1=1_{s}\)" src="images/4547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.652ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4547.svg">
(<a href="#_153_301" class="pginternal">*153·301</a>). But we do not have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{C} ʻʻ2=2_{r}\)" src="images/4548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.623ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4548.svg">;
<i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\((x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d} y\downarrow x)\in \breve{C}ʻʻ2\)" src="images/4549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.031ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4549.svg">
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_411.svg_2">, but <img alt="" data-tex="\((x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d} y\downarrow x){\sim}\in 2_{r}\)" src="images/4550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.266ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4550.svg">.
We have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !0_{r}\)" src="images/4551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.927ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_4551.svg"> (<a href="#_153_12" class="pginternal">*153·12</a>) and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!1_{s}\)" src="images/4552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.355ex; width: 3.956ex; height: 1.975ex;" id="img_images_4552.svg"> (<a href="#_153_34" class="pginternal">*153·34</a>),
but from our primitive propositions we cannot deduce <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !2_{r}\)" src="images/97.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.927ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_97.svg_1">
unless we rise above the lowest type of relations. The case is exactly
analogous to that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !2\)" src="images/96.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.018ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_96.svg_1"> (cf. <a href="#_101" class="pginternal">*101</a>); we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*153·26·262.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\exists !2_{r}\cap \text{Rl}ʻ(\text{Cls}\uparrow \text{Cls}).\exists !2_{r}\cap \text{Rel}^{2}\)" src="images/4553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.672ex; height: 2.584ex;" id="img_images_4553.svg"></p>

<p>But if, as monists aver, there is only one individual, we shall not
have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !2_{r}\)" src="images/97.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.927ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_97.svg_2"> in the type of relations of individuals to
individuals. Our primitive propositions do not suffice to disprove this
supposition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_153_212">*153·212</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻʻ2_{r} = 2   \quad[*55·15.*56·11.*54·101]\)" src="images/4578.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.804ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4578.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*153·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !2_{r}\cap t''ʻz.\equiv .\exists !2(z).\equiv .(\exists x,y).x\neq yx\in tʻz \quad[*153·211.*101·4]\)" src="images/4579.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.888ex; height: 2.283ex;" id="img_images_4579.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*153·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in 2_{r}.\supset .\text{Rl}ʻP\subset 0_{r}\cup 2_{r} \quad[*56·261]\)" src="images/4580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4580.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition illustrates the reasons for not putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 1_{r}=\hat{P} \{(\exists x).P=x\downarrow x\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.342ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_4581.svg"></span>
We want the inductive ordinals, like the inductive cardinals, to
form a series in order of magnitude; but, as the above proposition
illustrates, the relation-number of such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow x\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.976ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg_6">
is not in the same series with <img alt="" data-tex="\(0_{r}\)" src="images/2.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_2.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_9">. The above
proposition should be contrasted with *51·411.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_153_24">*153·24</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .2_{r}=\text{Nr}ʻ(\Lambda \downarrow \iota ʻx) \quad[*153·211.*51·161]\)" src="images/4582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.939ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4582.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*153·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .2_{r}\in \text{NR} \quad[*153·24.*152·41]\)" src="images/4583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.807ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4583.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_339">[Pg 339]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="id_154_RELATION-NUMBERS_OF_ASSIGNED_TYPES">
*154. RELATION-NUMBERS OF ASSIGNED TYPES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *154.</p>

<p>This number gives propositions analogous to those of *102. In
accordance with our general notations for typical definiteness,
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}(P)ʻQ\)" src="images/4608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4608.svg">" means "the class of relations like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_83"> and of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_106">," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr} (P_{Q})\)" src="images/4609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.25ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4609.svg">" means "the relation to
a relation of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_84"> of the class of relations like it and
of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_107">." By a special definition, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{NR}^{Q}(P)\)" src="images/4610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.274ex; height: 2.62ex;" id="img_images_4610.svg">"
is to mean all typically definite relation-numbers of the form
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}(P_{Q})ʻR\)" src="images/4611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 10.324ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4611.svg">," <i>i.e.</i> all relation-numbers generated
by the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}(P_{Q})\)" src="images/4612.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.25ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4612.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> the domain of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}(P_{Q})\)" src="images/4612.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.25ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4612.svg_1">.</p>

<p>Existence-theorems in this subject can be proved by means of <a href="#_154_14" class="pginternal">*154·14</a>,
which states that relations like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_85"> exist in the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_108">
when, and only when, classes similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_15"> exist in the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_11">. In virtue of this proposition, the existence-theorems of our
present topic are deducible from those for cardinals. In symbols, this
proposition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*154·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\text{Nr}(P)ʻQ.\equiv .\exists !\text{Nc}(CʻP)ʻCʻQ\)" src="images/4613.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.837ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4613.svg"></p>

<p>Hence by <a href="#_102_73" class="pginternal">*102·73</a> we deduce</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*154·242.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \Lambda  \in  \text{NR}^{\iota ^{;}P}(P)\)" src="images/4614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.949ex; height: 2.586ex;" id="img_images_4614.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence, by <a href="#_152_72" class="pginternal">*152·72</a>,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*154·9.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{NC}=Cʻʻʻ\text{NR}\)" src="images/4615.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.89ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4615.svg"></p>

<p>The remaining propositions are chiefly analogues of those in <a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a>. Very
few of them are subsequently referred to.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_154_14">*154·14</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\text{Nr}(P)ʻQ.\equiv .\exists !\text{Nc}(CʻP)ʻCʻQ   \quad[*154·13.(*65·04)]\)" src="images/4627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.459ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4627.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of *154·14 and the propositions of <a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a>, <a href="#_103" class="pginternal">*103</a>, <a href="#_104" class="pginternal">*104</a>, <a href="#_105" class="pginternal">*105</a>,
*106, we see that all homogeneous or ascending relation-numbers
exist, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_61"> is a member of every descending type of

homogeneous, we see that there are two kinds of steps by which their
types may be raised, namely (1) from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_109"> to relations of the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻCʻP\uparrow tʻCʻP\)" src="images/4628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.289ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4628.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_110"> to relations of the
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\downarrow CʻP\)" src="images/4629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.94ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4629.svg">, or of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ^{;}P\)" src="images/4509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 3.133ex; height: 1.568ex;" id="img_images_4509.svg_1">; (2) from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_111"> to
relations of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻP\uparrow tʻP\)" src="images/4630.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.135ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4630.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_112"> to
relations of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow P\)" src="images/4631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.786ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4631.svg">, or of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x^{;}P\)" src="images/4632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.385ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4632.svg">
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.998ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4515.svg_1">. Thus repetitions of the two steps from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_113"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ^{;}P\)" src="images/4509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 3.133ex; height: 1.568ex;" id="img_images_4509.svg_2">, and from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_114"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x^{;}P\)" src="images/4632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.385ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4632.svg_1">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4633.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.998ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4633.svg">,
will enable us, without changing the relation-number, to
raise its type indefinitely. It will be observed that, in accordance
with our general definitions for relative types, the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota^{;}P\)" src="images/4634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 3.133ex; height: 1.568ex;" id="img_images_4634.svg">
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{11}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.738ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4635.svg">, and the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x^{;}P\)" src="images/4632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.385ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4632.svg_2"> (where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in t_{0}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.998ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4515.svg_2">) is <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{11}ʻP\)" src="images/4636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.661ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4636.svg">.</p>

<p>The remaining propositions of this number (except <a href="#_154_9" class="pginternal">*154·9</a>) are the
analogues of those whose numbers have the same decimal part in <a href="#_102" class="pginternal">*102</a>.
They are here given without proof, because the proofs are, step by
step, analogous to the proofs of the corresponding propositions in *102.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_344">[Pg 344]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="id_155_HOMOGENEOUS_RELATION-NUMBERS">
*155. HOMOGENEOUS RELATION-NUMBERS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *155.</p>

<p>A relation-number is called homogeneous when it is generated by
a homogeneous relation of likeness, <i>i.e.</i> when it consists
of all relations which are like a given relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_117"> and of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_118">. For the homogeneous relation-number
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_119"> we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.628ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4692.svg">"; thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻP\cap tʻP\)" src="images/4693.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.673ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4693.svg">. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_120"> is given,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.628ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4692.svg_1"> is typically definite. We have always <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4694.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.093ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4694.svg">,
hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4695.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.515ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4695.svg">. Conversely, if a
typically definite relation-number is not null, it is a homogeneous
relation-number; in fact, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_121"> is a member of it, it is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.628ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4692.svg_2">. Thus the homogeneous relation-numbers are
all the relation-numbers except <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_62">.</p>

<p>Homogeneous relation-numbers play the same part in relation-arithmetic
as homogeneous cardinals play in cardinal arithmetic. The propositions
of this number (except <a href="#_155_6" class="pginternal">*155·6</a><a href="#_155_61" class="pginternal">·61</a>) are the analogues of those with the
same decimal part in <a href="#_103" class="pginternal">*103</a>. Their proofs are exactly analogous to the
proofs of their analogues in *103, and are therefore omitted.</p>

<p>The following propositions are the most useful in this number.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Q\in \text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP.\equiv .Q\,\text{smor}\,P.Q\in tʻP.\equiv .Q\in \text{Nr}ʻP.Q\in tʻP\)" src="images/4696.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 59.472ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4696.svg"></p>

<p>This merely embodies the definition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\in \text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.481ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4697.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\exists !\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4698.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.903ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4698.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻQ.\equiv .\text{Nr}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4699.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.176ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4699.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is used in the theory of well-ordered series (*253 and
*255). It requires that the equation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.388ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4488.svg_1">" on
the right-hand side should be subject to the convention <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{AT}\)" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.33ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_376.svg_35">.
Otherwise, the typical ambiguities might be so determined as to
give <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻQ=\Lambda\)" src="images/4700.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.975ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4700.svg">, which would not imply
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4701.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.376ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4701.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{R}.\equiv .(\exists P).\mu =\text{Nr}ʻP\cap tʻP.\equiv .(\exists P).\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\)" src="images/4702.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.529ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4702.svg"></p>

<p>This merely embodies the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{R}\)" src="images/4703.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 4.35ex; height: 1.92ex;" id="img_images_4703.svg">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_345">[Pg 345]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu \in \text{N}_{0}\text{R}.\supset .\exists !\mu\)" src="images/4704.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 18.143ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_4704.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \mu \in \text{NR}.\supset :P\in \mu .\equiv .\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\mu\)" src="images/4705.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 35.521ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4705.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·27.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\mu =\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP.\equiv .\mu \in \text{NR}.P\in \mu\)" src="images/4706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 31.749ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4706.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{NR}-\iota ʻ\Lambda \subset \text{N}_{0}\text{R}\)" src="images/4707.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4707.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{smor}ʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4708.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.183ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4708.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .0_{r}\in \text{N}_{0}\text{R}\)" src="images/4709.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 11.796ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_4709.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4710.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.29ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4710.svg"></p>

<p>This last proposition connects homogeneous relation-numbers with
homogeneous cardinals.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*155·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .2_{r}\cap \text{Rel}^{2}\in \text{N}_{0}\text{R}\)" src="images/4732.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 18.597ex; height: 2.393ex;" id="img_images_4732.svg"></p>

<p>The following propositions have no analogue in <a href="#_103" class="pginternal">*103</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_155_6">*155·6</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/4710.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.29ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4710.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*100·11.*103·11.&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in \text{N}_{0}\text{c}ʻCʻP.\equiv :\\ &amp;\alpha  \in  tʻCʻP:(\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻS=\alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=CʻP:\\ [*150·23] &amp;\equiv :\alpha \in tʻCʻP:(\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻS^{;}P=\alpha .\text{ᗡ}ʻS=CʻP:\\ [*151·11] &amp;\equiv :\alpha \in tʻCʻP:(\exists Q).Q\,\text{smor}\,P.\alpha =CʻQ:\\ [*64·24] &amp;\equiv :(\exists Q).Q\,\text{smor}\,P.Q\in tʻP.\alpha =CʻQ:\\ [*152·11.*155·11] &amp;\equiv :\alpha \in Cʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4733.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 81.625ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_4733.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_155_61">*155·61</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻʻʻ\text{N}_{0}\text{R}=\text{N}_{0}\text{C} \quad[*155·6]\)" src="images/4734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.676ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4734.svg"></p>

<p>On ascending and descending relation-numbers, propositions
analogous to those of <a href="#_104" class="pginternal">*104</a>, <a href="#_105" class="pginternal">*105</a>, and <a href="#_106" class="pginternal">*106</a> might be proved by
proofs analogous to those given in those numbers. It is, however,
scarcely necessary to add anything to the propositions already
proved, namely <a href="#_154_24" class="pginternal">*154·24</a><a href="#_154_241" class="pginternal">·241</a><a href="#_154_242" class="pginternal">·242</a><a href="#_154_25" class="pginternal">·25</a><a href="#_154_251" class="pginternal">·251</a> on descending relation-numbers,
<a href="#_154_26" class="pginternal">*154·26</a><a href="#_154_261" class="pginternal">·261</a><a href="#_154_262" class="pginternal">·262</a><a href="#_154_31" class="pginternal">·31</a><a href="#_154_311" class="pginternal">·311</a><a href="#_154_32" class="pginternal">·32</a><a href="#_154_321" class="pginternal">·321</a><a href="#_154_322" class="pginternal">·322</a><a href="#_154_33" class="pginternal">·33</a><a href="#_154_331" class="pginternal">·331</a> on ascending relation-numbers,
and <a href="#_155_23" class="pginternal">*155·23</a><a href="#_155_34" class="pginternal">·34</a> giving the relations of non-homogeneous to homogeneous
relation-numbers. Ascending relation-numbers all exist, and those
that start from the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_122">, wherever they end<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_13" id="FNanchor_13">[13]</a>, are the
correspondents<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_14" id="FNanchor_14">[14]</a> of the homogeneous relation-numbers of the type
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_123">, and are only some of the homogeneous relation-numbers of
the type in which they end. Descending relation-numbers consist of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_63"> together with the homogeneous relation-numbers of the type
in which they end: they are the correspondents of only some of the type
in which they begin, or rather, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_64"> is the common correspondent
of all those relation-numbers in the initial type which are not
correspondents of any homogeneous relation-number in the end-type.
These properties are exactly the same as in the case of cardinals, as
might be foreseen by <a href="#_154_14" class="pginternal">*154·14</a>.</p>
