<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_347">[Pg 347]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_B_II">SECTION B.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">ADDITION OF RELATIONS, AND THE PRODUCT OF TWO RELATIONS.</span></h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of Section B.</i></p>

<p>In the present section, we have to consider the kind of addition
of relations which is required in ordinal arithmetic. In cardinal
arithmetic, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_117"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg_11"> has the properties required of their sum, and thus we
do not require a new kind of logical addition before dealing with
arithmetical addition. But in ordinal arithmetic this is not so.
Suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_125"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_88"> are the generating relations of two series,
and we wish to add the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_89">-series at the end of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_126">-series.
Then we wish every term of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_127">-series to precede every term of
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_90">-series; thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x228d} Q\)" src="images/4737.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.846ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4737.svg"> is not the generating
relation of the new series, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x228d} Q\)" src="images/4737.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.846ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4737.svg_1"> gives no
relation between the terms of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_128">-series and the terms of the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_91">-series. The relation we want is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x228d} Q\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow CʻQ, \]" src="images/4738.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4738.svg"></span>
since this makes every term of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_129">-series precede every term of
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_92">-series. Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x2909}Q = P\unicode{x228d} Q\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow CʻQ \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4739.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.41ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4739.svg"></span>
It will be seen that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2909}Q\)" src="images/4740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.846ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4740.svg"> is in general different from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x2909}P\)" src="images/4741.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.846ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4741.svg">.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_12"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_16"> have no common terms, the sum of the
relation-numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_130"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_93"> is the relation-number of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2909}Q\)" src="images/4740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.846ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4740.svg_1"> (cf. <a href="#_180" class="pginternal">*180</a>).</p>

<p>The addition of a single term to a series requires a new definition,
and cannot be dealt with as a particular case of the addition of two
relations. It might be thought that, just as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \iota ʻx\)" src="images/4742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.415ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4742.svg">
gives the result of adding the one term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_100"> to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_231">,
so <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2909}(x\downarrow x)\)" src="images/4743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.793ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4743.svg"> would give the result of
adding the one term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_101"> to the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_131">. But this is not the
case, since, when we add a term to a series, we do not want this term
to precede itself, whereas <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2909}(x\downarrow x)\)" src="images/4743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.793ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4743.svg_1"> is a
relation which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_102"> has to itself. What we want is a relation which
every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_13"> has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_103"> but which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_104"> does not have to
itself; thus we take <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow \iota ʻx\)" src="images/4744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.673ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4744.svg"> as our
relation, and put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x21f8}x=P\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow \iota ʻx \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4745.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.353ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4745.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_348">[Pg 348]</span>
This definition defines the generating relation of the series obtained
by adding <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_105"> at the end of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_132">-series; similarly for adding
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_106"> at the beginning we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\unicode{x21f7}P=\iota ʻx\uparrow CʻP\unicode{x228d} P \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4746.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.353ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4746.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_107"> is not a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_14">, the relation-number of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x21f8}x\)" src="images/4747.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4747.svg"> is the sum of the relation-number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_133"> and
the ordinal 1, which we represent by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{1}\)" src="images/4748.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_4748.svg">. (The ordinal 1 has no
meaning by itself, but only as a summand.)</p>

<p>The sum of a series of series is defined in the same way as the sum
of two series was defined. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_134"> be a serial relation whose
field consists of serial relations. Then the sum of all the series
generated by members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_15">, when these series are taken in the
order generated by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_135">, must be a relation which holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_108">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_65"> whenever either (1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_109"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_66"> both belong to the
field of one of the series, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_110"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_67"> in this series,
or (2) <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_111"> belongs to the field of an earlier series than that to
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_68"> belongs. In the first case, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists Q) . Q\in CʻP.xQy\)" src="images/4749.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.344ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4749.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x (\dot{s} ʻCʻP)y\)" src="images/4750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.357ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_4750.svg">. In the second case, we
have <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists Q,R).QPR.x\in CʻQ.y\in CʻR\)" src="images/4751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.35ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4751.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists Q,R).QPR.xFQ.yFR\)" src="images/4752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.054ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4752.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x(F^{;}P)y\)" src="images/4753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.314ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4753.svg">. Hence the generating relation of the sum of
all the series is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻCʻP\unicode{x228d} F^{;}P\)" src="images/4754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.703ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4754.svg">. Hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Sigma ʻP=\dot{s} ʻCʻP\unicode{x228d} F^{;}P \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.723ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4755.svg"></span>
The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg"> has all the properties which we should
expect of the sum of a series of series.</p>

<p>If a series is to result from the addition of a series of series, it is
necessary that no two of the series should have any common terms. For
if we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ QPR.x\in CʻQ\cap CʻR, \]" src="images/4757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.076ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4757.svg"></span>
we shall also have <img alt="" data-tex="\(x(\Sigma ʻP)x\)" src="images/4758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.038ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4758.svg">.</p>

<p>Hence instead of a series, we shall have cycles; for it is essential to
a series that no term should precede itself. (What seem to be series
in which there is repetition are always the result of a one-many
correlation with series in which there is no repetition, so that a
term can be counted once as the correlate of one term, and again
as the correlate of a later term.) For this reason, as well as for
many others, it is important to consider relations between mutually
exclusive relations, <i>i.e.</i> between relations whose fields have no
common terms. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}=\hat{P} \{Q,R\in CʻP.Q\neq R.\supset _{Q,R}.CʻQ\cap CʻR=\Lambda\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 63.641ex; height: 3.028ex;" id="img_images_4759.svg"></span>
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg"> has much the same utility in
relation-arithmetic as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.974ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_4761.svg"> has in cardinal
arithmetic. We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :R\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv .F\upharpoonright CʻP\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1, \]" src="images/4762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 38.884ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_4762.svg"></span>
which is analogous to the proposition (*84·14)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\equiv .\in \upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1. \]" src="images/4763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 34.039ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_4763.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_349">[Pg 349]</span>
It will be found that in relation-arithmetic the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\)" src="images/4764.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.695ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_4764.svg"> often
appears where <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4765.svg"> appears in the analogous proposition of
cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p>Analogous to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sm sm}\)" src="images/4766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.118ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_4766.svg">" is the relation of double ordinal
similarity. This holds between two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_136"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_94"> when they
are ordinally similar relations between ordinally similar relations
with known correlators, <i>i.e.</i> when, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_17"> is an ordinal
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_137"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_95">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = T^{;}Q\)" src="images/4767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.858ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4767.svg">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(X\)" src="images/4768.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.928ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_4768.svg"> is
a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_16">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Y\)" src="images/4769.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.726ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_4769.svg"> is the corresponding member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_17">,
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(XTY\)" src="images/4770.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 5.247ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_4770.svg">, we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(X\,\text{smor}\,Y\)" src="images/4771.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 9.204ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_4771.svg">, and shall be able
to specify a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(X\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Y\)" src="images/4772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 9.204ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_4772.svg">. But as in
cardinals, so here, we have to frame our definition of double ordinal
similarity in such a way as to minimize the use of the multiplicative
axiom. We therefore take as our definition the following: <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_138"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_96"> are said to have double ordinal similarity when there is a
one-one relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_39"> which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.857ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4773.svg"> for its converse
domain, and is such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = S\dagger ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4774.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.608ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4774.svg">. A relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_40"> which
has these properties is called a <i>double correlator</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_139"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_97">, <i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P \,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\, Q = (1 \rightarrow  1) \cap  \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻCʻ\Sigma ʻQ \cap  \hat{S}  (P = S\dagger  ^{;}Q) \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/4775.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.415ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_4775.svg"></span>
a definition which, as will be perceived, is closely analogous to
that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \Lambda\)" src="images/4776.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 12.199ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_4776.svg">
in <a href="#_111" class="pginternal">*111</a>. Two relations have double similarity when they have a double
correlator, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{smor} \text{smor} = \hat{P} \hat{Q}  \{\exists  ! P \,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,  Q\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4777.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.766ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_4777.svg"></span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_41"> is a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_140"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_98"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_42"> is
a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger \upharpoonright CʻQ\)" src="images/4779.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.531ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4779.svg"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_141"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_99">. This might be
taken as the definition of a double correlator, since it is equivalent
to the above definition.</p>

<p>If we assume the multiplicative axiom, we can prove that double
similarity holds between similar relations of mutually exclusive
similar relations, <i>i.e.</i> between two relations of mutually
exclusive relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_142"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_100"> which have a correlator <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_43">
such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Y \in CʻQ\)" src="images/4780.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.359ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4780.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Y\)" src="images/4769.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.726ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_4769.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(SʻY\)" src="images/4781.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.543ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4781.svg"> are always
similar. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S \,\unicode{x2abd}\, \text{smor}\)" src="images/4782.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.367ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4782.svg">. Thus
if we assume the multiplicative axiom we have, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_143">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \in\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4783.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 12.674ex; height: 2.457ex;" id="img_images_4783.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P \,\text{smor}\,\text{smor}\,Q . \equiv  . \exists  ! P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q \cap  \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}. \]" src="images/4784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 40.497ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_4784.svg"></span>
In the particular case in which the fields of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_144"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_101">
consist of well-ordered relations (<i>i.e.</i> relations generating
<i>well-ordered</i> series), this equivalence can be proved without
the use of the multiplicative axiom, because two similar well-ordered
relations have only one correlator, so that the difficulty of selecting
among correlators does not arise.</p>

<p>Double ordinal correlators have the same importance in proving the
formal laws of relation-arithmetic that double cardinal correlators
have in cardinal arithmetic. The construction of double correlators in
various cases constitutes a large part of relation-arithmetic.</p>

<p>In defining the ordinal product of two relation-numbers, and in
defining exponentiation, we use a relation which has properties
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_350">[Pg 350]</span>analogous to those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_11">. This relation
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_2">, of which the structure is as follows:
Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_21">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/2358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2358.svg_4"> be two terms having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_102">; then form
the two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow z^{;}P\)" src="images/4785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.143ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4785.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow w^{;}P\)" src="images/4786.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.711ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4786.svg">. The
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow z^{;}P\)" src="images/4785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.143ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4785.svg_1"> holds between two couples <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow z\)" src="images/4787.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.734ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4787.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow z\)" src="images/4788.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.549ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4788.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_7">; thus it arranges couples
whose referents are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_17">, and whose relata are <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_22">,
in an order similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_145">. The relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow z^{;}P\)" src="images/4785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.143ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4785.svg_2"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow w^{;}P\)" src="images/4786.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.711ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4786.svg_1"> are (by <a href="#_150_03" class="pginternal">*150·03</a>) the same as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,}z\)" src="images/4789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.217ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4789.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} w\)" src="images/4790.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.784ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4790.svg">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_3"> arranges
such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow z^{;}P\)" src="images/4785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.143ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4785.svg_3"> in an order similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_103">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_4"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_104">, and every
member of its field is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_146">. Thus the relation-number
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_5"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.731ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4487.svg_1">, and every member
of its field has the relation-number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_7">. Moreover
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_6">, as it is easy to see, is a relation of
mutually exclusive relations. Hence it is suitable for defining the
product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_105"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_147">, and we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q\times P = \Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4791.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 24.529ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4791.svg"></span>
In the next section, after we have defined the product of a relation of
relations, we shall use the same relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_7"> for
the definition of exponentiation, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P \,\,\text{exp}\,\, Q = \text{Prod}ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 29.915ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4792.svg"></span>
These two definitions should be compared with those in <a href="#_113" class="pginternal">*113</a> and <a href="#_116" class="pginternal">*116</a>.</p>

<p>In virtue of the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_1">, the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\SigmaʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4793.svg"> holds between terms which either have one
of the relations of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} z\)" src="images/4794.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.217ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4794.svg">, or belong
respectively to the fields of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,}z\)" src="images/4789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.217ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4789.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} w\)" src="images/4790.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.784ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4790.svg_1">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(zQw\)" src="images/4125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.462ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4125.svg_2">. Thus the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\SigmaʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4793.svg_1"> holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow z\)" src="images/4787.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.734ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4787.svg_1"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow z\)" src="images/4788.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.549ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4788.svg_1"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\in CʻQ\)" src="images/4795.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.685ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4795.svg">, and also between
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow z\)" src="images/4787.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.734ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4787.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow w\)" src="images/4796.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4796.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y\in CʻP.zQw\)" src="images/4797.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 16.418ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4797.svg">.
Thus if, for the sake of illustration, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_148"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_106"> generate finite
series, so that their fields are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} 1_{P}, 2_{P} ..., \mu _{P},\\ 1_{Q}, 2_{Q} ..., \nu _{Q}, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4798.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.078ex; width: 13.453ex; height: 5.288ex;" id="img_images_4798.svg"></span>
then the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4799.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4799.svg"> will consist of the
couples
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} 1_{P}\downarrow 1_{Q}, 2_{P}\downarrow 1_{Q}, ..., \mu _{P}\downarrow 1_{Q};\\ 1_{P}\downarrow 2_{Q}, 2_{P}\downarrow 2_{Q}, ..., \mu _{P}\downarrow 2_{Q};\\ \ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots\\ 1_{P}\downarrow \nu _{Q}, 2_{P}\downarrow \nu _{Q}, ..., \mu _{P}\downarrow \nu _{Q}; \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4800.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.104ex; width: 29.91ex; height: 11.338ex;" id="img_images_4800.svg"></span>
and their order as arranged by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4799.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4799.svg_1"> is that
in which they are written above. Thus the above couples in the above
order constitute the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\times P\)" src="images/4801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4801.svg">, and it is evident that this
series has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \times \mu\)" src="images/4802.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.329ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_4802.svg"> terms.</p>

<p>When the factors of a product are not enumerated, but are given as the
field of a relation, a new definition of multiplication is required.
This definition, which has the advantage of being applicable to
infinite products, will be dealt with in the following section.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_351">[Pg 351]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_160">
*160. THE SUM OF TWO RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *160.</p>

<p>In this number, we introduce the definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x2909}Q=P\unicode{x228d} Q\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow CʻQ \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/4803.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.41ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4803.svg"></span>
which was explained in the introduction to this section. Although the
propositions of this and other numbers in this Part do not require
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_149"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_107"> should be such as to generate series, yet the
reader will find it convenient to imagine them to be such, since the
important applications of the ideas of this Part are to series. Thus we
may regard the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_150"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_108"> as a relation which holds between
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_112"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_69"> when either <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_113"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_70"> in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_151">-series,
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_114"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_71"> in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_109">-series, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_115"> belongs to the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_152">-series and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_72"> belongs to the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_110">-series.</p>

<p>The most important propositions of this number are :</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻ(P\unicode{x2909}Q)=CʻP\cup CʻQ\)" src="images/4804.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.246ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4804.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\unicode{x2909}\dot{\Lambda} =P\)" src="images/4805.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.731ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_4805.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\dot{\Lambda} \unicode{x2909}Q=Q\)" src="images/4806.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.912ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_4806.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(P\unicode{x2909}Q)\unicode{x2909}R=P\unicode{x2909}(Q\unicode{x2909}R)\)" src="images/4807.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.767ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4807.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which is the associative law, and</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(P\unicode{x228d} Q)\unicode{x2909}R=(P\unicode{x2909}R)\unicode{x228d} (Q\unicode{x2909}R)\)" src="images/4808.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.602ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4808.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :CʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.CʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.\supset .S^{;}(P\unicode{x2909}Q)=S^{;}P\unicode{x2909}S^{;}Q\)" src="images/4809.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4809.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which is also a kind of distributive law;</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·47.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :CʻP\cap CʻQ=\Lambda .CʻP'\cap CʻQ'=\Lambda .&amp;S\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P'.T\in Q\overline{\text{smor}} Q'.\supset .\\ &amp;S\unicode{x228d} T\in (P\unicode{x2909}Q)\overline{\text{smor}} (P'\unicode{x2909}Q')\end{align}\]" src="images/4810.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.17ex; width: 70.832ex; height: 5.47ex;" id="img_images_4810.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*160·48.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :CʻP\cap CʻQ=\Lambda .CʻP'\cap CʻQ'=\Lambda .P\,\text{smor}\,P'.&amp;Q\,\text{smor}\,Q'.\supset .\\ &amp;P\unicode{x2909}Q\,\text{smor}\,P'\unicode{x2909}Q'\end{align}\]" src="images/4811.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.17ex; width: 66.475ex; height: 5.47ex;" id="img_images_4811.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
whence it follows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_153"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_111"> are mutually exclusive, the

<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_154"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_112">;</p>

<p>The above two propositions state the distributive law for logical
and arithmetical addition. The three following propositions give the
generalized form of this law, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4837.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4837.svg"> replaces

but are inserted for the sake of their intrinsic interest.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_357">[Pg 357]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_161">
*161. ADDITION OF A TERM TO A RELATION.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *161.</p>

<p>The addition of a term has two forms, according as it occurs at the
beginning or end of the field of the relation in question. If we add
first <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_116"> and then <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_73"> at the end, the result is the same as if we
added <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1842.svg_3"> (<a href="#_161_22" class="pginternal">*161·22</a>); if at the beginning, it is the same
as if we added <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow x\)" src="images/4167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4167.svg_1"> (<a href="#_161_221" class="pginternal">*161·221</a>). The propositions of the
present number are all obvious, and offer no difficulties of any kind.
As explained in the introduction to this section, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} P\unicode{x21f8} x &amp;= P\unicode{x228d} CʻP\uparrow {℩}ʻx \quad\text{Df},\\ x\unicode{x21f7}P &amp;= {℩}ʻx\uparrow CʻP\unicode{x228d} P \quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4864.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 26.91ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_4864.svg"></span>
Most of the propositions of this number require the hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists} !P\)" src="images/4865.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.586ex; height: 2.305ex;" id="img_images_4865.svg">, because if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = \dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/4866.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.286ex; height: 2.541ex;" id="img_images_4866.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x21f8} x = x\unicode{x21f7}P = \dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/4867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.306ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_4867.svg">
(<a href="#_161_2" class="pginternal">*161·2</a><a href="#_161_201" class="pginternal">·201</a>). This is connected with the fact that there is no ordinal
number 1. Apart from propositions already mentioned, the chief
propositions of this number are the following (we omit propositions
about <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\unicode{x21f7}P\)" src="images/4868.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4868.svg"> when they are merely analogues of propositions
about <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x21f8} x\)" src="images/4869.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4869.svg">):</p>

<p>Note that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d} x\downarrow z\unicode{x228d}y\downarrow z\)" src="images/4896.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 16.789ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4896.svg">

ordinal arithmetic.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_362">[Pg 362]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_162">
*162. THE SUM OF THE RELATIONS OF A FIELD.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *162.</p>

<p>The form of summation defined in <a href="#_160" class="pginternal">*160</a> cannot be extended beyond a
finite number of summands, since it involves explicit mention of all
the summands. In the present number, we shall be concerned with a
form of summation which is not subject to this restriction. It will
be observed that, since relational summation is not permutative, we
cannot define the sum of a <i>class</i> of relations, for this would
not determine the order in which the summation is to be effected. Our
relations must be given as the field of some relation which orders
them; thus the sum appears not as the sum of a class, but as the sum
of a relation, namely of a relation whose field is the relations to
be summed. In the case of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_114"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_41">, the sum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\downarrow R\)" src="images/4928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.895ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4928.svg">, as defined in the present number, will be equal to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x2909}R\)" src="images/4929.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.864ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4929.svg">; similarly for three, the sum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\downarrow R\unicode{x228d} Q\downarrow S\unicode{x228d} R\downarrow S\)" src="images/4930.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.811ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4930.svg">
will be equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x2909}R\unicode{x2909}S\)" src="images/4931.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.681ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4931.svg">, and so on for
any finite number of summands.</p>

<p>As explained in the introduction to this Section, if P is a relation
between relations, we put</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Sigma ʻP=\dot{s} ʻCʻP\unicode{x228d} F^{;}P \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.723ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4755.svg_1"></span>
It is convenient to suppose that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_156"> is serial, and that every member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_18"> is also serial. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_2"> holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_119">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_76"> if either (1) there is a series, in the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_157">, in
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_120"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_77">, or (2) <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_121"> belongs to a series which is
earlier, in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_158">-series, than the series to which y belongs. The
following are the chief propositions of this number:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*162·22·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻ\Sigma ʻP=sʻCʻʻCʻP=Cʻ\dot{s} ʻCʻP=FʻʻCʻP=\overrightarrow{F}^{2}ʻP\)" src="images/4932.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 59.174ex; height: 3.636ex;" id="img_images_4932.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*162·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Sigma ʻ(P\unicode{x228d} Q)=\Sigma ʻP\unicode{x228d} \Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4933.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.831ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4933.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_162_35">*162·35</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset .\Sigma ʻR\dagger ^{;}Q=R^{;}\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4980.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 41.006ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4980.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*162·1.*150·22. \supset \vdash .\Sigma ʻR\dagger ^{;}Q&amp;=\dot{s} ʻR\dagger ʻʻCʻQ\unicode{x228d} F^{;}R\dagger ^{;}Q\\ [*150·16]    &amp;=R^{;}\dot{s} ʻCʻQ\unicode{x228d} F^{;}R\dagger ^{;}Q  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*162·343.  \supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\Sigma ʻR\dagger ^{;}Q&amp;=R^{;}\dot{s} ʻCʻQ\unicode{x228d} R^{;}F^{;}Q\\ [*150·3.*162·1]  &amp; =R^{;}\Sigma ʻQ:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4981.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.374ex; width: 75.38ex; height: 11.88ex;" id="img_images_4981.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is important, since it enables us to infer (with a
suitable hypothesis) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}M\)" src="images/4982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.728ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_4982.svg"> is always like <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_3"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\in CʻQ\)" src="images/4983.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.01ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4983.svg">,
then the arithmetical sum of all such relations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}M\)" src="images/4982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.728ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_4982.svg_1"> is
like <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_1">, being in fact <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4984.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.13ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4984.svg">. In other words,
if, whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\in CʻQ\)" src="images/4983.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.01ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4983.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright CʻM\)" src="images/4985.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.372ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4985.svg"> is a correlator of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}M\)" src="images/4982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.728ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_4982.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_4">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright \Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4986.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.698ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4986.svg"> is a correlator
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻR\dagger ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4987.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.14ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4987.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_2">. This proposition is
analogous in its uses to the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ sʻR_{\in}ʻʻ\kappa =Rʻʻsʻ\kappa , \]" src="images/4988.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.209ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4988.svg"></span>
which is *40·38. In general, in obtaining relational analogues of
cardinal propositions, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4989.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.735ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4989.svg"> is to be replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}Q\)" src="images/4990.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.139ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4990.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in }\)" src="images/4211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_4211.svg_1"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\dagger\)" src="images/4210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.722ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4210.svg_1">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/721.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_721.svg_5"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_3">. When these
substitutions are made in <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻR_{\in}ʻʻ\kappa =Rʻʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4991.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.58ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4991.svg">, <a href="#_162_35" class="pginternal">*162·35</a>
results, except for its hypothesis.</p>

<p>If we regard <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}Q\)" src="images/4990.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.139ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4990.svg_1"> as a kind of product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_42"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_115">, *162·35 becomes
a distributive law. For it asserts that if we multiply each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_18">
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_43">, and then sum the resulting products, we get the same relation as
if we first sum <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_19">, and then multiply by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_44">. The following application
of *162·35 to the sum of two relations makes its distributive character
more evident.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_369">[Pg 369]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="id_163_RELATIONS_OF_MUTUALLY_EXCLUSIVE_RELATIONS">
*163. RELATIONS OF MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *163.</p>

<p>In the present number we have to define mutually exclusive relations,
and to give a few of their properties. Mutually exclusive relations
play much the same part in relation-arithmetic as mutually exclusive
classes play in cardinal arithmetic. <i>Prima facie</i>, there are
various ways in which we might define them. We might define <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_160"> as a
relation of mutually exclusive relations when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} QPR . Q &amp;\neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . Q \dot{\cap}  R = \dot{\Lambda}  ,\\ \text{or when}\quad    Q,R \in  CʻP . Q &amp;\neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . Q \dot{\cap}  R = \dot{\Lambda}  , \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5011.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.779ex; width: 46.701ex; height: 6.689ex;" id="img_images_5011.svg"></span>
or when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q,R \in  CʻP . Q \neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . \text{D}ʻQ \cap  \text{D}ʻR = \Lambda  . \text{ᗡ}ʻQ \cap  \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \Lambda  , \]" src="images/5012.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 60.923ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5012.svg"></span>
or in several other ways. But in fact the most useful property to
choose is the property that any two members of the field have mutually
exclusive fields, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q,R \in  CʻP . Q \neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda  . \]" src="images/5013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 43.861ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5013.svg"></span></p>

<p>The principal applications of the subjects studied in this Part are to
series, and in series it is always the <i>fields</i> of the relations
that are important. We want, for instance, to define relations of
mutually exclusive relations in such a way that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_161"> is a serial
relation, and every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_20"> is a serial relation, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_3"> is a serial relation. For this purpose it is necessary
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_4"> should be contained in diversity, which requires
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(F^{;}P\)" src="images/5014.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.151ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_5014.svg"> should be contained in diversity, <i>i.e.</i> that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ QPR . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda  . \]" src="images/5015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 29.482ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5015.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_162"> is a serial relation, as we are supposing, this is equivalent
to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q,R \in  CʻP . Q \neq  P . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda  . \]" src="images/5016.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 43.842ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5016.svg"></span></p>

<p>Again we want to define relations of mutually exclusive relations in
such a way that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_163"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_116"> are two such relations, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_164">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_117"> have double likeness (cf. <a href="#_164" class="pginternal">*164</a>), then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_5"> is like
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_3">; <i>i.e.</i> if we are given a correlator <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_44"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_165">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_118">, and for every <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_5"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_2"> which <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_45"> correlates, we are
again given a correlator, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_6"> is to be like <img alt="" data-tex="\(\SigmaʻQ\)" src="images/5017.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5017.svg">.
That is, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_52"> is the class of relations which correlate
pairs of relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_3">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\in CʻQ.MSN\)" src="images/5018.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.494ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5018.svg">, we want<span class="pagenum" id="Page_370">[Pg 370]</span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4837.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4837.svg_1"> to be a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_166"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_119">. Now this
requires that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4837.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4837.svg_2"> should be a one-one relation, which
requires
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ M,M' \in  CʻP . M \neq  M' . \supset _{M,M'} . \text{D}ʻM \cap  \text{D}ʻM' = \Lambda  . \text{ᗡ}ʻM \cap  \text{ᗡ}ʻM' = \Lambda  . \]" src="images/5019.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 70.332ex; height: 2.48ex;" id="img_images_5019.svg"></span>
This is secured by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ M,M' \in  CʻP . M \neq  M' . \supset _{M,M'} . CʻM \cap  CʻM' = \Lambda  , \]" src="images/5020.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 51.271ex; height: 2.48ex;" id="img_images_5020.svg"></span>
but except for special classes of relations it is not secured by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ MPM' . \supset _{M,M'} . CʻM \cap  CʻM' = \Lambda  , \]" src="images/5021.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 34.893ex; height: 2.48ex;" id="img_images_5021.svg"></span>
since there may be two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(M'\)" src="images/5022.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.128ex; height: 1.717ex;" id="img_images_5022.svg"> which both belong to
the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_167">, but of which neither has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_168"> to the
other. Again, the analogy with cardinal arithmetic fails at many points
unless, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_169"> is a relation of mutually exclusive relations,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg_1"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes. But this is
not secured by any of the other possible definitions we have been
considering. There are further reasons, connected with the arithmetical
product of a relation of relations, for choosing as the definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q,R \in  CʻP . Q \neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda  . \]" src="images/5013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 43.861ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5013.svg_1"></span></p>

<p>From a technical point of view, the properties of a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/5023.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.974ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5023.svg"> depend mainly upon the fact that
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_118"> is such a class, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in \upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 14.954ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5024.svg"> (*84·14); in like manner the properties of a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_1"> depend upon
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ F\upharpoonright CʻP \in  \text{Cls} \rightarrow  1 , \]" src="images/5025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.87ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5025.svg"></span>
which requires our definition, and is equivalent to it (<a href="#_163_12" class="pginternal">*163·12</a>). We
thus become able to use the propositions of *81 on selections from
many-one relations, which would not otherwise be the case.</p>

<p>It should be observed that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q,R \in  CʻP . Q \neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda \]" src="images/5026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 43.232ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5026.svg"></span>
is not equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ CʻʻCʻP \in  \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl} , \]" src="images/5027.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.579ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_5027.svg"></span>
though it implies this. The converse implication will fail if <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_21">
contains two different relations with the same field. <i>E.g.</i>
take a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_170"> whose field consists of the four relations
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_46">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{S}\)" src="images/5028.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 2.514ex;" id="img_images_5028.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_18">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{T}\)" src="images/1667.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 2.4ex;" id="img_images_1667.svg_1">, and suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻS\cap CʻT=\Lambda\)" src="images/5029.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.308ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5029.svg">.
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP=\iota ʻCʻS\cup \iota ʻCʻT\)" src="images/5030.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.265ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5030.svg">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/5031.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.95ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_5031.svg">. But unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(S = \breve{S}\)" src="images/5032.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.936ex; height: 2.649ex;" id="img_images_5032.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(T=\breve{T}\)" src="images/5033.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.203ex; height: 2.586ex;" id="img_images_5033.svg"> we shall not have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q,R \in  CʻP . Q \neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda  . \]" src="images/5013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 43.861ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5013.svg_2"></span></p>

<p>The property by which we define relations of mutually exclusive
relations is a property which only depends on the field, so that we
might equally well put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Rel})\text{excl} = \hat{\lambda} \{Q,R \in  \lambda  . Q \neq  R . \supset _{Q,R} . CʻQ \cap  CʻR = \Lambda \} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/5034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 64.197ex; height: 3.052ex;" id="img_images_5034.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_371">[Pg 371]</span>But for our purposes this would be less convenient than the definition
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_2">.</p>

<p>We thus put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}=\hat{P} \{Q,R\in CʻP.Q\neq R.\supset _{Q,R}.CʻQ\cap CʻR=\Lambda\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/5035.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 63.012ex; height: 3.028ex;" id="img_images_5035.svg"></p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv :Q,R\in CʻP.\exists !CʻQ\cap CʻR.\supset _{Q,R}.Q=R\)" src="images/5036.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 60.533ex; height: 2.668ex;" id="img_images_5036.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv .F\upharpoonright CʻP\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5037.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 38.237ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_5037.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv .C\upharpoonright CʻP\in 1\rightarrow 1.CʻʻCʻP\in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}\)" src="images/5038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 56.819ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_5038.svg"></p>

<p>Any of the above might have been used to define
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_3">. The following propositions are important.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.S\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset .S\dagger ^{;}Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5039.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 49.15ex; height: 2.507ex;" id="img_images_5039.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of *84·53.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·4·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\dot{\Lambda} ,P\downarrow P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.636ex; height: 2.794ex;" id="img_images_5040.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}=\hat{P} \{Q,R\in CʻP.Q\neq R.\supset _{Q,R}.CʻQ\cap CʻR=\Lambda\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/5035.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 63.012ex; height: 3.028ex;" id="img_images_5035.svg_1"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·1.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv :Q,R\in CʻP.Q\neq R.\supset _{Q,R}.CʻQ\cap CʻR=\Lambda \\ &amp;[(*163·01)]\end{align}\]" src="images/5043.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.239ex; width: 63.862ex; height: 5.609ex;" id="img_images_5043.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*163·11.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv :Q,R\in CʻP.\exists !CʻQ\cap CʻR.\supset _{Q,R}.Q=R\\ &amp;[*163·1.\text{Transp}]\end{align}\]" src="images/5044.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.239ex; width: 61.162ex; height: 5.609ex;" id="img_images_5044.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_163_12">*163·12</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\equiv .F\upharpoonright CʻP\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1 \quad[*163·1.*74·632]\)" src="images/5045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.105ex; height: 2.584ex;" id="img_images_5045.svg"></p>

<p>For many purposes, this proposition gives the most useful equivalent of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.584ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg">.</p>

<p>Instead of the above proof, we may use *74·62, which gives us the
result in virtue of *33·5.</p>

<p>This proposition is important in connection with the multiplication
of relations, for we shall define as the product of a relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_171"> (whose field consists of relations) a relation whose field is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻF_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5056.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.552ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5056.svg">. Thus by the above proposition, whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_172"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_4">, the field of its product is the
product (in the cardinal sense) of the fields of its field, just as the
field of its sum is (by <a href="#_162_22" class="pginternal">*162·22</a>) the sum of the fields of its field.</p>
