<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_376">[Pg 376]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_164">*164. DOUBLE LIKENESS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *164.</p>

<p>The subject of this number is of great importance throughout
relation-arithmetic and its applications. Double likeness, or double
ordinal similarity, is a relation which is to hold between <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_173"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_120"> when (1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_174"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_121"> are like, (2) correlated members of the
fields of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_175"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_122"> are like, with a specific given correlator
in each case. (It is necessary, in general, to have a given correlator
in each case, to avoid the necessity of the multiplicative axiom
for selecting among correlators.) This definition can be somewhat
simplified by starting from a relation correlating <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_7"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_4">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_47"> is such a correlator, so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ.\Sigma ʻP=S^{;}\Sigma ʻQ, \]" src="images/5087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.016ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5087.svg"></span>
we want <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_48"> to be such that it not only correlates the whole of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_8"> with the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_5">, but also correlates
each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_22"> with the corresponding member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_20">,
<i>i.e.</i> such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_4"> is any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_21">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}N\)" src="images/5088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.218ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_5088.svg"> is
the corresponding member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_23">. This requires
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ NQN'.\equiv .(S^{;}N)P(S^{;}N'), \]" src="images/5089.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.364ex; height: 2.396ex;" id="img_images_5089.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> writing <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger ʻN\)" src="images/5090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.836ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5090.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger ʻN'\)" src="images/5091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 7.586ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_5091.svg"> in place of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}N, S^{;}N'\)" src="images/5092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 10.192ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_5092.svg">, it requires
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P=S\dagger ^{;}Q. \]" src="images/5093.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.237ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_5093.svg"></span>
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=S\dagger ^{;}Q\)" src="images/5094.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.608ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_5094.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS=Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/5095.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5095.svg">, we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP=S^{;}\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/5096.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.696ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5096.svg"> by <a href="#_162_35" class="pginternal">*162·35</a>. Hence double likeness will
subsist if there is a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_49"> such that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ.P=S\dagger ^{;}Q. \]" src="images/5097.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 37.927ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5097.svg"></span></p>

<p>A relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_50"> fulfilling this condition will be called a double
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_176"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_123">. Thus two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_177"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_124"> have
double likeness when there exists a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_178"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_125">, <i>i.e.</i> when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists S).S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ.P=S\dagger ^{;}Q. \]" src="images/5098.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.411ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5098.svg"></span>
A double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_179"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_126"> is a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_51"> which is
a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_6"> and is such that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger \upharpoonright CʻQ\)" src="images/5099.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.531ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5099.svg"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_180"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_127">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_377">[Pg 377]</span></p>

<p>It will be seen that this definition has the usual analogy to the
corresponding definition in cardinals (<a href="#_111_01" class="pginternal">*111·01</a>). The two inverted
commas of the cardinal definition are replaced by the semi-colon, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{\in }\)" src="images/4140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.642ex; height: 1.998ex;" id="img_images_4140.svg_3"> is replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\dagger\)" src="images/4139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.464ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4139.svg_5">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_8"> is replaced
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4778.svg_7"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/4773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.857ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4773.svg_1">. The propositions of the present
number consist largely of analogues of the propositions of <a href="#_111" class="pginternal">*111</a>, in
accordance with the above substitutions.</p>

<p>If it were not for the difficulty of choice among correlators, we could
define two relations as having double likeness when they are like
relations of like relations, <i>i.e.</i> when, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_181"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_128"> are
the two relations, they have a correlator <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_52"> such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(MSN\)" src="images/5100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 5.846ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_5100.svg">,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(M \text{smor} N\)" src="images/5101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 9.181ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_5101.svg">. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in P\overline{\text{smor}}Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}\)" src="images/5102.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.468ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5102.svg">.
Thus we have to consider the relations of the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}\)" src="images/5103.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.999ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5103.svg"> to the
class of double correlators, and we have to consider the relation
of the relation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap\text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}\)" src="images/5104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.886ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5104.svg">"
to the relation of double likeness. The propositions to be proved on
this subject in the present number are analogous to the propositions of
<a href="#_111" class="pginternal">*111</a>. But at a later stage (*251·61) we shall show that if the field of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_182"> consists entirely of relations which generate <i>well-ordered</i>
series, then the use of the multiplicative axiom ceases to be
necessary in identifying double likeness with the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}\)" src="images/5105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.886ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5105.svg">, the
reason being that two well-ordered series can never be correlated in
more than one way.</p>

<p>Our definitions are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q=(1\rightarrow 1)\cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻCʻ\Sigma ʻQ\cap \hat{S} (P=S\dagger ^{;}Q)   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/5106.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.786ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_5106.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{smor} \text{smor}=\hat{P} \hat{Q} (\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q)   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/5107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.635ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_5107.svg"></p>

<p>The principal propositions of this number are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·15.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\equiv .S\in \Sigma ʻP\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\Sigma ʻQ.(S\dagger )\upharpoonright CʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\)" src="images/5108.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.195ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5108.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164*151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P \,\text{smor}\,\text{smor}\,Q.\supset .\Sigma ʻP\,\text{smor}\,\Sigma ʻQ.P\,\text{smor}\,Q\)" src="images/5109.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 45.687ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5109.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164*18.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :S\upharpoonright Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,&amp;\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\equiv .\\ &amp;S\upharpoonright Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\in 1\rightarrow 1.Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS.P=S\dagger ^{;}Q\end{align}\]" src="images/5110.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.053ex; width: 71.528ex; height: 5.238ex;" id="img_images_5110.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is usually the most convenient proposition when a double
correlation has to be proved.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·201·211·221.</b> Double likeness is reflexive, symmetrical and transitive.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\equiv .S\in (CʻʻCʻP)\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (CʻʻCʻQ).P=S\dagger ^{;}Q\)" src="images/5111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.044ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5111.svg"></p>

<p>(Cf. note to *164·31, below.)</p>

<p>We then have a set of propositions (<a href="#_164_4" class="pginternal">*164·4</a> to the end) on the
identification of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap\text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}\)" src="images/5104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.886ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5104.svg_1">
with double likeness by means of the multiplicative axiom. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·43.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P,Q&amp;\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.S\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\\ &amp;\mu =\hat{\lambda}\{(\exists N).N\in CʻQ.\lambda =(SʻN)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,N\}.\supset :\\ &amp;R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\mu .\supset .\dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻR\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.S=(\dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻR)\dagger \upharpoonright CʻQ\end{align}\]" src="images/5112.svg" style="vertical-align: -4.04ex; width: 68.63ex; height: 9.21ex;" id="img_images_5112.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_378">[Pg 378]</span></p>

<p>That is to say, given that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_183"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_129"> are like relations of
like mutually exclusive relations, if we can pick out one correlator
for each pair of correlated members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_24"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_22">, then the
sum <img alt="" data-tex="\((\dot{s})\)" src="images/5113.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.821ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_5113.svg"> of such selected correlators is a double correlator
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_184"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_130">. Hence, observing that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_53"> is a double
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_185"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_131">, <img alt="" data-tex="\((S\dagger)\upharpoonright CʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}\)" src="images/5114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.056ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5114.svg"> (<a href="#_164_15" class="pginternal">*164·15</a><a href="#_164_16" class="pginternal">·16</a>), we
arrive at</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·45.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\colon &amp;\text{Mult ax}.\supset \colon\ldotp \\ &amp;P,Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\supset :\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}.\equiv .P \,\text{smor}\,\text{smor}\,Q\end{align}\]" src="images/5115.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 62.289ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5115.svg"></span></p>

<p>From <a href="#_164_43" class="pginternal">*164·43</a> we deduce also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·46.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp &amp;\text{Mult ax}.\supset :\\ &amp;P,Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}.\supset .\Sigma ʻP \,\text{smor}\,\Sigma ʻQ\end{align}\]" src="images/5116.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 60.081ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5116.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·48.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :R,S\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap &amp;\text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR,CʻS\in \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Nr}ʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;R\,\text{smor}\,\text{smor}\,S.\Sigma ʻR\,\text{smor}\,\Sigma ʻS\end{align}\]" src="images/5117.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 64.222ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5117.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> in effect, assuming the multiplicative axiom, if two
series <img alt="" data-tex="\((\Sigma ʻR\)" src="images/5118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.588ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5118.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻS\)" src="images/5119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.45ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5119.svg">) can each be divided into
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_155"> sets of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_232"> terms (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_233">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_156"> being
relation-numbers), then the two series are ordinally similar, and
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_157"> sets in the one case have double similarity with the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_158"> sets in the other. (Here we have written <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_234">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_159"> in place of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.731ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4487.svg_2"> of the
enunciation.)</p>

<p>It is by means of the above propositions that ordinal addition and
multiplication are connected, as will appear in <a href="#_166" class="pginternal">*166</a>.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*35·101.*150·1.&amp;\supset \vdash :M{(S\dagger  )\upharpoonright CʻQ}N.\equiv .N\in CʻQ.M=S^{;}N  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*164·1.*162·22.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :S\in 1\rightarrow 1:N\in CʻQ.\supset _{N}.CʻN\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻS:\\ [*151·23] &amp;\supset :N\in CʻQ.M=S^{;}N.\supset _{M,N}.M\,\text{smor}\,N\\ [(1)] &amp;\supset :M{(S\dagger  )\upharpoonright CʻQ}N.\supset _{M,N}.M\,\text{smor}\,N\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5137.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.401ex; width: 88.788ex; height: 11.933ex;" id="img_images_5137.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\text{smor}\,\text{smor}\,Q.\supset .\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}    \quad[*164·143·16]\)" src="images/5138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.478ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5138.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states that when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_186"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_132"> have double likeness,
there is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_187"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_133"> which couples like with
like relations; <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_54"> is the correlator, then, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(MSN\)" src="images/5100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 5.846ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_5100.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_5"> are ordinally similar. The converse of this
proposition, namely, that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_188"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_134"> have a correlator which
couples ordinally similar relations, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_189"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_135"> have double
likeness, can be proved if the multiplicative axiom is assumed, but not
otherwise, except in special cases, such as that of well-ordered series.</p>

<p>The following proposition is used frequently, owing to the fact that,
in the cases we are concerned with, double correlators generally have
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\upharpoonright Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\)" src="images/5139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.517ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5139.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_55"> is some relation
for which we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((y).\text{E}!Sʻy\)" src="images/4339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.97ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4339.svg_1">.</p>

<p>This proposition has the merit of reducing the ordinal element in
double likeness to a minimum. The proof of
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S \in  (CʻʻCʻP)\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, (CʻʻCʻQ) \]" src="images/5160.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.583ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5160.svg"></span>
is a cardinal problem, and what has to be added for ordinal purposes is
merely <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = S\dagger ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4774.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.608ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4774.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*164·34.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P \,\text{smor} R.Q\,\text{smor}\,S.CʻP \cap  CʻQ = \Lambda .&amp;CʻR \cap  CʻS =\Lambda .\supset .\\ &amp;P \downarrow  Q\,\text{smor smor}\,R \downarrow  S\\ [*164·33·11.*151·12]\end{align}\]" src="images/5166.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 61.763ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_5166.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned in showing that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_190">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_136"> are like relations, and the correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_191"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_137">
is contained in likeness (<i>i.e.</i> correlates relations which
have the relation of likeness), a correlator being given for each pair
of relations coupled by the correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_192"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_138">, then the
logical sum of such correlators is a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_193"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_139">, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_194"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_140"> are relations of mutually exclusive
relations. That is, assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_56"> to be the correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_195"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_141">, and assuming that <img alt="" data-tex="\(SʻN \,\text{smor}\, N\)" src="images/5167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.385ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5167.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(N \in CʻQ\)" src="images/5168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.642ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5168.svg">,
let it be possible to choose one correlator out of the class of
correlators <img alt="" data-tex="\((SʻN)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,N\)" src="images/5169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.145ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5169.svg">, for every <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_6"> which
belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_23">. That is, assume that it is possible to make a
selection from the class of classes of correlators. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_167"> is such
a selection, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ\mu\)" src="images/5170.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 3.783ex; height: 2.224ex;" id="img_images_5170.svg"> will be a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_196">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \)" src="images/5171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5171.svg">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_197">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 12.674ex; height: 2.457ex;" id="img_images_5172.svg">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_386">[Pg 386]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_165">
*165. RELATIONS OF RELATIONS OF COUPLES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *165.</p>

<p>In the present number, we shall give various propositions concerning
the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_8">, which has the same uses in
relation-arithmetic <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_12"> has in cardinal
arithmetic. The propositions of this number will be used in the
next number to establish the properties of the arithmetical product
of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_142"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_198">, which is defined as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\SigmaʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_4793.svg_2">.
Again in connection with exponentiation the propositions of the present
number will be useful, since, after the product of a relation of
relations has been defined (<a href="#_172" class="pginternal">*172</a>), we shall define exponentiation by
means of the definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P \,\,\text{exp}\,\, Q = \text{Prod}ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q  \text{Df}. \quad(Cf. *176.) \]" src="images/5197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 41.176ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5197.svg"></span>
There will also be occasional uses of the propositions of
this number throughout the theory of series. The relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_9"> is important because its structure is
thoroughly known. It is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_5"> which consists
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.731ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4487.svg_3"> relations, each like <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_199"> (<a href="#_165_27" class="pginternal">*165·27</a>); and if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\text{smor}\,P'.Q\,\text{smor}\,Q'\)" src="images/5198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.464ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_5198.svg">, we can construct a double correlator
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_10"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻ\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q'\)" src="images/5199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 8.939ex; height: 2.586ex;" id="img_images_5199.svg"> without invoking
the multiplicative axiom. In fact we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·362. </b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :R\upharpoonright CʻP'\in &amp;P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Pʻ.S\upharpoonright CʻQ'\in Q\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q'.\supset .\\ &amp;(R\parallel \breve{S} )\upharpoonright Cʻ\Sigma ʻP'\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q'\in (P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q)\,\overline{\text{smor}}     \,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(Pʻ\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q')\end{align}\]" src="images/5200.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.638ex; width: 71.053ex; height: 6.408ex;" id="img_images_5200.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition should be compared with <a href="#_113_127" class="pginternal">*113·127</a>. In virtue of
<a href="#_164_31" class="pginternal">*164·31</a>, together with various propositions of <a href="#_165" class="pginternal">*165</a> and <a href="#_166" class="pginternal">*166</a>, it will
appear that <a href="#_165_362" class="pginternal">*165·362</a> includes *113·127 as part of what it asserts.</p>

<p>In the present number, we begin with a set of propositions on fields.
We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .CʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=P\downarrow_{.,} ʻʻCʻQ\)" src="images/5201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 28.182ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5201.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .CʻP\downarrow_{.,} z=\downarrow zʻʻCʻP=(CʻP)\downarrow_{,,} z\)" src="images/5202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.444ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5202.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_387">[Pg 387]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .CʻʻCʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=(CʻP)\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻCʻQ\)" src="images/5203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 37.454ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5203.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which connects the theory of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_11"> with that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg_13"> (<a href="#_113" class="pginternal">*113</a> and <a href="#_116" class="pginternal">*116</a>). Hence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻ\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=CʻQ\times CʻP\)" src="images/5204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 30.836ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5204.svg"></p>

<p>In <a href="#_166" class="pginternal">*166</a>, we shall define <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\times P\)" src="images/4801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4801.svg_1"> as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,}^{;}Q\)" src="images/5205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5205.svg">;
thus the above will become
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .Cʻ(Q\times P)=CʻQ\times CʻP. \]" src="images/5206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.534ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5206.svg"></span></p>

<p>We next have a set of propositions concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,}\)" src="images/5207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.536ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_5207.svg">
as a relation, and with the circumstances under which we can infer
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y\)" src="images/5208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_5208.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=Q\)" src="images/5209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.506ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5209.svg"> from data as to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} x\)" src="images/5210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.459ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_5210.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\downarrow_{.,} y\)" src="images/5211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.364ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_5211.svg">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 20.227ex; height: 2.887ex;" id="img_images_5212.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·211.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !CʻP\downarrow_{.,} x\cap CʻP\downarrow_{.,} y.\supset .x=y\)" src="images/5213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 35.119ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5213.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} \in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5214.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.453ex; height: 2.955ex;" id="img_images_5214.svg"></p>

<p>We then have various propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg_4">, of
which the chief are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·241.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Q=\dot{\Lambda} .\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/5215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 24.33ex; height: 3.224ex;" id="img_images_5215.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·242.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P=\dot{\Lambda} .\dot{\exists} !Q.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=\dot{\Lambda} \downarrow \dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/5216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 32.88ex; height: 3.224ex;" id="img_images_5216.svg"></p>

<p>We have next four propositions which are constantly used, proving that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_12"> consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ\)" src="images/4487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.731ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4487.svg_4"> relations each
like <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_200">. These propositions are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\text{smor}Q.(P\downarrow_{.,} )\upharpoonright CʻQ\in (P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q)\overline{\text{smor}}     Q\)" src="images/5217.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 55.969ex; height: 3.175ex;" id="img_images_5217.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·251.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\downarrow_{.,} x\,\text{smor}\,P.(\downarrow x)\upharpoonright CʻP\in (P\downarrow_{.,} x)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P\)" src="images/5218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 47.126ex; height: 2.38ex;" id="img_images_5218.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .CʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\subset \text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/5219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 21.077ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5219.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·27.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap \text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\in     \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/5220.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 59.145ex; height: 3.175ex;" id="img_images_5220.svg"></p>

<p>From <a href="#_165_3" class="pginternal">*165·3</a> to *165·372, we are concerned with constructing a double
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_13"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻ\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q'\)" src="images/5199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 8.939ex; height: 2.586ex;" id="img_images_5199.svg_1">
when we are given simple correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_201"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(P'\)" src="images/5221.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.452ex; height: 1.717ex;" id="img_images_5221.svg"> and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_143">
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q'\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.417ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_1">. The result (<a href="#_165_362" class="pginternal">*165·362</a>) has already been given. Hence we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·37.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : P \,\text{smor}\,P'.Q \text{smor} Q'.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\,\text{smor smor}\,P'\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q'\)" src="images/5222.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 52.319ex; height: 2.586ex;" id="img_images_5222.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">and by <a href="#_164_48" class="pginternal">*164·48</a> and <a href="#_165_27" class="pginternal">*165·27</a> we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·38.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp &amp;\text{Mult ax}.\supset :\\ &amp;R\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap \text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR\subset \text{Nr}ʻP.\supset .R\, \text{smor smor}\, P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\end{align}\]" src="images/5223.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.349ex; width: 61.675ex; height: 5.828ex;" id="img_images_5223.svg"></span></p>

<p>Hence propositions concerning a series of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_160"> series, each
containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_235"> terms (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_236"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_161"> are
relation-numbers), which in general require the multiplicative
axiom, can be deduced, assuming that axiom, from propositions<span class="pagenum" id="Page_388">[Pg 388]</span> (not
requiring the axiom) concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_14">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP=\alpha\)" src="images/5224.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.105ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5224.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ=\beta\)" src="images/5225.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.028ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5225.svg">. Thus the use of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_15"> enables us to minimize the use of the
multiplicative axiom.</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned in proving that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_47"> is

and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q'\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.417ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_2"> then <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\parallel \breve{S}\)" src="images/2829.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.565ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_2829.svg_2"> (with its converse domain
limited) is a double correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\)" src="images/4293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 6.954ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_4293.svg_16"> and

<p>The above three propositions are of great utility in relation-arithmetic.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_395">[Pg 395]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·37.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :P\,\text{smor}\,P'.Q\text{smor}Q'.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\,\text{smor smor}\,P'\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q'\\ &amp;[*165·362.*164·11.*151·12]\end{align}\]" src="images/5312.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.255ex; width: 52.947ex; height: 5.641ex;" id="img_images_5312.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*165·38.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :R\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap &amp;\text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR\subset \text{Nr}ʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;R\,\text{smor smor}\,P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q\end{align}\]" src="images/5313.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.349ex; width: 52.846ex; height: 5.828ex;" id="img_images_5313.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*164·48.*165·27.&amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .R\,\text{smor smor}\,P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*153·17.*165·241.&amp;\supset \\ \vdash :Q=\dot{\Lambda} .R\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap \text{Nr}ʻQ.&amp;\supset .R=\dot{\Lambda} .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=\dot{\Lambda} .\\ [*164·32]   &amp;\supset .R\,\text{smor smor}\,P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q   &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*165*242&amp;.\supset \vdash :P=\dot{\Lambda} .\dot{\exists} !Q.\supset .P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q=\dot{\Lambda} \downarrow \dot{\Lambda}   &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .*153·17.*51·4.*151·32.\supset \\ \vdash :R\in \text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR\subset \text{Nr}ʻP.P=\dot{\Lambda} .\dot{\exists} !Q.&amp;\supset .CʻR={℩}ʻ\dot{\Lambda} .\\ [*56·381] &amp;\supset .R=\dot{\Lambda} \downarrow \dot{\Lambda}  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .(3).(4).*153·101.*164·34.\supset \\ \vdash :R\in \text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR\subset \text{Nr}ʻP.P=\dot{\Lambda} .\dot{\exists} !Q.&amp;\supset .R\,\text{smor smor}\,P\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q   &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).(5).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5314.svg" style="vertical-align: -19.112ex; width: 87.503ex; height: 39.355ex;" id="img_images_5314.svg"></span></p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_396">[Pg 396]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_166">
*166. THE PRODUCT OF TWO RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *166.</p>

<p>The product <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \times P\)" src="images/5315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5315.svg"> is defined as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,}^{;}Q\)" src="images/5205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 9.945ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5205.svg_1">.
This is a relation which has for its field all the couples that
can be formed by choosing the referent in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_25"> and the relatum in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_24">. These couples are arranged by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \times P\)" src="images/5315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5315.svg_1"> on the following
principle: If the relatum of the one couple has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_145"> to
the relatum of the other, we put the one before the other, and if the
relata of the two couples are equal while the referent of the one has
the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_203"> to the referent of the other, we put the one before
the other. Thus in advancing from any term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1842.svg_4"> in the
field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \times P\)" src="images/5315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5315.svg_2">, we first keep <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_78"> fixed and alter <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_122"> into
later terms as long as possible; then we alter <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_79"> into a later term,
move <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_123"> back to the beginning, and so on. Thus with a given <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_80">,
we get a series which is like <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_204">, and this series is wholly followed
or wholly preceded by the series with the referent <img alt="" data-tex="\(y'\)" src="images/5316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.736ex; height: 2.181ex;" id="img_images_5316.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y'\)" src="images/5316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.736ex; height: 2.181ex;" id="img_images_5316.svg_1">
follows or precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_81">.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are for the most part immediate
consequences of those of <a href="#_165" class="pginternal">*165</a>. The most important of them are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻ(P\times Q)=CʻP\times CʻQ\)" src="images/5317.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.905ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5317.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\times Q=\dot{\Lambda} .\equiv :P=\dot{\Lambda} .\lor.Q=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/5318.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 34.444ex; height: 2.794ex;" id="img_images_5318.svg"></p>

<p>Hence it follows that an ordinal product of a finite number of factors
vanishes when, and only when, one of its factors vanishes.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·16.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{B}ʻ(P\times Q)=\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\times \overrightarrow{B}ʻQ.\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\text{Cnv}ʻ(P\times Q)=\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P} \times \overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{Q}\)" src="images/5319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.858ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5319.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\text{smor}\,P'.Q\text{smor}Q'.\supset .Q\times P\,\text{smor}\,Q'\times P'\)" src="images/5320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 45.56ex; height: 2.156ex;" id="img_images_5320.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that the relation-number of a product <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \times P\)" src="images/5315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5315.svg_3">
depends only upon the relation-numbers of its factors.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·24.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :R\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap \text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR\subset \text{Nr}ʻ&amp;P.\supset .\\ &amp;\Sigma ʻR\,\text{smor}\,Q\times P\end{align}\]" src="images/5321.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 65.269ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5321.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition connects addition and multiplication (cf. note to
*166·24, below).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(P\times Q)\times R\,\text{smor}\,P\times (Q\times R)\)" src="images/5322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.933ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5322.svg"></p>

<p>This is the associative law. The distributive law has two forms:</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_397">[Pg 397]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Sigma ʻ\times P^{;}Q=(\Sigma ʻQ)\times P\)" src="images/5323.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.414ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5323.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .(Q\unicode{x2909}R)\times P=(Q\times P)\unicode{x2909}(R\times P)\)" src="images/5324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.809ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5324.svg"></p>

<p>We do not have in general (cf. note before *166·44, below)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\times (Q\unicode{x2909}R)=(P\times Q)\unicode{x2909}(P\times R). \]" src="images/5325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.05ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5325.svg"></span></p>

<p>We have also a distributive law for the addition of a single term,
<i>i.e.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !Q.\supset .(Q\unicode{x21f8} y)\times P=(Q\times P)\unicode{x2909}(P\downarrow_{.,} y)\)" src="images/5326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 40.992ex; height: 2.955ex;" id="img_images_5326.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·531.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !Q.\supset .(y\unicode{x21f7}Q)\times P=(P\downarrow_{.,} y)\unicode{x2909}(Q\times P)\)" src="images/5327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 40.992ex; height: 2.955ex;" id="img_images_5327.svg"></p>

<p>Here again the law does not hold in general for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\times(Q\unicode{x21f8} y)\)" src="images/5328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.481ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5328.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\times (y\unicode{x21f7}Q)\)" src="images/5329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.481ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5329.svg">.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*166·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\times P=\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/5330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 23.9ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5330.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Q\times P=\Sigma ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q \quad[(*166·01)]\)" src="images/5331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 35.307ex; height: 2.566ex;" id="img_images_5331.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·11.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp M(Q\times P)&amp;N.\equiv :(\exists x,y,z,w):x,y\in CʻP.z,w\in CʻQ:zQw.\lor.\\ &amp;z=w.xPy:M=x\downarrow z.N=y\downarrow w \quad[*165·17.*166·1]\end{align}\]" src="images/5332.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 68.615ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5332.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·111.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp M(P\times Q)&amp;N.\equiv :(\exists x,y,z,w):x,y\in CʻP.z,w\in CʻQ:xPy.\lor.\\ &amp;x=y.zQw:M=z\downarrow x.N=w\downarrow y \quad[*165·17.*166·1]\end{align}\]" src="images/5333.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 68.705ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5333.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·112.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp (x\downarrow z)(Q\times P)(y\downarrow w).&amp;\equiv :x,y\in CʻP.z,w\in CʻQ:zQw.\lor.\\ &amp;z=w.xPy \quad[*166·11.*55·202.*13·22]\end{align}\]" src="images/5334.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 67.13ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5334.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·113.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\colon x,y\in &amp;CʻP.z,w\in CʻQ.\supset \colon\ldotp \\ &amp;(x\downarrow z)(Q\times P)(y\downarrow w).\equiv :zQw.\lor.z=w.xPy \quad[*166·112]\end{align}\]" src="images/5335.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 66.203ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5335.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Cʻ(P\times Q)=CʻP\times CʻQ \quad[*165·16.*166·1]\)" src="images/5336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.772ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5336.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\times Q=\dot{\Lambda} .=:P=\dot{\Lambda} .\lor.Q=\dot{\Lambda}  \quad[*166·12.*113·114.*33·241]\)" src="images/5337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 67.63ex; height: 2.921ex;" id="img_images_5337.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P\times Q.\equiv .\dot{\exists} !P.\dot{\exists} !Q \quad[*166·13]\)" src="images/5338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.764ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_5338.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Cnv}ʻ(P\times Q)=\breve{P} \times \breve{Q}  \quad[*165·19 . *162·2]\)" src="images/5339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.357ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_5339.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·16.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{B}ʻ(P\times Q)=\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\times \overrightarrow{B}ʻQ.\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\text{Cnv}ʻ(P\times Q)=\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P} \times \overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{Q}\)" src="images/5319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.858ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5319.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*166·111.*93·103.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp M\in \overrightarrow{B}ʻ(P\times Q).&amp;\equiv :(\exists x,z):x\in CʻP.z\in CʻQ.M=z\downarrow x:\\ &amp;{\sim}(\exists y).yPx:{\sim}(\exists w).wQz:\\ [*93·103] &amp;\equiv :(\exists x,z).x\in \overrightarrow{B}ʻP.y\in \overrightarrow{B}ʻQ.M=z\downarrow x:\\ [*113·101] &amp;\equiv :M\in \overrightarrow{B}ʻP\times \overrightarrow{B}ʻQ &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*166·15.&amp;\supset \vdash .\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\text{Cnv}ʻ(P\times Q)=\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P} \times \overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{Q}  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5340.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.054ex; width: 79.15ex; height: 27.24ex;" id="img_images_5340.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_398">[Pg 398]</span></p>

<p>The above proposition is used in the ordinal theory of progressions
(*263·62·65).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·2.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :R\upharpoonright CʻPʻ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Pʻ.\supset .(R\mid )\upharpoonright Cʻ(Q\times Pʻ)\in (Q\times P)\overline{\text{smor}} (Q\times Pʻ)\\ &amp;[*165·36.*166·1.*164·14]\end{align}\]" src="images/5341.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.053ex; width: 74.494ex; height: 5.238ex;" id="img_images_5341.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·21.</b>
    <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :S\upharpoonright CʻQʻ\in Q\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Qʻ.\supset .(\mid \breve{S} )\upharpoonright Cʻ(Qʻ\times P)\in (Q\times P)\overline{\text{smor}} (Qʻ\times P)\\ &amp;[*165·361.*166·1.*164·14]\end{align}\]" src="images/5342.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.42ex; width: 74.249ex; height: 5.971ex;" id="img_images_5342.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·22.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :R\upharpoonright CʻP'\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P'.&amp;S\upharpoonright CʻQ'\in Q\overline{\text{smor}} Q'.\supset .\\ &amp;(R\parallel \breve{S} )\upharpoonright Cʻ(Q'\times P')\in (Q\times P)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(Q'\times P')\\ [*165·362.*166·1.*164·14]\end{align}\]" src="images/5343.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.957ex; width: 77.516ex; height: 9.045ex;" id="img_images_5343.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition gives the correlator for the product when correlators
are given for the factors.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·23.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :P \,\text{smor} P'.Q \text{smor} Q'.\supset .Q\times P \,\text{smor} \,Q'\times P'\\ &amp;[*166·22.*151·12]\end{align}\]" src="images/5344.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.103ex; width: 45.81ex; height: 5.337ex;" id="img_images_5344.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition enables us to use <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\times P\)" src="images/4801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4801.svg_2"> to define the
product of the relation-numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_146"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_205">, for it shows
that the relation-number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\times P\)" src="images/4801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4801.svg_3"> is determinate when the
relation-numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_147"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_206"> are given. We shall therefore (in
Section D of this part) define the product of two relation-numbers
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_151"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_168"> as the relation-number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\times P\)" src="images/4801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4801.svg_4"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻQ=\nu\)" src="images/5345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.935ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5345.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP=\mu\)" src="images/5346.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.009ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5346.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·24.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :R\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\cap \text{Nr}ʻQ.CʻR\subset \text{Nr}ʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;\Sigma ʻR\,\text{smor}\,Q\times P \quad[*165·38.*164·151.*166·1]\end{align}\]" src="images/5347.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 54.48ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5347.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition exhibits the connection of addition and
multiplication. If we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP=\mu\)" src="images/5348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.022ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5348.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻQ=\nu\)" src="images/5349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.947ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5349.svg">,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻR\)" src="images/5350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.708ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5350.svg"> in the above proposition is the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_152">
relations of which each is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_169">. In virtue of the above
proposition, it follows that (if the multiplicative axiom is assumed)
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻ\Sigma ʻR=\nu \times \mu\)" src="images/5351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 16.995ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5351.svg">. In other words, assuming the
multiplicative axiom, the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_153"> series (or other relations),
each of which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_170"> terms, has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu \times \mu\)" src="images/4802.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.329ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_4802.svg_1"> terms.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·3.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :\exists !Cʻ(P\times Q)\cap Cʻ(Pʻ\times Qʻ).\equiv .\exists !CʻP\cap CʻPʻ.\exists !CʻQ\cap CʻQʻ\\ &amp;[*166·12.*113·19]\end{align}\]" src="images/5352.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 68.149ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5352.svg"></span></p>

<p>The analogous proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{\exists} !(P\times Q)\dot{\cap} (Pʻ\times Qʻ).&amp;\equiv :\\ \dot{\exists} !(P\dot{\cap} Pʻ).&amp;\exists !CʻQ\cap CʻQʻ.\lor.\dot{\exists} !(Q\dot{\cap} Qʻ).\exists !CʻP\cap CʻPʻ \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5353.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.645ex; width: 68.192ex; height: 6.421ex;" id="img_images_5353.svg"></span>
is only true in general if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.Pʻ\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.852ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5354.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\dot{s} ʻCʻ(Q\times P)=CʻP\uparrow CʻQ \quad[*113·115.*166·12]\)" src="images/5355.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.076ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_5355.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·421.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \times  Q \times  R = (P \times  Q) \times  R \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/5364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.935ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5364.svg"></p>

<p>This definition serves merely for the avoidance of brackets.</p>

<p>The two following propositions give the distributive law. In
relation-arithmetic, this is in general only true in one of its two
forms, <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} (Q \unicode{x2909} R) \times  P &amp;= (Q \times  P) \unicode{x2909} (R \times  P),\\ \text{but not}\quad P \times  (Q \unicode{x2909} R) &amp;= (P \times  Q) \unicode{x2909} (P \times  R). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5365.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 41.543ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5365.svg"></span>
The latter is true for finite series, but not for infinite series or
(except in exceptional cases) for relations which are not serial.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*166·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  . \Sigma ʻ \times  P^{;}Q = (\Sigma ʻQ) \times  P\)" src="images/5366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.414ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5366.svg"></p>

the form in which it holds, is given in <a href="#_166_53" class="pginternal">*166·53</a><a href="#_166_531" class="pginternal">·531</a> (remembering
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\downarrow_{.,} y=\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/5382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 18.872ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5382.svg">). <a href="#_166_54" class="pginternal">*166·54</a><a href="#_166_541" class="pginternal">·541</a> exhibit the
failure of the other form.</p>
