<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_403">[Pg 403]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_C_II">SECTION C.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">THE PRINCIPLE OF FIRST DIFFERENCES, AND THE MULTIPLICATION
AND EXPONENTIATION OF RELATIONS.</span></h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section C.</i></p>

<p>In the present section, we have to consider various forms of a
principle which is of the utmost utility in relation-arithmetic. This
principle may be called "the principle of first differences." It has
been explained and used by Hausdorff in brilliant articles<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_15" id="FNanchor_15">[15]</a>. The
results there obtained by its use give some measure of its importance
in relation-arithmetic. It has, however, other uses besides those
that are concerned with the multiplication and exponentiation of
relation-numbers, as, for example, in the ordering of segments
and stretches in a series, or of any other set of classes which
are contained in the field of a given relation. In the present
section, after the first two numbers, we shall be concerned with its
arithmetical uses, but other uses will occur later.</p>

<p>The principle of first differences has various forms which, though
analogous, cannot, in the general case, be reduced to one common
genus. The simplest of these is the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg">, by
which the sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_26"> are ordered. This is defined as
follows. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_237"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_162"> are both contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_27">, we
say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta\)" src="images/5394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.524ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5394.svg"> if there are terms belonging
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_238"> but not to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_163"> such that no terms belonging to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_164"> and not to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_239"> precede them; <i>i.e.</i> if, after
taking away the terms (if any) which are common to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_240"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_165">, there are terms left in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_241"> which do not come after
any of the terms left in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_166">, <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\alpha-\beta -\breve{P} ʻʻ(\beta -\alpha )\)" src="images/5395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.815ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5395.svg">.
Thus the definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\text{cl}}=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\exists !\alpha -\beta -\breve{P} ʻʻ(\beta -\alpha )\}   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/5396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.833ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_5396.svg"></span>
It will be seen that this relation holds if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \subset \alpha.\beta \neq \alpha\)" src="images/5397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 12.497ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_5397.svg">.
Thus it holds between any existent member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.396ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5398.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_65">, and between <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_28"> and
any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.396ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5398.svg_1"> other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_29"> itself. When
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_207"> is a serial relation (which is the important case for all
the relations in this section), <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_1"> is transitive
<img alt="" data-tex="\((P^{2}_{\text{cl}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P_{\text{cl}})\)" src="images/5399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.714ex; width: 9.481ex; height: 2.601ex;" id="img_images_5399.svg"> and asymmetrical
<img alt="" data-tex="\((P_{\text{cl}}\dot{\cap} \breve{P} _{\text{cl}}=\dot{\Lambda})\)" src="images/5400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.447ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5400.svg">, but
not necessarily <i>connected</i>, <i>i.e.</i> there may<span class="pagenum" id="Page_404">[Pg 404]</span> be two members
of its field of which neither has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_2"> to
the other. This happens whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_208"> is not well-ordered; but when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_209"> is well-ordered, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_3"> is connected, and therefore
generates a series.</p>

<p>To illustrate the order generated by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_4"> in a simple
case, consider a series of three terms, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_124">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_82">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_25">. Let us for
the moment write <img alt="" data-tex="\((x\downarrow y\downarrow z)\)" src="images/5401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.991ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5401.svg"> for the relation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d} x\downarrow z\unicode{x228d} y\downarrow z,\,\, \textit{i.e.}\,\, (x\downarrow y)\unicode{x21f8} z, \]" src="images/5402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.12ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5402.svg"></span>
and similarly we will write <img alt="" data-tex="\((x\downarrow y\downarrow z\downarrow w)\)" src="images/5403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.999ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5403.svg">
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\downarrow z\unicode{x21f8} w\)" src="images/5404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.208ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5404.svg">, and so on. Then
assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y.x\neq z.y\neq z\)" src="images/4534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 17.973ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_4534.svg_2">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} (x\downarrow y\downarrow z)_{\text{cl}}=(\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy\cup \iota ʻz)&amp;\downarrow (\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy)\\ &amp;\downarrow (\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻz)\downarrow \iota ʻx\downarrow (\iota ʻy\cup \iota ʻz)\downarrow \iota ʻy\downarrow \iota ʻz\downarrow \Lambda . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5405.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 79.218ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5405.svg"></span>
In this series, a class containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_125"> is always earlier than one not
containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_126">; and of two classes of which both or neither contain
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_127">, one containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_83"> is earlier than one not containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_84">;
and of two classes of which both or neither contain <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_128">, and both
or neither contain <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_85">, one containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_26"> is earlier than one
not containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_27">. Thus our relation may be generated as follows:
Begin with <img alt="" data-tex="\((\iota ʻz)\downarrow \Lambda\)" src="images/5406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.929ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5406.svg">, which is <img alt="" data-tex="\((z\downarrow z)_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.595ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5407.svg">.
Add before these terms what results from adding <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻy\)" src="images/5408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.267ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5408.svg"> to each;
then we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((y\downarrow z)_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.652ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5409.svg">, which is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\iota ʻy\cup \iota ʻz)\downarrow \iota ʻy\downarrow \iota ʻz\downarrow \Lambda . \]" src="images/5410.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.593ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5410.svg"></span>
Now add at the beginning what results from adding <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg_6"> to each
of the above four classes, and we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((x\downarrow y\downarrow z)_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.334ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5411.svg">.
Thus generally, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x{\sim}\in CʻP\)" src="images/5412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.596ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5412.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x\unicode{x21f7}P)_{\text{cl}}=(\iota ʻx\cup )^{;}P_{\text{cl}}\unicode{x2909}P_{\text{cl}}. \]" src="images/5413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.402ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5413.svg"></span>
Thus by adding one term to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_210">, we double the number of terms in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_5">.</p>

<p>Again, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_211"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_148"> are two relations which have no common terms
in their fields, we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha P_{\text{cl}}&amp;\beta .\gamma ,\delta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻQ.\supset .(\alpha \cup \gamma )(P\unicode{x2909}Q)_{\text{cl}}(\beta \cup \delta )\\ &amp;\text{and}\quad \alpha \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\gamma Q_{\text{cl}}\delta .\supset .(\alpha \cup \gamma )(P\unicode{x2909}Q)_{\text{cl}}(\alpha \cup \delta ), \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5414.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 55.163ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5414.svg"></span>
while conversely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\gamma ,\delta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻQ.(\alpha \cup \gamma )(P\unicode{x2909}Q)_{\text{cl}}&amp;(\beta \cup \delta ).\supset :\\ &amp;\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta .\lor.\alpha =\beta .\gamma Q_{\text{cl}}\delta . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5415.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 68.091ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5415.svg"></span>
Hence
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} (\alpha \cup \gamma )(P\unicode{x2909}Q)_{\text{cl}}(\beta \cup \delta ).&amp;\equiv .(\gamma \downarrow \alpha )(P_{\text{cl}}\times Q_{\text{cl}})(\delta     \downarrow \beta )\\ &amp;\equiv .(\alpha \cup \gamma ){s^{;}C^{;}(P_{\text{cl}}\times Q_{\text{cl}})}(\beta \cup \delta ), \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5416.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 54.241ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5416.svg"></span>
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻ(P\unicode{x2909}Q)_{\text{cl}}=\text{Nr}ʻP_{\text{cl}}\times \text{Nr}ʻQ_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.483ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5417.svg">.</p>

<p>These propositions illustrate the connection of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_\text{cl}\)" src="images/5418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5418.svg"> with
multiplication.</p>

<p>Besides <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_6">, we often require (though not in this Part)
the relation which is the converse of <img alt="" data-tex="\((\breve{P})_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.802ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5419.svg">.
This relation we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg">, so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\text{lc}}=\text{Cnv}ʻ(\breve{P} )_{\text{cl}}   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/5421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.37ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5421.svg"></span>
This begins with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_66">, and ends with <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_30">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_405">[Pg 405]</span></p>

<p>Thus we shall have, for example,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} (x\downarrow y\downarrow z)_{\text{lc}} = \Lambda \downarrow \iota ʻx\downarrow \iota ʻy&amp;\downarrow (\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy)\\ &amp;\downarrow \iota ʻz\downarrow (\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻz)\downarrow (\iota ʻy\cup \iota ʻz)\downarrow (\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy\cup \iota ʻz). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5422.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 79.218ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_5422.svg"></span>
Here, if we start from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \downarrow \iota ʻx\)" src="images/5423.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.411ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5423.svg">, which is
<img alt="" data-tex="\((x\downarrow x)_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.079ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5424.svg">, the series grows by adding terms at
the end: we add <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻy\)" src="images/5408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.267ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5408.svg_1"> to each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \downarrow\iota ʻx\)" src="images/5425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.411ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5425.svg">
and put the resulting terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻy, \iota ʻx\cup \iotaʻy\)" src="images/5426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 13.507ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5426.svg">
after <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_67"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_407.svg_7">; we then add <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻz\)" src="images/5427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5427.svg"> to each
of the four terms we already have, and add the resulting terms at the
end; and so we can proceed indefinitely.</p>

<p>The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_1"> with its field limited arranges the
<i>segments</i> of P in ascending order of magnitude; if the class
of segments is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sigma\)" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.292ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_136.svg_40">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\sigma\)" src="images/5428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.445ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5428.svg">
generates what may be called the natural order among the segments (cf.
<a href="#_212" class="pginternal">*212</a>).</p>

<p>A variant of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_7"> is afforded by the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_1"> (<a href="#_171" class="pginternal">*171</a>), which is to hold between two members
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_242">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_167"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.396ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5398.svg_2"> when the first term of
either which does not belong to both belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_243">, <i>i.e.</i>
the "first difference" belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_244">. This relation implies
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_8">, and coincides with it if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_212"> is well-ordered; but
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_213"> is not well-ordered, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_9"> may hold between two
classes which have no first point of difference, <i>e.g.</i> (if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_214">
is "less than" among rationals) if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_245"> consists of rationals
between 0 and 1 (both excluded) and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_168"> of rationals between 1
and 2 (both excluded). The definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_2"> is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\text{df}}     = \hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP:(\exists z).z\in \alpha -\beta .\overrightarrow{P}ʻz\cap \alpha -\iota ʻz = \overrightarrow{P}ʻz\cap \beta\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/5429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 73.484ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5429.svg"></span></p>

<p>The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_3"> has the interesting property that
its relation-number is found by raising <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_10"> to the power
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_9"> (cf. <a href="#_177" class="pginternal">*177</a>). As the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_4">
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.396ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5398.svg_3">, this theorem is the ordinal analogue of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nc}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha = 2^{\text{Nc}ʻ\alpha}\)" src="images/5430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.357ex; height: 2.474ex;" id="img_images_5430.svg"> (<a href="#_116_72" class="pginternal">*116·72</a>).</p>

<p>A somewhat more complicated form of the relation of first differences
arises when we have a series of series. Let us suppose, to begin with,
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_215"> is a serial relation whose field consists of mutually
exclusive serial relations.</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 1200px;" id="i_405">
<img alt="Grid diagram showing four rows of dots with special markers. Each row has squares and circles at different positions among dots, with arrows pointing right to labels Q (top three rows) and R⋎p (bottom). The squares and circles shift diagonally downward, illustrating relation ordering." height="745" src="images/i_405.jpg" width="1200" id="img_images_i_405.jpg">
</figure>

<p>Thus in the accompanying figure, each row represents a series, the
generating relations of these series being <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_149">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_48">,... But the
series themselves form a series, which may be regarded as generated
by a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_216"> whose field consists of the relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_150">, ...
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_49">,... (It might be thought more natural to take <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_25">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_389.svg_3">,
... as the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_217">; but this would lead to confusion in the
case when two or more of the series have the same field.) Suppose
we now wish to find a relation which will order the multiplicative
class of the fields of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_151">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_50">, ..., <i>i.e.</i> the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻCʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.385ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5431.svg">. In the case illustrated in the figure, in which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_218"> generates a well-ordered series, and all the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_31">
are serial, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.584ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg_1">, we might use
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\Sigma ʻP)_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5432.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.793ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5432.svg">; this relation, with its field limited to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻCʻCʻʻP\)" src="images/5433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.385ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5433.svg">, will then give us what we want. This relation
will, in the case supposed, put<span class="pagenum" id="Page_406">[Pg 406]</span> a selected class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_171"> before
another selected class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_154"> if, where they first differ, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_172">
chooses an earlier term than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_155">. But if the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_219"> is not
well-ordered—if it is (say) of the type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻʻ\omega\)" src="images/3661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.208ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3661.svg_2"> (cf.
*263)—there may be no <i>first</i> member of the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_220"> where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_173"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_156"> differ. This will happen, for example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_174">
consists of all the first terms, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_157"> of all the second terms.
Our ordering relation can be so defined as to put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_175"> before
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_158"> in this case also, but if it is so defined, the associative
law of multiplication only holds if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_221"> is well-ordered. For this
reason, we define our ordering relation so that, in such a case,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_176"> comes neither before nor after <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_159">. Again, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_222"> is
not a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_6">, a member of a selected class may
occur twice, once as the representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_26">, and once as that
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_389.svg_4">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_27"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_389.svg_5"> have terms in common. We wish to
distinguish these two occurrences. Hence we proceed as follows: If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_177"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_160"> are two selected classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg_2">, let there
be one or more members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_32"> in which the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_178">-representative
precedes the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_161">-representative, and which are such that, among all
earlier<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_16" id="FNanchor_16">[16]</a> members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_33">, the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_179">-representative is identical
with the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_162">-representative.</p>

<p>But a further modification is desirable in order to meet the case
in which two or more of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_34"> have the same field.
Suppose, for example, we had to deal with a series consisting of all
the series that can be formed out of a given set of terms: in this
case, we should have to distinguish occurrences of any given term not
by the field, but by the generating relation. This requires that we
should make an <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\)" src="images/4764.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.695ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_4764.svg_1">-selection from <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_35">, not an <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4765.svg_1">-selection
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg_3">. Hence we take two members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5434.svg">, say
<img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_7">, and we arrange them or their domains on the following
principle: We put <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_10"> before <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_8"> (or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻM\)" src="images/5435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.464ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5435.svg"> before
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻN\)" src="images/5436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.095ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5436.svg">) if there is a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_152"> in the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_223"> such
that the <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_11">-representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_153">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻQ\)" src="images/5437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.525ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5437.svg">, has the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_154"> to the <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_9">-representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_155">, and such that, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_51"> is any earlier member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_36">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻR\)" src="images/5438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5438.svg"> is identical with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(NʻR\)" src="images/5439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.084ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5439.svg">. That is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_12"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_10"> if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists Q):(MʻQ)Q(NʻQ):RPQ.R\neq Q.\supset _{R}.MʻR = NʻR. \]" src="images/5440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.663ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5440.svg"></span></p>

<p>The relation between <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_13"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_11"> so defined has the properties
required of an arithmetical product; hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \Pi ʻP=\hat{M} \hat{N} &amp;\{M,N\in F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\colon\ldotp \\ &amp;(\exists Q):(MʻQ)Q(NʻQ):RPQ.R\neq Q.\supset _{R}.MʻR=NʻR\}  \quad\text{Df}.\\ \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5441.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.377ex; width: 74.635ex; height: 5.885ex;" id="img_images_5441.svg"></span></p>

<p>This relation is the ordinal analogue of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_18">.
The ordinal analogue of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/2205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.477ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2205.svg_8"> is the corresponding
relation of the domains of <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_12">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}\PiʻP\)" src="images/5442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.114ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5442.svg">;
hence we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Prod}ʻP= \text{D}^{;}\Pi ʻP   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/5443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.317ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5443.svg"></span></p>

<p>In case <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_224"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_7">, we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻ\text{Prod}ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.526ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5444.svg">. But when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_225"> is not
a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_8">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻP\)" src="images/5445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5445.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg"> are
in general not ordinally similar. We can, however, always make a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_9"> by replacing the members <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_129">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_86">, etc.
of<span class="pagenum" id="Page_407">[Pg 407]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_28"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\in CʻP\)" src="images/5447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.332ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5447.svg">) by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow Q,y\downarrow Q\)" src="images/5448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.764ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_5448.svg">,
etc. In this way, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_130"> occurs twice in <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/5449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.767ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5449.svg">, once as a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_29">, and once as a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_389.svg_6">, the two occurrences
are made to correspond to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow Q\)" src="images/5450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.472ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5450.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow R\)" src="images/5451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.399ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5451.svg">
respectively, and thus we get a new relation which <i>is</i> a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_10">.</p>

<p>If every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_37"> has a first term, <img alt="" data-tex="\(B\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/5452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.694ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5452.svg">
will be the first term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_1">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.208ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5453.svg"> will be the
first term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻP\)" src="images/5445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5445.svg_1">. If further there is a last member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_38">, <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.943ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5454.svg">, and if this last
member has a second term, the second member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_2"> is obtained
by taking this second term as the representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg">,
and leaving all the other representatives unchanged. In any case,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg_1"> exists, the earliest successors of any member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_3"> are those obtained by only varying the representative in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg_2">. Thus, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg_3"> exists, those members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_4"> which have a given set of representatives in all members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg_5"> form a consecutive stretch of the series, and this
stretch is like <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg_4">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg_5"> has an immediate
predecessor, the stretches obtained by varying only the representative
in this predecessor are again consecutive, and form a series like the
said predecessor; and so on. This makes it plain why <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_5"> has the
properties of a product.</p>

<p>As in the case of cardinals, the definition of exponentiation is
derived from that of multiplication. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} P\,\,\text{exp}\,\,Q&amp;=\text{Prod}ʻP\downarrow_{.,} ^{;}Q   &amp;\quad\text{Df}.\\ \text{We put also}\quad P^{Q}&amp;=\dot{s} ^{;}(P\,\,\text{exp}\,\,Q)   &amp;\quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5456.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.37ex; width: 43.163ex; height: 5.871ex;" id="img_images_5456.svg"></span>
This is an important relation, which deserves consideration apart from
the fact that it is useful in connection with exponentiation. It will
be found that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} P^{Q}=\hat{M} \hat{N} &amp;\{M,N\in (CʻP\uparrow CʻQ)_{\Delta }ʻCʻQ\colon\ldotp \\ &amp;(\exists y):y\in CʻQ.(Mʻy)P(Nʻy):xQy.x\neq y.\supset _{x}.Mʻx=Nʻx\}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5457.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.377ex; width: 72.826ex; height: 5.885ex;" id="img_images_5457.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is a form of the principle of first differences which is
appropriate when <i>two</i> relations are concerned, instead of only
one as in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_10">. The principle, in this case, is as
follows: Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_15">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_13"> be any two one-many relations which relate
part (or the whole) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_39"> to the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_30">. That is, each
of the two relations assigns a representative in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_40"> to every
term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_31">, but different terms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_32"> may have the same
representative. Then in travelling along the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_156">, there is to
be, sooner or later, a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_87"> whose <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_16">-representative is earlier
than its <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_14">-representative, and terms which come earlier than <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_88">
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_157"> are all to have their <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_17">-representatives identical with
their <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_15">-representatives.</p>

<p>The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{Q}\)" src="images/5458.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.278ex; height: 1.948ex;" id="img_images_5458.svg"> may be subjected to various restrictions which
give important results. This subject has been treated by Hausdorff.
For<span class="pagenum" id="Page_408">[Pg 408]</span> example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.507ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4536.svg_1"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_411.svg_3">), and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_158">
is of the ordinal type which Cantor calls <img alt="" data-tex="\(\omega\)" src="images/2870.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.407ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_2870.svg_6">, <i>i.e.</i> the
type of progressions (generated by transitive relations), then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_28">
is any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_33">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻz\)" src="images/2534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.787ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2534.svg_1"> is always either <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_131"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_89">.
If we impose the condition that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻz\)" src="images/2534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.787ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2534.svg_2"> is to be <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_132"> except for a
finite number of values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_29">, the resulting series is of the type
of the rationals in order of magnitude, <i>i.e.</i> the type called
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta\)" src="images/1345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.124ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_1345.svg_3">. If we impose the condition that there are to be an infinite
number of values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_30"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻz=y\)" src="images/5459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.913ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5459.svg">, the resulting series is
a continuum, <i>i.e.</i> it is of the ordinal type called <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/5460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_5460.svg">;
in this case, the contained "rational" series consists of those <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_18">'s
for which there are only a finite number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_31">'s having <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻz=x\)" src="images/5461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.099ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5461.svg">.
If we impose no limitation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{Q}\)" src="images/5458.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.278ex; height: 1.948ex;" id="img_images_5458.svg_1"> is of the type presented by the
real numbers when decimals ending in 9 recurring are counted separately
from the terminating decimals having the same value.</p>

<p>We may generalize <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{Q}\)" src="images/5458.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.278ex; height: 1.948ex;" id="img_images_5458.svg_2">, instead of restricting it. To begin with, we
may allow our <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_19"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_16"> to have only part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_34"> for their
converse domain, and remove the assumption that there is a <i>first</i>
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_35"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(Mʻy\)" src="images/5462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.844ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5462.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Nʻy\)" src="images/5463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.475ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5463.svg"> differ; this leads to
the relation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \hat{M} \hat{N} &amp;\{M,N\in (1\rightarrow \text{Cls})\cap \text{Rl}ʻ(CʻP\uparrow CʻQ)\colon\ldotp\\ &amp;(\exists y):(Mʻy)P(Nʻy):xQy.x\in \text{ᗡ}ʻN.\supset _{x}.(Mʻx)(P\unicode{x228d} I)(Nʻx)\}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5464.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.377ex; width: 66.609ex; height: 5.885ex;" id="img_images_5464.svg"></span>
Further, we may drop the restriction to one-many relations. It will be
observed that if <img alt="" data-tex="\((Mʻy)P(Nʻy)\)" src="images/5465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.538ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5465.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(y (\breve{M} \mid P\mid N)y\)" src="images/5466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.835ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5466.svg">.
Thus we may consider the relation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} MN[\hat{M} ,\hat{N} \in \text{Rl}ʻ&amp;(CʻP\uparrow CʻQ)\colon\ldotp \\ &amp;(\exists y):y(\breve{M} \mid P\mid N)y:xQy.\supset _{x}.x\{\breve{M} \mid (P\unicode{x228d} I)\mid N\}x]. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5467.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.735ex; width: 67.851ex; height: 6.602ex;" id="img_images_5467.svg"></span>
This relation has for its field all relations contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\uparrow CʻQ\)" src="images/5468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.031ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5468.svg">. We may, if we like, drop even this restriction,
and consider
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{M} \hat{N} [(\exists y):y\in CʻQ.y(\breve{M} \mid P\mid N)y:xQy.\supset _{x}.x\{\breve{M} \mid (P\unicode{x228d} I\upharpoonright CʻP)\mid N\}x]. \]" src="images/5469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.765ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5469.svg"></span>
This represents the most general form of the principle of first
differences as applied to a couple of relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_226"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_159">. In
ordinal arithmetic, however, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{Q}\)" src="images/5458.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.278ex; height: 1.948ex;" id="img_images_5458.svg_3"> is sufficiently general for the
uses we wish to make of it.</p>

<p>The formal laws, as far as they are true, can be proved without
excessive difficulty. We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :P\neq Q.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow Q)=\text{Nr}ʻ(P\times Q), \]" src="images/5470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.152ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5470.svg"></span>
which connects the two kinds of multiplication;
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :P \,\text{smor smor}\, Q.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻQ,\\ &amp;\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P=\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5471.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 52.23ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5471.svg"></span>
which is one form of the associative law, of which another form is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :P\neq Q.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ(\Pi ʻP\times \Pi ʻQ)=\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻ(P\unicode{x2909}Q). \]" src="images/5472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.23ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5472.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_409">[Pg 409]</span>
Also
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :P,\Sigma ʻP\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ\text{Prod}ʻ\text{Prod}^{;}P=\text{Nr}ʻ\text{Prod}ʻ\Sigma ʻP=\text{Nr}ʻ\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP, \]" src="images/5473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 81.36ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_5473.svg"></span>
which is the associative law for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}\)" src="images/2216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.817ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2216.svg_4">." We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :CʻQ\cap CʻR=\Lambda .\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ(P^{Q}\times P^{R})=\text{Nr}ʻP^{Q\unicode{x2909}R},\\ &amp;\vdash .\text{Nr}ʻ(P^{Q})^{R}=\text{Nr}ʻ(P^{R\times Q}). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5474.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.437ex; width: 51.813ex; height: 6.005ex;" id="img_images_5474.svg"></span>
But we do not have in general
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nr}ʻ(P^{R}\times Q^{R})=\text{Nr}ʻ(P\times Q)^{R}, \]" src="images/5475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.889ex; height: 2.593ex;" id="img_images_5475.svg"></span>
which obviously would require the commutative law for multiplication,
and therefore does not hold in general in spite of the fact that its
cardinal analogue does always hold.</p>

<p>As regards the connection with cardinals, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\supset .Cʻ\text{Prod}ʻP=\text{Prod}ʻCʻʻCʻP,\\ &amp;\vdash :\dot{\exists} !Q.\supset .Cʻ(P\,\,\text{exp}\,\,Q)=(CʻP)\,\,\text{exp}\,\,(CʻQ), \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5476.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.501ex; width: 49.605ex; height: 6.133ex;" id="img_images_5476.svg"></span>
and we have already had
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash .Cʻ(P\times Q)=CʻP\times CʻQ. \]" src="images/5477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.534ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5477.svg"></span>
Moreover the correlators by which similarity is established in
cardinals generally suffice to establish likeness in the analogous
cases in relation-arithmetic. Thus we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \vdash :S\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\supset .S_{\in }\upharpoonright \text{Cl}ʻCʻQ\in P_{\text{cl}}\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q_{\text{cl}},\\ \vdash :P,Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.S\upharpoonright Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\in P\overline{\text{smor}} &amp;\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\supset .\\ &amp;S_{\in }\upharpoonright Cʻ\text{Prod}ʻQ\in (\text{Prod}ʻP)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(\text{Prod}ʻQ),\\ \vdash :S\upharpoonright CʻP'\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,P'.&amp;T\upharpoonright CʻQʻ\in Q\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q'.\supset .\\ &amp;(S\parallel \breve{T} )\upharpoonright Cʻ(P'\,\,\text{exp}\,\,Q')\in (P\,\,\text{exp}\,\,Q)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(P'\,\,\text{exp}\,\,Q'), \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5478.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.061ex; width: 102.712ex; height: 15.253ex;" id="img_images_5478.svg"></span>
which are all closely analogous to propositions which were proved in
cardinals.</p>

<p>The applications of the propositions of this section are almost wholly
to series, and it is convenient to imagine our relations to be serial.
But the hypothesis that they are serial is not necessary to the
truth of any of the propositions of the present section, and it is a
remarkable fact that so many of the formal laws of ordinal arithmetic
hold for relations in general.</p>

<p>It should be observed that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_6"> is not always a series when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_227">
is a series and all the relations in the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_228"> are series.
A series (cf. <a href="#_204" class="pginternal">*204</a>) is a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_229"> which is (1) contained in
diversity, (2) transitive, (3) connected, <i>i.e.</i> such that every
term of the field of P has the relation P or the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_1">
to every other term of the field. It is the third condition which
may fail for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_7">, and which in fact does fail whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_230">
is not well-ordered. Thus suppose, for the sake of simplicity, that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_231"> is of the type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻʻ\omega\)" src="images/3661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.208ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3661.svg_3">, which we will call a
<i>regression</i>, <i>i.e.</i> the converse of a progression (cf.
*263); and suppose that the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_232"> consists entirely of
couples. Take a selection <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_20"> which chooses the first term of
every odd couple, and the second term of every even couple ; and take
another selection <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_17"> which chooses the second term of every odd
couple, and the first term of every even couple. Neither of these two
selections has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_8"> to the other, for whatever term
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_160"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_41"> we choose, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_21"> is the selection which chooses
the first term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_161">, there is an earlier term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_42"> (namely
the immediate predecessor of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_162">) in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_18"> chooses the first
term while <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_22"> chooses the second. Hence there is no such <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_163"> as
is required for <img alt="" data-tex="\(M(\Pi ʻP)N\)" src="images/5479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.9ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5479.svg">; and a similar argument holds against
<img alt="" data-tex="\(N(\Pi ʻP)M\)" src="images/5480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.9ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5480.svg">. In such a case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_9"> generates a number of
different series, and by suitable restrictions of the field, one of
these series can be extracted. Exactly similar remarks apply to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{Q}\)" src="images/5458.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.278ex; height: 1.948ex;" id="img_images_5458.svg_4">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_411">[Pg 411]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_170">
*170. ON THE RELATION OF FIRST DIFFERENCES AMONG THE
SUB-CLASSES OF A GIVEN CLASS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *170.</p>

<p>The definition to be given in this number of the relation of first
differences among the sub-classes of a given class is by no means
the only one possible, in fact a different definition will be
considered in <a href="#_171" class="pginternal">*171</a>. In the present number, the definition we choose
is this: <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_246"> is said to precede <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_169"> according to this
definition when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_247"> has at least one member which neither
belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_170"> nor follows any term belonging to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_171"> and
not to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_248"> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_249"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_172"> being both sub-classes
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_43">). In other words, if we consider the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha-\beta\)" src="images/5481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5481.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta -\alpha\)" src="images/5482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5482.svg">, there are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha -\beta\)" src="images/5483.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5483.svg">
which are not preceded by any members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta -\alpha\)" src="images/5482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5482.svg_1">. Pictorially,
we may conceive the relation as follows (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_234"> being supposed serial):
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_250"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_173"> each pick out terms from <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_44">, and these
terms have an order conferred by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_235">; we suppose that the earlier
terms selected by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_251"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_174"> are perhaps the same, but
sooner or later, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \beta\)" src="images/1362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_1362.svg_1">, we must come to terms which
belong to one but not to the other. We assume that the earliest terms
of this sort belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_252">, not to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_175">; in this case,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_253"> has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_176"> the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_11">. That
is, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_254"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_177"> begin to differ, it is terms of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_255"> that we come to, not terms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_178">. We do not assume
that there is a <i>first</i> term which belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_256"> and not
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_179">, since this would introduce undesirable restrictions in
case <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_236"> is not well-ordered.</p>

<p>A few of the propositions of the present number will be used in the
next number, which deals with a slightly different form of the relation
of first differences, but with this exception the propositions of this
number will not be referred to again until we come to series. Their
chief use occurs in the section on compact series, rational series, and
continuous series (Part V, Section F), especially in *274 and *276,
which respectively establish the existence of rational series (assuming
the axiom of infinity) and the fact that the cardinal number of terms
in a continuous series is the same as the number of classes contained
in the field of a progression, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{\aleph _{0}}\)" src="images/292.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.995ex; height: 1.932ex;" id="img_images_292.svg_3">. The
definitions and a few of the simpler propositions are also used in
connection with the series of segments of a series, since, as explained
above, the segments of a series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_237"> are arranged in the series
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_412">[Pg 412]</span>generated by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_2">.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number which will be used in dealing with
series are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta .\equiv .\alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\exists !\alpha -\beta -\breve{P} ʻʻ(\beta -\alpha )\)" src="images/5484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.654ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5484.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P_{\text{lc}}=\text{Cnv}ʻ(\breve{P} )_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.446ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5485.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·102.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha P_{\text{lc}}\beta .\equiv .\alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\exists !\beta -\alpha -Pʻʻ(\alpha -\beta )\)" src="images/5486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.654ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5486.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta .\equiv :\alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP:(\exists y).y\in \alpha -\beta .\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\cap \beta \subset \alpha\)" src="images/5487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.657ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5487.svg"></p>
