<p class="nind"><b>*170·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \subset CʻP.\beta \subset \alpha .\beta \neq \alpha .\supset .\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta\)" src="images/5488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 34.68ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5488.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> every sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_45"> has the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_12"> to every proper part of itself.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P_{\text{cl}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.P_{\text{lc}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.076ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5489.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·2.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP:(\exists y).ye\alpha -\beta .\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\cap \alpha =\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\cap \beta :\supset .\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta\)" src="images/5490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.625ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5490.svg"></p>

term y which belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_257"> and not to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_180">, and whose
predecessors all belong to both or neither.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·23.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \subset CʻP.y \in\alpha -\beta -\breve{P} ʻʻ&amp;(\beta -\alpha).\supset :\\ &amp;y \text{min}_{P}(\alpha -\beta ).\equiv .\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\cap \alpha =\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\cap \beta\end{align}\]" src="images/5491.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.141ex; width: 66.591ex; height: 7.414ex;" id="img_images_5491.svg"></span></p>

<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_181"> being supposed sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_46">).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\beta \subset CʻP.\beta \neq CʻP.\equiv .(CʻP)P_{\text{cl}}\beta\)" src="images/5492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.177ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5492.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x{\sim}\in CʻP.\supset .(x\unicode{x21f7}P)_{\text{cl}}=(\iota ʻx\cup )^{;}P_{\text{cl}}\unicode{x2909}P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5500.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.781ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5500.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that every term added to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_239"> doubles the
number of terms in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_13">; hence it is not surprising that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_14"> (when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_240"> is well-ordered) has a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_11">
for its relation-number (cf. <a href="#_177" class="pginternal">*177</a>).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170.67.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\dot{\exists} !Q.CʻP\cap CʻQ=\Lambda .\supset .(P\unicode{x2909}Q)_{\text{cl}}=s^{;}C^{;}(P_{\text{cl}}\times     Q_{\text{cl}})\)" src="images/5501.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.015ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_5501.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P_{\text{lc}}=\text{Cnv}ʻ(\breve{P} )_{\text{cl}} \quad[(*170·02)]\)" src="images/5506.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.149ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5506.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*170·102.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha P_{\text{lc}}\beta .\equiv .a,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\exists !\beta -\alpha -Pʻʻ(\alpha -\beta ) \quad[*170·1·101]\)" src="images/5507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.242ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5507.svg"></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha P_{\text{lc}}\beta\)" src="images/5508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.524ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5508.svg"> means, roughly speaking, that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta -\alpha\)" src="images/5482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5482.svg_2"> goes on longer than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha -\beta\)" src="images/5483.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5483.svg_2">, just as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta\)" src="images/5394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.524ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5394.svg_1"> means that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha -\beta\)" src="images/5483.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5483.svg_3"> begins
sooner. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_241"> is the relation of earlier and later in
time, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_259"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_182"> are the times when <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/5509.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_5509.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(B\)" src="images/5510.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_5510.svg"> respectively are out of bed, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha P_{\text{cl}}\beta\)" src="images/5394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.524ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5394.svg_2">"
will mean that <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/5509.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_5509.svg_1"> gets up earlier than <img alt="" data-tex="\(B\)" src="images/5510.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_5510.svg_1">, and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha P_{\text{lc}}\beta\)" src="images/5508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.524ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5508.svg_1">" will mean that <img alt="" data-tex="\(B\)" src="images/5510.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_5510.svg_2"> goes to bed later
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/5509.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_5509.svg_2">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_415">[Pg 415]</span></p>

<p>In order that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_15"> should be serial, we need further that
it should be transitive and connected. <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_16"> is transitive
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_242"> is transitive and connected. But <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_17"> may still
not be connected: there may be many distinct families in its field,
though all of them must begin with <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_47"> and end with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_68">.
For example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_243"> is a regression, the class which takes every
odd member does not have either of the relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_18">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P} _{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 2.771ex;" id="img_images_5526.svg"> to the class which takes every even member.
In order that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_19"> should be serial, we require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_244">
should be not only serial, but well-ordered, <i>i.e.</i> that every
existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_48"> should have a first term. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_245"> is
serial but not well-ordered, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_20"> will, however, generate
various series contained in it by imposing suitable limitations on the
field.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_423">[Pg 423]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_171">
*171. THE PRINCIPLE OF FIRST DIFFERENCES (<i>continued</i>).</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *171.</p>

<p>In this number, we shall consider a more restricted form of the
principle of first differences, which is applicable when there is a
definite first member of one class not belonging to the other class.
In this case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_32"> is the first differing member, the part of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_260"> which precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_33"> is to be the same as the part of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_183"> which precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_34">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_35"> belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_261"> and not
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_184">, we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_262"> before <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_185">; in the converse case,
we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_186"> before <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_263">. In case <img alt="" data-tex="\(zPz\)" src="images/5586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.803ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_5586.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_36"> itself is
not to be counted among its own predecessors; thus the predecessors
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_37"> are to be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻz-\iota ʻz\)" src="images/5587.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.085ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5587.svg">. Hence the
relation in question will hold between two sub-classes (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_264"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_187">) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_49"> when there is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_38"> such that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ z\in \alpha -\beta .\overrightarrow{P}ʻz-\iota ʻz\cap \alpha =\overrightarrow{P}ʻz-\iota ʻz\cap \beta , \]" src="images/5588.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 41.891ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5588.svg"></span>
or, what comes to the same thing (owing to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z{\sim}\in \beta\)" src="images/5589.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.859ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5589.svg">),
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ z\in \alpha -\beta .\overrightarrow{P}ʻz\cap \alpha -\iota ʻz=\overrightarrow{P}ʻz\cap \beta . \]" src="images/5590.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.915ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5590.svg"></span>
This relation between <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_265"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_188"> we denote by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_5">," where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{df}\)" src="images/5591.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.95ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_5591.svg">" stands for "difference."</p>

<p>Thus our definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\text{df}}=\hat{\alpha}     \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{Cl}ʻCʻP:(\exists z).z\in \alpha -\beta .\overrightarrow{P}ʻz\cap \alpha -\iota ʻz=\overrightarrow{P}ʻz\cap \beta\}   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/5592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 73.484ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5592.svg"></span></p>

<p>On the analogy of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_3">, we put also
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_\text{fd}=\text{Cnv}ʻ(\breve{P} )_{\text{df}}. \]" src="images/5593.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.135ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5593.svg"></span></p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_246"> is well-ordered, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_\text{fd}\)" src="images/5594.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5594.svg"> coincide
respectively with <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_21"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_4">. Their
properties are closely analogous to those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_22"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_5">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> the following propositions remain
true when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_7"> is substituted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_23">:
</p><p class="nindc">
<a href="#_170_17" class="pginternal">*170·17</a><a href="#_170_35" class="pginternal">·35</a><a href="#_170_36" class="pginternal">·36</a><a href="#_170_37" class="pginternal">·37</a><a href="#_170_38" class="pginternal">·38</a><a href="#_170_44" class="pginternal">·44</a><a href="#_170_5" class="pginternal">·5</a><a href="#_170_51" class="pginternal">·51</a><a href="#_170_52" class="pginternal">·52</a><a href="#_170_64" class="pginternal">·64</a><a href="#_170_67" class="pginternal">·67</a><a href="#_170_68" class="pginternal">·68</a><a href="#_170_69" class="pginternal">·69</a>.
</p>

and the following formulae suggesting an inductive identification

induction is applicable:</p>

well-ordered (*251·37).</p>

<img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3.svg_12"> to the power <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_10">. <div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_428">[Pg 428]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_172">
*172. THE PRODUCT OF THE RELATIONS OF A FIELD.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *172.</p>

<p>In this number we have to consider the form of product which is
applicable to any relation of relations, whether mutually exclusive
or not. If our relation were a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/4760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 8.119ex; height: 2.068ex;" id="img_images_4760.svg_11">, we
could take <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg_4">, and order selected classes from <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg_5">
by first differences. This would give us a relation whose field
would be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻCʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.385ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5431.svg_1">. But if any two fields overlap,
this method fails. We might substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻCʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.597ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5639.svg">
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻCʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.385ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5431.svg_2">, and order the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻCʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.597ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5639.svg_1"> by first differences; but this method will
not give what we want if two or more members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_50"> have the same
field. In order to avoid any confusion due to repetition, we must,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\in CʻP\)" src="images/5447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.332ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5447.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in CʻQ\)" src="images/5640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.927ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5640.svg">, consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_133"> in connection with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_166">, not merely with <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_36">. That is, the relations in the field
of the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_248"> must be such as concern themselves with the
ordered couple <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow Q\)" src="images/5450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.472ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5450.svg_1">, not merely with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_134">. The simplest
way of effecting this is to consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5434.svg_1">. A member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5434.svg_2">, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_23">, is a relation which picks out a
representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_167"> from the field of every <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_168"> which is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_51">; that is, whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\in CʻP\)" src="images/5447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.332ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5447.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻQ\in CʻQ\)" src="images/5641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.157ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5641.svg">.
Since we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻQ\)" src="images/5437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.525ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5437.svg_1">, not <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻCʻQ\)" src="images/5642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.602ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5642.svg">, two relations may have the same
field and yet we can distinguish the occurrence of a given term as the
representative of the one from its occurrence as the representative of
the other. Thus no degree of overlapping will cause confusion.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_429">[Pg 429]</span></p>

<p>The relations which compose <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5434.svg_3"> are to be ordered by
first differences, but in order to distinguish different occurrences of
a given term, we must give a slightly different form to the principle
of first differences from that employed in <a href="#_170" class="pginternal">*170</a> or <a href="#_171" class="pginternal">*171</a>. The new form
of the principle is as follows: Consider two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_24"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_19">
which are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5434.svg_4">. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_169"> be a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_52"> in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_25"> chooses a representative which precedes that
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_20">, <i>i.e.</i> in which <img alt="" data-tex="\((MʻQ)Q(NʻQ)\)" src="images/5643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.991ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5643.svg">; and let all earlier
relations than <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_170">, <i>i.e.</i> all relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_55"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(RPQ\)" src="images/5644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.206ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5644.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\neq Q\)" src="images/5645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 6.524ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_5645.svg">, have <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻR=NʻR\)" src="images/5646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.553ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5646.svg">. Then we say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_26"> precedes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_21">. This principle may also be stated as follows: We may divide
the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_53"> into four classes, not in general mutually
exclusive, namely:</p>

<p>(1) those in which <img alt="" data-tex="\((MʻQ)Q(NʻQ)\)" src="images/5643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.991ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5643.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i> in which the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_27">-representative precedes the <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_22">-representative;</p>

<p>(2) those in which <img alt="" data-tex="\((NʻQ)Q(MʻQ)\)" src="images/5647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.991ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5647.svg">,</p>

<p>(3) those in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻQ=NʻQ\)" src="images/5648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.698ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5648.svg">,</p>

<p>(4) those in which no one of the above three relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(MʻQ\)" src="images/5437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.525ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5437.svg_2"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(NʻQ\)" src="images/5649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5649.svg"> occurs.</p>

<p>Then we shall say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_28"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_23"> if there is a member of
class (1) whose predecessors all belong to class (3).</p>

<p>In case all the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_54"> are serial, the fourth of the above
classes is null, and the other three are mutually exclusive. If,
further,<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_249"> is well-ordered, any two different members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5650.svg">
must be such that one precedes the other in the above-defined
order. Thus in this case the product of a series of series is a series
(cf. *251).</p>

<p>The definition of the product <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_10"> is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \Pi ʻP=\hat{M} \hat{N} &amp;\{M,N\in F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\colon\ldotp \\ &amp;(\exists Q):(MʻQ)Q(NʻQ):RPQ.R\neq Q.\supset _{R}.MʻR=NʻR\}   \quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5651.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.377ex; width: 74.635ex; height: 5.885ex;" id="img_images_5651.svg"></span>
Owing to the complication of this definition, the proofs of
propositions of the present number are apt to be long.</p>

<p>Various other definitions might be adopted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_11">, but we have
found the above definition on the whole the best.</p>

<p>We might, for example, drop the condition <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\neq Q\)" src="images/5645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 6.524ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_5645.svg_1"> in the
definition; we could then write our definition in the simpler form:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Pi ʻP=\hat{M} \hat{N} \{M,N\in F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP:(\exists Q).(MʻQ)Q(NʻQ).M\upharpoonright \overrightarrow{P}ʻQ=N\upharpoonright \overrightarrow{P}ʻQ\}, \]" src="images/5652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 78.51ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5652.svg"></span>
which, with our definition, is only available when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg">.
But if we adopt this simplification, we no longer have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Pi ʻ(P\downarrow P)=P\downarrow_{.,} P   \quad(*172·2), \]" src="images/5654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 32.424ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5654.svg"></span>
which is a very useful proposition, required in the proofs of <a href="#_183_13" class="pginternal">*183·13</a>,
<a href="#_185_21" class="pginternal">*185·21</a> and other important propositions.</p>

<p>On the other hand, we might frame our definition on the analogy
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{cl}}\)" src="images/5393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5393.svg_26"> rather than, as above, on the analogy of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{df}}\)" src="images/5.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 3.019ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5.svg_11">. The definition would then be:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \Pi ʻP=\hat{M} \hat{N} &amp;\{M,N\in F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\colon\ldotp \\ &amp;(\exists Q):(MʻQ)Q(NʻQ):RPQ.\supset _{R}.(MʻR)(R\unicode{x228d} I)(NʻR)\}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5655.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.377ex; width: 68.9ex; height: 5.885ex;" id="img_images_5655.svg"></span></p>

<p>This definition does not assume that there is a first relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_171">
for which the <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_29">-representative precedes the <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_24">-representative.
Thus it might be thought that it would give better results in cases
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_250"> is not well-ordered. But in fact this is not the case. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_251"> is not well-ordered, it may happen that every <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_172"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\((MʻQ)Q(NʻQ)\)" src="images/5643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.991ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5643.svg_2"> is preceded by one for which <img alt="" data-tex="\((NʻQ)Q(MʻQ)\)" src="images/5647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.991ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5647.svg_1">, and
<i>vice versa</i>; in this case, we shall have neither <img alt="" data-tex="\(M(\Pi ʻP)N\)" src="images/5479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.9ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5479.svg_1">
nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(N(\Pi ʻP)M\)" src="images/5480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.9ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5480.svg_1">.<span class="pagenum" id="Page_430">[Pg 430]</span> Thus our suggested new definition does not secure
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_12"> shall be a series whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_252"> and all the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_55"> are series, and therefore has no substantial advantage over the
simpler definition which we have adopted, and has the disadvantage of
greater complication.</p>

<p>In the present number, we first prove that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\dot{\Lambda}=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/5656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.212ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_5656.svg">
(<a href="#_172_13" class="pginternal">*172·13</a>) and that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda} \in CʻP.\supset.\Pi ʻP=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/5657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.225ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_5657.svg">
(<a href="#_172_14" class="pginternal">*172·14</a>), so that a product is null if any one of its factors
is null. We then proceed to propositions about <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.83ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5658.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.828ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5659.svg">, etc. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·162.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\Pi ʻP=B_{\Delta }ʻCʻP.\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\text{Cnv}ʻ\Pi ʻP=B_{\Delta }ʻ\text{Cnv}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/5660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 63.681ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5660.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .Cʻ\Pi ʻP=F_{\Delta }ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.954ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_5661.svg"></p>

<p>Hence we derive propositions as to the existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_13">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·181.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :\Lambda {\sim}\in CʻP.\dot{\exists} !P.\equiv .\dot{\exists} !\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 41.028ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_5662.svg"></p>

<p>Thus assuming the multiplicative axiom, a product which has factors
none of which are null is not null.</p>

<p>We then consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow P)\)" src="images/5663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.601ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5663.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow Q)\)" src="images/5664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.691ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5664.svg">
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\neq Q\)" src="images/5665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 6.506ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_5665.svg">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow P)=P\downarrow_{.,} P\)" src="images/5666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.87ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5666.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which is a useful proposition, and</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\neq Q.\supset .\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow Q)\text{smor}P\times Q\)" src="images/5667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.658ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5667.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
which connects the two definitions of multiplication, showing that
they lead to equivalent results for any finite number of factors,
<i>i.e.</i> whenever the definition of <a href="#_166" class="pginternal">*166</a> is applicable.</p>

<p>We next consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ(P\unicode{x21f8} Z)\)" src="images/5668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.507ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5668.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Piʻ(P\unicode{x2909}Q)\)" src="images/5669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.661ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5669.svg">, proving</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Z{\sim}\in CʻP.\supset .\Pi ʻ(P\unicode{x21f8} Z)\text{smor}\Pi ʻP\times Z\)" src="images/5670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.806ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5670.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">with a similar proposition for <img alt="" data-tex="\(Z\unicode{x21f7}P\)" src="images/5671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.692ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5671.svg"> (<a href="#_172_321" class="pginternal">*172·321</a>), and</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\dot{\exists} !Q.CʻP\cap CʻQ=\Lambda .\supset .\Pi ʻ(P\unicode{x2909}Q)\text{smor}\Pi ʻP\times \Pi ʻQ\)" src="images/5672.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.249ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_5672.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which is a form of the associative law using both kinds of
multiplication. The kind which uses only <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\)" src="images/5673.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_5673.svg"> will be proved in <a href="#_174" class="pginternal">*174</a>.</p>

<p>We have next the proof (with its immediate consequences) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_253">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_173"> have double likeness, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\text{smor}\Pi ʻQ\)" src="images/5674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.391ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5674.svg">. We prove</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·43.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :T\upharpoonright Cʻ\Sigma ʻQ\in P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\, &amp;\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q.\supset .\\ &amp;(T\mid \text{Cnv}ʻT\dagger )\upharpoonright Cʻ\Pi ʻQ\in (\Pi ʻP)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(\Pi ʻQ)\end{align}\]" src="images/5675.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.07ex; width: 69.139ex; height: 5.271ex;" id="img_images_5675.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition should be compared with <a href="#_114_51" class="pginternal">*114·51</a>, which is its cardinal
analogue. It will be seen that the correlator only differs by the
substitution of <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\dagger\)" src="images/5676.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 2.597ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_5676.svg"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(T_{\in }\)" src="images/5677.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.576ex; height: 1.935ex;" id="img_images_5677.svg">. From <a href="#_172_43" class="pginternal">*172·43</a> we obtain</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\text{smor smor}\,Q.\supset .\Pi ʻP\,\text{smor}\,\Pi ʻQ\)" src="images/5678.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.957ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5678.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_431">[Pg 431]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·45.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :P,Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap \text{Rl}ʻ&amp;\text{smor}.\supset .\\ &amp;\Pi ʻP\,\text{smor}\,\Pi ʻQ\end{align}\]" src="images/5679.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.197ex; width: 63.775ex; height: 5.525ex;" id="img_images_5679.svg"></span></p>

<p>Other propositions about <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_14"> will be given in <a href="#_174" class="pginternal">*174</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \dot{\exists} !\Pi ʻP.\supset :Q\in CʻP.\supset _{Q}.\dot{\exists} !Q \quad[*172·14.\text{Transp}]\)" src="images/5690.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 51.922ex; height: 2.955ex;" id="img_images_5690.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_432">[Pg 432]</span></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.83ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5658.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.828ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5659.svg_1">, etc. <a href="#_172_15" class="pginternal">*172·15</a><a href="#_172_151" class="pginternal">·151</a><a href="#_172_16" class="pginternal">·16</a><a href="#_172_161" class="pginternal">·161</a> are lemmas for
<a href="#_172_162" class="pginternal">*172·162</a><a href="#_172_17" class="pginternal">·17</a>.</p>

<p>The following proposition is important. It shows that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_56">
consists of series, if any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_57"> has no first term, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\PiʻP\)" src="images/5698.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5698.svg">
has no first term, but if every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_58"> has a first
term, the selection of all these first terms is the first term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\PiʻP\)" src="images/5698.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5698.svg_1">.</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the nature of the
connection between <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow Q)\)" src="images/5664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.691ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5664.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\times Q\)" src="images/5714.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5714.svg">. The
connection is such as might be desired, except when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=Q\)" src="images/5209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.506ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5209.svg_1">, in which
case, as shown above, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ(P\downarrow P)\)" src="images/5663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.601ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5663.svg_1"> is like <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_254">, and is
therefore not like <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\times P\)" src="images/5715.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 6.164ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_5715.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·45.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\supset :P,Q\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\exists !P\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,Q\cap &amp;\text{Rl}ʻ\text{smor}.\supset .\\ &amp;\Pi ʻP\text{smor}\Pi ʻQ\\ [*164·44 . *172·44]\end{align}\]" src="images/5759.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.667ex; width: 58.362ex; height: 8.466ex;" id="img_images_5759.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following proposition shows that if two relations have the same
field, and if the parts of them that are contained in diversity
are the same, they have the same product. Thus <i>e.g.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\PiʻP_{\text{po}}=\Pi ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/5760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 14.896ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5760.svg">, in virtue of *91·541.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :CʻP=CʻQ.P\dot{\cap} J=Q\dot{\cap} J.\supset .\Pi ʻP=\Pi ʻQ\)" src="images/5761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 45.08ex; height: 2.541ex;" id="img_images_5761.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*50·11.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :RPS.R\neq S.\equiv .RQS.R\neq S &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*172·11.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5762.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 60.761ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_5762.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following proposition is used in <a href="#_182_42" class="pginternal">*182·42</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_172_51">*172·51</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Pi ʻP=\Pi ʻ(P\unicode{x228d} I\upharpoonright CʻP) \quad[*172·5]\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.958ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*172·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp Q\in \text{ᗡ}ʻP.\supset _{Q}.(\exists R).RPQ.R\neq Q:\supset .\Pi ʻP=\Pi ʻ(P\dot{\cap} J)\)" src="images/5764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 57.315ex; height: 2.738ex;" id="img_images_5764.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*50·11. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\text{ᗡ}ʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ(P\dot{\cap} J) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*33·14.*93·101.\text{Transp}.&amp;\supset \vdash :QPQ.\supset .Q{\sim}\in \overrightarrow{B}ʻP:\\ [\text{Transp}.*33·13] &amp;\supset \vdash :Q\in \overrightarrow{B}ʻP.\supset .(\exists R).QPR.R\neq Q.\\ [*50·11] &amp;\supset .Q\in Cʻ(P\dot{\cap} J) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).*93·103. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .CʻP\subset Cʻ(P\dot{\cap} J).\\ [*33·265] &amp;\supset .CʻP=Cʻ(P\dot{\cap} J) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(3).*172·5.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5765.svg" style="vertical-align: -12.344ex; width: 76.601ex; height: 25.819ex;" id="img_images_5765.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus we shall always have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP=\Pi ʻ(P\dot{\cap} J)\)" src="images/5766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.225ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_5766.svg"> unless there

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_173">
*173. THE PRODUCT OF THE RELATIONS OF A FIELD (continued).</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *173.</p>

<p>In this number, we shall consider the relation between the
domains of relations related by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_19">, <i>i.e.</i> we shall
consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}^{;}\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.114ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5767.svg">. This relation bears to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_20"> a
relation analogous to that which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/2205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.477ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2205.svg_9"> bears to
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/1376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1376.svg_19">. We shall denote it by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻP\)" src="images/5445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5445.svg_2">."
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.584ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻP\)" src="images/5445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5445.svg_3"> is like
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_21">, and is often more convenient than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_22">. When
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.584ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻP\)" src="images/5445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5445.svg_4"> arranges the
multiplicative class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg_6"> by first differences, taking first
differences to mean that the earliest member <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_175"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_59"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \cap CʻQ\neq \nu \cap CʻQ\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 20.343ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg"> has the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_180">-member earlier than
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_163">-member in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_176">-series.</p>

<p>The properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻP\)" src="images/5445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.873ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5445.svg_5"> all result immediately from those
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_23">, and offer no difficulty of any kind. The most important
of them are:</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_447">[Pg 447]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_174">
*174. THE ASSOCIATIVE LAW OF RELATIONAL MULTIPLICATION.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *174.</p>

<p>In the present number, we have to prove the associative law for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\)" src="images/5673.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_5673.svg_1">
and for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}\)" src="images/2216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.817ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2216.svg_6">, <i>i.e.</i> we have to prove (with a suitable
hypothesis)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\text{smor}\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP \]" src="images/5810.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.621ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5810.svg"></span>
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻ\text{Prod}^{;}P\text{smor}\text{Prod}ʻ\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/5811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.981ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5811.svg">.</p>

<p>The first of these requires <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.584ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg_5"> and either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_1"> or
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ QPQ.\supset _{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1; \]" src="images/5812.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 23.542ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5812.svg"></span>
the second requires not only this, but also
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\in\text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5813.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.575ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_5813.svg">. When both <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_258"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\SigmaʻP\)" src="images/5814.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5814.svg"> are relations of mutually exclusive relations, we call
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_259"> an <i>arithmetical</i> relation, which we denote by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}^{3}\text{arithm}\)" src="images/5815.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 10.956ex; height: 2.066ex;" id="img_images_5815.svg">." Arithmetical relations serve exactly
analogous purposes to those served by arithmetical classes in cardinal
arithmetic.</p>

<p>The proof of the associative law for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\)" src="images/5673.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_5673.svg_2"> consists in showing that,
under a suitable hypothesis, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} \mid \text{D}\)" src="images/2808.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.675ex; height: 2.299ex;" id="img_images_2808.svg_2"> (with its
converse domain limited) is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/5816.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.744ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5816.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\)" src="images/5817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.083ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5817.svg"> (<a href="#_174_221" class="pginternal">*174·221</a><a href="#_174_23" class="pginternal">·23</a>). To prove this, we first prove</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*174·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\supset .\dot{s}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻʻCʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P=Cʻ\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/5818.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 51.213ex; height: 2.471ex;" id="img_images_5818.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">and</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*174·19.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.\supset .(\dot{s} \mid \text{D})\upharpoonright Cʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5819.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.339ex; height: 2.584ex;" id="img_images_5819.svg"></p>

<p>This gives what we may call the cardinal part of the proof, <i>i.e.</i>
it shows that <img alt="" data-tex="\((\dot{s} \mid \text{D})\upharpoonright Cʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\)" src="images/5820.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.796ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_5820.svg">
is a cardinal correlator of the fields of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/5816.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.744ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5816.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Piʻ\Pi ^{;}P\)" src="images/5821.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.083ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5821.svg">.
We then prove that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(M\)" src="images/1671.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.378ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1671.svg_30"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/3795.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_3795.svg_25"> belong to the field
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\)" src="images/5817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.083ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5817.svg_1">, they have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\)" src="images/5817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.083ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5817.svg_2"> when the
relational sums of their domains have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/5816.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.744ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5816.svg_2">.
Here, in addition to the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.584ex; height: 2.109ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg_6">,
we require that if any relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_178"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_260"> to itself,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_37"> is not to have more than one term. Thus we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*174·215.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}:QPQ.\supset _{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1:\supset :\\ &amp;M(\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P)N.\equiv .M,N\in F_{\Delta }ʻ\Pi ʻʻCʻP.(\dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻM)(\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP)(\dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻN)\end{align}\]" src="images/5822.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.258ex; width: 68.108ex; height: 5.647ex;" id="img_images_5822.svg"></span></p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(QPQ.\supset _{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/5823.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.913ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5823.svg"> is verified if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_2"> (<a href="#_174_216" class="pginternal">*174·216</a>); thus for most purposes it is more
convenient to substitute the simpler hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_3">
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(QPQ.\supset _{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/5823.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.913ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5823.svg_1">. We shall, however, have
occasion to use the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(QPQ.\supset _{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/5823.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.913ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5823.svg_2"> in
<a href="#_182_42" class="pginternal">*182·42</a><a href="#_182_43" class="pginternal">·43</a><a href="#_182_431" class="pginternal">·431</a>, where our <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_261"> is a relation whose field consists
entirely of relations of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\downarrow Q\)" src="images/5824.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.967ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5824.svg">, whose<span class="pagenum" id="Page_448">[Pg 448]</span> fields are
always unit classes, so that our <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_262"> satisfies the above hypothesis
even if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_263"> is not contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(J\)" src="images/5825.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.432ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_5825.svg">.</p>

<p>The proof of <a href="#_174_215" class="pginternal">*174·215</a> (above) is effected by first proving</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*174·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.Q\in CʻP.M\in Cʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P.\supset .Mʻ\Pi ʻQ=(\dot{s} ʻ\text{D}ʻM)\upharpoonright CʻQ\)" src="images/5826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 73.949ex; height: 2.584ex;" id="img_images_5826.svg"></p>

<p>From <a href="#_174_17" class="pginternal">*174·17</a><a href="#_174_19" class="pginternal">·19</a><a href="#_174_215" class="pginternal">·215</a> we deduce</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*174·221.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}:QPQ.\supset _{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1:\supset .\\ &amp;\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP=\dot{s} ^{;}\text{D}^{;}\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P.(\dot{s} \mid \text{D})\upharpoonright Cʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\in     (\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P)\end{align}\]" src="images/5827.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.258ex; width: 68.364ex; height: 5.647ex;" id="img_images_5827.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">whence we obtain the more convenient proposition</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*174·23.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :&amp;P\in \text{Rel}^{2}\text{excl}.P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .\\ &amp;\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP=\dot{s} ^{;}\text{D}^{;}\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P.(\dot{s} \mid \text{D})\upharpoonright Cʻ\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\in     (\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP)\,\overline{\text{smor}}\,(\Pi ʻ\Pi ^{;}P)\end{align}\]" src="images/5828.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.216ex; width: 70.375ex; height: 5.563ex;" id="img_images_5828.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus if the hypothesis of <a href="#_174_221" class="pginternal">*174·221</a> or of <a href="#_174_23" class="pginternal">*174·23</a> holds, the associative
law holds for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\)" src="images/5673.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_5673.svg_3"> (<a href="#_174_241" class="pginternal">*174·241</a><a href="#_174_25" class="pginternal">·25</a>).</p>

<p>To prove the associative law for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}\)" src="images/2216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.817ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2216.svg_7">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in \text{Rel}^{3}\text{arithm}.P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .\text{Prod}ʻ\Sigma ʻP \,\text{smor} \text{Prod}ʻ\text{Prod}^{;}P, \]" src="images/5829.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 55.431ex; height: 2.469ex;" id="img_images_5829.svg"></span>
we observe that, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻ\Sigma ʻP=\dot{s} ^{;}\text{D}^{;}\Pi ʻ\Pi^{;}P\)" src="images/5830.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.899ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_5830.svg">
(<a href="#_174_23" class="pginternal">*174·23</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ =\dot{s} ^{;}\text{Prod}ʻ\Pi ^{;}P,\, \text{by the definition of Prod}, \]" src="images/5831.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 40.164ex; height: 2.197ex;" id="img_images_5831.svg"></span>
we have (<a href="#_174_41" class="pginternal">*174·41</a>) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prod}ʻ\Sigma ʻP=\text{D}^{;}\dot{s}^{;}\text{Prod}ʻ\Pi ^{;}P\)" src="images/5832.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.139ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_5832.svg">
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;=s^{;}\text{D}_{\in }^{;}\text{Prod}ʻ\Pi ^{;}P, &amp;&amp;\quad\text{by *41·33},\\ &amp;=s^{;}\text{Prod}ʻ\text{D}\dagger ^{;}\Pi ^{;}P, &amp;&amp;\quad\text{by *173·33},\\ &amp;=s^{;}\text{Prod}ʻ\text{Prod}^{;}P, &amp;&amp;\quad\text{by the definition of Prod}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/5833.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.558ex; width: 51.196ex; height: 8.246ex;" id="img_images_5833.svg"></span>
Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\upharpoonright Cʻ\text{Prod}ʻ\text{Prod}^{;}P\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5834.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.209ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5834.svg">,
by <a href="#_115_46" class="pginternal">*115·46</a>. Hence the associative law follows (<a href="#_174_43" class="pginternal">*174·43</a>). It will
be observed that in this case the correlator is simply s with its
converse domain limited (<a href="#_174_42" class="pginternal">*174·42</a>).</p>

<p>As in the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi\)" src="images/5673.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_5673.svg_4">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_4">" is a stronger
hypothesis than we really need: what we need is <img alt="" data-tex="\(QPQ.\supset_{Q}.CʻQ\in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/5835.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.913ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5835.svg">.</p>
