<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_511">[Pg 511]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="PART_V">PART V.<br>
<br>
SERIES.</h2>
</div>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_513">[Pg 513]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SUMMARY_OF_PART_V">SUMMARY OF PART V.</h2>
</div>


<p><span class="allsmcap">A RELATION</span> is said to be <i>serial</i>, or to generate a
series, when it possesses three different properties, namely (1) being
contained in diversity, (2) transitiveness, (3) connexity, <i>i.e.</i>
the property that the relation or its converse holds between any two
different members of its field. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_301"> is a serial relation if
(1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_5">, (2) <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P\)" src="images/6534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.624ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6534.svg">, (3)<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y\in CʻP.x\neq y.\supset _{x,y}:xPy.\lor.yPx\)" src="images/6535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 35.456ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_6535.svg">.
The third characteristic, that of connexity, may be written more shortly
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\in CʻP.\supset _{x}.\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup \iota ʻx\cup \overleftarrow{P}ʻx=CʻP, \]" src="images/6536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 40.253ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6536.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in CʻP.\supset _{x}.\overleftrightarrow{P}ʻx=CʻP\)" src="images/6537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.792ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6537.svg">,
using the notation of *97; and this, in virtue of *97·23, is equivalent
to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overleftrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\in 0\cup 1. \]" src="images/6538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.299ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6538.svg"></span></p>

<p>In virtue of *50·47, the first two characteristics are equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\dot{\cap} \breve{P} =\dot{\Lambda} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P. \]" src="images/6539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.754ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_6539.svg"></span>
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{\cap} \breve{P} =\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.494ex; height: 2.6ex;" id="img_images_6540.svg">, we say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_302"> is
"asymmetrical." Thus serial relations are such as are asymmetrical,
transitive, and connected.</p>

<p>It might be thought that a serial relation need not be contained
in diversity, since we commonly speak of series in which there are
repetitions, <i>i.e.</i> in which an earlier term is identical with a
later term. Thus, <i>e.g.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ a,\, b,\, c,\, a,\, e,\, f,\, b,\, g,\, h \]" src="images/6541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 21.066ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_6541.svg"></span>
would be called a series of letters, although the letters <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_5"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/5930.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_5930.svg_3"> recur. But in all such cases, there is some means (in the above
case, position in space) by which one <i>occurrence</i> of a given
term is distinguished from another occurrence, and this will be found
to mean that there is some other series (in the above case, the
series of positions in a line) free from repetitions, with which our
pseudo-series has a one-many correlation. Thus, in the above instance,
we have a series of nine positions, which we may call
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 1,\, 2,\, 3,\, 4,\, 5,\, 6,\, 7,\, 8,\, 9, \]" src="images/6542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.881ex; height: 1.971ex;" id="img_images_6542.svg"></span>
which form a true series without repetitions; we have a one-many
relation, that of <i>occupying</i> these positions, by means of which
we distinguish occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_6">, the first occurrence being a as
the correlate of 1, the second being<span class="pagenum" id="Page_514">[Pg 514]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_7"> as the correlate of 4. All
series in which there are repetitions (which we may call pseudo-series)
are thus obtained by correlation with true series, i.e, with series
in which there is no repetition. That is to say, a pseudo-series has
as its generating relation a relation of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}P\)" src="images/4202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.908ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4202.svg_1">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_303"> is a serial relation, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_65"> is a one-many relation whose
converse domain contains the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_304">. Thus what we may call
self-subsistent series must be series without repetitions, <i>i.e.</i>
series whose generating relations are contained in diversity.</p>

<p>For our purposes, there is no use in distinguishing a series from
its generating relation. A series is not a class, since it has a
definite order, while a class has no order, but is capable of many
orders (unless it contains only one term or none). The generating
relation determines the order, and also the class of terms ordered,
since this class is the field of the generating relation. Hence the
generating relation completely determines the series, and may, for all
mathematical purposes, be taken to be the series.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_305"> is transitive, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\text{po}}=P.P_{*}=P\unicode{x228d} I\upharpoonright CʻP. \]" src="images/6543.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 26.311ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_6543.svg"></span>
Hence all the propositions of Part II, Section E become greatly
simplified when applied to series.</p>

<p>Also, since the field of a connected relation consists of a single
family, a series has one first term or none, and one last term or none.</p>

<p>In the case of a serial relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_306">, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_1"> (defined
in <a href="#_121_02" class="pginternal">*121·02</a>) becomes <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.272ex; height: 2.24ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i> the relation
"immediately preceding." In a <i>discrete</i> series, the terms in
general immediately precede other terms. A <i>compact</i> series, on
the contrary, is defined as one in which there are terms between any
two: in such a series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6544.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 7.027ex; height: 2.695ex;" id="img_images_6544.svg">.</p>

<p>It very frequently occurs that we wish to consider the relations of
various series which are all contained in some one series; for example,
we may wish to consider various series of real numbers, all arranged
in order of magnitude. In such a case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_307"> is the series in which
all the others are contained, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_266">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_189">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_46">,
... are the fields of the contained series, the contained series
themselves are <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\beta\)" src="images/6546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.337ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6546.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\gamma\)" src="images/6547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.285ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_6547.svg">, .... Thus when series are given as
contained in a given series, they are completely determined by their
fields.</p>

<p>In what follows, Section A deals with the elementary properties of
series, including maximum and minimum points, sequent points and limits.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_515">[Pg 515]</span></p>

<p>Section B will deal with the theory of segments and kindred topics;
in this section we shall define "Dedekindian" series, and shall prove
the important proposition that the series of segments of a series is
always Dedekindian, <i>i.e.</i> that every class of segments has either
a maximum or a limit.</p>

<p>Section C, which stands outside the main developments of the book,
is concerned with convergence and the limits of functions and the
definition of a continuous function. Its purpose is to show how these
notions can be expressed, and many of their properties established, in
a much more general way than is usually done, and without assuming that
the arguments or values of the functions concerned are either numerical
or numerically measurable.</p>

<p>Section D will deal with "well-ordered" series, <i>i.e.</i> series in
which every class containing members of the field has a first term. The
properties of well-ordered series are many and important; most of them
depend upon the fact that an extended variety of mathematical induction
is possible in dealing with well-ordered series. The term "ordinal
number" is confined by usage to the relation-number of a well-ordered
series; ordinal numbers will also be considered in our fourth section.</p>

<p>Section E will deal with finite and infinite. We shall show that the
distinction between "inductive" and "non-reflexive" does not arise in
well-ordered series.</p>

<p>Section F will deal with "compact" series, <i>i.e.</i> series in which
there is a term between any two, <i>i.e.</i> in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg">. In
particular we shall consider "rational" series (<i>i.e.</i> series
like the series of rationals in order of magnitude) and continuous
series (<i>i.e.</i> series like the series of real numbers in order of
magnitude). Our treatment of this subject will follow Cantor closely.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_516">[Pg 516]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_A_III">SECTION A.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">GENERAL THEORY OF SERIES.</span></h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of Section A.</i></p>

<p>In the present section, we shall be concerned with the properties
common to all series. Such properties, for the most part, are very
simple, and present no difficulties of any kind. Many of the properties
of series do not require all the three characteristics by which serial
relations are defined, but only one or two of these properties: we
therefore begin with numbers in which, though the properties proved
derive their chief importance from their applicability to series, the
hypotheses are only that the relations in question have one or two
of the properties of serial relations. Thence we proceed to the most
elementary properties peculiar to series, and thence to the theory
of minimum and maximum members of classes contained in a series,
and of the successors and limits of classes. We then proceed to the
correlation of a series with part of itself. The ground covered is
familiar, and the difficulties encountered are less than in most
previous sections.</p>

<p>It will be observed that where series are concerned, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_267"> is an existent class contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_72">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg"> is correlative to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg"> (which
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.281ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6551.svg">): <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_1"> is "predecessors of
some <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_268">," and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg_1"> is "successors
of all <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_269">'s." If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_270"> is an existent class contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_73">, the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_74">, with the exception of the last term
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_271"> (if there is such a term), belongs to one or other of
the classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg_2">, of which
the first wholly precedes the second. The division of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_75"> into
these two classes is the Dedekind "cut" defined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_272">. But
when only part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_273"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_76">, we must replace
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg_3"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha\cap CʻP)\)" src="images/6552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.345ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6552.svg">,
since <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =\Lambda\)" src="images/6553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.881ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6553.svg"> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_274"> has any member not belonging to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_77">. Again, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP=\Lambda\)" src="images/6554.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.326ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6554.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha\cap CʻP)=\text{V}\)" src="images/6555.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.059ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6555.svg">.
But what we want is the complement to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_3">, which in this case is null. Hence we must
replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)\)" src="images/6556.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.345ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6556.svg"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)\)" src="images/6557.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.636ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6557.svg">: this is <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_78"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha =\Lambda\)" src="images/6558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.449ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6558.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP=\Lambda\)" src="images/6554.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.326ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6554.svg_1">.
In any other event it is equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha\cap CʻP)\)" src="images/6552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.345ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6552.svg_1">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_275"><span class="pagenum" id="Page_517">[Pg 517]</span> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_79"> and is not null,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)=pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.947ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6559.svg">.
Thus the Dedekind "cut" defined by a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_276">, whether or not
this class is contained in whole or part in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_80">, is always the two
classes
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Pʻʻ\alpha , CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP). \]" src="images/6560.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.133ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6560.svg"></span></p>

<p>Throughout the elementary propositions of this section, we have
been careful to avoid stronger hypotheses than are required: we
have not assumed <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_308"> to be serial, if our conclusion would follow
(<i>e.g.</i>) from the hypothesis that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_309"> is transitive and
connected. It will be found that many properties of series depend
upon the fact that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_144">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_94"> are two different terms of a
series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_310">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy.\equiv .{\sim}(yPx)\)" src="images/6561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.496ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6561.svg"> (<a href="#_204_3" class="pginternal">*204·3</a>). Here the
implication <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy.\supset .{\sim}(yPx)\)" src="images/6562.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.496ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6562.svg"> requires that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_311"> should be
asymmetrical, <i>i.e.</i> that we should have <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{\cap} \breve{P}=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6563.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.494ex; height: 2.6ex;" id="img_images_6563.svg">,
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/6564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.357ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6564.svg">. The implication
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(yPx).\supset .xPy\)" src="images/6565.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.496ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6565.svg"> requires that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_312"> should be connected.
Thus the hypothesis required is not that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_313"> should be serial, but
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_314"> should be connected and asymmetrical (<a href="#_202_5" class="pginternal">*202·5</a>).</p>

<p>Again, consider the proposition that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_315"> is a series,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}=P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/2894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 11.729ex; height: 2.394ex;" id="img_images_2894.svg_2">. This relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_2"> is the very useful
relation "immediately preceding"; thus the above proposition is
important, as is the further proposition that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_316"> is a series,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_3"> is a one-one relation. It will be remembered that (by
<a href="#_121" class="pginternal">*121</a>) "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{1}y\)" src="images/6566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.843ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6566.svg">" means that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\vdash\dashv y)\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_3"> consists of
two terms. It was shown in <a href="#_121_304" class="pginternal">*121·304</a><a href="#_121_305" class="pginternal">·305</a> that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_6">
is contained in diversity, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{1}y\)" src="images/6566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.843ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6566.svg_1">" implies "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/3595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3595.svg_9">" and is
equivalent to the statement that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_145"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_95"> constitute the
whole interval <img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\vdash\dashv y)\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_4"> and are not identical. Also
by <a href="#_121_254" class="pginternal">*121·254</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}=(P_{\text{po}})_{1}\)" src="images/6567.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 11.535ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_6567.svg">. It is evident that, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_7"> is contained in diversity, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{1}y\)" src="images/6566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.843ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6566.svg_2">, we
cannot have <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP^{2}y\)" src="images/6568.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.215ex; height: 2.351ex;" id="img_images_6568.svg">, because there is no term other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_146">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_96"> in the interval <img alt="" data-tex="\(P(x\vdash\dashv y)\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_5">, and we cannot have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPx\)" src="images/6569.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.287ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_6569.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(yPy\)" src="images/3592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.916ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3592.svg_1">. Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_5">, we
have <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.126ex; height: 2.507ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg">. Hence by what was said
above (<a href="#_121_305" class="pginternal">*121·305</a>), if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_6">, we shall have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/6571.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.825ex; height: 2.507ex;" id="img_images_6571.svg">. On the other hand, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_317"> is
transitive, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{-} P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P_{1}\)" src="images/6572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.825ex; height: 2.507ex;" id="img_images_6572.svg"> (<a href="#_201_61" class="pginternal">*201·61</a>).
Combining these two facts, and remembering that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_318"> is transitive,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P=P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/6573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.046ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_6573.svg"> (<a href="#_201_18" class="pginternal">*201·18</a>), we find that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}=P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/2894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 11.729ex; height: 2.394ex;" id="img_images_2894.svg_3">
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_319"> is transitive and contained in diversity. We find further
(<a href="#_202_7" class="pginternal">*202·7</a>) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_320"> is connected, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.272ex; height: 2.24ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg_2"> is one-one. Hence
we need the full hypothesis that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_321"> is a series in order to prove
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_4"> is a one-one (<a href="#_204_7" class="pginternal">*204·7</a>). This is a good example of the
way in which the various separate characteristics that make up the
definition of series are relevant in proving the properties of series.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_518">[Pg 518]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_200">
*200. RELATIONS CONTAINED IN DIVERSITY.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *200.</p>

<p>Some of the propositions of this number are repetitions or
immediate consequences of previous propositions, especially those
of the propositions of *50 which deal with diversity. But we are
chiefly concerned here with propositions which will be useful in
the theory of series; this leads us to introduce propositions
on <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg_4"> and on matters connected
with relation-arithmetic and other topics. It will be seen that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/6564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.357ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6564.svg_1">" (<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_322"> is asymmetrical") is an
important hypothesis, as is also <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_7">, of
the use of which we have already had examples in *96 and <a href="#_121" class="pginternal">*121</a>.</p>

<p>The following are among the most useful propositions in this number:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Rl}ʻJ.\supset .CʻP{\sim}\in 1\)" src="images/6574.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6574.svg"></p>

<p>This is the proposition which makes it impossible to define an ordinal
number 1 which shall take its place among relation-numbers applicable
to series.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\alpha \in 1.\supset .P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha =\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6575.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.351ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_6575.svg"></p>

<p>This is a consequence of <a href="#_200_12" class="pginternal">*200·12</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·36.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/6576.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.014ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6576.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·361.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\,     J.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cap ({℩}ʻx\cup \overleftarrow{P}ʻx)=\Lambda .\overleftarrow{P}ʻx\cap (\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup {℩}ʻx)=\Lambda\)" src="images/6577.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.823ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6577.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/6564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.357ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6564.svg_2">, no term precedes itself or
any of its predecessors, and no term succeeds itself or any of its
successors.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·38.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P_{\text{po}}=P_{*}\dot{\cap} J\)" src="images/6578.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.015ex; height: 2.738ex;" id="img_images_6578.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·39.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.x\in CʻP.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\cap \overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx={℩}ʻx\)" src="images/6579.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 44.037ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_6579.svg"></p>

<p>We then have a collection of propositions concerned with
relation-arithmetic.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·211.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.P\,\,\text{smor}\,\,Q.\supset .Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/6580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.791ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6580.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the property of being contained in diversity is invariant
for likeness-transformations;</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\unicode{x2909}Q\in \text{Rl}ʻJ.\equiv .P,Q\in \text{Rl}ʻJ.CʻP\cap CʻQ=\Lambda\)" src="images/6581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 49.203ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6581.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_519">[Pg 519]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P \unicode{x21f8}  x \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . \equiv  . x \unicode{x21f7} P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . \equiv  . P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . x {\sim} \in  CʻP\)" src="images/6582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.823ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6582.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">and other such propositions.</p>

<p>We then have a set of propositions concerned with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.357ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6583.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg_5">.
The most important are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . \supset  . \alpha  \cap  pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha  = \Lambda  . \alpha  \cap  pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha  = \Lambda\)" src="images/6584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 47.414ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6584.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . \supset  . CʻP {\sim} \in  \overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/6585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.149ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6585.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P^{2}     \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . \supset  . Pʻʻ\alpha  \cap  Pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha  = \Lambda  . \breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha  \cap  pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha  = \Lambda\)" src="images/6586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 57.916ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6586.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_323"> is asymmetrical, the terms which precede part of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_277"> do not succeed the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_278">, and vice versa.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P \in  \text{Rl}ʻJ . \equiv  . \breve{P}  \in  \text{Rl}ʻJ \quad[*50·23]\)" src="images/6587.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.321ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_6587.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : T \in  1 \rightarrow  1 . \supset  . T^{;}(P \dot{\cap}  J) = T^{;}P \dot{\cap}  J\)" src="images/6590.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.314ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_6590.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : T \in  \text{Cls} \rightarrow  1. P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,J. \supset  . T^{;}P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J\)" src="images/6592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 32.045ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6592.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*150·1.*50·24. \supset  \vdash  \colon\ldotp  \text{Hp} . &amp;\supset  : x (T^{;}P) y . \supset  . <p class="nind"><b><a id="_200_211">*200·211</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . P \,\,\text{smor}\, \,Q . \supset  . <p>The properties of relations are very frequently common to all
relations which are like a given relation, and this applies specially
to the kinds of properties with which we are most concerned. The
above proposition is an illustration of this fact: it shows that
the property of being contained in diversity is invariant for
likeness-transformations.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash  : P \,\unicode{x2abd}\,  J . \equiv  . \text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP \subset  \text{Rl}ʻJ . \equiv  . \exists  ! \text{N}_{0}\text{r}ʻP \cap  \text{Rl}ʻJ\)" src="images/6595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.27ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6595.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_520">[Pg 520]</span></p>

<p>We have, without the need of typical definiteness,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻP\subset \text{Rl}ʻJ\\ \text{and}\quad     &amp;\vdash :\exists !\text{Nr}ʻP\cap \text{Rl}ʻJ.\supset .P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/6597.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 33.949ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_6597.svg"></span>
both of which are immediate consequences of <a href="#_200_211" class="pginternal">*200·211</a>. The converse
implications, however, fail if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP\)" src="images/4146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.64ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4146.svg_13"> is taken in a type in
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Nr}ʻP=\Lambda\)" src="images/6598.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.228ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6598.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\dot{\Lambda} \in \text{Rl}ʻJ  \quad[*25·12]\)" src="images/6599.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.619ex; height: 2.921ex;" id="img_images_6599.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x\neq y.\equiv .x\downarrow y\in \text{Rl}ʻJ      \quad[*55·3]\)" src="images/6600.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.152ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6600.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \uparrow \beta \,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\equiv .\alpha \cap \beta =\Lambda  \quad[*50·55]\)" src="images/6601.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.715ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6601.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha \,\unicode{x2abd}\, J  \quad[*35·442]\)" src="images/6602.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.648ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6602.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha \,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\equiv .P\upharpoonright \alpha \,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\equiv .\alpha \upharpoonleft P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J   \quad[*50·58]\)" src="images/6603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.83ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6603.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\alpha \in 1.\supset .P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha =\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6575.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.351ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_6575.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*52·16.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :x,y\in \alpha .&amp;\supset _{x,y}.{\sim}(xJy).\\ [*23·81]  &amp;\supset _{x,y}.{\sim}(xPy):\\ [*11·521] &amp;\supset :(x,y).{\sim}\{x,y\in \alpha .xPy\}\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6604.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.835ex; width: 70.507ex; height: 8.801ex;" id="img_images_6604.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·36.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J \quad[*50·45]\)" src="images/6605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.825ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_6605.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition is frequently used. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_280"> is
an existent class contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_81">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_4"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.294ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg_7"> are the two parts of the Dedekind "cut"
determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_281"> (excluding the maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_282">, if any).
The above proposition shows that these two parts are mutually exclusive.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*200·54.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ{CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha }=pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻpʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 58.964ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6636.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*40·62. &amp;\supset \vdash :\exists !\alpha.\supset .CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*40·2.  \supset \vdash :\alpha=\Lambda .&amp;\supset .pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha=\text{V}. &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ [*40·16]  &amp;\supset .pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻpʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha \subset pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(3).*200·51.&amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\alpha =\Lambda .\supset .pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻpʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =\Lambda  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .(2).*24·26. &amp;\supset \vdash :\alpha =\Lambda .\supset .CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =CʻP  &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash .(5).*200·51.&amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\alpha =\Lambda .\supset .pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ(CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha )=\Lambda   &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ \vdash .(1).(4).(6).&amp;\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6637.svg" style="vertical-align: -14.548ex; width: 80.82ex; height: 30.226ex;" id="img_images_6637.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is a lemma whose purpose is to avoid the necessity of
introducing the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\alpha\)" src="images/6638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.335ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_6638.svg"> or in proofs in which it
is not really necessary. The first use of this proposition occurs in
<a href="#_206_551" class="pginternal">*206·551</a>.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_525">[Pg 525]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_201">
*201. TRANSITIVE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *201.</p>

<p>There are two main varieties of transitive relations, namely
those that are symmetrical <img alt="" data-tex="\((P=\breve{P})\)" src="images/6639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.175ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_6639.svg">, and those that are
asymmetrical <img alt="" data-tex="\((P\dot{\cap} \breve{P} =\dot{\Lambda})\)" src="images/6640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.255ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_6640.svg">. Transitive
<i>symmetrical</i> relations have the formal properties of equality:
examples of such relations have occurred above, <i>e.g.</i> identity,
similarity, and likeness. The propositions of the present number,
however, are rather such as will be useful in connection with
transitive <i>asymmetrical</i> relations, since they are intended to be
applied to series.</p>

<p>We denote the class of transitive relations by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{trans}\)" src="images/6641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.048ex; height: 1.416ex;" id="img_images_6641.svg">"; thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{trans}=\hat{P} (P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.461ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_6642.svg"></span>
Many propositions of this number are analogous to propositions whose
numbers have the same decimal part in <a href="#_200" class="pginternal">*200</a>. Such are: If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_324"> is
transitive, so is its converse (<a href="#_201_11" class="pginternal">*201·11</a>), and so is any relation
which is like P (<a href="#_201_211" class="pginternal">*201·211</a>); <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg_5"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1842.svg_5">
are transitive (<a href="#_201_3" class="pginternal">*201·3</a><a href="#_201_31" class="pginternal">·31</a>); if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_325"> is transitive, so is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg_1"> (<a href="#_201_33" class="pginternal">*201·33</a>). The propositions <a href="#_201_4" class="pginternal">*201·4</a>—<a href="#_201_42" class="pginternal">·42</a>,
which deal with the ideas of relation-arithmetic, are also analogous to
<a href="#_200_4" class="pginternal">*200·4</a>—<a href="#_200_42" class="pginternal">·42</a>.</p>

<p>Most of the other propositions of this number, however, have no
analogues in <a href="#_200" class="pginternal">*200</a>. Among the most important of these are the following :</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.xPy.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\subset \overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/6643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 32.565ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_6643.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .R_{*}\in \text{trans}\)" src="images/6644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 12.907ex; height: 1.854ex;" id="img_images_6644.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·18.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset .P_{\text{po}}=P.P_{*}=P\unicode{x228d} I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/6645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.719ex; height: 2.536ex;" id="img_images_6645.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is very important, since it effects an immense
simplification in the use of all propositions involving
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_8"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg">, when these propositions are to be
applied to transitive relations. Owing to the above proposition,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_9"> drops out where transitive relations are concerned.
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg_1">, on the other hand, remains useful: If <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in CʻP\)" src="images/6647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.651ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_6647.svg">,
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(xP_{*}y\)" src="images/2897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.843ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2897.svg_1">" will mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_147"> precedes or is <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_97">," which, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_326">
generates a series of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_148"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_98"> are members, is equivalent
to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_149"> does not follow <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_99">."</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_526">[Pg 526]</span></p>

<p>We have a series of propositions (<a href="#_201_5" class="pginternal">*201·5</a>—<a href="#_201_5" class="pginternal">·56</a>) on <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_5"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.357ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6583.svg_2">. The chief of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\supset .PʻʻPʻʻ\alpha \subset Pʻʻ\alpha \)" src="images/6648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.08ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6648.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·501.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\supset .Pʻʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\subset \overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/6649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 32.057ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6649.svg"></p>

<p>These two propositions express the fact that a predecessor of a
predecessor is a predecessor.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\supset .P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha =Pʻʻ\alpha \cup (\alpha \cap CʻP)\)" src="images/6650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.42ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6650.svg"></p>

<p>Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset CʻP,P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.85ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6651.svg"> consists of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_283">
together with the predecessors of its members.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·521.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.x\in CʻP.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻx=\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup {℩}ʻx\)" src="images/6652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.75ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6652.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\supset .Pʻʻ(\alpha \cup Pʻʻ\alpha )=Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.802ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6653.svg"></p>

<p>We have next a set of important propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.272ex; height: 2.24ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg_3"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_5">. The chief are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·63.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{Rl}ʻJ.\supset .P_{1}=P\dot{-} P^{2}\)" src="images/6654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.252ex; height: 2.507ex;" id="img_images_6654.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·65.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{Rl}ʻJ.\supset :P_{1}=\dot{\Lambda} .\equiv .P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.857ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_6655.svg"></p>

<p>On these two propositions, see the notes appended to them below.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*201·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{trans}=\hat{P} (P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.832ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_6656.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\equiv .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P \quad[(*201·01)]\)" src="images/6657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.251ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_6657.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_201_11">*201·11</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\equiv .\breve{P} \in \text{trans}\)" src="images/6658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 25.437ex; height: 2.505ex;" id="img_images_6658.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*201·1.*31·4.\supset \vdash :P\in \text{trans}.&amp;\equiv .\text{Cnv}ʻP^2\,\unicode{x2abd}\, \breve{P} .\\ [*34·63.*201·1] &amp;\equiv .\breve{P} \in \text{trans}:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6659.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.867ex; width: 58.036ex; height: 6.864ex;" id="img_images_6659.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{trans}.\supset :P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\equiv .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\equiv .P\dot{\cap} \breve{P} =\dot{\Lambda}   \quad[*50·47]\)" src="images/6660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.382ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_6660.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, being contained in diversity is
equivalent (where transitive relations are concerned) to asymmetry.
This is not in general the case with relations which are not
transitive; thus <i>e.g.</i> diversity itself is contained in
diversity, but is symmetrical.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{Rl}ʻI\subset \text{trans}\)" src="images/6661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.245ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6661.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*34·34.\supset \vdash :R\,\unicode{x2abd}\, I.&amp;\supset .R^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, R\mid I.\\ [*50·4] &amp;\supset .R^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, R:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6662.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.339ex; width: 42.722ex; height: 5.81ex;" id="img_images_6662.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.xPy.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\subset \overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/6643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 32.565ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_6643.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*201·1.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.zPx.\supset .zPy      &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*32·18.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6663.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 40.653ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_6663.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_527">[Pg 527]</span></p>

<p>The following propositions (<a href="#_201_15" class="pginternal">*201·15</a>—<a href="#_201_19" class="pginternal">·19</a>) are concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{*}\)" src="images/6664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6664.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_3">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_201_15">*201·15</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .R_{*}\in \text{trans} \quad[*90·17]\)" src="images/6665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.718ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6665.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .R_{\text{po}}\in \text{trans} \quad[*91·56]\)" src="images/6666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 24.607ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_6666.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is important, since it often happens that a series is
given as defined by a one-one relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_67">, as in <a href="#_122" class="pginternal">*122</a> for example,
and in such cases <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_4"> is a serial relation in our
present sense. By the above proposition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_5"> is always
transitive; by *96·421, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_6"> is connected when confined to
the posterity of a given term, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/3535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3535.svg_3">;
by *96·23, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/726.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_726.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(xBR\)" src="images/6667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.729ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_6667.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_7"> is contained in diversity throughout the posterity of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_150">. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_68"> is a one-one, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_8"> confined to any
family which has a beginning will be a serial relation.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.Q\in \text{Pot}ʻP.\supset .Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P\)" src="images/6668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.808ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6668.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*34·34.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset _{S}.S\mid P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*91·171  \frac{S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P}{\phi S}. \supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp Q\in \text{Pot}ʻP:S\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset _{S}.S\mid P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P:P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P:\supset .Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).*23·42.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6669.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.884ex; width: 62.266ex; height: 12.9ex;" id="img_images_6669.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is important, since it simplifies all propositions
concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_10"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg_2"> in case <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_327"> is transitive.
The following proposition is an instance of this simplification.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_201_19">*201·19</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\supset .P(x-y)=\overleftarrow{P}ʻx\cap \overrightarrow{P}ʻy \quad[*201·18.(*121·01)]\)" src="images/6671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.29ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6671.svg"></p>

belongs to every member of a relation-number or to none.</p>

<p>The following propositions (<a href="#_201_5" class="pginternal">*201·5</a>—<a href="#_201_56" class="pginternal">·56</a>) are concerned with

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_201_63">*201·63</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{Rl}ʻJ.\supset .P_{1}=P\dot{-} P^{2}  \quad[*201·62]\)" src="images/6715.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.194ex; height: 2.62ex;" id="img_images_6715.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition is of fundamental importance. The relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_8"> (defined in <a href="#_121" class="pginternal">*121</a>) plays a great part in the theory of series.
It is the relation<span class="pagenum" id="Page_532">[Pg 532]</span> "immediately preceding." Its domain consists of
those terms which have immediate successors; its converse domain,
of those that have immediate predecessors. In well-ordered series,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{1}=\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/6716.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.328ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6716.svg">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP_{1}\)" src="images/6717.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6717.svg"> consists
of all terms (except the first) which do not belong to the first
derivative (cf. <a href="#_216" class="pginternal">*216</a>). In any series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP-\text{ᗡ}ʻP_{1}\)" src="images/6718.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.335ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6718.svg">
consists of all the terms which are limits of ascending series, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP-\text{D}ʻP_{1}\)" src="images/6719.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6719.svg">. consists of all the terms which are
limits of descending series.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*201·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{trans}.\supset :P\dot{-} P^{2}=\dot{\Lambda} .\equiv .P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6720.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 39.09ex; height: 2.541ex;" id="img_images_6720.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*23·41.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :P^{2}=P.&amp;\equiv .P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P^{2}.\\ [*25·3] &amp;\equiv .P\dot{-} P^{2}=\dot{\Lambda} \colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6721.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.573ex; width: 58.092ex; height: 6.278ex;" id="img_images_6721.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_201_65">*201·65</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{Rl}ʻJ.\supset :P_{1}=\dot{\Lambda} .\equiv .P^{2}=P    \quad [*201·64·63]\)" src="images/6722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.696ex; height: 2.921ex;" id="img_images_6722.svg"></p>

a <i>compact</i> series, <i>i.e.</i> one in which there are terms

predecessor.</p>
