<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_533">[Pg 533]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_202">*202. CONNECTED RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *202.</p>

<p>A relation is said to be <i>connected</i> when either it or its
converse holds between any two different members of its field,
<i>i.e.</i> when, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_151">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in CʻP . x \neq y\)" src="images/6728.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 15.076ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_6728.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy. \lor . yPx\)" src="images/6729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.725ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6729.svg">.
Thus the field of a connected relation consists of
a single family, unless the relation is null, in which case it has
no families. Conversely, a relation which has one family or none is
connected. Connection is necessary, in addition to transitiveness and
asymmetry, in order that a relation may generate a single series.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_58"> is a class of transitive or asymmetrical relations,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4837.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4837.svg_3"> is transitive or asymmetrical; but if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_59">
is a class of connected relations, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4837.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_4837.svg_4"> is not in
general connected. Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_60"> is a class of series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_6730.svg">
is not one series, but many detached series. This is one
reason why the arithmetical sum of a relation of relations is not
defined as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻCʻP\)" src="images/6731.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.195ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_6731.svg">, but as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s} ʻCʻP \unicode{x228d}F^{;}P\)" src="images/6732.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.703ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_6732.svg">
(cf. <a href="#_162" class="pginternal">*162</a>), because the latter, but not in general the former,
is connected when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_329"> and all the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_82"> are connected
(<a href="#_202_42" class="pginternal">*202·42</a>).</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_330"> is connected, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_284"> is any class contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_83">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ CʻP = Pʻʻ\alpha  \cup  \alpha  \cup  (CʻP \cap  pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha ), \]" src="images/6733.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.106ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6733.svg"></span>
and there is at most one member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_285"> belonging neither
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_7"> nor to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP \cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.585ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6734.svg">.
This member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_286">, if it exists, is the maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_287">.
If, further, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2} \,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/6735.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.357ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6735.svg"> (<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_331">
is asymmetrical), <img alt="" data-tex="\((Pʻʻ\alpha \cup \alpha ) \cap (CʻP \cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha) = \Lambda\)" src="images/6736.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.032ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6736.svg">.
Thus when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_332"> is both connected and asymmetrical, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\cup \alpha\)" src="images/6737.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.825ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6737.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP \cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.585ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6734.svg_1"> are each
other's complements, and the two together constitute the Dedekind
cut defined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha , Pʻʻ\alpha \cup \alpha\)" src="images/6738.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.279ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6738.svg"> being all the
terms that do not follow the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_288">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP \cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.585ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6734.svg_2">
being all the terms that do follow the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_289">.</p>

<p>More generally, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_290"> is any class, not necessarily contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_84">, then when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_333"> is connected, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ CʻP - pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha  \cap  CʻP) \subset  Pʻʻ\alpha  \cup  (\alpha  \cap  CʻP), \]" src="images/6739.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.408ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6739.svg"></span>
and when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_334"> is asymmetrical, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Pʻʻ\alpha  \cup  (\alpha  \cap  CʻP) \subset  CʻP - pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha . \\]" src="images/6740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.3ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6740.svg"></span>
Thus when both conditions are fulfilled, we have (<a href="#_202_503" class="pginternal">*202·503</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ CʻP - pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha  \cap  CʻP) = Pʻʻ\alpha  \cup  (\alpha  \cap  CʻP). \]" src="images/6741.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.408ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6741.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_534">[Pg 534]</span></p>

<p>The above inclusions and the consequent equality will be constantly
required throughout what follows. The division of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_85"> into the two
mutually exclusive parts
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Pʻʻ\alpha \cup (\alpha \cap CʻP) \,\text{and}\, CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP) \]" src="images/6742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.914ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6742.svg"></span>
is the Dedekind "cut" defined by the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_291">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\subset CʻP\)" src="images/6743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.241ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6743.svg">,
the two parts become, as above mentioned,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Pʻʻ\alpha \cup \alpha  \,\text{and}\, CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/6744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.441ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6744.svg"></span>
If, further, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_292"> is not null, they become
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Pʻʻ\alpha \cup \alpha  \,\text{and}\, pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/6745.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.15ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6745.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_293"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_86"> and contains all its own
predecessors, they become
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha\, \text{and}\, CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha. \]" src="images/6746.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.064ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6746.svg"></span>
In this simplified form, Dedekind "cuts" will be considered later
(<a href="#_211" class="pginternal">*211</a>).</p>

<p>We take as our definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{connex}  = \hat{P} \{x\in CʻP.\supset _{x}.\overleftrightarrow{P}ʻx = CʻP\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6747.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.933ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6747.svg"></span></p>

<p>Some of the propositions of the present number are analogues of
propositions in <a href="#_200" class="pginternal">*200</a> and <a href="#_201" class="pginternal">*201</a>. Such are: If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_335"> is connected,
so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_2"> (<a href="#_202_11" class="pginternal">*202·11</a>); if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_336"> is connected, so is any
similar relation (<a href="#_202_211" class="pginternal">*202·211</a>); <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/1842.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1842.svg_6">
are connected (<a href="#_202_3" class="pginternal">*202·3</a><a href="#_202_31" class="pginternal">·31</a>); if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_337"> is connected, so is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg_2"> (<a href="#_202_33" class="pginternal">*202·33</a>); and various propositions
connected with relation-arithmetic (<a href="#_202_4" class="pginternal">*202·4</a>—<a href="#_202_42" class="pginternal">·42</a>). The majority of the
propositions of this number, however, deal with properties peculiar to
connexity. Among the most important of these are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in  \text{connex} . \equiv  :x\in CʻP.\supset _{x}.\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup \iota ʻx\cup \overleftarrow{P}ʻx = CʻP\)" src="images/6748.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 58.358ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6748.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·103.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\colon P\in  \text{connex} . \equiv  \colon\ldotp x,y\in CʻP.\supset _{x,y}:xPy.\lor.x = y.\lor.yPx\)" src="images/6749.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 57.46ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_6749.svg"></p>

<p>These are merely alternative forms of the definition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :R_{*}\in  \text{connex} . \equiv  .R_{\text{po}}\in  \text{connex}\)" src="images/6750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 31.945ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_6750.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·501.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in  \text{connex} .\supset .CʻP-\alpha -Pʻʻ\alpha \subset pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)\)" src="images/6752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.707ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6752.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·503.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in  \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .CʻP-pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP) = (\alpha \cap CʻP)\cup Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.87ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6753.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha \in  \text{connex} .\alpha \subset CʻP.\alpha {\sim}\in 1.\supset .CʻP\unicode{x0294f}\alpha  = \alpha\)" src="images/6757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 51.19ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6757.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition (and others) if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_338"> is a series
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_294"> is a class (not a unit class) contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_87">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg_3"> is the generating relation of the series
consisting of the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_295"> in the order which it has in the
series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_339">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*202·7.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\supset .P\dot{-} P^{2}\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 32.547ex; height: 2.24ex;" id="img_images_6758.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is to be taken in connection with <a href="#_201_63" class="pginternal">*201·63</a>. The two
together show that when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_340"> is a series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{1}\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.885ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg_9"> is one-one.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_536">[Pg 536]</span></p>

<p>The following propositions, down to <a href="#_202_181" class="pginternal">*202·181</a> inclusive (excepting
<a href="#_202_16" class="pginternal">*202·16</a><a href="#_202_161" class="pginternal">·161</a>) are concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{*}\)" src="images/6664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6664.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/3713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_3713.svg_9">.
It often happens that these are connected when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_69"> is not so,

cardinals.</p>

<p>The following propositions (<a href="#_202_511" class="pginternal">*202·511</a>—<a href="#_202_524" class="pginternal">·524</a>) are concerned with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/3663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3663.svg_7">. <a href="#_202_52" class="pginternal">*202·52</a> shows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{connex}\)" src="images/6835.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 11.316ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_6835.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_342"> cannot have more than one first term or more than one last
term, and <a href="#_202_523" class="pginternal">*202·523</a> shows that this still holds if only <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg_3">
is connected. *202·511 shows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_343"> is a connected relation
which has a first term, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_296"> is any class, there are
predecessors of the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP\)" src="images/6836.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.739ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6836.svg"> when and only when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_13"> is such a predecessor, and when and only when <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP{\sim}\in \alpha\)" src="images/6837.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.748ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6837.svg">.
<a href="#_202_524" class="pginternal">*202·524</a> shows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_344"> is connected and has a first
term, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/4354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.414ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4354.svg_2"> consists of the successors of the first term.
These propositions are much used.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_202_53">*202·53</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Q\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset .Q=P\unicode{x0294f}CʻQ\)" src="images/6848.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.519ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6848.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*33·17.*36·13. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :xQy.\supset .x(P\unicode{x0294f}CʻQ)y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*50·43. \supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :xPy.\supset .{\sim}(yPx).\\ [*23·81]  &amp;\supset .{\sim}(yQx).  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*200·36.&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :xPy.\supset .x\neq y  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(2).(3).*202·104.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :x,y\in CʻQ.xPy.\supset .xQy:\\ [*36·13]&amp;\supset :x(P\unicode{x0294f}CʻQ)y.\supset .xQy  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .(1).(4).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6849.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.068ex; width: 73.857ex; height: 21.267ex;" id="img_images_6849.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_544">[Pg 544]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is important in series. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_345"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_211"> are
serial relations, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P\)" src="images/6850.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.602ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6850.svg">, they verify the above
hypothesis; hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_212"> is a series contained in a given series
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_346">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_213"> is simply <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_347"> with its field limited. Thus series
contained in a given series are completely determined by their fields.</p>

or successor. *202·72 is used in <a href="#_204_71" class="pginternal">*204·71</a>, which is an important
proposition.</p>

<p>The above proposition shows that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_214"> is connected, and any class

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_547">[Pg 547]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_204">
*204. ELEMENTARY PROPERTIES OF SERIES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *204.</p>

<p>In this number we give the definition and a few of the simpler
properties of series. Most of the propositions of this number result
immediately from those of <a href="#_200" class="pginternal">*200</a>, <a href="#_201" class="pginternal">*201</a>, and <a href="#_202" class="pginternal">*202</a>. Our definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Ser} =\text{Rl}ʻJ\cap \text{trans}\cap \text{connex}   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6874.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.49ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6874.svg"></span></p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\equiv .P\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.P^{3}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\equiv .P\in \text{connex} .P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\,     J\)" src="images/6875.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 63.038ex; height: 2.536ex;" id="img_images_6875.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">either of which might have been taken as the definition.</p>

<p>After a few propositions giving other possible forms of the definition
of series, we proceed to a set of propositions which follow immediately
from those of *200, *201, and *202. Such are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\equiv .\breve{P} \in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/6876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 21.641ex; height: 2.505ex;" id="img_images_6876.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.P\,\,\text{smor}\,\,Q.\supset .Q\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/6877.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 32.531ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_6877.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\dot{\Lambda} \in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/6878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 9.874ex; height: 2.446ex;" id="img_images_6878.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x\neq y.\equiv .x\downarrow y\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/6879.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 22.538ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_6879.svg"></p>

<p>Another important proposition on couples is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·272.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Ser}.\supset :\text{D}ʻP\in 1.\equiv .P\in 2_{r}.\equiv .\text{ᗡ}ʻP\in 1\)" src="images/6880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6880.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">so that couples are the only series having unit classes for their
domains or converse domains.</p>

<p>We then proceed to a set of propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/6881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6881.svg">.
We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Ser}.x,y\in CʻP.\supset :x\neq y.\overrightarrow{P}ʻyC\overrightarrow{P}ʻx.\equiv .yPx\)" src="images/6882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 51.524ex; height: 3.676ex;" id="img_images_6882.svg"></p>

<p>Also, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Ser},\overrightarrow{P}\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/6883.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.296ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6883.svg"> is a
one-one and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\,\,\text{smor}\,\,P\)" src="images/6884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 12.161ex; height: 3.215ex;" id="img_images_6884.svg"> (*204·34·35).</p>

<p>We then have some propositions (<a href="#_204_4" class="pginternal">*204·4</a>—<a href="#_204_44" class="pginternal">·44</a>) on relations with limited
fields. The most important of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha \in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/6885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.446ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6885.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P,Q\in \text{Ser}.Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset .Q=P\unicode{x0294f}CʻQ\)" src="images/6886.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.16ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6886.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_548">[Pg 548]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is important, since it shows that any series contained
in a given series is wholly determined when its field is given.</p>

<p>We have next a number of propositions (<a href="#_204_45" class="pginternal">*204·45</a>—<a href="#_204_59" class="pginternal">·59</a>) applying
relation-arithmetic to series. The first set of these (<a href="#_204_45" class="pginternal">*204·45</a>—<a href="#_204_483" class="pginternal">·483</a>)
are concerned with the proof that if a "cut" is made in a series, the
series is the sum of the two parts into which the cut divides it, where
the sum is taken in the sense of <a href="#_160" class="pginternal">*160</a> or <a href="#_161" class="pginternal">*161</a>, according as one part
of the cut does not or does consist of a single term. Most of these
propositions do not require the full hypothesis that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_350"> is a series, but
only some part of it. Thus we have for instance</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·46.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash  : &amp;P \in  \text{connex}  . \text{E}! BʻP . \text{ᗡ}ʻP {\sim} \in  1 . \supset  .\\ &amp;P = BʻP \unicode{x21f7} P \unicode{x0294f} \text{ᗡ}ʻP . \text{Nr}ʻP = \dot{1}  \dot{+}  \text{Nr}ʻ(P \unicode{x0294f} \text{ᗡ}ʻP)\end{align}\]" src="images/6887.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.309ex; width: 46.056ex; height: 5.749ex;" id="img_images_6887.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">with a similar proposition for <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/5455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5455.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg_6">
(<a href="#_204_461" class="pginternal">*204·461</a>).</p>

<p>We next prove that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_351">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_216"> are mutually exclusive series,
their sum <img alt="" data-tex="\((P \unicode{x2909} Q)\)" src="images/6888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.606ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6888.svg"> is a series, and vice versa
(<a href="#_204_5" class="pginternal">*204·5</a>); that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_352"> is a series to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_152"> does not belong,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x21f8} x\)" src="images/6889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6889.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \unicode{x21f7} P\)" src="images/6890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6890.svg"> are series, and
vice versa (<a href="#_204_51" class="pginternal">*204·51</a>); that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_353"> is a series of mutually exclusive
series, its sum <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Sigma ʻP\)" src="images/4756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4756.svg_10"> is a series (<a href="#_204_52" class="pginternal">*204·52</a>); that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_354">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_217"> are series, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \times Q\)" src="images/4117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.254ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4117.svg_2"> (<a href="#_204_55" class="pginternal">*204·55</a>); that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_355"> is
a series of series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_28"> is contained in diversity and is
transitive (<a href="#_204_561" class="pginternal">*204·561</a>), while if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_356"> is also well-ordered, <i>i.e.</i>
such that every existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_88"> has a first term, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Pi ʻP\)" src="images/5446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.753ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5446.svg_29"> is a series (<a href="#_204_57" class="pginternal">*204·57</a>); and that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_357"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_218"> are
series, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_219"> is well-ordered, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{Q}\)" src="images/5458.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 3.278ex; height: 1.948ex;" id="img_images_5458.svg_13"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \,\text{exp}\,\, Q\)" src="images/6891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.079ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_6891.svg"> are series (<a href="#_204_59" class="pginternal">*204·59</a>). These propositions are essential to ordinal
arithmetic, but they will not be referred to again until we reach that
stage (Sections D and E of this Part).</p>

<p>The three following propositions deal with couples. Couples
often require special treatment, owing to the fact that,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_358"> is a couple, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP =\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.429ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_6922.svg">, so that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ(P\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP) \neq\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/6923.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.481ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6923.svg">, whereas in any other case,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_359"> is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_550">[Pg 550]</span> a series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ(P\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP)=\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/6924.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.481ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6924.svg">.
Hence the following propositions are often required.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_551">[Pg 551]</span></p>

<p>The three following propositions only require <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Rl}ʻJ\cap\text{connex}\)" src="images/6935.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.914ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6935.svg">,
but are required for application to series, and are
therefore convenient in the form here given.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·331.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Ser}.x,y\in CʻP.\supset :\overrightarrow{P}ʻx=\overrightarrow{P}ʻy.\equiv .x=y\\ &amp;[*202·161.*71·55]\end{align}\]" src="images/6936.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.783ex; width: 48.343ex; height: 6.697ex;" id="img_images_6936.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}\upharpoonright CʻP\in 1\rightarrow 1.\overrightarrow{P}\upharpoonright CʻP\in (\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P)\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}     P \quad[*202·161]\)" src="images/6937.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 69.559ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6937.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\,\,\text{smor}\,\,P  \quad[*204·34]\)" src="images/6938.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.129ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6938.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that the series of segments which have upper
limits is like the original series, for a segment whose upper limit is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_153"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/6881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6881.svg_1">, and the series of such segments is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\)" src="images/6939.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.156ex; height: 3.19ex;" id="img_images_6939.svg">.</p>

<p>The following propositions (<a href="#_204_4" class="pginternal">*204·4</a>—<a href="#_204_44" class="pginternal">·44</a>) are concerned with relations
with limited fields.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_204_4">*204·4</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha \in \text{Ser}  \quad[*200·33.*201·33.*202·33]\)" src="images/6940.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.501ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6940.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*204·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P,Q\in \text{Ser}.Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset .Q=P\unicode{x0294f}CʻQ  \quad[*202·53.*204·13]\)" src="images/6941.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.158ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6941.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of the above two propositions, the series contained in a
given series are the relations resulting from limitations of the field;
the process of limiting the field is merely the process of selecting a
part of the original series without changing the order.</p>

<p>The following propositions (<a href="#_204_45" class="pginternal">*204·45</a>—<a href="#_204_483" class="pginternal">*204·483</a>) are concerned with the
division of a series into two parts, one of which wholly precedes
the other. The case where one of the parts consists of a single term
requires special treatment, and so does the case where both parts
consist of single terms, <i>i.e.</i> where the series is a couple.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_559">[Pg 559]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="id_205_MAXIMUM_AND_MINIMUM_POINTS">
*205. MAXIMUM AND MINIMUM POINTS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *205.</p>

<p>The minimum points of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_298"> with respect to a relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_361"> are those members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_299"> which belong to the field of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_362"> but to which no members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_300"> have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_363">;
that is, they are those members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_301"> which belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_90">
but have no predecessors in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_302">. Similarly the maximum points
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_303"> are those members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_304"> which belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_91">
but have no successors in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_305">. Both these notions have been
already defined in *93, but they were there only used for the special
purpose of studying generations. Their chief utility is in connection
with <i>series</i>, and it is in this connection that we shall now
consider them. Many of the properties of maxima and minima in series do
not demand the whole hypothesis "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/7003.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.614ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_7003.svg">," but only "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in\text{connex}\)" src="images/7004.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 11.316ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_7004.svg">."
This is the case, in particular, with the fundamental
property of maxima and minima in series, namely that each class has at
most one maximum and one minimum. The minimum of a class, if it exists,
is the first term of the class, and the maximum, if it exists, is the
last term. The maxima with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_364"> are the minima with respect
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_3">; hence properties of maxima result immediately from
the corresponding properties of minima, and will be set down without
proof in what follows.</p>

<p>It will be seen that the maxima and minima of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_306"> depend only
upon <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP\)" src="images/6836.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.739ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6836.svg_1">: the part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_307"> (if any) which is not
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_92"> is irrelevant.</p>

<p>In accordance with the definitions of *93, the class of minima of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_308"> is denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7005.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.569ex; height: 4.132ex;" id="img_images_7005.svg">,
where
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{p}ʻ\alpha =(\alpha \cap CʻP)-\breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha , \]" src="images/7006.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 30.342ex; height: 4.132ex;" id="img_images_7006.svg"></span>
the definition being
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{min}_{P}=\hat{x} \hat{\alpha} \{x\in (\alpha \cap CʻP)-\breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha\}. \]" src="images/7007.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.998ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7007.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/7008.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_7008.svg"> is a relation contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4765.svg_2">. When
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_365"> is connected, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha\in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/7009.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.509ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7009.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> (by *71·12)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{min}_{P}\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}. \]" src="images/7010.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 16.36ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_7010.svg"></span>
It follows that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_119"> is a set of classes which all have
minima, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\upharpoonright \kappa\)" src="images/7011.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.664ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_7011.svg"> is a selective
relation for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_120">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{min}_{P}\upharpoonright \kappa \in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa . \]" src="images/7012.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.749ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7012.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_560">[Pg 560]</span>
Owing to this fact, the existence of selections can sometimes be proved
in dealing with series (especially with well-ordered series), in cases
where such proof would be impossible if no serial arrangement were
given.</p>

<p>The definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/7008.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_7008.svg_1"> is so chosen as to exclude
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7013.svg"> whatever
part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_309"> is not contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_93">, and to make
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ{℩}ʻx={℩}ʻx\)" src="images/7014.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.553ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7014.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}ʻ{℩}ʻx=x\)" src="images/7015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.838ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7015.svg">, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in CʻP.{\sim}(xPx)\)" src="images/7016.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.65ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7016.svg">. For
these two reasons we have to reject two simpler definitions which might
otherwise be thought preferable. One of these would give
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\alpha -\breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha , \]" src="images/7017.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.688ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7017.svg"></span>
which might be obtained by putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{min}_{P}=\in \dot{-} \in \mid \breve{P}   \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/7018.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 21.853ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_7018.svg"></span>
This agrees with our definition whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\subset CʻP\)" src="images/6743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.241ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6743.svg_1">,
but not otherwise, since it includes in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7013.svg_1"> any part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_310"> not
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_94">. Hence it necessitates the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_311">
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\subset CʻP\)" src="images/7019.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.165ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7019.svg"> in many propositions which, with our definition, do not
require this hypothesis, and in particular in the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in \text{connex} .\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha \in 0\cup 1, \]" src="images/7020.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.226ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7020.svg"></span>
so that instead of having (as with our definition)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in \text{connex} .\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} \]" src="images/7021.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 30.819ex; height: 3.821ex;" id="img_images_7021.svg"></span>
we should only have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in \text{connex} .\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}\upharpoonright \text{Cl}ʻCʻP\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}. \]" src="images/7022.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.044ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7022.svg"></span>
For these reasons, this definition is less convenient than the one we
have adopted.</p>

<p>The other definition which suggests itself is one which will give
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\unicode{x0294f}\alpha . \]" src="images/7023.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.191ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7023.svg"></span>
If this definition were adopted, we might dispense
with a special notation altogether, using
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/7024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.579ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7024.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/7025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7025.svg"> in place of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7013.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7026.svg">.
This definition, however, has the drawback that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in 1\)" src="images/7027.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.345ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_7027.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_6">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha =\dot{\Lambda} , \]" src="images/7028.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.721ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_7028.svg"></span>
so that we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\dot{\Lambda}\,\text{when}\, \alpha \in 1.\alpha \subset CʻP. \]" src="images/7029.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 34.307ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7029.svg"></span>
This necessitates the addition of the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha{\sim}\in 1\)" src="images/7030.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.105ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_7030.svg">
(as in <a href="#_204_45" class="pginternal">*204·45</a> above, for example) in cases where,
with our definition, no such hypothesis is required. If we take
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\alpha \upharpoonleft P\)" src="images/7031.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.422ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7031.svg">, instead of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/7024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.579ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7024.svg_1">, as the class
of minimum points, we secure <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}ʻ{℩}ʻx=x\)" src="images/7015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.838ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7015.svg_1"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/7032.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.845ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7032.svg">, but not when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/7033.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.834ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7033.svg">. Thus we still have exceptions to
provide against which do not arise with the definition we have adopted.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_561">[Pg 561]</span></p>

<p>The first few propositions of this number have already been proved in
*93, but are repeated here for convenience of reference.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are numerous and much used. Among the
elementary properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{max}_{P}\)" src="images/61.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.6ex; height: 1.353ex;" id="img_images_61.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/7008.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_7008.svg_2"> with
which the number begins, the following should be noted:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{B}ʻP=\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\text{D}ʻP=\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/7034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.794ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7034.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·123.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\Lambda .\equiv .\alpha \cap CʻP\subset Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7035.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 37.022ex; height: 3.434ex;" id="img_images_7035.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\hat{x} \{x\in \alpha \cap CʻP.\alpha \cap \overrightarrow{P}ʻx= \Lambda \}\)" src="images/7036.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.633ex; height: 4.048ex;" id="img_images_7036.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)=\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7037.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.389ex; height: 4.048ex;" id="img_images_7037.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\Lambda =\Lambda\)" src="images/7038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.064ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7038.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·18.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :{\sim}(xPx).x\in CʻP.\supset .\text{min}_{P}ʻ{℩}ʻx=\text{max}_{P}ʻ{℩}ʻx=x\)" src="images/7039.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.884ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7039.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·19.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}.\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ(\alpha      \cup \breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha )=\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\breve{P} _{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.149ex; height: 4.048ex;" id="img_images_7040.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·194.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x\text{min}_{P}\alpha .\supset .{\sim}(xPx)\)" src="images/7041.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.123ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7041.svg"></p>

<p>Owing to this proposition, we can sometimes dispense with the
hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/5653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5653.svg_8"> in propositions about minima which
would otherwise require this hypothesis.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·197.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Rl}ʻJ\cap \text{trans}.\supset :x\in CʻP.\equiv .x=\text{max}_{P}ʻ(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup {℩}ʻx)\)" src="images/7042.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.04ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7042.svg"></p>

<p>Our next set of propositions (<a href="#_205_2" class="pginternal">*205·2</a>—<a href="#_205_27" class="pginternal">·27</a>) introduces the hypothesis
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_366"> is connected, or transitive and connected. The chief of them
are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\text{E}!\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha .y\in \alpha \cap CʻP-{℩}ʻ\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha .\supset .\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha Py\)" src="images/7043.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 66.709ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_7043.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if the minimum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_312"> exists, it precedes every other member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP\)" src="images/6836.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.739ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6836.svg_2">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex} .\text{E}!\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha .\supset .\breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha =\overleftarrow{P}ʻ\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7044.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 57.27ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7044.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the terms which come after some part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_313"> are
those that come after its minimum (when the minimum exists).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻx=(\overleftarrow{P}\dot{-} P^{2})ʻx\)" src="images/7045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.831ex; height: 4.048ex;" id="img_images_7045.svg"></p>

<p>We have next the fundamental proposition:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha \in 0\cup 1.\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{P}ʻ\alpha \in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/7046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 49.814ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_7046.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">whence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\supset .\text{min}_{P},\text{max}_{P}\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/7047.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 40.065ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_7047.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">which leads to</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\kappa \subset  \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.\supset .\text{min}_{P}\upharpoonright \kappa \in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/7048.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 48.05ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7048.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is useful in the theory of well-ordered series.
Observe that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/7049.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.196ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7049.svg">" means that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_121"> consists of classes which have minima.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_562">[Pg 562]</span></p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions (<a href="#_205_4" class="pginternal">*205·4</a>—<a href="#_205_44" class="pginternal">·44</a>) dealing with the
relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7026.svg_1"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/7025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7025.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\alpha \upharpoonleft P\)" src="images/7050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.422ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7050.svg">; next we have propositions on the
relations of the minima of two different classes, of which the most
useful is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .BʻP\in \alpha .\supset .BʻP=\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7051.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 43.478ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7051.svg"></p>

<p>We have next various propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha\cap CʻP)\)" src="images/7052.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.408ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7052.svg">,
of which the chief is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·65.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex} .\text{E}!\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha     .\supset .pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)=\overrightarrow{P}ʻ\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7053.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 67.88ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7053.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the predecessors of the whole of a class contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_95"> are the predecessors of its minimum (if it has one).</p>

<p>A useful proposition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·68.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha \subset \alpha .\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{\text{min}}(P_{\text{po}})ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7054.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 39.389ex; height: 4.132ex;" id="img_images_7054.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_314"> is a hereditary class, its minima with
respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_367"> are the same as its minima with respect to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_11">.</p>

<p>We prove next that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_9"> has a maximum, so has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_315">
(<a href="#_205_7" class="pginternal">*205·7</a>), and that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{connex}\)" src="images/6835.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 11.316ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_6835.svg_2">, only a unit class can
have its maximum identical with its minimum (<a href="#_205_73" class="pginternal">*205·73</a>).</p>

<p><a href="#_205_8" class="pginternal">*205·8</a>—<a href="#_205_85" class="pginternal">·85</a> are concerned with relation-arithmetic. The chief
proposition here is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·8.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S\in P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,Q.\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =Sʻʻ\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{Q}ʻ\breve{S} ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7055.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 47.793ex; height: 4.132ex;" id="img_images_7055.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> in any correlation, the minima of the correlates of a class
are the correlates of the minima.</p>

<p>We end with two propositions on relations with limited fields. The more
useful of these is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·9.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} ·\kappa \subset CʻP.\kappa {\sim}\in 1.\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}(P\unicode{x0294f}\kappa )ʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ(\alpha     \cap \kappa )\)" src="images/7056.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.934ex; height: 4.048ex;" id="img_images_7056.svg"></p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*205·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x\text{min}_{P}\alpha .\equiv .x\in \alpha \cap CʻP-\breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha       \quad[*93·11]\)" src="images/7057.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.552ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7057.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*205·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :x\text{max}_{P}\alpha .\equiv .x\in \alpha \cap CʻP-Pʻʻ\alpha .\equiv .x \text{min}(\breve{P} )\alpha       \quad[*93·115]\)" src="images/7058.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.867ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7058.svg"></p>

reference in the sequel, we shall refer to the corresponding
propositions for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/7008.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_7008.svg_4">, in case no reference exists for

<p>Observe that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim} (\alpha \cap CʻP = {℩}ʻBʻ\breve{P})\)" src="images/7195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.765ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7195.svg"> is not in
