<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_605">[Pg 605]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="id_208_THE_CORRELATION_OF_SERIES">
*208. THE CORRELATION OF SERIES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *208.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are chiefly important on account of
their consequences in the theory of well-ordered series (*250 ff.) and
in the theory of vector-families (*330 ff.). When two well-ordered
series are ordinally similar, they have only one correlator; and a
well-ordered series is not ordinally similar to any of its segments.
Of these two propositions, the first is an immediate consequence of
<a href="#_208_41" class="pginternal">*208·41</a>, and the second is an immediate consequence of <a href="#_208_47" class="pginternal">*208·47</a>.</p>

<p>Propositions concerning correlators of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_391"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_220">
are obtained from propositions concerning correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_392"> with
itself, by means of the fact that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_66">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_21"> are two correlators
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_393"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_221">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid \breve{T}\)" src="images/7514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.938ex; height: 2.964ex;" id="img_images_7514.svg"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_394"> with
itself. Again, correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_395"> with itself are considered, in
this number, as a special case of correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_396"> with parts of
itself. This latter is a notion which will prove important for other
reasons than those for which it is used in our present context. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_397"> is connected, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_67"> correlates <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_398"> with part of itself (so
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S^{;}P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P\)" src="images/7515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.72ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7515.svg">), <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_106"> will contain terms of three
kinds, (1) those for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻx=x\)" src="images/7516.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.422ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7516.svg">, (2) those for which <img alt="" data-tex="\((Sʻx)Px\)" src="images/7517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.864ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7517.svg">,
(3) those for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(xP(Sʻx)\)" src="images/7518.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.864ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7518.svg">. Our propositions result from the
non-existence (under certain circumstances) of maxima or minima of
classes (2) and (3).</p>

<p>The following definition defines "correlations of P with parts (or the
whole) of itself." The letters "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{cror}\)" src="images/7519.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.91ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_7519.svg">" stand for "ordinal
correlation." For a cardinal correlation, should occasion arise, we
should use "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{cr}\)" src="images/7520.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.891ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_7520.svg">," <i>i.e.</i> we should put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{cr}ʻ\alpha =sʻ\,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \alpha ʻʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha   \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/7521.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.338ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_7521.svg"></span>
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in \text{cr}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\alpha .\text{D}ʻS\subset \alpha\)" src="images/7522.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 41.986ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7522.svg">.
For the present, we are concerned with the corresponding ordinal
notion; thus we require
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\equiv .S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=CʻP.S^{;}P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P. \]" src="images/7523.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.922ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7523.svg"></span>
This is secured by putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{cror}ʻP=sʻ\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,Pʻʻ\text{Rl}ʻP  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/7524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.784ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_7524.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_606">[Pg 606]</span></p>

<p>It will be observed that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_376"> is what we called
a "non-reflexive" class (cf. <a href="#_124" class="pginternal">*124</a>), <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{cr}ʻ\alpha={℩}ʻI\upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/7525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.217ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7525.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in \text{cr}ʻ\alpha .\supset.\text{D}ʻS=\alpha\)" src="images/7526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.705ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7526.svg">. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_107">
is non-reflexive, the same is true of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_399">; and when <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_108"> is
reflexive, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_400"> is also reflexive, in the sense that it contains
proper parts similar to itself, though if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_401"> is well-ordered, such
proper parts cannot be segments of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_402">, but must extend to the end of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_109">.</p>

<p>The class of correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_403"> with the whole of itself, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P\)" src="images/7527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 9.704ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_7527.svg">, is a sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{cror}ʻP\)" src="images/7528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.966ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7528.svg">, and
is specially important. This class differs widely in its properties
from the corresponding cardinal class. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_377"> has more than one
member, the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \,\overline{\text{ sm }}\, \alpha\)" src="images/7529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.559ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_7529.svg"> (which is the
"permutations" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_378"> in the usual elementary sense) always
has more than one member. But the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P\)" src="images/7527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 9.704ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_7527.svg_1">
(which consists of such permutations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_110"> as keep the order
unchanged) will consist of the single term <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/3388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3388.svg_1">,
unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_111"> contains classes which have neither a minimum nor a
maximum, in which case there will be many correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_404"> with
itself. As a simple illustration, take the series of negative and
positive integers in their natural order. Then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_172"> is any one
of these integers, <img alt="" data-tex="\(+\nu\)" src="images/7530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 2.959ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_7530.svg"> is a correlator of the whole series with
itself. If we take only the positive integers, <img alt="" data-tex="\(+\nu\)" src="images/7530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 2.959ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_7530.svg_1"> is no longer
a correlator of the whole series with itself, since all integers less
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_173"> are omitted from the correlate.</p>

<p>The first important use of the propositions of this number is in the
beginning of the theory of well-ordered series (*250). The propositions
there used are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·41.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ&amp;\text{min}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.\\ &amp;S,T\in P \,\,\text{smor}\, \,Q.\supset .(P \overline{\,\text{smor}\,}Q) \in 1\end{align}\]" src="images/7531.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.205ex; width: 74.304ex; height: 5.541ex;" id="img_images_7531.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_405"> is connected and asymmetrical, and every existent
sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_112"> has either a minimum or a maximum, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_406"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_222">
cannot have more than one correlator.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·42.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{In the same circumstances},\, P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P={℩}ʻ(I\upharpoonright CʻP)\)" src="images/7532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.251ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_7532.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\supset .{\sim}(\exists x).(Sʻx)Px\)" src="images/7533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.605ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7533.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if every existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_113"> has a minimum, a
correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_407"> with part of itself can never move terms backwards.
Thus for example, to take a simple instance, an infinite series
consisting of some of the natural numbers in order of magnitude cannot
have its <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_190">th term less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_139.svg_191">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.\supset .\text{Rl}ʻP\cap \text{Nr}ʻP={℩}ʻP\)" src="images/7534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 72.553ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7534.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_408"> is connected and every existent sub-class of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_114"> has both a maximum and a minimum, no proper part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_409"> is
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_410">. This proposition is important in the theory of finite
series and finite ordinals.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·46.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\supset .CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS=\Lambda\)" src="images/7535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 64.932ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7535.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_607">[Pg 607]</span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if every existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_115"> has a minimum, a
part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_411"> which is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_412"> must go up to the end of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_413">,
<i>i.e.</i> must not wholly precede any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_116">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·47.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\exists !CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻCʻQ.\supset .{\sim}(Q\,\,\text{smor}\,\,P)\)" src="images/7536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.284ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7536.svg"></p>

<p>This is an immediate consequence of <a href="#_208_46" class="pginternal">*208·46</a>.</p>

<p>The proof of the above propositions proceeds simply by showing that
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in \text{cror}ʻP\)" src="images/7537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.191ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7537.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\((Sʻx)Px\)" src="images/7517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.864ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7517.svg_1">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\((SʻSʻx)P(Sʻx)\)" src="images/7538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.258ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7538.svg">,
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_174"> is not the earliest term for which <img alt="" data-tex="\((Sʻx)Px\)" src="images/7517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.864ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7517.svg_2">,
since <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻx\)" src="images/4163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.111ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4163.svg_1"> is an earlier term for which the same thing holds.
Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\{(Sʻx)Px\}\)" src="images/7539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.421ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_7539.svg"> can have no minimum; and similarly
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\{xP(Sʻx)\}\)" src="images/7540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.421ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_7540.svg"> can have no maximum (<a href="#_208_14" class="pginternal">*208·14</a>). So far we
require no hypothesis as to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_414">. Assuming now <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{connex}.P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/7541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.679ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_7541.svg">,
we show similarly that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_68"> correlates the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_415"> with itself,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\{(Sʻx)Px\}\)" src="images/7539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.421ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_7539.svg_1"> can have no maximum and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\{xP(Sʻx)\}\)" src="images/7540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.421ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_7540.svg_1">
can have no minimum.</p>

<p>Propositions about correlators of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_416"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_223"> follow from the
above by taking two correlators <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_69"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/1448.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_1448.svg_22">, and applying the above
propositions to <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid \breve{T}\)" src="images/7514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.938ex; height: 2.964ex;" id="img_images_7514.svg_1">, which is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_417">
with the whole of itself.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :S,T\in P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,Q.\supset .S\mid \breve{T} \in P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P  \quad[*151·131·141]\)" src="images/7566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.539ex; height: 2.966ex;" id="img_images_7566.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·32.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P&amp;\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.S,T\in P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,Q.\supset .\\ &amp;{\sim}\exists !\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\hat{x} \{(Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx)Px\}.{\sim}\exists !\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{P}ʻ\hat{x}\{(Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx)Px\}.\\ &amp;{\sim}\exists !\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\hat{x}\{xP(Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx)\}.{\sim}\exists !\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{P}ʻ\hat{x}\{xP(Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx)\}\\\ &amp;[*208·3·31.*34·41]\end{align}\]" src="images/7567.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.914ex; width: 57.485ex; height: 14.959ex;" id="img_images_7567.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·4.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ&amp;\text{min}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.\\ &amp;S,T\in P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,Q.\supset .S=T\end{align}\]" src="images/7568.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.205ex; width: 65.677ex; height: 5.541ex;" id="img_images_7568.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*208·32. &amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .\hat{x}\{(Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx)Px\}=\Lambda .\hat{x}\{xP(Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx)\}=\Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*208·31.*34·41.  &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :x\in CʻP.\supset .Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx\in CʻP   &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .(1).(2).*202·103.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :x\in CʻP.\supset .Sʻ\breve{T} ʻx=x.\\ [*72·241] &amp;\supset .\breve{T} ʻx=\breve{S} ʻx:\\ [*150·23] &amp;\supset :x\in \text{D}ʻS\cup \text{D}ʻT.\supset .\breve{T} ʻx=\breve{S} ʻx:\\ [*33·46] &amp;\supset :S=T\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7569.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.307ex; width: 93.723ex; height: 21.744ex;" id="img_images_7569.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_208_41">*208·41</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ&amp;\text{min}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.\\ &amp;P\,\,\text{smor}\,\,Q.\supset .(P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,Q)\in 1\\ [*208·4.*151·12.*52·16]\end{align}\]" src="images/7570.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.675ex; width: 68.236ex; height: 8.482ex;" id="img_images_7570.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_610">[Pg 610]</span></p>

<p>The above proposition is of great importance in the theory of
well-ordered series.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·42.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .P^{2}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}\cup &amp;\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.\supset     .\\ &amp;P\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P={℩}ʻ(I\upharpoonright CʻP)\\ [*208·4.*51·141.*151·121]\end{align}\]" src="images/7571.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.675ex; width: 71.2ex; height: 8.482ex;" id="img_images_7571.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\supset .{\sim}(\exists x).(Sʻx)Px  \quad[*208·14]\)" src="images/7572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.548ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7572.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·431.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\supset .{\sim}(\exists x).xP(Sʻx)  \quad[*208·14]\)" src="images/7573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.987ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7573.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·44.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}\cap &amp;\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;S=I\upharpoonright CʻP\end{align}\]" src="images/7574.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 62.431ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_7574.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*208·43·431.*202·103.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :x\in CʻP.\supset .Sʻx=x.\\ [*50·14.*35·7] &amp;\supset .Sʻx=(I\upharpoonright CʻP)ʻx:\\ [*208·1.*50·5·52] &amp;\supset :x\in \text{ᗡ}ʻS\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ(I\upharpoonright CʻP).\supset .Sʻx=(I\upharpoonright CʻP)ʻx:\\ [*33·45] &amp;\supset :S=I\upharpoonright CʻP\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7575.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 90.328ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_7575.svg"></span></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_419"> is a finite series, no proper
part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_420"> is ordinally similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_421">. (It will be shown later
that a finite series is one in which every existent contained class has
both a maximum and a minimum.) The following proposition gives a more
explicit form of the above result.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}.\supset .\text{Rl}ʻP\cap \text{Nr}ʻP={℩}ʻP\)" src="images/7534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 72.553ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7534.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*208·441.  \supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=CʻP.S^{;}P\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\supset .S=I\upharpoonright CʻP.\\ [*150·534] &amp;\supset .S^{;}P=P  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*13·12.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=CʻP.Q=S^{;}P.\supset .Q=P:\\ [*151·1] &amp;\supset :Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.Q\,\,\text{smor}\,\,P.\supset .Q=P:\\ [*152·1] &amp;\supset :\text{Rl}ʻP\cap \text{Nr}ʻP\subset {℩}ʻP &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*61·34.*152·3.&amp;\supset \vdash .{℩}ʻP\subset \text{Rl}ʻP\cap \text{Nr}ʻP  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(2).(3).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7576.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.068ex; width: 88.998ex; height: 21.267ex;" id="img_images_7576.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following propositions are useful in the theory of segments of
well-ordered series, since they show that a well-ordered series is
never ordinally similar to any of its segments.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_208_46">*208·46</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\supset .CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS=\Lambda\)" src="images/7535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 64.932ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7535.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*208·1. \supset \vdash \colon\ldotp S\in \text{cror}ʻP.&amp;\supset :x\in CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS.\supset .(Sʻx)Px:\\ [\text{Transp}]  &amp;\supset :{\sim}\{(Sʻx)Px\}.\supset .x{\sim}\in CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).*208·43.&amp;\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.\supset .(x).x{\sim}\in CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS:\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7577.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.973ex; width: 90.765ex; height: 13.077ex;" id="img_images_7577.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_611">[Pg 611]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*208·461.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.S\in \text{cror}ʻP.\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS=\Lambda\\ &amp;[*208·46·1.*40·62]\end{align}\]" src="images/7578.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.783ex; width: 62.862ex; height: 6.697ex;" id="img_images_7578.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_208_47">*208·47</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Cl ex}ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{P}.Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\exists !CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻCʻQ.\supset .{\sim}(Q\,\,\text{smor}\,\,P)\)" src="images/7536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.284ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7536.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*208·46.(*208·01).\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.S\in Q\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P.\supset .CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻS=\Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .(1).\text{Transp}.*151·11.*150·23.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, P.\exists !CʻP\cap pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻCʻQ.\supset .(S).S{\sim}\in Q\,\overline{\,\text{smor}\,}\,P.\\ [*151·12] &amp;\supset .{\sim}(Q\,\,\text{smor}\,\,P)\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7579.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.394ex; width: 103.71ex; height: 17.919ex;" id="img_images_7579.svg"></span></p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_612">[Pg 612]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_B_III">SECTION B.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">ON SECTIONS, SEGMENTS, STRETCHES, AND DERIVATIVES.</span></h2>
</div>


<p>In this section, our chief topic will be <i>sections</i> and
<i>segments</i>. This topic will occupy <a href="#_211" class="pginternal">*211</a>, <a href="#_212" class="pginternal">*212</a> and <a href="#_213" class="pginternal">*213</a>, and
<a href="#_210" class="pginternal">*210</a> will consist of propositions whose chief utility lies in their
application to segments. In <a href="#_214" class="pginternal">*214</a>, we shall consider Dedekindian
series, which are intimately connected with segments, owing to the
fact that one of the chief propositions in the subject is that
the series of segments of a series is Dedekindian. In <a href="#_215" class="pginternal">*215</a>, we
shall consider "stretches," which consist of any consecutive piece
of a series, and are constituted by the product of an upper and
lower section. Finally, in <a href="#_216" class="pginternal">*216</a>, we shall consider the derivative
of a series, or of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_379"> contained in a series: the
former is the series of limit-points of the series, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻ\text{lt}_P\)" src="images/7396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.041ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7396.svg_2">, the latter is the class of
limits of existent sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP\)" src="images/6836.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.739ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6836.svg_14">, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{lt}_Pʻʻ\text{Cl ex}ʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)\)" src="images/7580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.497ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7580.svg">.</p>

<p>A class is called a <i>section</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_422"> when it is contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_117">, and contains all the predecessors of its members, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_380"> is a section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_423"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset CʻP.Pʻʻ\alpha\subset \alpha\)" src="images/7581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.574ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7581.svg">.
Thus a section consists of all the field up to a certain point.
It may consist of all the predecessors of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_175">, <i>i.e.</i> it
may be of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/6881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6881.svg_8">; or again, it may
consist of these together with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_176">, in which case it is of the
form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup {℩}ʻx\)" src="images/7582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.874ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7582.svg">; or again, it may be not
definable by means of a single sequent or maximum, but be of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_14">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_381"> is a class without a limit or maximum.
The class of sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_424"> is denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg">. A
section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_5"> will be called an "upper section" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_425">.</p>

<p>The idea of a <i>segment</i> is slightly less general than that of a
<i>section</i>. We define a segment of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_426"> as any class of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_15">, <i>i.e.</i> as any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg">.
Provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_427"> is transitive, segments are contained among sections.
But even in a series sections are not, in general, contained among
segments: if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_428"> is a series, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_177"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_118">
which has no immediate successor, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup {℩}ʻx\)" src="images/7582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.874ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7582.svg_1">
will be a section but not a segment.</p>

<p>If a segment has a maximum, it must also have a sequent. Segments which
have no maximum form a specially important class of segments: these are
classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_382"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7585.svg">; they form the class
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_613">[Pg 613]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.203ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7586.svg">.</p>

<p>The properties of sections and segments considered as classes of
classes are many and various: they are considered in <a href="#_211" class="pginternal">*211</a>. In <a href="#_212" class="pginternal">*212</a>,
we pass to the consideration of the series of sections and segments.
These series are <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7587.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.99ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7587.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP_{\in}\)" src="images/7588.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.946ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7588.svg"> (cf.
<a href="#_170" class="pginternal">*170</a>). The series of such segments as have no maximum is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7589.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.356ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7589.svg">. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \varsigma ʻP&amp;=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP_{\in }      \quad\text{Df},\\ \text{sgm}ʻP&amp;=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)  \quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/7590.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.232ex; width: 29.649ex; height: 5.595ex;" id="img_images_7590.svg"></span>
It then appears that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \varsigma ʻP_{*}=\text{sgm}ʻP_{*}=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{sect}ʻP, \]" src="images/7591.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 30.072ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_7591.svg"></span>
so that it is unnecessary to introduce a special notation for the
series of sections.</p>

<p>Whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_429"> is connected and transitive,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP_{\in}\)" src="images/7588.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.946ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7588.svg_1"> turns out to be
equivalent to logical inclusion combined with diversity (with the field
limited to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_1">). That is to say (<a href="#_212_23" class="pginternal">*212·23</a>),
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex} .\supset .\varsigma ʻP=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta}\{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta\}. \]" src="images/7592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.697ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7592.svg"></span>
Hence it follows (<a href="#_212_24" class="pginternal">*212·24</a>) that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :P_{*}\in \text{connex} .\supset .\varsigma ʻP_{*}=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{sect}ʻP.\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta\}· \]" src="images/7593.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.661ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7593.svg"></span>
We have also (<a href="#_211_6" class="pginternal">*211·6</a><a href="#_211_17" class="pginternal">·17</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp P_{*}\in \text{connex} .\alpha ,\beta \text{sect}ʻP.\supset :\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset \alpha \]" src="images/7594.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.065ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7594.svg"></span>
Hence it easily follows that whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg_4"> is connected,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg"> is a series. Similarly <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg"> will be a
series if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_430"> is transitive and connected.</p>

<p>The fact of connection, which is required in order that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigmaʻP\)" src="images/7597.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7597.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg_1"> may be a series, results from
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha ,\beta \in \text{sect}ʻP.&amp;\supset :\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset \alpha \\ \text{or}\quad  \alpha ,\beta \in \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.&amp;\supset :\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset \alpha . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/7598.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 36.491ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_7598.svg"></span>
In order to deal with such cases generally, we study, in a preliminary
number (<a href="#_210" class="pginternal">*210</a>), the consequences to be deduced from the hypothesis
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\supset _{\alpha ,\beta }:\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset \alpha . \]" src="images/7599.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 30.03ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_7599.svg"></span>
We find that, with this hypothesis, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} (\alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta ), \]" src="images/7600.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.231ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7600.svg"></span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\kappa\)" src="images/7601.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.263ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7601.svg"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \subset\text{Cl}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/7602.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.716ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7602.svg">
(<a href="#_210_13" class="pginternal">*210·13</a>), and thus in the same circumstances
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\kappa\)" src="images/7603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.456ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7603.svg"> is a series (<a href="#_210_14" class="pginternal">*210·14</a>).</p>

<p>The interesting point about such series is their behaviour with
regard to limits. Assuming that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_123"> is not a unit class (so
as to insure <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists} !Q)\)" src="images/7604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.557ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_7604.svg">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_61"> is any sub-class
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_124">, the logical product <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7605.svg"> is the minimum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_62"> if it is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_63"> (<a href="#_210_21" class="pginternal">*210·21</a>), and the
lower limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_64"> if it is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_125"> but not
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_65"> (<a href="#_210_23" class="pginternal">*210·23</a>). Similarly <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_9"> is the maximum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_66"> if it is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_67"> (<a href="#_210_211" class="pginternal">*210·211</a>), and the upper
limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_68"> if it is not a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_69"> but is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_126"> (<a href="#_210_231" class="pginternal">*210·231</a>). Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_127"> is such that,
whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \subset \kappa\)" src="images/7606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.639ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_7606.svg">, we have<span class="pagenum" id="Page_614">[Pg 614]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda \in \kappa\)" src="images/7607.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.807ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7607.svg">,
it follows that every sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_128"> has either a maximum or a
limit, <i>i.e.</i> the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\kappa\)" src="images/7603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.456ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7603.svg_1">
is Dedekindian. Now each of the three classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.203ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7586.svg_1"> verifies
this condition, <i>i.e.</i> the sum of any sub-class of any one of
these classes belongs to the class in question (<a href="#_211_63" class="pginternal">*211·63</a><a href="#_211_64" class="pginternal">·64</a><a href="#_211_65" class="pginternal">·65</a>). (This
holds without any hypothesis as to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_431">.) Hence we arrive at the
result that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg_2"> (<i>i.e.</i> the series of sections)
is a Dedekindian series whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg_5"> is connected and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_432"> is
not null (<a href="#_214_32" class="pginternal">*214·32</a>), while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_1"> (<i>i.e.</i> the series of
segments) is a Dedekindian series whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_433"> is transitive and
connected and not null (<a href="#_214_33" class="pginternal">*214·33</a>), and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻP\)" src="images/7608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.964ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_7608.svg"> (the series of
segments having no maximum) is a Dedekindian series whenever it exists
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_434"> is connected (<a href="#_214_34" class="pginternal">*214·34</a>). These propositions are important, and
are the source of much of the utility of sections and segments.</p>

<p>For many purposes, especially in ordinal arithmetic, it is necessary
to consider sections not as classes, but as series. That is to say, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_383"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_2">, we want to deal with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f} \alpha\)" src="images/7609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7609.svg"> rather than with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_384">. The series of
all such terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x0294f} \alpha\)" src="images/7610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7610.svg"> might be supposed to
be <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x0294f} ^{;}\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.403ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_7611.svg">. But here a limitation is
necessary owing to the fact that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg_15"> exists, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_73"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻBʻP\)" src="images/7612.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.932ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7612.svg"> are both sections, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x0294f} \Lambda\)" src="images/7613.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.627ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7613.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x0294f} \iota ʻBʻP\)" src="images/7614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.989ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7614.svg"> are both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg_9">, so
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x0294f} ^{;}\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.403ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_7611.svg_1"> will be a relation which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_718.svg_10"> will have to itself. In order to avoid this, we first
exclude <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_74"> from the sections to be considered, and thus put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}^{;}(\varsigma ʻP_{*})\unicode{x0294f}(-\iota ʻ\Lambda )    \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/7615.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.387ex; height: 2.333ex;" id="img_images_7615.svg"></span>
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/7616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7616.svg"> is the series of segments considered as series.
Provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_12"> is a series, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma}\)" src="images/7617.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7617.svg">
holds between any two members <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_224"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_71"> of its field
when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, R.Q\neq R\)" src="images/7618.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 13.15ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_7618.svg">. The subject
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/7616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7616.svg_1"> is considered in <a href="#_213" class="pginternal">*213</a>; the utility of the
propositions of this number will not appear until we come to ordinal
arithmetic.</p>

<p>The subject of Dedekindian relations is next considered (<a href="#_214" class="pginternal">*214</a>). We
define a Dedekindian relation as one such that every class has either
a maximum or a sequent. A Dedekindian series must have a first and a
last term, since the first term must be the sequent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_75">, and
the last must be the maximum of the field. A Dedekindian series may be
discrete, or compact (<i>i.e.</i> such that there is a term between
any two, <i>i.e.</i> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg_2">), or partly one and partly
the other. A finite series must be Dedekindian: a well-ordered series
is Dedekindian if it has a last term. But the chief importance of the
Dedekindian property is in connection with compact series. A compact
Dedekindian series is said to possess "Dedekindian continuity"; such
series have many important properties. They are a wider class than
series possessing Cantorian continuity; these latter will be considered
in Section F of this Part.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_615">[Pg 615]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_210">
*210. ON SERIES OF CLASSES GENERATED BY THE RELATION
OF INCLUSION.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *210.</p>

<p>In the theory of series it frequently happens that we have to deal
with a class of classes such that, of any two, one is contained in the
other. <i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_129"> is the class of classes, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\supset _{\alpha ,\beta }:\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset \alpha . \]" src="images/7599.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 30.03ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_7599.svg_1"></span></p>

<p>Instances of this are afforded by the various classes of sections, to
be considered in <a href="#_211" class="pginternal">*211</a>. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_130"> fulfils the above condition,
the classes composing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_131"> can be arranged in a series by the
relation of inclusion (combined with inequality), <i>i.e.</i> by the
relation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} (\alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta ), \]" src="images/7619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.425ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7619.svg"></span>
or, what comes to the same,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} (\alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\exists !\beta -\alpha ). \]" src="images/7620.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.308ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7620.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_435"> is any relation such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \subset \text{Cl}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/7621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.716ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7621.svg">,
the above relation of inclusion is equal to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\kappa . \]" src="images/7622.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.085ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7622.svg"></span>
(For the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_6">, see <a href="#_170" class="pginternal">*170</a>.) Thus under the
above circumstances, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\kappa\)" src="images/7603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.456ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7603.svg_2"> is a
series, whatever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_436"> may be.</p>

<p>The importance of such relations of inclusion, as generators of series,
is in connection with the existence of maxima and minima or limits. If
we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} (\alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\exists !\beta -\alpha ). \]" src="images/7623.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.115ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7623.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_132"> satisfies the above condition, then if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\subset \kappa\)" src="images/7624.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.639ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_7624.svg"> and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda \in \kappa\)" src="images/7607.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.807ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7607.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_10"> is
the maximum or the upper limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_70"> with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_225">,
according as <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_11"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_71"> or not. Similarly
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda \in \kappa\)" src="images/7625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.884ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7625.svg">, p<img alt="" data-tex="\(ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7626.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 2.676ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7626.svg"> is the minimum or lower
limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_72">, according as <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7605.svg_1"> is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_73"> or not. Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_133"> is such that the sum of any
sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_134"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_135">, every sub-class of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_136"> has either a maximum or an upper limit; and if the product
of every sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_137"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_138">, every
sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_139"> has either a minimum or a lower limit.</p>

<p>In order that every sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_140"> should have a minimum or
a lower limit, it is sufficient that the sum of every sub-class of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_141"> should be a member<span class="pagenum" id="Page_616">[Pg 616]</span> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_142">. For, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_74"> is
any sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_143">, consider those members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_144"> which
are contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7605.svg_2">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda \]" src="images/7627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.252ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7627.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda \in \kappa\)" src="images/7625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.884ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7625.svg_1">, the sum of these classes = <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7605.svg_3">,
and is the lower limit or minimum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_145">. But if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda{\sim}\in \kappa\)" src="images/7628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.644ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7628.svg">, then every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_146"> which is not
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ(\kappa \cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda )\)" src="images/7629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.431ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7629.svg"> is also not
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7605.svg_4">, and is therefore not contained in some
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_75">. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ(\kappa \cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda )\)" src="images/7629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.431ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7629.svg_1">
is the lower limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_76">.</p>

<p>It is owing to these propositions that segments of series are of such
great importance in connection with limits.</p>

<p>The hypothesis that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \subset \kappa\)" src="images/7606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.639ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_7606.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7605.svg_5"> is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_147">, will usually fail to be verified in the case when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda =\Lambda\)" src="images/7630.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.906ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_7630.svg">, since in this case <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda =\text{V}\)" src="images/7631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.528ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7631.svg">. But
all the results desired can be obtained from the hypothesis that, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \subset \kappa\)" src="images/7606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.639ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_7606.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\((pʻ\lambda \cap sʻ\kappa )\in \kappa\)" src="images/7632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.88ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7632.svg">.
This hypothesis is equivalent to the other except in the case of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_76">, in which case it requires <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa \in \kappa\)" src="images/7633.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.791ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7633.svg">, which
is much more often verified than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\in \kappa\)" src="images/7634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.766ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_7634.svg">, which was
required by the other hypothesis.</p>

<p>The principal propositions of this number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\colon\alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\supset _{\alpha ,\beta }:\alpha     \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset \alpha \colon\ldotp \supset \colon\ldotp \alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\supset :\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta .\equiv .\exists !\beta -\alpha\)" src="images/7635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 74.058ex; height: 2.27ex;" id="img_images_7635.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Q=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} (\alpha ,\beta \in \kappa .\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta ).\supset .Q\in \text{trans}\cap \text{Rl}ʻJ\)" src="images/7636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.216ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_7636.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·1·11.\supset .Q\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/7637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 29.516ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_7637.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·12.\kappa \subset \text{Cl}ʻCʻP.\supset .Q=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\kappa\)" src="images/7638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.402ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7638.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·12.\kappa {\sim}\in 1.\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{Q}ʻ\lambda =\lambda \cap \kappa \cap \iota ʻpʻ(\lambda \cap \kappa )\)" src="images/7639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 56.755ex; height: 4.132ex;" id="img_images_7639.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·2.\lambda \subset \kappa .pʻ\lambda \in \lambda .\supset .\text{min}_{Q}ʻ\lambda =pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 47.569ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_7640.svg"></p>

<p><a href="#_210_211" class="pginternal">*210·211</a> gives an analogous proposition for <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_12"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{max}_{Q}\)" src="images/7641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.664ex; height: 1.663ex;" id="img_images_7641.svg">. We shall not here mention such analogues, unless
for some special reason.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·2.\lambda \subset \kappa .pʻ\lambda -\lambda .\supset .pʻ\lambda =\text{prec}_{Q}ʻ\lambda =\text{tl}_{Q}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.829ex; width: 56.607ex; height: 2.526ex;" id="img_images_7642.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·232.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·2.\lambda \subset \kappa .pʻ\lambda \in \kappa .\supset .pʻ\lambda =\text{limin}_Pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/7643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 48.747ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7643.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·251.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·2:\lambda \subset \kappa .\supset _{\lambda }.sʻ\lambda     \in \kappa :\supset :\lambda \in \kappa .\supset .sʻ\lambda (\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{Q}ʻ\lambda \cup \overrightarrow{\text{seq}} _{Q}ʻ\lambda )\)" src="images/7644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.829ex; width: 71.123ex; height: 3.811ex;" id="img_images_7644.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·252.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :&amp;\text{Hp} *210·2:\lambda \subset \kappa .\supset _{\lambda }.pʻ\lambda \cap sʻ\kappa :\supset :\\ &amp;\lambda \subset \kappa .\supset .pʻ\lambda \cap sʻ\lambda \in (\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{Q}ʻ\lambda \cup \overrightarrow{\text{prec}} _{Q}ʻ\lambda     ).pʻ\lambda \cap sʻ\kappa =\text{limin}_{Q}ʻ\lambda\end{align}\]" src="images/7645.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.061ex; width: 67.948ex; height: 7.252ex;" id="img_images_7645.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·254.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·251.\supset .(\lambda ).\lambda \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{Q}\)" src="images/7646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.829ex; width: 46.499ex; height: 2.526ex;" id="img_images_7646.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·26.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·2.\lambda \subset \kappa .pʻ\lambda {\sim}\in \lambda .&amp;sʻ(\kappa \cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda )\in \kappa .\supset .\\ &amp;sʻ(\kappa \cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda )=\text{prec}_{Q}ʻ\lambda\end{align}\]" src="images/7647.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.168ex; width: 58.185ex; height: 5.467ex;" id="img_images_7647.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·28.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :\text{Hp} *210·2.sʻʻ&amp;\text{Cl}ʻ\kappa \subset \kappa .\supset .\\ &amp;(\lambda ).\lambda \in (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{Q})(\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{prec}_{Q})\end{align}\]" src="images/7648.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.168ex; width: 66.914ex; height: 5.467ex;" id="img_images_7648.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_148"> is a class of not less than two classes such that,
of any two of its members, one must be contained in the other, and if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_226"> is the relation<span class="pagenum" id="Page_617">[Pg 617]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta\)" src="images/7649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 12.497ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_7649.svg">
confined to members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_149">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_227"> is a series (<a href="#_210_12" class="pginternal">*210·12</a>)
in which, provided the sums of sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_150"> are always
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_151">, every class has either a maximum or an upper
limit, and every class has either a minimum or a lower limit (<a href="#_210_28" class="pginternal">*210·28</a>).</p>

<p>The reader will observe that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_385">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \in \kappa.\supset _{\alpha ,\beta }:\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset\alpha\)" src="images/7650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 26.947ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_7650.svg">,
any <i>finite</i> sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_152"> must contain its own sum and
product as members. For example, if we have two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_386"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_193">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset \beta\)" src="images/7651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_7651.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =pʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha\cup \iota ʻ\beta )\)" src="images/7652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.281ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7652.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =sʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup \iota ʻ\beta)\)" src="images/7653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.036ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7653.svg">; if we have three
classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_387">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_194">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_47">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset \beta.\beta \subset \gamma\)" src="images/7654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.278ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_7654.svg">,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =pʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup \iotaʻ\beta \cup \iota ʻ\gamma )\)" src="images/7655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.182ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7655.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma =sʻ(\iota ʻ\alpha \cup\iota ʻ\beta \cup \iota ʻ\gamma )\)" src="images/7656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.886ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7656.svg">;
and so on. Thus the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\kappa \subset \kappa\)" src="images/7657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.019ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7657.svg">
is only required in order to enable us to deal with infinite
sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_153">.</p>
