have <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa =\text{V}\)" src="images/7706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.436ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7706.svg">. But the hypothesis of <a href="#_210_252" class="pginternal">*210·252</a> only

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_210_281">*210·281</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :\text{Hp}*210·2.pʻʻ&amp;\text{Cl}ʻ\kappa \subset \kappa .\supset .\\ &amp;(\lambda ).\lambda \in (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{Q})\cap (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{prec}_{Q})\end{align}\]" src="images/7720.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.168ex; width: 69.506ex; height: 5.467ex;" id="img_images_7720.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_210_282">*210·282</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}*210·2:\lambda &amp;\subset \kappa .\supset _{\lambda }.pʻ\lambda \cap sʻ\kappa \in \kappa :\supset .\\ &amp;(\lambda ).\lambda \in (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{Q})\cap (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}_{Q}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{prec}_{Q})\end{align}\]" src="images/7721.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.168ex; width: 68.983ex; height: 5.467ex;" id="img_images_7721.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus when either of the hypotheses of <a href="#_210_281" class="pginternal">*210·281</a><a href="#_210_282" class="pginternal">·282</a> is fulfilled, the
series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_228"> is Dedekindian both upwards and downwards.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·29.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Hp}*210·251.\supset .(\lambda ).\lambda \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{limax}_P\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{limin}_P \quad[*210·28.*207·44]\)" src="images/7722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.566ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7722.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*210·291.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :\text{Hp}*210·252.\supset .(\lambda ).\lambda \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{limax}_P\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{limin}_P\\ &amp;[*210·282.*207·44]\end{align}\]" src="images/7723.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 70.435ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_7723.svg"></span></p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_624">[Pg 624]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_211">
*211. ON SECTIONS AND SEGMENTS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *211.</p>

<p>The theory of the modes of separation of a series into two classes,
one of which wholly precedes the other, and which together make up the
whole series, is of fundamental importance. When one out of a pair
of such classes is given, the other is the rest of the series; we
may therefore, for most purposes, confine our attention to that one
of the two classes which comes first in the serial order. Any class
which can be the first of such a pair we shall call a <i>section</i>
of our series. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_438"> is the series, we shall denote the class of
its sections by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_3">." If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_388"> is a section of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_439">, we shall call <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP - \alpha\)" src="images/7724.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.99ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7724.svg"> (which is the second class of our
pair) the <i>complement</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_389">. The class of complements of
sections is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (CʻP -)ʻʻ\text{sect}ʻP, \]" src="images/7725.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.477ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7725.svg"></span>
which is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/7726.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7726.svg"> (<a href="#_211_75" class="pginternal">*211·75</a>).</p>

<p>In order that a class may be a section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_440">, it is necessary and
sufficient that it should be contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_119"> and should contain
all its own predecessors; thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{sect}ʻP = \hat{\alpha}  (\alpha  \subset  CʻP . Pʻʻ\alpha  \subset  \alpha ) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/7727.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.949ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_7727.svg"></span>
We have also, by *90·23,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{sect}ʻP = \hat{\alpha}  (\alpha  = P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha ) \quad(*211·13). \]" src="images/7728.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.204ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_7728.svg"></span></p>

<p>Among sections, a specially important class consists of classes which
are composed of all the predecessors of some class, <i>i.e.</i> classes
of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/7729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.695ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7729.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> classes which are members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in}\)" src="images/7730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7730.svg">. Whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_441"> is transitive, <img alt="" data-tex="\(PʻʻPʻʻ\beta\subset Pʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/7731.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.82ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7731.svg">;
hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/7729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.695ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7729.svg_1"> is a section according to
the above definition. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_442"> is a series, the complement of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/7729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.695ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7729.svg_2"> (when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_195"> exists and is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_120">) is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{max}} _Pʻ\beta  \cup  pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta . \]" src="images/7732.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.508ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7732.svg"></span></p>

<p>The members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in}\)" src="images/7730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7730.svg_1"> are called <i>segments</i> of the
series generated by P. In a series in which every sub-class has a
maximum or a sequent, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in} = \overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7733.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7733.svg">
(<a href="#_211_38" class="pginternal">*211·38</a>), <i>i.e.</i> the predecessors of a class are always the
predecessors of a single term, namely the maximum of the class if it
exists,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_625">[Pg 625]</span> or the sequent if no maximum exists. But if there are classes
which have neither a maximum nor a sequent, the predecessors of such
classes are not coextensive with the predecessors of any single term.
Thus in general the series of segments will be larger than the original
series. For example, if our original series is of the type of the
series of rationals in order of magnitude, the series of segments is
of the type of the series of real numbers, <i>i.e.</i> the type of the
continuum.</p>

<p>Among segments, a specially important class consists of those which
have no maximum. In this case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_390"> is such a segment, we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7734.svg">; and since (provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_443"> is transitive)
we also have, for all segments, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha \subset \alpha\)" src="images/7735.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7735.svg">, the
segments having no maximum are those for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7736.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.327ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7736.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> they are the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in} \dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7737.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.203ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7737.svg">.
In compact series, all segments belong to this latter class, but
in general only those segments belong to it which correspond to a
"Häufungsstelle." In all cases in which the existence of a limit is not
known, the segment fulfils the functions of a limit; that is to say,
in those places in the series where a limit might be expected, we have
a segment having no limit or maximum, which takes the same place in
the series of segments as would be taken by the limit in the original
series if the limit existed. Segments having no limit or maximum are
limiting points in the series of segments, and every class of segments
which has no maximum in the series of segments has a limit in that
series.</p>

<p>We have thus three classes to deal with, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;(1)\quad \text{sect}ʻP,\\ &amp;(2) \quad\text{D}ʻP_{\in },\\ &amp;(3) \quad\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in } \dot{\cap}  I). \end{aligned} \]" src="images/7738.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.702ex; width: 15.986ex; height: 8.536ex;" id="img_images_7738.svg"></span>
Of these the second is contained in the first when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_444"> is transitive
(<a href="#_211_15" class="pginternal">*211·15</a>), and the third is contained in the first and second
(<a href="#_211_14" class="pginternal">*211·14</a>). The second consists of those members of the first which have
either a sequent or no maximum (<a href="#_211_32" class="pginternal">*211·32</a>); the third consists of those
members of the first which have no maximum (<a href="#_211_41" class="pginternal">*211·41</a>). If every member
of the third class has a limit, <i>i.e.</i> if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{D}ʻ(P_{\in } \dot{\cap}  I) \subset  \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}, \]" src="images/7739.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.044ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7739.svg"></span>
then every class has either a sequent or a maximum, <i>i.e.</i> the
series is Dedekindian; and the converse also holds (<a href="#_211_47" class="pginternal">*211·47</a>).</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_445"> is connected, of any two sections one must be contained
in the other (<a href="#_211_6" class="pginternal">*211·6</a>). Moreover, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_77"> is contained in any
one of the three classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_3">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in } \dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.203ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7740.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_13"> is a member
of that class (<a href="#_211_63" class="pginternal">*211·63</a><a href="#_211_64" class="pginternal">·64</a><a href="#_211_65" class="pginternal">·65</a>). Hence the propositions of <a href="#_210" class="pginternal">*210</a> become
available. It is thus that the existence of limits in series of
segments or sections is proved: the maximum or upper limit of any
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_78"> consisting of segments or sections is <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg_14">,
and the minimum or lower limit is the sum of the segments that are
contained in every <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_79">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_626">[Pg 626]</span></p>

<p>We begin, in this number, with elementary properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_5">. The sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_446"> are the segments of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}\)" src="images/6646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.44ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6646.svg_6">
(<a href="#_211_13" class="pginternal">*211·13</a>) and the sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_13"> (<a href="#_211_17" class="pginternal">*211·17</a>). We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .CʻP \in  \text{sect}ʻP.sʻ\text{sect}ʻP=CʻP\)" src="images/7741.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 34.822ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7741.svg"></p>

<p>We then proceed to the elementary properties of segments, <i>i.e.</i>
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_4"> (<a href="#_211_3" class="pginternal">*211·3</a>—<a href="#_211_38" class="pginternal">·38</a>). We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\subset \text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.389ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7742.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·301.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{D}ʻP \in  \text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.733ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7743.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·302.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P \in  \text{Ser}.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP=\text{sect}ʻP\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\)" src="images/7744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.519ex; width: 42.78ex; height: 3.709ex;" id="img_images_7744.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·351.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P \in  \text{Ser}.\supset .\text{sect}ʻP - \text{D}ʻP_{\in }=\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻʻ(CʻP - \text{D}ʻP_{1})\)" src="images/7745.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.423ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7745.svg"></p>

<p>We then proceed to elementary properties of segments having no maximum,
<i>i.e.</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.203ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7586.svg_2"> (<a href="#_211_4" class="pginternal">*211·4</a>—<a href="#_211_47" class="pginternal">·47</a>). We
have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P \in  \text{trans}.\supset .\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)=\text{D}ʻP_{\in } - \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\)" src="images/7746.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.018ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7746.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\Lambda \in \text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I).\Lambda \in \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.\Lambda \in \text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7747.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.242ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7747.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·451.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\in \text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I).\supset .x{\sim}\in \text{ᗡ}ʻ(P\dot{-} P^{2})\)" src="images/7748.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.298ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7748.svg"></p>

<p>Our next set of propositions (<a href="#_211_5" class="pginternal">*211·5</a>—<a href="#_211_553" class="pginternal">·553</a>) is concerned with compact
series, <i>i.e.</i> with the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg_3">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}=P.\supset .\text{D}ʻP_{\in }=\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7749.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.954ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7749.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·551.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P \in  \text{Ser}.\supset :\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}=\Lambda .\equiv .P=P^{2}\)" src="images/7750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.519ex; width: 48.944ex; height: 2.406ex;" id="img_images_7750.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> a series is compact when, and only when, no class has both
a maximum and a sequent.</p>

<p>We come next to the application of the propositions of <a href="#_210" class="pginternal">*210</a>
(<a href="#_211_56" class="pginternal">*211·56</a>—<a href="#_211_692" class="pginternal">·692</a>). These propositions proceed from</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·56.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P \in  \text{connex} .\alpha ,\beta  \in  \text{sect}ʻP.\supset :\alpha \subset \beta .\lor.\beta \subset Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.504ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7751.svg"></p>

<p>(Here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}} \in \text{connex}\)" src="images/7752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 12.946ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_7752.svg">" may be substituted in the
hypothesis: cf. <a href="#_211_561" class="pginternal">*211·561</a>.) The propositions of this set, which are very
important, have been already mentioned.</p>

<p>Our next set of propositions (<a href="#_211_7" class="pginternal">*211·7</a>—<a href="#_211_762" class="pginternal">·762</a>) are concerned with the
complements of sections and segments. Some of these propositions have
been already mentioned; others of importance are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·7.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP.\supset .CʻP-\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/7753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.056ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7753.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·703.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P \in  \text{connex} .\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻCʻP.\supset .\exists !pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 50.666ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7754.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·726.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P \in  \text{connex} \cap &amp;\text{Rl}ʻJ.\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{\text{prec}} _{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha ).\overrightarrow{\text{seq}} _{P}ʻ\alpha     =\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha )\end{align}\]" src="images/7755.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.929ex; width: 73.113ex; height: 6.989ex;" id="img_images_7755.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·727.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{connex} \cap \text{Rl}ʻJ.\alpha \in &amp;\text{sect}ʻP.\supset :\\ &amp;\text{E}!\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha .\equiv .\text{E}!\text{limin}_Pʻ(CʻP-\alpha )\end{align}\]" src="images/7756.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 63.201ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_7756.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·728.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{connex} \cap &amp;\text{Rl}ʻJ.\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP:{\sim}\text{E}!\text{max}_{P}ʻ\alpha .\lor.\\ &amp;{\sim}\text{E}!\text{min}_{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha ):\supset .\overrightarrow{\text{limax}} _{P}ʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{\text{limin}} _{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha )\end{align}\]" src="images/7757.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.957ex; width: 72.647ex; height: 7.045ex;" id="img_images_7757.svg"></span></p>

<p>The remaining propositions are mainly occupied with
relation-arithmetic. The most important of them is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·82.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\colon P\in \text{Ser}.&amp;Q\in \text{D}ʻP\unicode{x0294f}.\supset \colon\ldotp \\ &amp;CʻQ\in \text{sect}ʻP.\equiv :(\exists R).P=Q\unicode{x2909}R.\lor.(\exists x).P=Q\unicode{x21f8} x:\\ &amp;\equiv :(\exists R).P=Q\unicode{x2909}R.\lor.P=Q\unicode{x21f8} Bʻ\breve{P}\end{align}\]" src="images/7758.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.865ex; width: 64.707ex; height: 8.862ex;" id="img_images_7758.svg"></span></p>

<p>That is, given any series contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_447">, if something can be added
to make it into <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_448">, its field is a section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_449">, and vice versa.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*160·1.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset .CʻQ\uparrow CʻR\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\\ [*200·32]  &amp; \supset .CʻQ\cap CʻR=\Lambda :\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7810.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 50.934ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_7810.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_6">.
This is to be compared with two other classes, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_7">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg">. The members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_8"> which
do not belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_7"> are those which have a maximum
but no sequent, <i>i.e.</i> (if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_451"> is a series), those classes which
consist of a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_178"> together with all its predecessors, where x
has no immediate successor. In series in which every term except the
last has an immediate successor, <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_121"> will be the only member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP-\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7812.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.396ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7812.svg">, if the series has a last term; if
the series has no last term, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP=\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7813.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.648ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7813.svg">.</p>

<p>The members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_8"> which are not members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_1"> are those that have no sequent, <i>i.e.</i>
those that have no upper limit (for a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in}\)" src="images/7730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7730.svg_2">
which has no sequent has also no maximum). These are the members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_9"> corresponding to a "gap," <i>i.e.</i> to a
Dedekind section in which neither the earlier terms have a maximum
nor the later terms a minimum. Hence in a Dedekindian series,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }=\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7814.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7814.svg">; and conversely,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }=\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7814.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7814.svg_1">, the series is
Dedekindian. These properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_10"> are proved in
the following propositions.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_211_3">*211·3</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\subset \text{D}ʻP_{\in } \quad[*53·301.*211·11]\)" src="images/7815.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.387ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7815.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*211·302.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP=\text{sect}ʻP\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\)" src="images/7817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.519ex; width: 42.78ex; height: 3.709ex;" id="img_images_7817.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition and the two following propositions enable us
in certain cases to prove propositions concerning the relations of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_11"> without assuming that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_452">
is transitive. An example of the use of these propositions occurs
in <a href="#_211_754" class="pginternal">*211·754</a>, where the hypothesis assumes <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\in }\text{Rl}ʻJ\cap\text{connex}\)" src="images/7827.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.156ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7827.svg">.
If we used <a href="#_211_31" class="pginternal">*211·31</a> and its consequences instead of
<a href="#_211_314" class="pginternal">*211·314</a> and its consequences, the hypothesis of *211·754 would have to
assume <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/7003.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.614ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_7003.svg_1">.</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in}\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/7852.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.203ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7852.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> with those sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_453"> which
have no maximum. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_454"> is compact (<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg_4">),
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)=\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7853.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.013ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_7853.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_455">
is also a Dedekindian series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap}I)=\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7854.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.41ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7854.svg">.
This is the mark of Dedekindian continuity, since it states that, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_16"> has no maximum, there is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_179"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha=\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/7855.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.23ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7855.svg">, and this <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_180"> is the upper limit of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/6881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6881.svg_9"> has no maximum, so that the series is compact.</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with certain consequences of
the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}=P\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg_5">. This hypothesis is important because it is
the defining characteristic of compact series.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_211_5">*211·5</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P^{2}=P.\alpha =Pʻʻ\beta .\supset .\alpha =Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.433ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_7876.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*37·33.\supset \vdash :\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset .Pʻʻ\beta =PʻʻPʻʻ\beta .\\ [\text{Hp}.*13·12] &amp;\supset .\alpha =Pʻʻ\alpha :\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7877.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 44.498ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_7877.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus in compact series there is no distinction between the two sorts of
segments.</p>

<p>In the hypothesis of <a href="#_211_61" class="pginternal">*211·61</a>, it is necessary that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_456"> should be

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{P}ʻy=\iota ʻx.\overrightarrow{P}ʻz=\iota ʻy. \]" src="images/7901.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 22.662ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_7901.svg"></span>

the hypotheses of <a href="#_210" class="pginternal">*210</a>. The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{lc}}\)" src="images/5420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.795ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_5420.svg_7"> with its
field limited to sections or segments, which occurs in the following
propositions, is important, and will be considered at length in the
following number.</p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the relations
of sections and segments of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_458"> to sections and segments of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_6">. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7779.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.051ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7779.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP - \alpha \in\text{sect}ʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/7926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.593ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7926.svg">,
and vice versa. Also, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_459"> is connected, the maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_391">
(if any) is the precedent with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_460"> (<i>i.e.</i> the
sequent with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_7"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP - \alpha\)" src="images/7724.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.99ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7724.svg_1">, and the
sequent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_392"> (if any) is the minimum with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_461">
(<i>i.e.</i> the maximum with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_8">) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP -\alpha\)" src="images/7927.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.99ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7927.svg">.
Hence the relations to be proved follow easily.</p>

<p>The above hypothesis is not sufficient to secure
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{seq}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\text{min}_{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha)\)" src="images/7944.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.57ex; height: 3.548ex;" id="img_images_7944.svg">,
as may be seen by putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P=\alpha \uparrow (\alpha \cup \iota ʻx),\,\text{where}\,\exists !\alpha .x{\sim}\in \alpha . \]" src="images/7945.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.515ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7945.svg"></span>
We then have <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{connex} .Pʻʻ\alpha =\alpha .CʻP-\alpha=\iota ʻx.pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =\alpha \cup \iota ʻx\)" src="images/7946.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 59.847ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7946.svg">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha )=\iotaʻx.\overrightarrow{\text{seq}}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\Lambda\)" src="images/7947.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.616ex; height: 4.048ex;" id="img_images_7947.svg">.
It will be seen that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \uparrow (\alpha \cup \iota ʻx)\in\text{trans}\)" src="images/7948.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.825ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7948.svg">,
so that it is useless to add <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{trans}\)" src="images/7949.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 9.513ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_7949.svg"> to
the hypothesis of <a href="#_211_714" class="pginternal">*211·714</a>. A sufficient addition is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\,\unicode{x2abd}\,J\)" src="images/7950.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7950.svg">, as is proved in the following proposition.</p>

<p>We have always, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in \text{connex} .\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.373ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7958.svg">,

<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_10"> in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_464">) from the note to <a href="#_211_714" class="pginternal">*211·714</a>. secure the converse implication, it is sufficient to assume

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_211_75">*211·75</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \subset CʻP.Q=\breve{P} .\supset :\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP.\equiv .CʻP-\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻQ    \quad[*211·7]\)" src="images/7977.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.488ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7977.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*211·32.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset :\alpha \in \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.\equiv .\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP\cap (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\cup     -\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}).\\ [*211·75·726]   &amp;\equiv .CʻP-\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻQ\cap (\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{Q}\cup -\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{Q})\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7979.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.281ex; width: 79.682ex; height: 5.694ex;" id="img_images_7979.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above proposition, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \in \text{trans}\)" src="images/7980.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 9.513ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_7980.svg">" is necessary in
order that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\)" src="images/7584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.793ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7584.svg_13"> may be contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sect}ʻP\)" src="images/7583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.837ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7583.svg_13">,
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \in \text{Rl}ʻJ\)" src="images/7981.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.549ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7981.svg">" is necessary in order that "<img alt="" data-tex="\((CʻP-\alpha){\sim}\in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{Q}\)" src="images/7982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.829ex; width: 22.535ex; height: 2.526ex;" id="img_images_7982.svg">"
may imply "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha {\sim}\in\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\)" src="images/7983.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.289ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7983.svg">." Hence the
full hypothesis "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in\text{Ser}\)" src="images/7984.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.614ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_7984.svg">" becomes necessary.</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .*211·1·26.&amp;\supset \vdash .\Lambda \in \text{sect}ʻ(x\downarrow y).\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy\in \text{sect}ʻ(x\downarrow y)  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .*55·13.   &amp;\supset \vdash :x\neq y.\supset .(x\downarrow y)ʻʻ\iota ʻx=\Lambda  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .*55·13.   &amp;\supset \vdash :x=y.\supset .(x\downarrow y)ʻʻ\iota ʻx=\iota ʻx  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .(2).(3).  &amp;\supset \vdash .(x\downarrow y)ʻʻ\iota ʻx\subset \iota ʻx.\\ [*211·1]    &amp;\supset \vdash .\iota ʻx\in \text{sect}ʻ(x\downarrow y) &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .*211·1.*54·4.\supset \\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \beta \in \text{sect}ʻ(x\downarrow y).&amp;\supset :\beta =\Lambda .\lor.\beta =\iota ʻx.\lor.\beta =\iota ʻy.\lor.\beta =\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash .*55·13.      \supset \vdash :x\neq y.&amp;\supset .x\in (x\downarrow y)ʻʻ\iota ʻy-\iota ʻy\\ [*211·1]  &amp;\supset .\iota ʻy{\sim}\in \text{sect}ʻP   &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ \vdash .*51·23.  &amp; \supset \vdash :x=y.\supset .\iota ʻy=\iota ʻx   &amp;\qquad \text{(7)}\\ \vdash .(5).(6).(7).&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \beta \in \text{sect}ʻ(x\downarrow y).\supset :\beta =\Lambda .\lor.\beta =\iota ʻx.\lor.\beta =\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy  &amp;\qquad \text{(8)}\\ \vdash .(1).(4).(8).\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/8013.svg" style="vertical-align: -17.986ex; width: 94.093ex; height: 37.104ex;" id="img_images_8013.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_651">[Pg 651]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_212">
*212. THE SERIES OF SEGMENTS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *212.</p>

<p>The series of segments or sections of a series may be ordered by the
relation of inclusion, after the manner considered in <a href="#_210" class="pginternal">*210</a>. Since, as
was shown in <a href="#_211" class="pginternal">*211</a>, sections and segments have the properties assigned
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_159"> in the hypothesis of *210, the resulting series are
such that every class has either a maximum or a sequent, and either a
minimum or a precedent; <i>i.e.</i> the series of segments or sections
are Dedekindian. Most of the properties of the series of sections and
of the series of segments which have no maximum, only require that the
original relation should be connected. The properties of the series
of segments in general <img alt="" data-tex="\((\text{D}ʻP_{\in })\)" src="images/8014.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.553ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8014.svg"> require also that the
original relation should be transitive.</p>

<p>We denote the series of segments by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_2">, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \varsigma ʻP=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻP_{\in }  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.248ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8015.svg"></span></p>

<p>We then have, in virtue of <a href="#_210_13" class="pginternal">*210·13</a> and <a href="#_211_61" class="pginternal">*211·61</a>,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex} .\supset .\varsigma ʻP=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.\alpha     \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta\}\)" src="images/8016.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.068ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_8016.svg"></p>

<p>In like manner, for the series of segments which have no maximum, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{sgm}ʻP=P_{\text{lc}}\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)  \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/8017.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.649ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_8017.svg"></span>
and we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\supset .\text{sgm}ʻP=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap}     I).\alpha \subset \beta .\alpha \neq \beta\}\)" src="images/8018.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.906ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_8018.svg"></p>

<p>We do not need a special notation for the series of sections, since, in
virtue of <a href="#_211_13" class="pginternal">*211·13</a>, it is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigmaʻP_{*}\)" src="images/8019.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8019.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/8020.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 7.705ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_8020.svg">.
Thus, by <a href="#_212_23" class="pginternal">*212·23</a>,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{*}\in \text{connex} .\supset .\varsigma ʻP_{*}=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} \{\alpha ,\beta \in \text{sect}ʻP.\alpha \subset \beta .a\neq \beta\}\)" src="images/8021.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.781ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_8021.svg"></p>

<p>We begin the number with various propositions on the fields, etc. of
these relations, and on the conditions for their existence. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·132.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{D}ʻ\varsigma ʻP=\text{D}ʻP_{\in }-\iota ʻ\text{D}ʻP.\text{ᗡ}ʻ\varsigma ʻP=\text{D}ʻP_{\in }-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/8022.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 50.965ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8022.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·133.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .Cʻ\varsigma ʻP=\text{D}ʻP_{\in }.Bʻ\varsigma ʻP=\Lambda .Bʻ\text{Cnv}ʻ\varsigma ʻP=\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/8023.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 59.798ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_8023.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\equiv .\dot{\exists} !\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/8024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.858ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_8024.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_652">[Pg 652]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·152.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{sgm}ʻP=\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)-\iota ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/8025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.781ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_8025.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !\varsigma ʻP_{*}.\equiv .\exists !\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\Lambda .\equiv .\text{sect}ʻP{\sim}\in 1.\equiv .\dot{\exists} !P\)" src="images/8026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.107ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_8026.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·172.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .Cʻ\varsigma ʻP_{*}=\text{sect}ʻP.Bʻ\varsigma ʻP_{*}=\Lambda .Bʻ\text{Cnv}ʻ\varsigma ʻP_{*}=CʻP\)" src="images/8027.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 63.056ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_8027.svg"></p>

<p>Of the next set of propositions (<a href="#_212_2" class="pginternal">*212·2</a>—<a href="#_212_25" class="pginternal">·25</a>), several have already
been mentioned. An important proposition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P=(\varsigma ʻP)\unicode{x0294f}\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/8028.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.48ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_8028.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">for this shows that the series of segments contains a series similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_465">.</p>

<p>We take up next the application of the propositions of *210 to
the series of sections and segments. We show that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in\text{connex}\)" src="images/7004.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 11.316ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_7004.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻP\)" src="images/7608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.964ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_7608.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg_3"> are series
(<a href="#_212_3" class="pginternal">*212·3</a>), and that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_466"> is also transitive, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_3"> is a
series (<a href="#_212_31" class="pginternal">*212·31</a>). We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·322.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !P.\lambda \subset \text{sect}ʻP.\supset .sʻ\lambda =\text{limax}(\varsigma ʻP_{*})ʻ\lambda \)" src="images/8029.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.873ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_8029.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !P.\lambda \subset \text{sect}ʻP.\supset .pʻ\lambda \cap CʻP=\text{limin}(\varsigma ʻP_{*})ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/8030.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.801ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_8030.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">so that every class of sections has both an upper limit or maximum and
a lower limit or minimum (<a href="#_212_35" class="pginternal">*212·35</a>).</p>

<p>We then prove similar propositions for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_4"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻP\)" src="images/7608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.964ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_7608.svg_2">, except that in place of <a href="#_212_34" class="pginternal">*212·34</a> we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·431.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !&amp;P.\lambda \subset \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.\supset .\\ &amp;sʻ(\text{D}ʻP_{\in }\cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda )=\text{limin}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\lambda\end{align}\]" src="images/8031.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.34ex; width: 60.788ex; height: 5.812ex;" id="img_images_8031.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·53.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !\text{sgm}ʻP.\lambda \subset \text{D}ʻ&amp;(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I).\supset .\\ &amp;sʻ{\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda }=\text{limin}(\text{sgm}ʻP)ʻ\lambda \end{align}\]" src="images/8032.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.536ex; width: 74.258ex; height: 6.204ex;" id="img_images_8032.svg"></span></p>

<p>The reason of the difference from *212·34 is that the product of
an existent class of segments may not be a segment. Suppose, for
example, the segments are all those that contain a given term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_181">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_182"> has no immediate successor; then their logical product is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\cup \iota ʻx\)" src="images/8033.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.318ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8033.svg">, which is a section but not a
segment.</p>

<p>We have next (<a href="#_212_6" class="pginternal">*212·6</a>—<a href="#_212_667" class="pginternal">·667</a>) a number of propositions on the limits and
maxima of sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_2"> in the series
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_5">. The interest of this subject lies in its relation to
irrationals. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_396"> is a class contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_122"> and having
no limit or maximum, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg"> is contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/8035.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.05ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8035.svg">, and has a limit in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_6">. We may call
this limit an irrational segment. There is no irrational term in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_123">, because in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_467"> there is no limit to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_397">; but the
limit, in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_7">, of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_1"> may be
called irrational, because it corresponds to no term in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_124">. It
should be observed that (as will be proved in Section F) if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_468"> is
similar to the series of rationals, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_8"> is similar to the
series of real numbers.</p>

<p>The most useful propositions in this subject are:</p>

<p><b>*212·6.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\alpha \subset CʻP.&amp;\supset .\\ &amp;\overrightarrow{\text{max}}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =\overrightarrow{\text{max}}(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha     =\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{\text{max}}_{P}ʻ\alpha \end{align}\]" src="images/8036.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.783ex; width: 74.493ex; height: 6.697ex;" id="img_images_8036.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_653">[Pg 653]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·601.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in &amp;\text{Ser}.\alpha \subset CʻP.\supset :\\ &amp;\text{E}!\text{max}_{P}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .\text{E}!\text{max}(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha     .\equiv .\text{E}!\text{max}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha \end{align}\]" src="images/8037.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.783ex; width: 64.199ex; height: 6.697ex;" id="img_images_8037.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·602.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Ser}.\dot{\exists} !P.\alpha \subset CʻP.\supset :\text{E}!\text{max}_{P}ʻ\alpha .\equiv .Pʻʻ\alpha \in \overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 58.708ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8038.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !P.\supset .\text{limax}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha =Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8039.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.182ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_8039.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·632.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\dot{\exists} !P.\alpha \subset CʻP.Pʻʻ\alpha {\sim}\in \overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP.\supset .Pʻʻ\alpha =\text{lt}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.79ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_8040.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·661.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\kappa \subset \text{D}ʻP_{\in }.\text{E}!\text{lt}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ&amp;\kappa .\supset .\\ &amp;\text{lt}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\kappa =\text{lt}(\varsigma ʻP)ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻsʻ\kappa =sʻ\kappa\end{align}\]" src="images/8041.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.783ex; width: 69.543ex; height: 6.697ex;" id="img_images_8041.svg"></span></p>

<p>This shows that every limit in the series of segments is a limit of
a class of what we may call <i>rational</i> segments (<i>i.e.</i>
segments of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/6881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6881.svg_10">), namely it is the limit
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/8042.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.136ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8042.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·667.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\text{D}ʻ\text{lt}(\varsigma ʻP)-\iota ʻ\Lambda =\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{sgm}ʻP\)" src="images/8043.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.544ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8043.svg"></p>

<p>This shows that the segments (other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_79">) which are limits
of classes of segments are the segments (other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_80">) which
have no maximum in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_469">.</p>

<p>The number ends with a set of propositions (<a href="#_212_7" class="pginternal">*212·7</a>—<a href="#_212_72" class="pginternal">·72</a>) on the
relations of the sections and segments of two correlated series. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_70"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_470"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_229">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(S_{\in }\)" src="images/4140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.642ex; height: 1.998ex;" id="img_images_4140.svg_4"> (with
its converse domain limited) is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg_4">
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻQ_{*}\)" src="images/8044.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.051ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8044.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_9"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻQ\)" src="images/8045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.063ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8045.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻP\)" src="images/7608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.964ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_7608.svg_3"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻQ\)" src="images/8046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 7.054ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_8046.svg"> (<a href="#_212_71" class="pginternal">*212·71</a><a href="#_212_711" class="pginternal">·711</a><a href="#_212_712" class="pginternal">·712</a>). Hence</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·72.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\,\,\text{smor}\,\,Q.\supset .\varsigma ʻP_{*}\,\text{smor}\,\varsigma ʻQ_{*}.\varsigma ʻP\,\text{smor}\,\varsigma ʻQ.\text{sgm}ʻP\,\text{smor}\,\text{sgm}ʻQ\)" src="images/8047.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 66.687ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_8047.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is used in the next number, and also in *271.</p>

<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda \in\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\)" src="images/8143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.783ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_8143.svg">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ sʻ\{\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda\}=pʻ\lambda . \]" src="images/8144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.293ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_8144.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·53.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in &amp;\text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !\text{sgm}ʻP.\lambda \subset \text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I).\supset .\\ &amp;sʻ\{\text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\cap \text{Cl}ʻpʻ\lambda\}=\text{limin}(\text{sgm}ʻP)ʻ\lambda \quad[*212·51·52]\end{align}\]" src="images/8145.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.536ex; width: 66.595ex; height: 6.204ex;" id="img_images_8145.svg"></span></p>

<p>The proof proceeds as in <a href="#_212_431" class="pginternal">*212·431</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*212·54.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :P\in \text{connex} .\dot{\exists} !\text{sgm}ʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;(\lambda ).\lambda \in \{\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}(\text{sgm}ʻP)\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}(\text{sgm}ʻP)\}\cap \{\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{min}(\text{sgm}ʻP)\cap\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{prec}(\text{sgm}ʻP)\}\end{align}\]" src="images/8146.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.34ex; width: 81.221ex; height: 5.812ex;" id="img_images_8146.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_212_55">*212·55</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{connex} .\supset :\lambda \in Cʻ\text{sgm}ʻ\text{sgm}ʻP.\supset .\text{E}!\text{seq}(\text{sgm}ʻP)ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/8147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.557ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8147.svg"></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with the relations of maxima,
limits and sequents in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_472"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_13"> respectively. The
series <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\)" src="images/6939.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.156ex; height: 3.19ex;" id="img_images_6939.svg_1">, which is ordinally similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_473">,
is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_14">; and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_398"> has a maximum or
limit in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_474">, the maximum or limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_2">
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_15"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻ\text{max}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.462ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8148.svg"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻ\text{lt}_Pʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.76ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8149.svg">. In this way, a series
(namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\)" src="images/6939.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.156ex; height: 3.19ex;" id="img_images_6939.svg_2">) which has the same ordinal
properties as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_475"> can be placed in a certain Dedekindian series
(namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_16">) in such a way that the classes which have
limits in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_476"> are those whose correlates have<span class="pagenum" id="Page_662">[Pg 662]</span> limits which are
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_3">, while those whose correlates
have limits which are not members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_4">
are those which have neither a maximum nor a limit in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_477">. These
relations are important in many connections. For example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_478"> is
of the type of the rationals, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_17"> is of the type of the
real numbers: <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\varsigma ʻP-\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/8150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.006ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8150.svg"> corresponds to
the irrationals, and classes contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_5">
but having a limit not belonging to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_6">
correspond to series of rationals having an irrational limit.
In the original series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_479">, there are no irrational limits;
but if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_399"> is a class in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_126"> and having no limit,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_3"> has an irrational limit in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigmaʻP\)" src="images/7597.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7597.svg_1">.</p>
