<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_668">[Pg 668]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_213">
*213. SECTIONAL RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *213.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_400"> is a section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_480">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg_5"> is
called a <i>sectional relation</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_481">; and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_401"> is a
segment of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_482">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg_6"> is called a <i>segmental
relation</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_483">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_14"> is serial, sectional
relations may be arranged in a series by the relation of inclusion
(<a href="#_213_153" class="pginternal">*213·153</a>). That is, if we call the series of sectional relations
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma}\)" src="images/7617.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7617.svg_1">, we shall so define <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/7616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7616.svg_2"> as to secure
that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_15"> is serial,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ QP_{\varsigma }R.\equiv .Q,R\in P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ(\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\Lambda ).Q\,\unicode{x2abd}\, R.Q\neq R  \quad(*213·21). \]" src="images/8197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 64.938ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8197.svg"></span>
The natural definition to take would be
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}^{;}\varsigma ʻP_{*}. \]" src="images/8198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 14.337ex; height: 2.278ex;" id="img_images_8198.svg"></span>
But this has the disadvantage that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(xBP\)" src="images/8199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.71ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_8199.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x0294f}\iota ʻx=P\unicode{x0294f}\Lambda .\Lambda ,\iota ʻx\in \text{sect}ʻP. \]" src="images/8200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.42ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8200.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\alpha =P\unicode{x0294f}\beta\)" src="images/8201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.859ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8201.svg">
does not imply <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =\beta\)" src="images/8202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_8202.svg">; and when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_484"> is serial,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}^{;}\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/8203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.403ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_8203.svg"> is not serial, because
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda} (P\unicode{x0294f}^{;}\varsigma ʻP_{*})\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/8204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.303ex; height: 2.921ex;" id="img_images_8204.svg">.
In order to obviate this inconvenience, we confine ourselves to
sections which are not null, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}^{;}(\varsigma ʻP_{*})\unicode{x0294f}(-\iota ʻ\Lambda )  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.387ex; height: 2.333ex;" id="img_images_8205.svg"></span>
With the above definition, we have (<a href="#_213_151" class="pginternal">*213·151</a><a href="#_213_152" class="pginternal">·152</a>), if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/8206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.245ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_8206.svg">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (P\unicode{x0294f})\upharpoonright Cʻ{(\varsigma ʻP_{*})\unicode{x0294f}-\iota ʻ\Lambda }\in 1\rightarrow 1 \]" src="images/8207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.968ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8207.svg"></span>
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\,\text{smor}\,(\varsigmaʻP_{*})\unicode{x0294f}(-\iota ʻ\Lambda )\)" src="images/8208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.918ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8208.svg">.</p>

<p>The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/7616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7616.svg_3"> is very useful in dealing with
well-ordered series; in this case, we have (as will be shown later)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}^{;}\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\unicode{x0294f}\text{ᗡ}ʻP\unicode{x21f8}P. \]" src="images/8209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 22.608ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8209.svg"></span>
It will be seen that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/8206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.245ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_8206.svg_1">, whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_485"> exists, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=Bʻ\breve{P} _{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 10.079ex; height: 2.925ex;" id="img_images_8210.svg"> (<a href="#_213_158" class="pginternal">*213·158</a>); and whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/3663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3663.svg_9"> exists, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda} =BʻP_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 9.95ex; height: 2.866ex;" id="img_images_8211.svg">
(<a href="#_213_155" class="pginternal">*213·155</a>).</p>

<p>We have, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}\)" src="images/8206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.245ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_8206.svg_2">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ QP_{\varsigma }R.\equiv .R\in CʻP_{\varsigma }.Q\in \text{D}ʻR_{\varsigma } \quad(*213·245). \]" src="images/8212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.821ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8212.svg"></span>
Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in CʻP_{\varsigma }.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}_{\varsigma}ʻR=\text{D}ʻR_{\varsigma }.R_{\varsigma }=P_{\varsigma}\unicode{x0294f}CʻR_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 43.491ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8213.svg">
    (<a href="#_213_246" class="pginternal">*213·246</a><a href="#_213_242" class="pginternal">·242</a>).</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_486"> is serial, the sectional relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_487"> are all relations
such that by adding something to them they become <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_488">, <i>i.e.</i>
they are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{Q} \{(\exists R).P=Q\unicode{x2909} R.\lor.(\exists x).P=Q\unicode{x21f8}x\} \quad(*213·4). \]" src="images/8214.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.313ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_8214.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_669">[Pg 669]</span>
Hence their relation-numbers are those that can be made equal to that
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_489"> by being added to. This fact is important in connection with
the theory of greater and less among relation-numbers.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are rendered complicated by the
necessity of taking account of the possibility of a section being a
unit class. This necessitates a good many propositions which are merely
lemmas; but in the end the complications mostly disappear.</p>

<p>We begin with propositions on the field, etc., of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/7616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7616.svg_4">.
We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{D}ʻP_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ(\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\Lambda -\iota ʻCʻP)\)" src="images/8215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.343ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8215.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·142.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J.\supset .CʻP_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ(\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\Lambda )\)" src="images/8216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 42.532ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8216.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\text{D}ʻP_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ(\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\Lambda )-\iota ʻP\)" src="images/8217.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.266ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8217.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·161.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\,     J.\exists !\overrightarrow{B}ʻP.\supset . P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ\text{sect}ʻP= P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ(\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\Lambda )=CʻP_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 65.824ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_8218.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·162.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\text{ᗡ}ʻP_{\varsigma }=P\unicode{x0294f}ʻʻ\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻ\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/8219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 42.78ex; height: 3.005ex;" id="img_images_8219.svg"></p>

<p>We then prove:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·17.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}.\supset .\text{Nr}ʻ\varsigma ʻP_{*}=\dot{1} \dot{+} &amp;\text{Nr}ʻP_{\varsigma }.\\ &amp;\text{Nr}ʻ(\varsigma ʻP_{*})\unicode{x0294f}(\text{ᗡ}ʻ\varsigma ʻP_{*})=\text{Nr}ʻP_{\varsigma }\end{align}\]" src="images/8220.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.351ex; width: 60.429ex; height: 5.833ex;" id="img_images_8220.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_490"> is finite, it follows from the above that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg_6">
is not similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/7616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 2.288ex; height: 2.056ex;" id="img_images_7616.svg_5">; but if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_491"> is infinite and has
a beginning and is well-ordered, we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Nr}ʻ\varsigma ʻP_{*}=\text{Nr}ʻP_{\varsigma }. \]" src="images/8221.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 18.531ex; height: 2.207ex;" id="img_images_8221.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·172.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{\text{po}},Q_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}.P \,\,\text{smor}\, \,Q.\supset .P_{\varsigma } \,\text{smor}\, Q_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8222.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 41.593ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_8222.svg"></p>

<p>We then have a set of propositions (<a href="#_213_2" class="pginternal">*213·2</a>—<a href="#_213_251" class="pginternal">·251</a>) chiefly concerned
with the sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_72">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in CʻP_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 9.848ex; height: 2.207ex;" id="img_images_8223.svg">. Besides
those already mentioned, the following are important:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\beta \in \text{sect}ʻP.R=P\unicode{x0294f}\beta .\supset .\text{sect}ʻR=\text{sect}ʻP\subset \text{Cl}ʻCʻR\)" src="images/8224.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 55.514ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8224.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·243.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\overrightarrow{P}_{\varsigma }ʻP=\text{D}ʻP_{\varsigma }\)" src="images/8225.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.511ex; width: 16.124ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8225.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*213·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}.Q,R\in CʻP_{\varsigma }.\supset :Q\in \text{D}ʻR_{\varsigma }.\lor.R\in     \text{D}Q_{\varsigma }.\lor.Q=R\)" src="images/8226.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 62.91ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8226.svg"></p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_8">, in the above
proposition, restricts <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_494"> more than is necessary for the truth
of the conclusion. What we really require is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = \dot{\Lambda}.\lor.(\exists x).x\in CʻP .\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\neq CʻP\)" src="images/8245.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.853ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_8245.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻʻCʻP\neq \iota ʻCʻP\)" src="images/8246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 19.883ex; height: 3.676ex;" id="img_images_8246.svg">. This holds
if either (1) the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_495"> does not consist of a single family,
or (2) there is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_127"> which does not have the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.33ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg_16"> to itself. Thus the only case excluded is that of a
single cyclic family. The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻʻCʻP\neq\iota ʻCʻP\)" src="images/8247.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 19.883ex; height: 3.676ex;" id="img_images_8247.svg">
may be substituted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\,J\)" src="images/8248.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8248.svg"> in most of the
subsequent propositions of this number in which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\, J\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg_9"> occurs in the hypothesis. We have,
however, preferred the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\text{po}}\,\unicode{x2abd}\,J\)" src="images/8248.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.875ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8248.svg_1">,
as it gives a more immediate application to the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in\text{Ser}\)" src="images/7984.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.614ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_7984.svg_1">,
which is the case in which the propositions of the present number are
important.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_684">[Pg 684]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_214">
*214. DEDEKINDIAN RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *214.</p>

<p>We call a relation "Dedekindian" when it is such that every class
has either a maximum or a sequent with respect to it. As a rule, the
hypothesis that a relation is Dedekindian is only important in the case
of serial relations. Dedekindian series have considerable importance,
especially in connection with limits.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_496"> is transitive, the hypothesis that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_497"> is Dedekindian
is equivalent to the hypothesis that every section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_498"> has a
maximum or a sequent (<a href="#_214_13" class="pginternal">*214·13</a>); it is also equivalent to the assumption
that every segment of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_499"> has a maximum or a sequent (<a href="#_214_131" class="pginternal">*214·131</a>),
<i>i.e.</i> to the assumption that every segment of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_500"> which has no
maximum has a limit, <i>i.e.</i> to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{D}ʻ(P_{\in }\dot{\cap} I)\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{lt}_P. \]" src="images/8350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.462ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_8350.svg"></span>
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_501"> is a series, the hypothesis that it is Dedekindian is
equivalent to the hypothesis that every segment has a sequent
(<a href="#_214_15" class="pginternal">*214·15</a>), <i>i.e.</i> to the hypothesis that the class of segments
is the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/7811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7811.svg_7"> (<a href="#_214_151" class="pginternal">*214·151</a>). If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_502"> is a
Dedekindian series, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_11">, and vice versa (<a href="#_214_14" class="pginternal">*214·14</a>).
Whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_503"> is connected and not null, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP_{*}\)" src="images/7595.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.714ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7595.svg_7"> is
a Dedekindian series (<a href="#_214_32" class="pginternal">*214·32</a>), and so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sgm}ʻP\)" src="images/7608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.964ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_7608.svg_7"> if it
exists (<a href="#_214_34" class="pginternal">*214·34</a>); whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_504"> is transitive and connected and not
null, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_18"> is a Dedekindian series (<a href="#_214_33" class="pginternal">*214·33</a>). All these
propositions have been virtually proved already: almost the only thing
new in the present number is the definition, which is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Ded}=\hat{P}\{(\alpha ).\alpha \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.734ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_8351.svg"></span></p>

<p><a href="#_214_4" class="pginternal">*214·4</a>—<a href="#_214_43" class="pginternal">·43</a> give properties of series which have Dedekindian
continuity. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P^{2}=P.P\in \text{connex} .\supset :P\in \text{Ded}.\equiv .\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}=-\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\)" src="images/8352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.519ex; width: 59.783ex; height: 2.406ex;" id="img_images_8352.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in \text{Ser}.\supset :P^{2}=P.P\in \text{Ded}.\equiv .\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}=-\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\)" src="images/8353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.519ex; width: 56.082ex; height: 2.406ex;" id="img_images_8353.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_685">[Pg 685]</span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> in a series, Dedekindian continuity is equivalent to the
assumption that the classes which have a maximum are the same as the
classes which have no sequent.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in  \text{Ser} \cap  \text{Ded}.P^{2} = P.\alpha \in  \text{sect}ʻP.\supset .\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha  = \text{limin}_Pʻ(CʻP-\alpha )\)" src="images/8354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.329ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_8354.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is important in dealing with Dedekind "cuts."</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·43.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp P\in  &amp;\text{Ser} \cap  \text{Ded}.\alpha \in  \text{sect}ʻP.\supset :\\ &amp;\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha  = \text{limin}_Pʻ(CʻP-\alpha ).\lor.\text{max}_{P}ʻ\alpha P_{1} \text{min}_{P}ʻ(CʻP-\alpha )\end{align}\]" src="images/8355.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 70.071ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_8355.svg"></span></p>

<p><a href="#_214_5" class="pginternal">*214·5</a> shows that a Dedekindian relation has a beginning and an end;
the following propositions deal with <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\dot{\cap} J\)" src="images/8356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.64ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_8356.svg"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_505"> is
Dedekindian.</p>

<p><a href="#_214_6" class="pginternal">*214·6</a> shows that a relation which is similar to a Dedekindian relation
is Dedekindian.</p>

<p>We call a relation "semi-Dedekindian" if it becomes Dedekindian by the
addition of one term at the end; the definition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{semi Ded} = \hat{P} (\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P})  \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/8357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.704ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_8357.svg"></p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*214·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Ded} = \hat{P}\{(\alpha ).\alpha \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/8358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.105ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_8358.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{semi Ded} = \hat{P} (\text{sect}ʻP-\iota ʻCʻP\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/8359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.704ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_8359.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in  \text{Ded}. \equiv  .(\alpha ).\alpha \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P} \quad[(*214·01)]\)" src="images/8360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.022ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8360.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·101.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp; \vdash :P\in  \text{Ded}. \equiv  .-\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}. \equiv  .-\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\subset     \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{lt}_P\\ &amp;[*214·1.*24·312.*207·12]\end{align}\]" src="images/8361.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 58.26ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_8361.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*21·411.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp; \vdash :P\in  \text{Ded}. \equiv  .(\alpha ).\alpha \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup     \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{lt}_P. \equiv  .(\alpha ).\alpha \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{limax}_P\\ &amp;[*214·1.*207·14·44]\end{align}\]" src="images/8362.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 62.14ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_8362.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*214·12.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp; \vdash \colon\ldotp P\in  \text{Ded}. \equiv  :\alpha \subset CʻP.\supset _{\alpha }.\alpha \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{P}\cup     \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{seq}_{P}\\ &amp;[*214·1.*205·151.*206·131]\end{align}\]" src="images/8363.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 52.965ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_8363.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_691">[Pg 691]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_215">*215. STRETCHES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *215.</p>

<p>A <i>stretch</i> of a series is any piece taken out of it, and not
having any gaps; that is, it is a class contained in the series, and
containing all terms which come between any two of its terms. Thus it
is defined as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{\alpha} (\alpha \subset CʻP.Pʻʻ\alpha \cap \breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha \subset \alpha ). \]" src="images/8411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.788ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8411.svg"></span></p>

<p>We denote the class of stretches by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{str}ʻP\)" src="images/8412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.715ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8412.svg">," where
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{str}\)" src="images/8413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.658ex; height: 1.416ex;" id="img_images_8413.svg">" stands for "stretch" or "Strecke." A stretch which
has no predecessors is a section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_506">; one which has no successors
is a section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_12">. The properties of stretches are chiefly
important in connection with compact series. In discrete series,
stretches are the same as intervals.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_507"> is transitive, stretches of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_508"> are the products of sections
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_509"> and sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_13">, <i>i.e.</i> of upper and lower
sections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_510"> (<a href="#_215_16" class="pginternal">*215·16</a>). If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_511"> is connected, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_402"> is
a lower section, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_196"> an upper section, then if the two have a
stretch <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/8414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_8414.svg"> in common, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha =Pʻʻ(\alpha \cap \beta )\cup (\alpha \cap \beta ).\beta =\breve{P} ʻʻ(\alpha \cap \beta )\cup (\alpha \cap \beta ) \quad(*215·161). \]" src="images/8415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.844ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8415.svg"></span>
A slightly more general form of this proposition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*215·165.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\in \text{connex} .\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP.\beta \in \text{sect}ʻ\breve{P} .\exists !\alpha \cap \beta .\supset .\\ &amp;\alpha =P_{*}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap \beta ).\beta =\breve{P} _{*}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap \beta ).Pʻʻ\alpha =P_{\text{po}}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap \beta ).\breve{P} ʻʻ\beta =\breve{P} _{\text{po}}ʻʻ(\alpha     \cap \beta )\end{align}\]" src="images/8416.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.838ex; width: 79.784ex; height: 6.806ex;" id="img_images_8416.svg"></span></p>

<p>A specially important case is when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_403"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_197"> have just one term
in common. In this case we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*215·166.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}.\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP.\beta \in \text{sect}ʻ\breve{P} .\alpha \cap \beta \in 1.\supset .\\ &amp;\alpha \cap \beta =\iota ʻ\text{max}_{P}ʻ\alpha =\iota ʻ\text{min}_{P}ʻ\beta\end{align}\]" src="images/8417.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.437ex; width: 50.253ex; height: 6.005ex;" id="img_images_8417.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_692">[Pg 692]</span></p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/8414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_8414.svg_1"> has more than one term, if the upper limit
or maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_404"> and the lower limit or minimum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_198">
both exist, the latter precedes the former (<a href="#_215_52" class="pginternal">*215·52</a>); if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_405">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_199"> have no common part, but together exhaust the field of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_512">, we have either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha =\text{limin}_Pʻ\beta\)" src="images/8418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.737ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8418.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha P_{1}\text{limin}_Pʻ\beta\)" src="images/8419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.16ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8419.svg">, assuming
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha .\text{E}!\text{limin}_Pʻ\beta\)" src="images/8420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.065ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8420.svg">
(<a href="#_215_54" class="pginternal">*215·54</a>). Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.663ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8421.svg"> has no immediate
successor, it must be identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{limin}_Pʻ\beta\)" src="images/8422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.057ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8422.svg">. Thus we
have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*215·543.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.&amp;\alpha \in \text{sect}ʻP.\beta \in \text{sect}ʻ\breve{P} .\alpha \cup \beta =CʻP.\alpha \cap \beta \in 0\cup 1.\\ &amp;\text{E}!\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha .\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha {\sim}\in \text{D}ʻP_{1}.\supset .\text{limax}_Pʻ\alpha =\text{limin}_Pʻ\beta\end{align}\]" src="images/8423.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.395ex; width: 68.946ex; height: 5.921ex;" id="img_images_8423.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above propositions will be useful in Section C (<a href="#_231" class="pginternal">*231</a> and <a href="#_233" class="pginternal">*233</a>).</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*215·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{str}ʻP=\hat{\alpha} (\alpha \subset CʻP.Pʻʻ\alpha \cap \breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha \subset \alpha )   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/8424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.574ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8424.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*215·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{str}ʻP.\equiv .\alpha \subset CʻP.Pʻʻ\alpha \cap \breve{P} ʻʻ\alpha \subset \alpha   \quad[(*215·01)]\)" src="images/8425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.994ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8425.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_700">[Pg 700]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_216">*216. DERIVATIVES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *216.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_406"> is any class, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_513"> is any series, the
<i>derivative</i> (or <i>first derivative</i>) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_407"> with
respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_514"> is the class of limits of existent sub-classes of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap CʻP\)" src="images/6836.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.739ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6836.svg_15">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{lt}_{p}ʻʻ\text{Cl ex}ʻ(\alpha\cap CʻP)\)" src="images/8485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.1ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8485.svg">.
That is, a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_183"> belongs to the derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_408"> if a set
of terms exists which is contained both in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_409"> and in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_128">,
and has <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_184"> for its limit. The derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_410"> with respect
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_515"> will be denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta _{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.802ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8486.svg">.</p>

<p>In general, there will be members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_411"> not contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta_{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.802ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8487.svg">, and members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta _{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.802ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8486.svg_1"> not
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_412">. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_413"> is said to be <i>dense</i> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_516">
if all its terms except the first (if there is a first) belong to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta _{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 4.802ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8486.svg_2">, that is, if all its terms except the first are
limits of existent classes contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_414">. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_415"> is said
to be <i>closed</i> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_517"> if every existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_416">
which has no maximum has a limit which belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_417">,
<i>i.e.</i> if every existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_418"> has a limit or a
maximum, and the derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_419"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_420">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_421"> is both dense and closed, it is called <i>perfect</i>.
In this case, all its terms are limits of classes chosen out of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_422">, and every class chosen out of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_423"> has a limit or
maximum in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_424">.</p>

<p>The second derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_425"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta _{p}ʻ\delta_{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.157ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8488.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta _{p}^{2}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.869ex; width: 4.802ex; height: 2.756ex;" id="img_images_8489.svg">, and so on.
(Derivatives of infinite order cannot be dealt with till a later
stage.) If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_518"> is serial, the second derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_426"> is
always contained in the first (<a href="#_216_14" class="pginternal">*216·14</a>).</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_519"> is a Dedekindian series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_427"> is closed whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta _{p}ʻ\alpha \subset \alpha\)" src="images/8490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.267ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8490.svg">. In order to secure a Dedekindian
series, it is sometimes convenient to replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_520"> by the ordinally
similar series <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}^{;}P\)" src="images/6939.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 4.156ex; height: 3.19ex;" id="img_images_6939.svg_3">, which is contained in
the Dedekindian series <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_19">. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_428"> is replaced
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_4">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_429"> is closed if
the derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_5"> with respect to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_20"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_6">. The
relation of the derivative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_430"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_521"> to the derivative of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_7"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_21"> has been treated
in <a href="#_212_6" class="pginternal">*212·6</a> and following propositions. This subject is resumed below
(<a href="#_216_5" class="pginternal">*216·5</a> ff.).</p>

<p>The derivative of the series P will be defined as the series of its
limit-points, and denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nabla ʻP\)" src="images/8491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.941ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8491.svg">. Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \nabla ʻP=P\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻ\text{lt}_{p}. \]" src="images/8492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 17.231ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8492.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_701">[Pg 701]</span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_522"> is a series, the derivative of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_431"> consists of
those members <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_185"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/4354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.414ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4354.svg_3"> which are such that members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_432"> exist in every interval which ends in <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_186">, <i>i.e.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*216·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\colon P\in \text{Ser}.\supset \colon\ldotp x\in \delta _{p}ʻ\alpha .\equiv :x\in \text{ᗡ}ʻP:yPx.\supset _{y}.\exists     !\alpha \cap \overleftarrow{P}ʻy\cap \overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/8493.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 65.696ex; height: 3.857ex;" id="img_images_8493.svg"></p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*216·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\delta _{p}ʻCʻP=\text{D}ʻ\text{lt}_{p}-\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/8494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 26.663ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_8494.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*216·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{dense}ʻP.\equiv .\alpha -\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{p}ʻ\alpha \subset \delta _{p}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.701ex; height: 4.132ex;" id="img_images_8495.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*216·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \in \text{closed}ʻP.\equiv .\text{Cl ex}ʻ(\alpha \cap CʻP)\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{limax}_{p}.\delta _{p}ʻ\alpha \subset \alpha\)" src="images/8496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 58.951ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8496.svg"></p>

<p>We prove (<a href="#_216_4" class="pginternal">*216·4</a>—<a href="#_216_412" class="pginternal">·412</a>) that the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_433"> with respect
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_523">, as regards being dense, closed, or perfect, belong to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{S} ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8497.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.622ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_8497.svg"> with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_231"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/26.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_26.svg_71"> is a correlator
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_524"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_232">.</p>

<p>We next consider the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_434"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_525"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_8"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_22"> (<a href="#_216_5" class="pginternal">*216·5</a>—<a href="#_216_56" class="pginternal">·56</a>).
The point of these propositions is that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_23"> is
Dedekindian, so that a class is closed in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_24"> if
it contains its first derivative. (It is usual to <i>define</i>
a class as closed whenever it contains its first derivative;
but this involves the tacit assumption that the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_526"> is
Dedekindian. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_527"> is the series of real numbers, this assumption
is of course verified.) We prove (<a href="#_216_52" class="pginternal">*216·52</a>) that the derivative of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_9"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_25"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻʻ(\text{Cl ex}ʻ\alpha -\text{ᗡ}ʻ\text{max}_{p})\)" src="images/8498.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 26.048ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8498.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> is the class of segments defined by such existent
sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_435"> as have no maximum; we show that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_436"> is dense, closed, or perfect in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_528"> according
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_10"> is dense, closed, or
perfect in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\varsigma ʻP\)" src="images/7596.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.973ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7596.svg_26"> (<a href="#_216_53" class="pginternal">*216·53</a><a href="#_216_54" class="pginternal">·54</a><a href="#_216_56" class="pginternal">·56</a>), and that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_437"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_11"> are closed if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8034.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8034.svg_12"> contains its first derivative (<a href="#_216_54" class="pginternal">*216·54</a>).</p>

<p>We end with various propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nabla ʻP\)" src="images/8491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.941ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8491.svg_1"> (<a href="#_216_6" class="pginternal">*216·6</a>—<a href="#_216_621" class="pginternal">·621</a>), of which
the chief is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*216·611.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P\in \text{Ser}.\dot{\exists} !\nabla ʻP.\supset .Cʻ\nabla ʻP=CʻP-\text{ᗡ}ʻP_{1}=\delta _{p}ʻCʻP\cup \overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/8499.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 64.028ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_8499.svg"></p>

<p>This subject will be resumed in connection with well-ordered series in
*264.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_710">[Pg 710]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="id_217_ON_SEGMENTS_OF_SUMS_AND_CONVERSES">
*217. ON SEGMENTS OF SUMS AND CONVERSES.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *217.</p>

<p>The purpose of the present number is to prove <a href="#_217_43" class="pginternal">*217·43</a>, which is
required in the theory of real numbers (Part VI, Section A), where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_233"> will be the series of positive ratios including zero, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_529"> will
be the series of negative ratios in the order from zero to -<img alt="" data-tex="\(\infty\)" src="images/8580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_8580.svg">
(both excluded), <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_438"> the real number zero, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Z\)" src="images/8581.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.636ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_8581.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(W\)" src="images/2484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.371ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_2484.svg_2">
two different series either of which may be taken as the series of
negative and positive real numbers. In virtue of *217·43, these two
series are ordinally similar.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*217·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\alpha \cap CʻQ=\Lambda .\supset .(P\unicode{x2909} Q)ʻʻ\alpha =Pʻʻ\alpha      \quad[*160·1]\)" src="images/8582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.288ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8582.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*217·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\exists !\alpha \cap CʻQ.\supset .(P\unicode{x2909} Q)ʻʻ\alpha =CʻP\cup Qʻʻ\alpha    \quad[*160·1]\)" src="images/8583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.968ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8583.svg"></p>
