<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_715">[Pg 715]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_C_III">SECTION C.<br>
<span class="allsmcap">ON CONVERGENCE, AND THE LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS.</span></h2>
</div>


<p>The purpose of this section is to express in a general form the
definitions of convergence, the limits of functions, the continuity
of functions, and kindred notions, and to give such elementary
consequences of these definitions as may seem illustrative.</p>

<p>In the definitions usually given in treatises on analysis, it is
assumed that both the arguments and the values of the function are
numbers of some kind, generally real numbers, and limits are taken with
respect to the order of magnitude. There is, however, nothing essential
in the definitions to demand so narrow a hypothesis. What is essential
is that the arguments should be given as belonging to a series, and
that the values should also be given as belonging to a series, which
need not be the same series as that to which the arguments belong. In
what follows, therefore, we assume that all the possible arguments
to our function, or at any rate all the arguments which we consider,
belong to the field of a certain relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_234">, which, in cases where
our definitions are useful, will be a serial relation; we assume
similarly that the values of our function, at least for arguments
belonging to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_47">, belong to the field of a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_530">, which,
in all important cases, will be a serial relation. The function itself
we represent by the relation of the value to the argument; that is, the
relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(x)\)" src="images/8625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.299ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8625.svg"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_187"> is to be <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_73">, so that, if the function
is one-valued, <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(x) = Rʻx\)" src="images/8626.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.685ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8626.svg">. (If the function is not one-valued,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(x)\)" src="images/8625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.299ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8625.svg_1"> is any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/8627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8627.svg">.) Thus we may speak
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_74"> as the function, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_235"> as the argument-series, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_531"> as
the value-series.</p>

<p>To take an illustration: Suppose we are given a set of real numbers
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/1380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1380.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg_1">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8628.svg">, ..., where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_174"> may be
any finite integer. Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8628.svg_1"> is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_175">; the
argument-series is that of the finite integers in order of magnitude,
the value-series is that of the real numbers (or any part of this
series which contains all the values <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/1380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1380.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg_2">, ...
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8628.svg_2">, ...). The function <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_75"> is the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu}\)" src="images/8629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8629.svg">
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_176">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu } = Rʻ\nu\)" src="images/8630.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.621ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8630.svg">. In this case, calling
the argument-series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_236"> and the value-series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_532"> (as will be done
throughout this section), we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR = CʻQ = \text{the finite integers}\)" src="images/8631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 32.385ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_8631.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(RʻʻCʻQ = \text{D}ʻR = \text{the class}\,\, x_{1}\)" src="images/8632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.429ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8632.svg">,
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_716">[Pg 716]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg_3">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8628.svg_3">, ..., and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}Q\)" src="images/4990.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.139ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4990.svg_2">= the <i>series</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/1380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1380.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg_4">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8628.svg_4">, .... The series which arranges
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/1380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1380.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg_5">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_8628.svg_5">, ... in the order of their
own magnitudes, instead of the order of magnitude of their suffixes,
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/8633.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.86ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8633.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x0294f}RʻʻCʻQ\)" src="images/8634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.355ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8634.svg">.
This will not be equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{;}Q\)" src="images/4990.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.139ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_4990.svg_3"> unless the function is one which
continually increases, <i>i.e.</i> one for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \lt \nu .\supset.x_{\mu } \lt x_{\nu }\)" src="images/8635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 17.146ex; height: 1.907ex;" id="img_images_8635.svg">.</p>

<p>In general, the propositions of the present section are only
important when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_533"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_237"> are series. If our assertions are
not to be trivial, we must have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !CʻQ\cap \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/8636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.071ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8636.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !CʻP\cap RʻʻCʻQ\)" src="images/8637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.476ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8637.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> there must be arguments
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_48"> which lead to values in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_129">. It will also generally
happen that the function is one-valued, <i>i.e.</i> that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/726.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_726.svg_5">.
But the above conditions, though necessary to the <i>importance</i> of
our propositions, are in general much narrower than the hypotheses that
are necessary for the truth of our propositions.</p>

<p>The present section is wholly self-contained, that is to say, its
propositions are not referred to in the sequel. We have, in this
section, carried the subject as far as seemed suitable for the present
work; its further development belongs to treatises on analysis.</p>

<p>We begin (<a href="#_230" class="pginternal">*230</a>) with a general conception which is involved in the
notion of convergency. We shall say that the values of a function
converge (or, simply, that the function itself converges) into the
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_439">, if for late enough arguments the values always belong
to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_440">, <i>i.e.</i> if there is a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_100"> such
that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(yQ_{*}z\)" src="images/8638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.938ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_8638.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻz\in \alpha\)" src="images/8639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.341ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8639.svg">, or, to avoid assuming that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_76"> is one-valued, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻz\subset \alpha\)" src="images/8640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.592ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_8640.svg">. Thus the
values of the function converge into the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_441"> if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists y).y\in CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR.Rʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\subset \alpha . \]" src="images/8641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.257ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8641.svg"></span>
If a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_101"> is one such that, from <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_102"> onward, all values belong
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_442">, we write <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in R\overline{Q}_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 10.617ex; height: 2.846ex;" id="img_images_8642.svg"> (where
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{cn}\)" src="images/8643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_8643.svg">" stands for "convergent"), <i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\overline{Q}_{\text{cn}}\alpha =\hat{y} \{y\in CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR.Rʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\subset \alpha\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.938ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8644.svg"></span>
When there is such a <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_103">, <i>i.e.</i> when the function converges
into the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_443">, we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8645.svg">,"
<i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Q_{\text{cn}} = \hat{R} \hat{\alpha} (\exists !R\overline{Q}_{\text{cn}}\alpha ) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.461ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_8646.svg"></span>
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8645.svg_1">" may be read "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_77"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_238">-convergent
into <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_444">." This means that for arguments sufficiently late in
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_239">-series, the value of the function is always a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_445">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx = \dfrac{1}{x}\)" src="images/8647.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.577ex; width: 9.675ex; height: 4.613ex;" id="img_images_8647.svg">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha= \hat{y} (y \lt 1)\)" src="images/8648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.591ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_8648.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8645.svg_2">, and if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z \gt 1\)" src="images/8649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.2ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_8649.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\in R\overline{Q}_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 10.56ex; height: 2.846ex;" id="img_images_8650.svg">.</p>

<p>We next consider (<a href="#_231" class="pginternal">*231</a>) <i>limiting sections</i> and <i>ultimate
oscillations</i> of functions. For this purpose, we proceed as
follows. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8645.svg_3">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7413.svg_1"> is
a section of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_534">-series such that, for sufficiently late
arguments, the values of the function must belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7413.svg_2">.
Hence if we take all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_446"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8645.svg_4">, and take the logical product of all the
resulting sections <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7413.svg_3">, we get a section containing all
the "ultimate" values of the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_717">[Pg 717]</span> function; moreover this is obviously
the smallest section which has this property, because, if we take any
section <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_200"> which contains all the "ultimate" values, we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(RQ_{\text{cn}}\beta\)" src="images/8651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.575ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_8651.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\beta = \beta\)" src="images/8652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.733ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8652.svg">, and therefore
the logical product in question is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/36.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_36.svg_201">. The logical
product in question is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR. \]" src="images/8653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 16.95ex; height: 3.774ex;" id="img_images_8653.svg"></span>
In order to avoid trivial exceptions which arise when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\cap\text{ᗡ}ʻR = \Lambda\)" src="images/8654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.4ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8654.svg">, we define the "limiting section" as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR\cap CʻP. \]" src="images/8655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 24.241ex; height: 3.774ex;" id="img_images_8655.svg"></span>
This "limiting section" we denote by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg">, where
the letters "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sc}\)" src="images/8657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.896ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_8657.svg">" stand for "section." Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q = pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR\cap CʻP \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 38.675ex; height: 3.774ex;" id="img_images_8658.svg"></span></p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg_1"> is the class of those members <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_188">
of the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_535"> which are such that, given any argument however
late, there are still arguments as late or later for which the value
of the function is not less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_189">. In like manner, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8659.svg">,
which we will call the "limiting upper section," consists of those
members <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_190"> of the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_536"> which are such that, given any
argument however late, there are still arguments as late or later
for which the value of the function is not greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_191">.
Thus the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8659.svg_1">
is the smallest stretch which contains all the "ultimate" values of
the function, <i>i.e.</i> it is the stretch consisting of those terms
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_192"> which are such that, however late an argument we take, there
are arguments as late or later for which the value of the function is
not greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_193">, and also arguments for which it is not less
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_194">. Thus the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg_3"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P} \overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8660.svg"> represents what we may call
the "ultimate oscillation" of the function. We shall denote it by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg">, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q = P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\cap \breve{P} \overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 31.136ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8662.svg"></span>
We may express <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg_4"> in a form not involving
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{cn}}\)" src="images/8663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.577ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8663.svg">, namely (<a href="#_231_12" class="pginternal">*231·12</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q = pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻRʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻʻ(CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR)\cap CʻP. \]" src="images/8664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.195ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8664.svg"></span></p>

<p>This formula for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg_5"> may be elucidated
by the following considerations. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_104"> is any member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_49">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\cap \overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\)" src="images/8665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 12.851ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8665.svg"> consists
of all arguments from <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_105"> onwards. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\cap\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy)\)" src="images/8666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.044ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8666.svg">.
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\)" src="images/8667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.337ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8667.svg">,
consists of all values of the function for arguments from <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_106">
onwards. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻRʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\)" src="images/8668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 15.492ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8668.svg"> consists of all
members of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_537">-series which are equalled or surpassed by values
of the function for arguments equal to or later than <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_107">. Now if a
term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_195"> belongs to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻRʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\)" src="images/8668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 15.492ex; height: 3.701ex;" id="img_images_8668.svg_1">
for every argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_108">, it is a term such that, however far up the
argument-series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_240"> we go, we shall still find values as great as
or greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_196">. When this is the case, we may say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_197">
is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_718">[Pg 718]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_538">-persistent. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_198"> may be regarded as not
greater than the "ultimate" values of the function. Now the class of
arguments concerned is <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.813ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8669.svg">. Hence the class of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_539">-persistent terms is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻRʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻʻ(CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR), \]" src="images/8670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.154ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8670.svg"></span>
where the factor <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_130"> may be added in order to accommodate the
formula to the trivial case where <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \Lambda\)" src="images/8671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.4ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8671.svg"> (the
only case in which the factor <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_131"> makes any difference). Thus the
class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_540">-persistent terms is the limiting section. Similarly the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_14">-persistent terms are the limiting upper section. These
are the terms which are not less than the "ultimate" values of the
function. Thus the product <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg_1"> is the terms
which are neither greater than all ultimate values, nor less; hence it
is the class of ultimate values, which may be appropriately called the
"ultimate oscillation."</p>

<p>It will be seen that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg_2">, being the product
of an upper and lower section, is itself a stretch: we may call it
(alternatively) the "limiting stretch." It consists of all members
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_199"> of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_541">-series such that the function does not, however
great we make the argument, become and remain less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_200">, nor yet
become and remain greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_201">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg_3">
consists of a single term, that term is the limit of the function
as the argument travels up the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_241">. (This is, of course,
in general different from the limit of the values of the function
considered simply as a class of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_132">, <i>i.e.</i> it is
different from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{lt}_PʻRʻʻCʻQ\)" src="images/8672.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.554ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8672.svg">.) If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg_4">
does not consist of a single term or none, we shall have two limits
to consider, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{limax}_PʻP\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8673.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.039ex; height: 2.715ex;" id="img_images_8673.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{limin}_PʻP\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.6ex; height: 2.715ex;" id="img_images_8674.svg">, which give the two
boundaries of the ultimate values of the function. When the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg_5"> is null, the function may be regarded as
having a definite limit: in this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8656.svg_6">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P} \overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8660.svg_1"> are the two parts
of an "irrational" Dedekind cut, <i>i.e.</i> a cut in which the
first portion has no maximum and the second no minimum. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\in 0\cup 1\)" src="images/8675.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 14.367ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8675.svg"> is the condition for a
definite limit of the function as the argument grows indefinitely.</p>

<p>The above gives the generalization of the limit of a function when
the argument may be any member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.813ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8669.svg_1">. In order to
obtain limits for other classes of arguments, it is only necessary,
as a rule, to limit the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_242"> to the class of arguments in
question, <i>i.e.</i> to replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_243"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/8676.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.595ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8676.svg">
(cf.<a href="#_232" class="pginternal">*232</a>). In order, however, to avoid vexatious and trivial
exceptions arising when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in 1\)" src="images/7027.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.345ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_7027.svg_1">, it is more convenient
to replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_244"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{*}\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/8677.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.583ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8677.svg">. Thus the
section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_542"> defined by the class of arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_447"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}(Q_{*}\unicode{x0294f}\alpha\)" src="images/8678.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.407ex; height: 2.828ex;" id="img_images_8678.svg">). We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\alpha  = P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}} (Q_{*}\unicode{x0294f}\alpha ) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8679.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.917ex; height: 2.828ex;" id="img_images_8679.svg"></span>
This definition is useful because we very often wish to be able to
exhibit the limiting section defined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_448"> as a function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_449">. The section <img alt="" data-tex="\((P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8680.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.3ex; height: 2.828ex;" id="img_images_8680.svg"> is such
that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_202"> is any member of it, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_109"> is any argument belonging
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_450">, there is in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_451"> an argument equal to or later
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_110">, for which the function<span class="pagenum" id="Page_719">[Pg 719]</span> has a value equal to or later than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_203">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_204"> is such that the function does not ultimately become
less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_205"> as the argument increases in the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_452">. The
limit or maximum of such terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_206"> is the limit or maximum of the
ultimate values of the function as the argument approaches the top of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_453">. The class of ultimate values is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\alpha  \cap  (\breve{P} \overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\alpha ,\, \text{which we call}\, (P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{os}}ʻ\alpha . \]" src="images/8681.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.84ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8681.svg"></span>
If the function has a definite limit as the argument increases in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_454">, the class of ultimate values must not contain more than one
term.</p>

<p>Our next number (<a href="#_233" class="pginternal">*233</a>) deals with the limit of a function for a
given argument. The limit or maximum of the class of ultimate values
is not necessarily the value for the limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_455">. It will
be found, however, that, with a suitable hypothesis, the limiting
section <img alt="" data-tex="\((P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8680.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.3ex; height: 2.828ex;" id="img_images_8680.svg_1"> depends only upon
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{*}ʻʻ(\alpha \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR)\)" src="images/8682.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.647ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8682.svg">, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8683.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.395ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8683.svg">
has no maximum, it depends only upon <img alt="" data-tex="\(Qʻʻ(\alpha \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR)\)" src="images/8684.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.659ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8684.svg">.
Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8683.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.395ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8683.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8685.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.227ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8685.svg"> both
have the same limit, they define the same limiting section. Hence if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_8"> is the limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_456">, the limiting section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_457"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\((P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\overrightarrow{Q}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/8686.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.447ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8686.svg">. The upper
limit of this is the upper limit of the ultimate values as the argument
approaches <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_9"> from below. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R (PQ)ʻa = \text{limax}_Pʻ(P\overline{R}Q)_{\text{sc}}ʻ\overrightarrow{Q}ʻa  \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/8687.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.261ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8687.svg"></span>
We have thus four limits of the function as the argument approaches
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_10">, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R(PQ)ʻa,\quad R(\breve{P} Q)ʻa,\quad R(P\breve{Q} )ʻa,\quad R(\breve{P} \breve{Q} )ʻa . \]" src="images/8688.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.516ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_8688.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_78"> is a continuous function, these four are all equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻa\)" src="images/8689.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.271ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8689.svg">;
but in general they are different from each other and from <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻa\)" src="images/8689.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.271ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8689.svg_1">.
The subject of the continuity of functions is dealt with in <a href="#_234" class="pginternal">*234</a>. When
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(PQ)ʻa= R(\breve{P} Q)ʻa\)" src="images/8690.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.058ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8690.svg">, each is the limit of the function for
the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/3545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_3545.svg_11"> for approaches from below. It should be observed
that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_79"> is defined for a set of arguments which are dense in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_245">, <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta_{Q}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR = CʻQ\)" src="images/8691.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 16.131ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8691.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(PQ)ʻa\)" src="images/8692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.52ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8692.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(\breve{P} Q)ʻa\)" src="images/8693.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.52ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8693.svg"> are defined for all arguments in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_50">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_720">[Pg 720]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_230">
*230. ON CONVERGENTS.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *230.</p>

<p>In the present number, we have to consider the notion of a function
converging into a given class, or, as we may express it, the notion
that the value of the function "ultimately" belongs to the given class.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_80"> is the function in question, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_458"> the given class,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_246"> a series to which the arguments belong, we say that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_81">
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_247">-convergent into <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_459">" if there is an argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_111">
such that, for all arguments from <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_112"> onward (in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_248">-order),
the value of the function is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_460">. That is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_82"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_249">-convergent into <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_461"> if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists y) . y\in CʻQ \cap  \text{ᗡ}ʻR.Rʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy \subset  \alpha . \]" src="images/8694.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.257ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8694.svg"></span>
A term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_113"> which is of this nature is said to belong to the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8695.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.846ex;" id="img_images_8695.svg">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_83"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_250">-convergent
into <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_462"> if the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}\alpha\)" src="images/8695.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 6.742ex; height: 2.846ex;" id="img_images_8695.svg_1"> is
not null. Hence we have the following pair of definitions:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}\alpha  &amp;= CʻQ \cap  \text{ᗡ}ʻR \cap  \hat{y}  (Rʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy \subset  \alpha ) \quad\text{Df},\\ Q_{\text{cn}} &amp;= \hat{R}  \hat{\alpha}  (\exists ! R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}\alpha ) \quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/8696.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.147ex; width: 47.07ex; height: 7.425ex;" id="img_images_8696.svg"></span></p>

<p>In all the cases that have any importance, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_84"> will be a one-valued
function (<i>i.e.</i> a one-many relation), <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_251"> will be a series,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.813ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8697.svg"> will be a class having no maximum in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_252">. For, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.813ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8697.svg_1"> has a maximum in <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_253">, then
the classes into which <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_85"> converges are simply those to which the
value for this maximum belongs. The following propositions, though
only <i>important</i> under the above circumstances, are in general
<i>true</i> under much wider hypotheses.</p>

<p>It is possible to generalize still further the notion of convergence,
so as to apply to any property which belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_86"> when confined to
sufficiently late arguments. For this purpose, we have to consider
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\unicode{x0294f}\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻz\)" src="images/8698.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.463ex; width: 8.923ex; height: 3.7ex;" id="img_images_8698.svg"> where <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/2071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2071.svg_39"> is to be confined
to terms later than or equal to some term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_114">. If, under these
circumstances, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x0294f} \overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻz\)" src="images/8699.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.463ex; width: 8.923ex; height: 3.7ex;" id="img_images_8699.svg"> always
belongs to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_80">, we may say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_87"> ultimately
becomes a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg_81">. We may put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} R\overline{Q} _{\text{cng}} \lambda &amp;= \hat{y}\{y \in  CʻQ \cap  \text{ᗡ}ʻR : yQ_{*}z .\supset _{z} . R \unicode{x0294f} \overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻz     \in  \lambda\} \quad\text{Df},\\ Q_{\text{cng}} &amp;= \hat{R}  \hat{\lambda}  (\exists ! R\overline{Q} _{\text{cng}}\lambda ) \quad\text{Df}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/8700.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.442ex; width: 59.337ex; height: 8.016ex;" id="img_images_8700.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_721">[Pg 721]</span></p>

<p>This is the general conception of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{cn}}\)" src="images/8663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.577ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8663.svg_1"> is a
particular case; in fact,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash :RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha .\equiv .RQ_{\text{cng}}(\breve{\text{D}} ʻʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha ). \]" src="images/8701.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.669ex; width: 31.149ex; height: 3.083ex;" id="img_images_8701.svg"></span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{cng}}\)" src="images/8702.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.669ex; width: 4.377ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8702.svg"> will have to be used when the ultimate properties
of the function with which we are concerned are not properties of its
values; but when they are properties of its values, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{cn}}\)" src="images/8663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.577ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_8663.svg_2">
enables us to deal with them more easily than <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\text{cng}}\)" src="images/8702.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.669ex; width: 4.377ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8702.svg_1">.</p>

<p>In this number, we prove the following propositions among others:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*230·171.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :y\in R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}(\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx).\supset .x\in P_{*}ʻʻRʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻy\)" src="images/8703.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.168ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8703.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*230·211.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \subset \beta .\supset :RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha .\supset .RQ_{\text{cn}}\beta\)" src="images/8704.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 30.253ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_8704.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*230·253.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp RʻʻCʻQ\subset \alpha .\supset :RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha .&amp;\equiv .\exists !CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\\ &amp;\equiv .\exists !RʻʻCʻQ.\equiv .\dot{\exists} !(R\upharpoonright CʻQ)\end{align}\]" src="images/8705.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.34ex; width: 59.337ex; height: 5.812ex;" id="img_images_8705.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*230·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}\alpha =\text{ᗡ}ʻR\cap \breve{Q} _{*}ʻʻ(R\overline{Q} _{\text{cn}}\alpha )\)" src="images/8706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.089ex; height: 3.027ex;" id="img_images_8706.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*230·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp Q_{*}\in \text{connex}  .\supset :RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha .RQ_{\text{cn}}\beta .\equiv .RQ_{\text{cn}}(\alpha \cap \beta )\)" src="images/8707.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.205ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_8707.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*230·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp Q\in \text{trans}\cap \text{connex}  .\text{E}!\text{max}_{Q}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset :RQ_{\text{cn}}\alpha     .\equiv .\overrightarrow{R}ʻ\text{max}_{Q}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset \alpha\)" src="images/8708.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 70.523ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_8708.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, the case when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!\text{max}_{Q}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8709.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 13.623ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_8709.svg"> is uninteresting, and in
order to obtain interesting interpretations of our propositions,
it is necessary to suppose that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/2905.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2905.svg_1"> has no maximum.
Similarly when, in later numbers, we consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\cap\overrightarrow{Q}ʻx\)" src="images/8710.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.388ex; height: 3.69ex;" id="img_images_8710.svg">,
we shall only obtain interesting results when this has no maximum,
which requires that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_254"> should be a compact series <img alt="" data-tex="\((Q^{2}=Q)\)" src="images/8711.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.344ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_8711.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/2905.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2905.svg_2"> should be dense in <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_255">. These assumptions are,
however, not usually required for the <i>truth</i> of our propositions.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_727">[Pg 727]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_231">
*231. LIMITING SECTIONS AND ULTIMATE OSCILLATION
OF A FUNCTION.</h2>
</div>


<p class="nind"><i>Summary of</i> *231.</p>

<p>In the present number we are concerned with the limiting section
defined in a series <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_543">, to which the values of a function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_88"> belong, as the arguments to the function increase in the
argument-series <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_256">. That is, we are concerned with the section
consisting of those terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_207"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_133"> which are such that,
however great the argument to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_89"> becomes, there are still values
at least as great as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_208">. Such terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_209"> may be said to be
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_544">-persistent; <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_210"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_545">-persistent if the function does not
ultimately become and remain less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_211">. The class of persistent
terms is called the <i>limiting section</i>. The limiting section
may be defined as follows. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_463"> is any class into which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_90"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_257">-convergent, then the section <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7413.svg_4"> is such
that the values of the function are ultimately contained in it. The
product of such terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7413.svg_5"> is the smallest section
having this property. Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_212"> be any member of this section,
then ultimately (<i>i.e.</i> for arguments far enough along the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_258">
series) the values of the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/25.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_25.svg_91"> do not persistently remain
less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_213"> in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_546"> series. Thus the product of such terms as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{*}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/7413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.603ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7413.svg_6"> is the limiting section, and we may therefore put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q=pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR\cap CʻP  \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/8779.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 38.675ex; height: 3.774ex;" id="img_images_8779.svg"></span>
where the letters "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sc}\)" src="images/8657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.896ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_8657.svg_1">" are intended to suggest "section."
(The factor <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_134"> on the right is superfluous except when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR=\Lambda\)" src="images/8780.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 11.9ex; height: 3.774ex;" id="img_images_8780.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\cap\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\Lambda\)" src="images/8781.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.4ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8781.svg">.)</p>

<p>We will call the limiting section of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg_15">, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8782.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8782.svg">, the "limiting upper
section." It will be seen that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_214"> is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8783.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8783.svg">, then the function does not ultimately
become and remain, as far as some of its arguments are concerned,
greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_215">, that is, however great we make the argument, we
still find values not greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_216">. Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_217"> belongs to
both <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8784.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P} \overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.734ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8660.svg_2">,
we find values not less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_218"> and values not greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_219">
however great we make the argument. This class, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\cap \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.983ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8785.svg">,
may therefore be regarded as the class of ultimate values of the
function. We will call it the "ultimate oscillation" of the function,
since, as the argument approaches <img alt="" data-tex="\(\infty\)" src="images/8580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_8580.svg_1">, the value of the function
ultimately oscillates in this stretch of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_547">, and no smaller stretch
has the same property. We will denote this class by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R}_{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8661.svg_6">,"
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{os}\)" src="images/8786.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_8786.svg">" is intended to suggest "oscillation."
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8787.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.824ex; height: 2.701ex;" id="img_images_8787.svg"> is a stretch in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_135">, because it is
the product of two sections. Hence we shall also call it the "limiting<span class="pagenum" id="Page_728">[Pg 728]</span>
stretch." When the function has a definite limit as the argument
approaches <img alt="" data-tex="\(\infty\)" src="images/8580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_8580.svg_2">, the limiting stretch must not contain more than
one term.</p>

<p>Limits of functions for arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_220"> in the middle of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\cap\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/8788.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.813ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8788.svg">,
which will be considered later, are derived from the
limits considered in the present number by limiting the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/3372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_3372.svg_259">
to predecessors of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_221">.</p>

<p>In this number we prove the following propositions among others:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·103.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q=P_{\text{po}}\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q=P_{*}\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q\)" src="images/8789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 31.266ex; height: 2.912ex;" id="img_images_8789.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q=pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻRʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{*}ʻʻ(CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR)\cap CʻP\)" src="images/8790.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.955ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8790.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :Q_{*}\in \text{connex}  .RQ_{\text{cn}}(\overleftarrow{P}_{*}ʻx).\supset .x\in P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.936ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_8792.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·191.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\in \text{connex}  .&amp;\exists !P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q.\supset .\\ &amp;P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q=P_{*}ʻʻ(P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q).Pʻʻ(P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q)=P_{\text{po}}ʻʻ(P\overline{R}     _{\text{os}}Q)\end{align}\]" src="images/8793.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.686ex; width: 71.266ex; height: 6.503ex;" id="img_images_8793.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·193.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P_{\text{po}}\in \text{Ser}.P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q&amp;\in 1.\supset .\\ &amp;P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q=\iota ʻ\text{max}_{P}ʻ(P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q)=\iota ʻ\text{min}_{P}ʻ(\breve{P}     \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q)\end{align}\]" src="images/8795.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.72ex; width: 67.354ex; height: 6.571ex;" id="img_images_8795.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is frequently used in the present section.</p>

<p>In all ordinary circumstances, we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP=P\overline{R}_{\text{sc}}Q\cup \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8796.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.776ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_8796.svg">,
so that if the upper and lower limiting sections do not have more than
one term in common (<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q\in 1)\)" src="images/8797.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.601ex; height: 2.828ex;" id="img_images_8797.svg">, they define a Dedekind cut in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_548">. The following propositions
are concerned with this fact:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·202.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{*},Q_{*}\in \text{connex}  .\exists !P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q.\supset .CʻP-(P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q)\subset     \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8798.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.667ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8798.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·21.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash :P_{*},Q_{*}\in \text{connex}  .CʻQ\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset Q_{*}ʻʻ\breve{R} ʻʻ&amp;CʻP.\supset .\\ &amp;CʻP=P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\cup \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\end{align}\]" src="images/8799.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.753ex; width: 68.017ex; height: 6.638ex;" id="img_images_8799.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{*},Q_{*}\in \text{connex}  .RʻʻCʻQ\subset CʻP.\supset .CʻP=P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\cup \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8800.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 64.126ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_8800.svg"></p>

<p>Note that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(RʻʻCʻQ\subset CʻP\)" src="images/8801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.092ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_8801.svg">" is the hypothesis that for arguments belonging
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_51">, the values belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/4110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4110.svg_136">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :P_{*}\in \text{connex}  .RʻʻCʻQ\subset CʻP.{\sim}\{RQ_{\text{cn}}(\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻx)\}.\supset .\overrightarrow{P}_{*}ʻx\subset     P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\)" src="images/8802.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.585ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_8802.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q=pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR\cap CʻP   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/8803.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.537ex; width: 38.046ex; height: 3.774ex;" id="img_images_8803.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q=P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\cap \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/8804.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 30.507ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_8804.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_729">[Pg 729]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q=pʻP_{*}ʻʻʻ\overleftarrow{Q}_{\text{cn}}ʻR\cap CʻP  \quad[(*231·01)]\)" src="images/8805.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.454ex; height: 3.803ex;" id="img_images_8805.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*231·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .P\overline{R} _{\text{os}}Q=P\overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q\cap \breve{P} \overline{R} _{\text{sc}}Q   \quad[(*231·02)]\)" src="images/8806.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.915ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_8806.svg"></p>

argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_115"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻQ\)" src="images/4111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4111.svg_52">, we can find an argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y'\)" src="images/5316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.736ex; height: 2.181ex;" id="img_images_5316.svg_2"> greater than
